title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
text:
Overview
Farmers learn about seeds, disease advisories, and practices mostly from other farmers, and mostly from farmers nearby. Extension systems therefore face a network question: which farmers should be trained first so knowledge spreads furthest?
This case study uses the synthetic farmer advice network in Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/ with geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis for participation, diffusion centrality, seeding strategies, and simple / complex contagion.
Topics:

Directed advice graph and within- vs between-village ties
Distance decay and dyadic tie formation
Communities vs villages; leaders and bridges
Simple vs complex contagion and seeding strategies
Spatial pattern of adoption

title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
text:
Part A: The advice network
Direction matters. An edge i → j means i seeks advice from j, so information flows j → i. A farmer’s in-degree (times named) measures how often others turn to them: a standard proxy for opinion leadership.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Build the directed advice graph and summarise structure / geography.
# ===================================================================

# Directed graph: source asks target for advice.
A = nx.from_pandas_edgelist(ties, "source", "target", create_using=nx.DiGraph)  # NetworkX graph built from the edge table
A.add_nodes_from(farmers.index)  # include isolates with no ties
nx.set_node_attributes(A, farmers.drop(columns="geometry").to_dict("index"))  # run this analysis or plotting step
pos = {f: (p.x, p.y) for f, p in farmers.geometry.items()}  # map layout

# In-degree = how often named as an adviser; out-degree = how many named.
farmers["named_by"] = pd.Series(dict(A.in_degree()))  # run this analysis or plotting step
farmers["names"] = pd.Series(dict(A.out_degree()))  # run this analysis or plotting step

xy = np.c_[farmers.geometry.x, farmers.geometry.y]  # coordinate matrix
idx = {f: k for k, f in enumerate(farmers.index)}  # farmer_id -> row index
# Euclidean tie length (km) and same-village flag for every observed tie.
ties["km"] = [np.hypot(*(xy[idx[s]] - xy[idx[t]])) / 1000 for s, t in zip(ties.source, ties.target)]  # run this analysis or plotting step
ties["same_village"] = [farmers.village[s] == farmers.village[t] for s, t in zip(ties.source, ties.target)]  # run this analysis or plotting step

summary = pd.Series({  # one-line network structure summary
    "farmers": A.number_of_nodes(),  # continue multi-line call
    "ties": A.number_of_edges(),  # continue multi-line call
    "reciprocity": nx.reciprocity(A),  # continue multi-line call
    "share of ties within village": ties.same_village.mean(),  # continue multi-line call
    "median tie length (km)": ties.km.median(),  # continue multi-line call
    "90th pct tie length (km)": ties.km.quantile(0.9),  # continue multi-line call
    "max in-degree (named by)": farmers.named_by.max(),  # continue multi-line call
    "farmers never named": (farmers.named_by == 0).mean(),  # continue multi-line call
    "weakly connected components": nx.number_weakly_connected_components(A),  # continue multi-line call
})
summary.round(3).to_frame("value")  # run this analysis or plotting step

The picture is typical of rural information networks: dense local clusters (villages), a thin web of between-village ties, and a handful of heavily consulted farmers in each village. Notice that farmers with extension contact (red rings) are not necessarily the ones others consult.

title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
section: Part B: What makes two farmers connect?
text:
Part B: What makes two farmers connect?

B1. Distance-decay curve
As in 03.06.1, compute the probability that a pair of farmers is tied as a function of distance, separately for pairs in the same village and in different villages.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Empirical P(tie) vs distance, split by same vs different village.
# ===================================================================

n = len(farmers)  # number of nodes / farmers
D = np.hypot(xy[:, None, 0] - xy[None, :, 0], xy[:, None, 1] - xy[None, :, 1]) / 1000  # km matrix
vil = farmers.village.to_numpy(dtype=object)  # village labels as an object array
SV = vil[:, None] == vil[None, :]  # same-village boolean matrix
Adj = nx.to_numpy_array(A, nodelist=list(farmers.index))  # directed adjacency
U = np.maximum(Adj, Adj.T)  # undirected presence of a tie in either direction
iu = np.triu_indices(n, 1)  # unique unordered pairs
pairs = pd.DataFrame({"km": D[iu], "same_village": SV[iu], "tie": U[iu]})  # unique unordered farmer pairs
bins = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 60]  # distance bands for empirical P(link)
pairs["band"] = pd.cut(pairs.km, bins)  # run this analysis or plotting step
curve = pairs.groupby(["band", "same_village"], observed=True).tie.mean().unstack()  # P(tie) by distance band and village match

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))  # create figure and primary axes
mids = [b.mid for b in curve.index]  # bin midpoints for plotting
ax.plot(mids, curve[True], marker="o", label="same village")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
ax.plot(mids, curve[False], marker="s", label="different village")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
ax.set(  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    xscale="log", yscale="log",  # xscale argument
    xlabel="distance between farmers (km)", ylabel="P(tie)",  # x-axis label
    title="Distance decay of advice ties",  # plot or map title
)
ax.legend()  # add a legend for mapped layers
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Two effects are visible at once: tie probability falls steeply with distance, and at the same distance, farmers in the same village are much more likely to be tied. Village membership is a social boundary over and above geography.


B2. A dyadic tie-formation model
A logistic regression on dyads separates these effects and adds characteristics of the potential adviser. With 175,000 directed pairs and few ties, we use case-control sampling: all ties plus a random sample of non-ties. Coefficients on the predictors are unaffected by this sampling; only the intercept shifts.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Dyadic logit for directed ties: distance, village, adviser attributes.
# Down-sample non-ties for a tractable case-control design.
# ===================================================================

src, tgt = np.where(~np.eye(n, dtype=bool))  # all ordered pairs i != j
dy = pd.DataFrame({"i": src, "j": tgt, "tie": Adj[src, tgt]})  # dyadic case-control sample for the logit
# Keep all observed ties and a random sample of non-ties.
dy = pd.concat([dy[dy.tie == 1], dy[dy.tie == 0].sample(20 * int(dy.tie.sum()), random_state=1)])  # dyadic case-control sample for the logit
dy["log_km"] = np.log(D[dy.i, dy.j] + 0.05)  # distance with a small offset
dy["same_village"] = SV[dy.i, dy.j].astype(int)  # run this analysis or plotting step
dy["adviser_log_farm"] = np.log(farmers.farm_ha.values[dy.j])  # target (adviser) farm size
dy["adviser_educ"] = farmers.education_yrs.values[dy.j]  # notebook step
dy["adviser_extension"] = farmers.extension_contact.values[dy.j].astype(int)  # run this analysis or plotting step
Xcols = ["log_km", "same_village", "adviser_log_farm", "adviser_educ", "adviser_extension"]  # logit predictor column names
Xs = (dy[Xcols] - dy[Xcols].mean()) / dy[Xcols].std()  # standardised design matrix
logit = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(dy[Xcols], dy.tie)  # raw-scale coefs
logit_s = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(Xs, dy.tie)  # comparable magnitudes
pd.DataFrame({  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "coef": logit.coef_[0],  # continue string literal
    "odds ratio": np.exp(logit.coef_[0]),  # continue multi-line call
    "standardised coef": logit_s.coef_[0],  # continue string literal
}, index=Xcols).round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

Reading the table: each doubling of distance multiplies the odds of a tie by about \(2^{\beta_{\log km}}\); sharing a village multiplies it several-fold; larger and more educated farmers are sought out more often. Extension contact has little effect, consistent with how the data were generated: having access to extension does not by itself make a farmer someone others consult. This is precisely the situation in which “train the farmers you already reach” may be a weak seeding rule.

Caution. Dyadic models treat pairs as independent, which they are not (reciprocity, transitivity). For inference use ERGMs or dyadic-cluster-robust standard errors; here the model is descriptive.

Part C: Communities, leaders, and bridges

C1. Do network communities match villages?


Code
# ===================================================================
# Louvain communities on the undirected advice graph vs village labels.

High agreement: villages are the network’s main communities, with occasional merging of neighbouring villages that exchange many ties. The between-village ties are therefore the scarce channel through which knowledge leaves a village.


C2. Opinion leaders and bridging farmers
Three roles matter for diffusion:

Opinion leaders: high in-degree within their village.
Bridges: high betweenness, or many ties to other villages. The participation coefficient \(P_i = 1 - \sum_c (k_{ic}/k_i)^2\) measures how evenly a farmer’s ties spread across communities (0 = all in one village).
Diffusion centrality (Banerjee et al., 2013): expected number of farmers reached if information passes along each tie with probability q for T rounds, \(\sum_{t=1}^{T} (qA)^t \mathbf{1}\).



Code
# ===================================================================
# Role measures: betweenness, participation, diffusion centrality.
# Diffusion centrality uses information flow adviser -> asker (Adj.T).
# ===================================================================

bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(Gu, k=200, seed=1)  # sampled betweenness
# Diffusion centrality on the "information flows j -> i" matrix (transpose of asks-matrix).
Ainfo = Adj.T  # information-flow matrix (adviser -> asker)
q, T_ = 0.25, 4  # transmission probability and horizon used by DC
DC = sna.diffusion_centrality(Ainfo, q=q, T=T_)  # diffusion centrality scores

farmers["betweenness"] = farmers.index.map(bc)  # run this analysis or plotting step
farmers["participation"] = farmers.index.map(  # continue multi-line call
    sna.participation_coefficient(Gu, farmers.village.to_dict())  # cross-village bridging
)
farmers["diffusion_centrality"] = DC  # notebook step
roles = farmers[[  # define roles
    "village", "farm_ha", "education_yrs", "extension_contact", "named_by",  # continue string literal
    "betweenness", "participation", "diffusion_centrality",  # continue string literal
]]
roles.sort_values("diffusion_centrality", ascending=False).head(8).round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
text:
Part D: Simulating technology diffusion

The diffusion models
Each period, a non-adopter considers the adopters among the people they ask for advice (\(k_i^{adopt}\) of their \(k_i\) advisers):

Simple contagion (information): adopt with probability \(1 - (1-q)^{k_i^{adopt}}\), plus a small spontaneous rate. One informed adviser can be enough. Appropriate for awareness of a disease advisory or a market price.
Complex contagion (persuasion): adopt with probability p only once the share of adopting advisers reaches a threshold \(\theta_i\). Appropriate for costly or risky practices, such as a new variety, zero tillage, or machinery, where farmers want to see several peers succeed first (Beaman et al., 2021).



Seeding strategies (budget = 14 seed farmers, one per village on average)







Strategy
Rule




Random
14 farmers at random


Extension contacts
farmers who already have extension contact (status quo)


Top in-degree
the 14 most-consulted farmers overall


Leader per village
the most-consulted farmer in each village (spatially dispersed)


Bridges
highest participation coefficient (ties to other villages)


Pairs per village
the two most-consulted farmers in 7 villages: concentrates seeds for complex contagion





Code
# ===================================================================
# Compare seeding strategies for K=14 initial adopters.
# ===================================================================

K = 14  # seed budget
vill_list = sorted(farmers.village.unique())  # define vill_list
order_in = farmers.sort_values(["named_by", "diffusion_centrality"], ascending=False)  # used inside select_seeds
ext_ids = farmers.index[farmers.extension_contact].tolist()  # farmers with extension contact

strategies = [  # seeding strategies to compare
    "Random", "Extension contacts", "Top in-degree",  # continue string literal
    "Leader per village", "Bridges", "Pairs per village",  # continue string literal
]
print(f"{len(ext_ids)} farmers have extension contact")  # status line for the notebook reader
for s in strategies:  # iterate over the collection
    sd = sna.select_seeds(farmers, s, K, rng=np.random.default_rng(0))  # sd argument
    print(  # status line for the notebook reader
        f"{s:20s} seeds in {farmers.loc[sd, 'village'].nunique():2d} villages, "  # run this analysis or plotting step
        f"mean in-degree {farmers.loc[sd, 'named_by'].mean():.1f}"  # run this analysis or plotting step
    )



30 farmers have extension contact
Random               seeds in 11 villages, mean in-degree 3.4
Extension contacts   seeds in 11 villages, mean in-degree 4.4
Top in-degree        seeds in  8 villages, mean in-degree 9.4
Leader per village   seeds in 14 villages, mean in-degree 9.0
Bridges              seeds in  6 villages, mean in-degree 4.4
Pairs per village    seeds in  7 villages, mean in-degree 8.6




Code
# ===================================================================
# Monte Carlo simple vs complex contagion under each seeding strategy.
# ===================================================================

advisers = Adj  # row i: whom i asks (influence comes from named advisers)
theta_i = np.random.default_rng(3).uniform(0.3, 0.6, n)  # heterogeneous persuasion thresholds
results = {}  # collect index / scenario result rows
for model, kw in [("simple", {}), ("complex", {"theta": theta_i})]:  # iterate over the collection
    for s in strategies:  # iterate over the collection
        results[(model, s)] = sna.monte_carlo_contagion(  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
            advisers, farmers, s, model=model, reps=200, k=K, seed=11, periods=20, **kw  # notebook step
        )





Code
# ===================================================================
# Mean adoption trajectories with 10-90% bands over 200 Monte Carlo runs.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.4), sharey=False)  # create a grid of subplot axes

What the simulations suggest (for this network and these parameters):

Under simple contagion, coverage of villages matters most. Putting one well-connected seed in every village reaches nearly everyone; strategies that leave villages without a seed plateau lower because information must cross the scarce between-village ties. Centrality within the village mainly buys speed.
Under complex contagion, the strategy decides whether the practice takes off at all. Isolated seeds stall because their neighbours never see enough adopting peers; seeds that are well connected within their village, and seeds clustered so that neighbours hear from several of them, do far better.
Seeding the existing extension contacts performs close to random in this network, because extension access is not what makes someone a sought-after adviser (Part B).

These are the same qualitative conclusions reached by field experiments, but magnitudes here depend entirely on assumed parameters (q, p, θ). Simulation is for comparing designs and understanding mechanisms, not for forecasting adoption rates.

title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
section: Part F: From analysis to program design
text:
Part F: From analysis to program design
Practical recommendations an extension program could draw from this workflow:

Collect network data cheaply. A single name-generator question (“Who do you ask for farming advice?”) in a baseline survey is enough to compute in-degree, village leaders, and bridges. Where surveys are infeasible, the distance-decay and village-homophily model from Part B can generate a plausible proxy network.
Match seeding to the technology. Information (advisories, prices) behaves like simple contagion: spread seeds widely. Costly practices behave like complex contagion: concentrate on locally central farmers and ensure each target village has more than one early adopter.
Do not assume extension contacts are opinion leaders. Check, using in-degree or diffusion centrality.
Watch the bridges. Between-village ties are scarce; a few bridging farmers determine whether a practice leaves its village.

Caveats for causal claims. Observing that farmers adopt after their advisers did does not prove peer influence. Homophily (similar farmers befriend each other), shared local conditions (same soils, same market), and the reflection problem (Manski, 1993) all generate the same correlation. Credible estimates of network effects need randomised seeding (as in the field experiments cited above) or quasi-experimental designs from the causal inference toolkit.

title: Farmer Information Networks and Technology Diffusion
text:
Summary

Farmer advice networks are spatial networks: strong distance decay, village communities, few long ties.
Dyadic models separate geography, social boundaries and adviser characteristics in tie formation.
In-degree / diffusion centrality identify leaders; betweenness / participation identify bridges.
Simulated diffusion: for simple contagion, seed every village; for complex contagion, concentrate seeds among well-connected farmers so neighbours see several adopters.
Network distance to seeds predicts adoption timing better than geographic distance.


Exercises

Increase the seed budget from 14 to 28. Which strategy gains most under complex contagion?
Make θ depend on farm size (larger farms need fewer adopting peers). Do larger-farm seeds now outperform village leaders?
Remove the 10 highest-participation farmers (they migrate away) and rerun the simple-contagion simulation. How much slower is diffusion?
Replace the survey network with a synthetic one built only from the Part B logit model, run the simulations again, and compare the ranking of strategies. When is a modelled network “good enough”?



References

Bandiera, O., & Rasul, I. (2006). Social networks and technology adoption in northern Mozambique. Economic Journal, 116, 869-902.
Banerjee, A., Chandrasekhar, A. G., Duflo, E., & Jackson, M. O. (2013). The diffusion of microfinance. Science, 341, 1236498.
Beaman, L., BenYishay, A., Magruder, J., & Mobarak, A. M. (2021). Can network theory-based targeting increase technology adoption? American Economic Review, 111(6), 1918-1943.

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Overview
Landslides occur in every U.S. state, and the four states of this capstone, Colorado, Wyoming, New Mexico and Kansas, span the full range of exposure: steep, wildfire-prone mountains in the west and nearly flat plains in the east. A susceptibility map answers one question: where are landslides most likely to occur, given the terrain, climate, soils and vegetation? It says nothing about when, which makes it a planning tool rather than a warning system.
This capstone builds that map at 1 km resolution over about 1,050,000 km², using

the environmental covariate grid assembled for Ahmed et al. (2017), Assessing soil carbon vulnerability in the Western USA by geospatial modeling of pyrogenic and particulate carbon stocks (Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences 122: 354-369). The paper mapped soil carbon fractions over these four states with random forests on terrain, climate, soil, vegetation and fire-regime covariates. The same covariates, grid and random-forest workflow are reused here for a different response: landslide occurrence;
the USGS Landslide Inventories across the United States, version 3.0 (Belair et al. 2025), as training and test data.

Three families of model are built and compared, following Module 03: a bivariate statistical model (frequency ratio), a knowledge-driven multi-criteria model (AHP-weighted fuzzy overlay) and machine learning (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting).

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Problem statement and study area
Study area. Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico and Wyoming, the study region of Ahmed et al. (2017). Elevation rises from about 200 m in eastern Kansas to more than 4,300 m in the Colorado Rockies. Mean annual precipitation ranges from under 150 mm in the New Mexico basins to over 2,000 mm on the highest ranges.
Landslides in the region are of several kinds: deep-seated slides and earthflows in weak shales of the Colorado Plateau and the Wyoming basins, rockfall and debris flows in the high mountains, and post-wildfire debris flows, which have become a leading hazard in Colorado and New Mexico. This last link to fire is why the fire-regime layer of the soil carbon study is useful here.
Question. Which parts of the four states are most susceptible to landslides, which environmental factors explain the pattern, and how far can a national inventory compiled from many sources be trusted to say so?

The landslide inventory
The USGS compilation brings together inventories from state geological surveys, the USGS, universities and other agencies. Each record carries a Confidence code:



Code
Meaning




1
Possible landslide in the area


2
Probable landslide in the area


3
Likely landslide at or near this location


5
Moderate confidence in the extent or nature of the landslide


8
High confidence in the extent or nature of the landslide



Codes 1 and 2 locate a landslide only to “the area”, often a whole quadrangle or a report region, which is too vague for a 1 km model. Training uses Confidence ≥ 3. All records, including codes 1 and 2, are still used in Section 5 to decide where the region has been surveyed at all.

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Sampling design
A susceptibility model learns by comparing landslide cells with non-landslide cells. Where nobody looked, a cell without a record is not evidence of stability, and sampling it as a negative teaches the model that unsurveyed terrain is safe. Three rules reduce that bias:

Surveyed tiles only. The region is divided into 50 km tiles. Negatives are drawn only from tiles that contain at least one inventory record of any confidence, a simple form of the target-group background used in species distribution modelling.
Exclusion buffer. Cells within 2 km of a landslide cell are not used as negatives, because records are positioned only to within a few hundred metres and landslide clusters extend beyond mapped points.
Several draws. Five independent negative samples, each twice the number of landslide cells, are drawn; models are fitted to each and averaged.



Code
TILE = 50_000.0
grid["tile"] = (np.floor((grid.x - grid.x.min()) / TILE).astype(int) * 1000
                + np.floor((grid.y - grid.y.min()) / TILE).astype(int))
surveyed_tiles = set(grid.loc[grid.n_all > 0, "tile"])
grid["surveyed"] = grid.tile.isin(surveyed_tiles)

ls_ras = to_raster(grid.landslide) == 1
buffer = ndimage.binary_dilation(ls_ras, structure=np.ones((5, 5)))  # 2 cells either side = 2 km
grid["near_landslide"] = buffer[grid.row.values, grid.col.values] & (grid.landslide == 0)

neg_pool = np.flatnonzero(grid.surveyed.values & (grid.landslide.values == 0) & ~grid.near_landslide.values)

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Model 1: frequency ratio
The frequency ratio (FR) of a factor class is the share of landslide cells that fall in the class divided by the share of area it covers:
\[
FR_{ij} = \frac{N_{ij}^{ls} / N^{ls}}{N_{ij} / N}
\]
\(FR > 1\) means landslides are more common than average in the class. The landslide susceptibility index of a cell is the sum of the log frequency ratios of its classes across all factors, \(LSI = \sum_i \ln FR_{ij}\). The method is transparent, needs no model fitting, and is a standard baseline in landslide studies.
Continuous factors are split into deciles; categorical factors use their classes. Frequency ratios are computed on surveyed tiles only, for the reason given in Section 5.


Code
FR_CONT = ["slope_g", "tpi_2000", "elev", "preci", "temp", "ndvi", "silt_clay", "kfactor", "v_curvatur", "h_curvatur"]
FR_CAT = ["topo_2000", "nlcd", "frg"]


def fr_classes(df):
    """Class label of every node for every factor (deciles for continuous factors)."""
    cls = {}
    for f in FR_CONT:
        edges = np.unique(np.nanquantile(grid.loc[grid.surveyed, f], np.linspace(0, 1, 11)))
        cls[f] = np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges, df[f].values, side="right") - 1, 0, len(edges) - 2)
    for f in FR_CAT:
        cls[f] = df[f].values.astype(int)
    return cls


CLS = fr_classes(grid)


def fr_tables(train_mask):
    """Frequency-ratio table for every factor, from the nodes in ``train_mask`` (surveyed only)."""
    m = train_mask & grid.surveyed.values
    y = grid.landslide.values[m]
    tabs = {}
    for f, c in CLS.items():
        cm = c[m]
        classes = np.unique(c)
        area = np.array([(cm == k).sum() for k in classes], float)
        lsn = np.array([y[cm == k].sum() for k in classes], float)
        fr = ((lsn + 0.5) / (y.sum() + 0.5)) / ((area + 1) / m.sum())  # small offsets avoid log(0)
        tabs[f] = pd.Series(fr, index=classes)
    return tabs


def lsi(tabs, idx=slice(None)):
    """Landslide susceptibility index (sum of log FR) for the nodes in ``idx``."""
    return sum(np.log(tabs[f].reindex(CLS[f][idx]).fillna(1.0).values) for f in tabs)


fr_all = fr_tables(np.ones(len(grid), bool))
grid["fr_lsi"] = lsi(fr_all)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(20, 8))
for ax, f in zip(axes.ravel(), ["slope_g", "tpi_2000", "preci", "ndvi", "topo_2000", "frg", "nlcd", "silt_clay"]):

    elif f == "nlcd":
        labels = [nlcd_names.get(k, k) for k in t.index]
    else:
        labels = [f"D{k + 1}" for k in t.index]
    ax.bar(range(len(t)), t.values, color=np.where(t.values > 1, "firebrick", "steelblue"))
    ax.axhline(1, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(t)), labels, rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=7)
    ax.set_title(f, fontsize=10)

axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Frequency ratio")

plt.tight_layout()

Reading the frequency ratios. Bars above 1 (red) mark classes where landslides are more common than average. Three things to check:

Does the ratio rise steadily through the slope deciles? A clean monotonic rise means slope is behaving as the dominant control.
Do steep slopes and canyon bottoms sit above 1 and gentle slopes below?
Precipitation, NDVI, fire regime and land cover often show strong ratios too. In this region the wet, green, fire-prone land is the mountains, so these bars can repeat the terrain signal through other variables. A bivariate method cannot separate such overlapping effects; Model 3 can.

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Model 2: AHP multi-criteria model
A knowledge-driven model encodes what geomorphology says controls slope stability, without fitting it to the inventory. Seven criteria are used:








Criterion
Membership
Reasoning




Slope
large, midpoint 15°, spread 4
Shear stress rises with slope; most slides start on slopes above 15°


Local relief
large on |TPI 2,000 m|, midpoint 60 m, spread 3
Relief supplies the height a slide needs


Slope position
steep slope 1.0, canyon bottom 0.6, ridgeline 0.5, gentle slope 0.1
Steep side-slopes fail; canyon bottoms receive debris flows


Precipitation
linear, 250 to 900 mm
Wetter slopes reach failure pore pressures more often


Fire regime
FRG IV 1.0, FRG III 0.7, barren 0.7, FRG V 0.6, FRG I 0.5, FRG II 0.4
Stand-replacing fire in forest (FRG IV) strips the canopy and triggers debris flows; FRG II is mostly grassland, where frequent fire does far less to slope stability


Vegetation (NDVI)
small, midpoint 0.35, spread 4
Roots reinforce soil; sparse cover means weaker slopes


Silt + clay
linear, 20 to 80 %
Fine-grained soils lose strength when wet



A weighted linear combination is compensatory: a flat, wet, clay-rich field in eastern Kansas collects points for precipitation and soil and can score as high as a dry mountain slope, although flat land cannot slide. The combined score is therefore multiplied by a slope gate that is 0 below 2°, rises linearly to 1 at 8°, and leaves steeper land unchanged. This is the hybrid “constraint × score” design of Module 03.04.
Weights come from the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP; Saaty 1980). Each pair of criteria is judged on the 1-9 scale (“slope is moderately more important than precipitation” = 3); the weights are the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix, and the consistency ratio (CR) checks that the judgments do not contradict each other. CR < 0.10 is the usual acceptance threshold.
GeoLattice has no AHP function, so a short one is written here.


Code
CRITERIA = ["slope", "relief", "slope_position", "precipitation", "fire_regime", "vegetation", "silt_clay"]
# Upper-triangle judgments: (row criterion, column criterion) -> how much more important row is.
JUDGMENTS = {
    ("slope", "relief"): 2, ("slope", "slope_position"): 3, ("slope", "precipitation"): 3, ("slope", "fire_regime"): 4,
    ("slope", "vegetation"): 5, ("slope", "silt_clay"): 5,
    ("relief", "slope_position"): 2, ("relief", "precipitation"): 2, ("relief", "fire_regime"): 3,
    ("relief", "vegetation"): 4, ("relief", "silt_clay"): 4,
    ("slope_position", "precipitation"): 1, ("slope_position", "fire_regime"): 2, ("slope_position", "vegetation"): 3,
    ("slope_position", "silt_clay"): 3,
    ("precipitation", "fire_regime"): 2, ("precipitation", "vegetation"): 3, ("precipitation", "silt_clay"): 3,
    ("fire_regime", "vegetation"): 2, ("fire_regime", "silt_clay"): 2,
    ("vegetation", "silt_clay"): 1,
}
RANDOM_INDEX = {1: 0.0, 2: 0.0, 3: 0.58, 4: 0.90, 5: 1.12, 6: 1.24, 7: 1.32, 8: 1.41, 9: 1.45, 10: 1.49}


def ahp(criteria, judgments):
    """AHP weights (principal eigenvector) and consistency ratio for a reciprocal matrix."""
    n = len(criteria)
    A = np.ones((n, n))
    for (a, b), v in judgments.items():
        i, j = criteria.index(a), criteria.index(b)
        A[i, j], A[j, i] = v, 1.0 / v
    vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
    k = np.argmax(vals.real)
    w = np.abs(vecs[:, k].real)
    w = w / w.sum()
    ci = (vals[k].real - n) / (n - 1)
    return pd.Series(w, index=criteria), A, ci / RANDOM_INDEX[n]


W_AHP, A_MATRIX, CR = ahp(CRITERIA, JUDGMENTS)
display(pd.DataFrame(A_MATRIX, index=CRITERIA, columns=CRITERIA).round(2))
display(W_AHP.rename("weight").to_frame())
print(f"Consistency ratio: {CR:.3f} ({'acceptable' if CR < 0.10 else 'revise the judgments'})")

text:
Model 3: machine learning

Predictors
The predictors are the covariates of Ahmed et al. (2017). Aspect is turned into northness (\(\cos\)) and eastness (\(\sin\)) so that 359° and 1° are neighbours; flat cells get 0 for both. Slope length is log-transformed. The three categorical layers (slope position, land cover, fire regime) are one-hot encoded.
The paper reports strong correlation between elevation, temperature, precipitation and NDVI. As in the paper, all are kept: tree ensembles handle correlated predictors, and the logistic model is used only as a reference.


Code
asp = np.radians(grid.aspect.clip(lower=0).values)
flat = grid.aspect.values < 0
X_num = pd.DataFrame({
    "elev": grid.elev, "slope_g": grid.slope_g, "log_slopeleng": np.log1p(grid.slopeleng),
    "northness": np.where(flat, 0, np.cos(asp)), "eastness": np.where(flat, 0, np.sin(asp)),
    "tpi_2000": grid.tpi_2000, "h_curvatur": grid.h_curvatur, "v_curvatur": grid.v_curvatur,
    "ndvi": grid.ndvi, "preci": grid.preci, "temp": grid.temp, "silt_clay": grid.silt_clay, "kfactor": grid.kfactor,
})
frg_group = grid.frg.where(grid.frg <= 5, 9).astype(int)  # FRG I-V, and 9 = no fire regime
X_cat = pd.concat([
    pd.get_dummies(grid.topo_2000.map(slope_pos_names), prefix="pos"),
    pd.get_dummies(grid.nlcd.map(nlcd_names), prefix="lc"),
    pd.get_dummies(frg_group.map({1: "I", 2: "II", 3: "III", 4: "IV", 5: "V", 9: "none"}), prefix="frg"),
], axis=1).astype(float)
X = pd.concat([X_num, X_cat], axis=1)
FEATURES = list(X.columns)
XA = X.values.astype(np.float32)
y_all = grid.landslide.values

Spatial cross-validation
Landslides cluster, so a random split puts near-identical neighbours in training and test sets and inflates the scores. Here folds are 100 km blocks: a model is always tested on blocks it never saw. Each of the five negative draws is cross-validated, and out-of-fold predictions are kept for validation in Section 10.


Code
def make_models():
    return {
        "Logistic": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=3000)),
        "RandomForest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, max_features="sqrt",
                                               n_jobs=-1, random_state=1),
        "GradientBoosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.08, max_iter=250,
                                                           random_state=1),
    }


def tss_max(y, p):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p)
    return float(np.max(tpr - fpr))


MODEL_NAMES = list(make_models())
oof = {m: np.full((N_DRAWS, len(grid)), np.nan) for m in MODEL_NAMES}  # out-of-fold predictions
oof_fr = np.full((N_DRAWS, len(grid)), np.nan)  # frequency ratio, refitted on training folds
rows = []
t0 = time.time()
for d, neg in enumerate(neg_draws):
    idx = np.r_[pres_idx, neg]
    y = y_all[idx]
    groups = grid.block.values[idx]
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(GroupKFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS).split(idx, y, groups)):
        if y[te].sum() == 0 or y[tr].sum() == 0:
            continue
        for name, model in make_models().items():
            p = model.fit(XA[idx[tr]], y[tr]).predict_proba(XA[idx[te]])[:, 1]
            oof[name][d, idx[te]] = p
            rows.append((d, k, name, roc_auc_score(y[te], p), tss_max(y[te], p)))
        # Frequency ratio from the training blocks only.
        train_mask = ~np.isin(grid.block.values, np.unique(groups[te]))
        p_fr = lsi(fr_tables(train_mask), idx[te])
        oof_fr[d, idx[te]] = p_fr
        rows.append((d, k, "FrequencyRatio", roc_auc_score(y[te], p_fr), tss_max(y[te], p_fr)))
    # The AHP model uses no training data: score it on the same test rows.
    rows.append((d, -1, "AHP-MCDA", roc_auc_score(y, grid.mcda.values[idx]), tss_max(y, grid.mcda.values[idx])))
cv = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["draw", "fold", "model", "AUC", "TSS"])
print(f"Cross-validation: {len(cv)} scores in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

perf = cv.groupby("model")[["AUC", "TSS"]].agg(["mean", "std"]).sort_values(("AUC", "mean"), ascending=False)
display(perf.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
order = perf.index.tolist()

Final models and susceptibility maps
Each machine-learning model is refitted on all data for every negative draw and applied to all 1 million cells; the five predictions are averaged. The random forest, the method of Ahmed et al. (2017), is the headline model; gradient boosting and logistic regression are kept for comparison.


Code

pred = {name: np.zeros(len(grid)) for name in MODEL_NAMES}
rf_draws = []  # random-forest predictions per draw, for the uncertainty map

    idx = np.r_[pres_idx, neg]

            model.set_params(n_estimators=150)

        p = model.predict_proba(XA)[:, 1]
        pred[name] += p / N_DRAWS
        if name == "RandomForest":

text:
What drives susceptibility?
Permutation importance measures how much the held-out AUC of the random forest falls when one predictor is shuffled. One-hot columns of the same layer are shuffled together so that each layer is judged as a whole. Partial dependence shows the average modelled response to one predictor, as Ahmed et al. (2017) did for soil carbon.


Code
model, idx_fit = fitted_rf[0]
# Use a held-out block set: refit on four folds, score the fifth.
idx = np.r_[pres_idx, neg_draws[0]]
groups = grid.block.values[idx]
tr, te = next(GroupKFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS).split(idx, y_all[idx], groups))
rf_imp = make_models()["RandomForest"].fit(XA[idx[tr]], y_all[idx[tr]])
layers_of = {c: c for c in X_num.columns}
layers_of.update({c: "slope_position" for c in X_cat.columns if c.startswith("pos_")})
layers_of.update({c: "land_cover" for c in X_cat.columns if c.startswith("lc_")})
layers_of.update({c: "fire_regime" for c in X_cat.columns if c.startswith("frg_")})
Xte, yte = XA[idx[te]].copy(), y_all[idx[te]]
base = roc_auc_score(yte, rf_imp.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1])
imp = {}
for layer in dict.fromkeys(layers_of.values()):
    cols = [FEATURES.index(c) for c, l in layers_of.items() if l == layer]
    drops = []
    for rep in range(3):
        Xp = Xte.copy()
        perm = RNG.permutation(len(Xp))
        Xp[:, cols] = Xp[perm][:, cols]
        drops.append(base - roc_auc_score(yte, rf_imp.predict_proba(Xp)[:, 1]))

imp = pd.Series(imp).sort_values(ascending=False)

title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Validation of all models
Two curves are standard in landslide studies (Chung and Fabbri 2003):

the success-rate curve uses the landslides the model was fitted on and measures goodness of fit;
the prediction-rate curve uses landslides the model did not see and measures predictive skill.

Cells are ranked from most to least susceptible; the curve plots the cumulative share of landslide cells against the cumulative share of area. A curve that rises steeply means a small fraction of the land captures most landslides. The area under the prediction-rate curve is the headline comparison.
Prediction-rate curves use out-of-fold predictions (averaged over draws) and are computed within surveyed tiles, where absence of a record means something.


Code
def rate_curve(score, mask):
    """Cumulative share of landslide cells vs cumulative share of area, ranked by score."""
    s, y = score[mask], y_all[mask]
    order = np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")
    cum_ls = np.cumsum(y[order]) / y.sum()
    cum_area = np.arange(1, len(s) + 1) / len(s)
    return cum_area, cum_ls, float(np.trapezoid(cum_ls, cum_area))

Susceptibility classes
Planners use classes, not continuous scores. Classes are set by share of area, so that each model’s classes cover the same land and can be compared directly: very low (lowest 50 %), low (next 20 %), moderate (next 15 %), high (next 10 %) and very high (top 5 %). A good map concentrates landslides in the upper classes, so the landslide density should rise steadily from class to class.

CLASS_CUTS = [0.50, 0.70, 0.85, 0.95]

Uncertainty
Two sources of uncertainty are quantified:

Training sample (Model 3). Each negative draw gives a slightly different random forest. The standard deviation across the five draws shows where the map depends on which negatives were chosen.
Weights (Model 2). monte_carlo_weights draws 500 weight vectors from a Dirichlet distribution around the AHP weights and reports the spread of the score and how often each cell stays in the top 10 percent.

A susceptibility model can also audit its own training data. title: Landslide Susceptibility of the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains and Western Great Plains
text:
Limitations

Inventory heterogeneity. The national compilation joins inventories of very different scope, date and method. The surveyed-tile background reduces the bias this causes, but cannot remove it: a tile with one mapped landslide counts as surveyed even if most of it was never examined.
Resolution. A 1 km node carries the 90 m slope at one point. Landslides start on slopes a few tens of metres across, so the map is a regional screen. Site decisions need 10 m terrain and field mapping; the USGS national susceptibility map (Mirus et al. 2024) works at about 10 m.
Mixed landslide types. Rockfall, debris flows, shallow slides and deep-seated slides are modelled together. Their controls differ, and type-specific models would be sharper where the inventory’s LS_Type field is filled.
Missing geology. Lithology and structure strongly control deep-seated landslides in the Colorado Plateau and Wyoming basins, and are not among the covariates. Soil texture and land cover partly stand in for them.
Static covariates. Fire regime describes historical fire, not recent burn scars. Post-fire debris-flow hazard changes year by year and is mapped separately by the USGS for individual fires.
Excluded land. Developed land, water and wetlands are outside the grid, so landslides recorded in towns and along reservoirs do not enter the model.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Overview
A watershed characterization describes how a drainage basin is built: where its boundary runs, how its stream network is organised, how steep and how wet its terrain is, and which parts of it respond fastest to rainfall. Planners use it as the first step before flood studies, erosion control, or water-quality work.
This capstone applies the terrain and hydrology tools from Module 03.02 to one real basin, the Onondaga Lake watershed in central New York, and adds the morphometric analysis that turns raster outputs into numbers a watershed manager can compare across sub-basins.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Setup
Locate the repository root, import the GeoLattice tools and the shared capstone helpers in data_processing.py, and create the output folder.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Problem statement and study area
Onondaga Lake lies on the north side of Syracuse, New York. Its watershed of roughly 738 km² sits almost entirely inside Onondaga County and spans two very different landscapes:

the Appalachian Plateau in the south, with relief of several hundred metres and deep, glacially carved “through valleys” such as the Tully Valley;
the Ontario Lake Plain in the north, a low, nearly flat surface that carries the city of Syracuse.

Two tributaries, Onondaga Creek and Ninemile Creek, deliver most of the inflow. Ley Creek and Harbor Brook drain the urban area.
Question. What are the physical and hydrologic characteristics of the Onondaga Lake watershed and its sub-basins, and which sub-basins should be looked at first for runoff and erosion management?
Data. Only one input is needed for the core analysis:








Layer
File
Notes




Elevation
Data/00_shared/raster_data/USA/Onondaga_DEM.tif
Clipped to the county, geographic coordinates, about 92 m x 126 m cells


County boundary
Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/NY_County_PROJ.shp
Map context



Land cover and soil layers are optional and handled in Section 12.


Code
# Project the county DEM to UTM 18N on a 100 m grid (cached after the first run).
DEM = dp.prepare_onondaga_dem(ROOT, resolution=100.0)

dem, GT, CRS = dp.read_band(DEM)  # elevation array, geotransform, CRS
CELL = abs(GT[1])  # cell size in metres
CELL_KM2 = CELL * CELL / 1e6  # cell area in km2
EXTENT = dp.extent_of(DEM)  # imshow extent for every map below
valid = np.isfinite(dem)  # cells inside the county

print(f"Grid:        {dem.shape[1]} x {dem.shape[0]} cells at {CELL:.0f} m, {CRS}")
print(f"Data area:   {valid.sum() * CELL_KM2:,.0f} km2")
print(f"Elevation:   {np.nanmin(dem):.0f} to {np.nanmax(dem):.0f} m")

# Hillshade backdrop used under most maps.
HS = OUT / "hillshade.tif"
hillshade(DEM, HS, azimuth=315, altitude=45, overwrite=True)
hs, _, _ = dp.read_band(HS)

# Onondaga County outline in the DEM's CRS.
county = gpd.read_file(ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "NY_County_PROJ.shp")
name_col = "COUNTY" if "COUNTY" in county.columns else county.columns[0]
county = county[county[name_col].astype(str).str.contains("Onondaga", case=False)].to_crs(dp.ONONDAGA_CRS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
ax.imshow(hs, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)
im = ax.imshow(dem, cmap="terrain", extent=EXTENT, alpha=0.6)
county.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=1)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04, label="Elevation (m)")
ax.set_title("Onondaga County DEM (UTM 18N, 100 m)")
ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m)")
ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m)")
plt.show()

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
DEM preparation and conditioning
Flow routing needs a surface on which every cell has a lower neighbour until the water leaves the map. Two properties of this DEM need care:

It is clipped to the county. The data are bounded by nodata, not by the edge of the raster, so water must be allowed to leave through any valid cell that touches nodata.
It contains large flats. Onondaga Lake, Otisco Lake and the valley floors are level in the DEM. A flat has no downslope neighbour, so flow stops there unless a small gradient is imposed.

fill_depressions with fix_flats=True handles both with Priority-Flood + epsilon (Barnes, Lehman and Mulla, 2014). The flood starts from every cell on the data boundary and moves inward in order of elevation. A cell that is not higher than the cell it was reached from is raised by the smallest representable increment, which fills depressions and drains flats in one pass.


Code
# Condition the DEM and report what changed.
DEM_COND = OUT / "dem_conditioned.tif"
fill_depressions(DEM, DEM_COND, fix_flats=True, overwrite=True)

cond, _, _ = dp.read_band(DEM_COND)
fill_depth = cond - dem  # metres added by conditioning
raised = fill_depth > 0.1  # ignore the epsilon-only changes
diag = pd.Series(
    {
        "cells": int(valid.sum()),
        "cells raised by more than 0.1 m": int(raised.sum()),
        "share of cells raised (%)": 100 * raised.sum() / valid.sum(),
        "maximum fill (m)": float(np.nanmax(fill_depth)),
        "mean fill where raised (m)": float(np.nanmean(fill_depth[raised])),
    }
)
display(diag.to_frame("value"))
fill_show = np.where(fill_depth > 0.1, fill_depth, np.nan)  # hide the epsilon-only changes

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7))
axes[0].imshow(hs, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)
im0 = axes[0].imshow(fill_show, cmap="magma_r", extent=EXTENT, vmin=0, vmax=10)
axes[0].set_title("Fill depth > 0.1 m")
plt.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.04, label="m")
axes[1].hist(fill_depth[fill_depth > 0.1], bins=40, color="steelblue")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Fill depth (m)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Cells")
axes[1].set_title("Distribution of fill depth")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Reading the result. About six percent of the cells are raised by more than 0.1 m. They sit in closed depressions on the plateau, in kettle holes on the valley floors and in quarries near Syracuse. Fill depths of several metres on a 100 m DEM usually mean a real feature (a reservoir, a quarry, a road embankment that blocks a valley), not noise. For a design study each large fill would be checked against imagery.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Flow direction and flow accumulation
D8 sends all flow from a cell to its steepest downslope neighbour. It gives clean, single-thread channels and is the standard for delineation. D-infinity splits flow between two neighbours according to the true downslope angle, which represents dispersion on hillslopes better. We route with both, use D8 for the network and basins, and use D-infinity for the wetness index.


Code
# D8 pointer and accumulation from the conditioned DEM.
D8 = OUT / "d8_pointer.tif"
FA = OUT / "d8_flow_accumulation.tif"
d8_pointer(DEM_COND, D8, overwrite=True)
d8_flow_accumulation(DEM_COND, FA, out_type="cells", pointer=D8, overwrite=True)

# D-infinity specific catchment area for comparison.
SCA = OUT / "dinf_sca.tif"
dinf_flow_accumulation(DEM_COND, SCA, out_type="sca", overwrite=True)

fa, _, _ = dp.read_band(FA)
sca, _, _ = dp.read_band(SCA)
ptr, _, _ = dp.read_band(D8)

# Cells with no flow direction should only be outlets on the data boundary.
no_dir = valid & ~np.isfinite(ptr)
print(f"Cells without a flow direction: {no_dir.sum()} (all on the county boundary: outlets)")
print(f"Largest contributing area:      {np.nanmax(fa) * CELL_KM2:,.0f} km2")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7.5))
for ax, arr, title in zip(
    axes,
    [np.log10(np.maximum(fa * CELL_KM2, CELL_KM2)), np.log10(np.maximum(sca, 1.0))],
    ["D8 contributing area, log10(km2)", "D-infinity specific catchment area, log10(m)"],
):
    im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap="Blues", extent=EXTENT)
    county.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Cells without a flow direction: 476 (all on the county boundary: outlets)
Largest contributing area:      953 km2









The D8 map shows the organised network: Onondaga Creek running north through the Tully Valley, Ninemile Creek leaving Otisco Lake in the south-west, and the Seneca and Oneida rivers collecting flow across the lake plain. The D-infinity surface is smoother on hillslopes, which is why it is preferred for the wetness index in Section 10.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Stream network and threshold sensitivity
A cell is called a stream when its contributing area exceeds a threshold. The threshold is a modelling choice: a small value draws channels up every hollow, a large value keeps only the main rivers. Drainage density, one of the key morphometric indices, depends directly on it, so the choice must be reported.
\[
D_d = \frac{\sum L_{stream}}{A}
\]


Code
# Drainage density of the whole data area for a range of thresholds.
recv, step = dp.d8_receivers(ptr)  # downstream cell and step length for every cell
step_km = step.reshape(dem.shape) * CELL / 1000.0  # channel length carried by each cell (km)

rows_ = []
for thr_km2 in [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0]:
    mask = fa * CELL_KM2 >= thr_km2
    length = np.nansum(step_km[mask])
    rows_.append({"threshold_km2": thr_km2, "stream_cells": int(mask.sum()), "length_km": length,
                  "drainage_density_km_per_km2": length / (valid.sum() * CELL_KM2)})
thr_table = pd.DataFrame(rows_)
display(thr_table)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.loglog(thr_table["threshold_km2"], thr_table["drainage_density_km_per_km2"], "o-")
ax.set_xlabel("Stream initiation threshold (km2)")
ax.set_ylabel("Drainage density (km / km2)")
ax.set_title("Drainage density depends on the threshold")
ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

STREAM_THRESHOLD_KM2 = 1.0
STREAMS = OUT / "streams.tif"
extract_streams(FA, STREAMS, threshold=STREAM_THRESHOLD_KM2 / CELL_KM2, overwrite=True)

# Strahler order of every stream cell (helper; see data_processing.py).

text:
Watershed delineation and validation
A delineation is only as good as its outlets. We use five: the outlet of Onondaga Lake and four stream gauges on its tributaries. Gauge coordinates are approximate, so each point is snapped to the stream cell with the largest contributing area within a search distance.
Published drainage areas give an independent check:

Code
# Outlets: name, longitude, latitude, published area (km2), snap distance (m).
# Coordinates other than Spencer Street are approximate and rely on snapping.
outlets = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ("Onondaga Creek at Spencer St", -76.1620, 43.0574, 284.9, 600),
        ("Ninemile Creek at Lakeland", -76.2264, 43.0806, 297.8, 600),
        ("Ley Creek at Park St", -76.1697, 43.0775, 66.1, 600),
        ("Harbor Brook at Hiawatha Blvd", -76.1836, 43.0564, 31.4, 600),
        ("Onondaga Lake outlet", -76.2478, 43.1178, 738.0, 1000),
    ],
    columns=["outlet", "lon", "lat", "published_km2", "snap_m"],
)

to_utm = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", dp.ONONDAGA_CRS, always_xy=True)
outlets["x"], outlets["y"] = to_utm.transform(outlets["lon"].values, outlets["lat"].values)

# Snap each outlet to the largest stream within its search distance.
snapped = []
for _, o in outlets.iterrows():
    sx, sy = snap_pour_points([(o.x, o.y)], STREAMS, snap_distance=float(o.snap_m), prefer_flow_accumulation=FA)[0]
    snapped.append((sx, sy))
outlets["x_snap"] = [s[0] for s in snapped]
outlets["y_snap"] = [s[1] for s in snapped]
outlets["moved_m"] = np.hypot(outlets.x_snap - outlets.x, outlets.y_snap - outlets.y)

# Delineated area = flow accumulation at the snapped cell.
rc = [dp.xy_to_rowcol(x, y, GT) for x, y in snapped]
outlets["delineated_km2"] = [fa[r, c] * CELL_KM2 for r, c in rc]
outlets["difference_pct"] = 100 * (outlets.delineated_km2 - outlets.published_km2) / outlets.published_km2
display(outlets[["outlet", "published_km2", "delineated_km2", "difference_pct", "moved_m"]])

Reading the validation table.

The lake outlet and Ninemile Creek agree with the published areas to within a few percent. Their divides run along plateau ridges that a 100 m DEM resolves well.
Onondaga Creek and Ley Creek are over-estimated by roughly 13 to 15 percent.
Harbor Brook is not recovered: the snapped outlet drains under 3 km² against a published 31 km². The basin is small, narrow and largely urban, and its lower course runs through culverts. On this DEM most of its area is routed to a neighbouring stream, which is a likely contributor to the Onondaga Creek surplus. The gauge coordinates used here are approximate, which adds to the uncertainty for an outlet this small.

The lesson is general: a coarse DEM delineates large, high-relief basins well and small, low-relief or engineered basins poorly. Where storm sewers or culverts control drainage, the terrain surface is no longer the right model, and a finer DEM with a burned-in drainage network is required.


Code
# Delineate the lake watershed and the gauged tributary basins.
lake_xy = snapped[-1]
WS = OUT / "watershed_lake.tif"
watershed(D8, [lake_xy], WS, overwrite=True)
ws, _, _ = dp.read_band(WS)
in_ws = np.isfinite(ws)  # True inside the Onondaga Lake watershed

GAUGE_WS = OUT / "watersheds_gauges.tif"
watershed(D8, snapped[:3], GAUGE_WS, overwrite=True)  # Harbor Brook omitted (not resolved)
gws, _, _ = dp.read_band(GAUGE_WS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 8.5))
ax.imshow(hs, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)

ax.scatter(outlets.x_snap, outlets.y_snap, c="red", s=40, zorder=5, edgecolor="white")
label_offsets = [(30, -32), (-110, 14), (26, 22), (-118, -22), (8, 10)]  # keep the labels apart
for (_, o), off in zip(outlets.iterrows(), label_offsets):
    ax.annotate(o.outlet.replace(" at ", "\nat "), (o.x_snap, o.y_snap), xytext=off, textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="black", lw=0.6),
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc="white", alpha=0.85, lw=0))
county.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Sub-basins
Management decisions are made for parts of a watershed, so the basin is split into sub-basins. dp.subbasin_outlets places an outlet at the end of every branch that drains at least 25 km² where it meets another such branch. watershed then labels the area above each outlet. The result is one unit per major tributary plus the inter-basin areas along the main stems.


Code
SUB_THRESHOLD_KM2 = 25.0
sub_xy = dp.subbasin_outlets(FA, D8, threshold_cells=SUB_THRESHOLD_KM2 / CELL_KM2, mask=in_ws)
sub_xy = sub_xy + [lake_xy]  # the lake outlet closes the last unit

SUB = OUT / "subbasins_raw.tif"
watershed(D8, sub_xy, SUB, overwrite=True)
sub_raw, _, _ = dp.read_band(SUB)
sub_raw[~in_ws] = np.nan

# Renumber from largest to smallest and keep units of at least 5 km2 for analysis.
ids, counts = np.unique(sub_raw[np.isfinite(sub_raw)], return_counts=True)
order_by_area = ids[np.argsort(-counts)]
sub = np.full(sub_raw.shape, np.nan)
outlet_of = {}  # new id -> outlet (x, y)
for new_id, old_id in enumerate(order_by_area, start=1):
    sub[sub_raw == old_id] = new_id
    outlet_of[new_id] = sub_xy[int(old_id) - 1]
SUBBASINS = OUT / "subbasins.tif"
dp.write_band(SUBBASINS, sub, DEM, nodata=0.0)

MIN_AREA_KM2 = 5.0
area_km2 = {i: float((sub == i).sum() * CELL_KM2) for i in outlet_of}
analysis_ids = [i for i in outlet_of if area_km2[i] >= MIN_AREA_KM2]
print(f"Sub-basins: {len(outlet_of)} delineated, {len(analysis_ids)} of at least {MIN_AREA_KM2:g} km2 kept for analysis")
print(f"Area covered by the analysed units: {sum(area_km2[i] for i in analysis_ids) / (in_ws.sum() * CELL_KM2):.1%}")

# Polygons for mapping, perimeter and the output GeoPackage.
SUB_GPKG_RAW = OUT / "subbasins_raw.gpkg"
polygonize(SUBBASINS, SUB_GPKG_RAW, field_name="sub_id", overwrite=True)
sub_gdf = gpd.read_file(SUB_GPKG_RAW)
sub_gdf = sub_gdf[sub_gdf["sub_id"] > 0].dissolve(by="sub_id").reset_index()
sub_gdf["sub_id"] = sub_gdf["sub_id"].astype(int)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 8.5))
ax.imshow(hs, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)
ax.imshow(sub, cmap="tab20", extent=EXTENT, alpha=0.55, interpolation="nearest")
ax.imshow(np.where(streams & in_ws, 1.0, np.nan), cmap="Blues", extent=EXTENT, vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")
sub_gdf.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
for _, row in sub_gdf[sub_gdf.sub_id.isin(analysis_ids)].iterrows():
    p = row.geometry.representative_point()
    ax.text(p.x, p.y, str(row.sub_id), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.2", fc="white", alpha=0.85, lw=0))
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = sub_gdf.total_bounds
ax.set_xlim(xmin - 1500, xmax + 1500)
ax.set_ylim(ymin - 1500, ymax + 1500)
ax.set_title(f"Sub-basins of the Onondaga Lake watershed (confluence threshold {SUB_THRESHOLD_KM2:g} km2)")
plt.show()


Sub-basins: 13 delineated, 12 of at least 5 km2 kept for analysis
Area covered by the analysed units: 99.5%

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Morphometric analysis
Morphometry describes a basin with dimensionless or simply scaled numbers so that basins of different size can be compared. Three groups are computed for every sub-basin.
Geometry (shape)








Index
Formula
Meaning




Form factor
\(F_f = A / L_b^2\)
Low values: elongated basin, flatter and longer flood peak


Circularity ratio
\(R_c = 4\pi A / P^2\)
1 for a circle


Elongation ratio
\(R_e = 2\sqrt{A/\pi} / L_b\)
Near 1: circular; below 0.7: elongated


Compactness coefficient
\(C_c = P / (2\sqrt{\pi A})\)
1 for a circle, larger for irregular outlines



Relief








Index
Formula
Meaning




Basin relief
\(H = z_{max} - z_{min}\)
Potential energy of the basin


Relief ratio
\(R_h = H / L_b\)
Overall steepness


Ruggedness number
\(R_n = H \cdot D_d\)

\(D_d = \sum L / A\)

Here \(A\) is area, \(P\) perimeter, \(L_b\) basin length, \(N_u\) the number of stream segments of Strahler order \(u\) and \(N\) their total. Basin length is taken as the longest flow path to the sub-basin outlet. Perimeter is measured on polygons simplified by one cell width, because the stair-step edge of a raster zone overstates perimeter.


Code
# Flow distance from every cell to the outlet of its own sub-basin.
targets = np.zeros(dem.shape, dtype=bool)
for i, (x, y) in outlet_of.items():
    r, c = dp.xy_to_rowcol(x, y, GT)
    targets[r, c] = True
FLOWLEN = OUT / "flow_length_to_subbasin_outlet.tif"
flow_len = dp.flow_distance_to_targets(D8, DEM_COND, targets, FLOWLEN)  # metres

# Stream segments are counted at their downstream end: a stream cell whose
# downstream cell has a different order, is not a stream, or lies outside the region.
order_flat = np.nan_to_num(order, nan=0).ravel()
down_order = np.where(recv >= 0, order_flat[np.clip(recv, 0, None)], 0)


def segment_ends(region):
    """Boolean array of segment-end cells for the stream network inside ``region``."""
    reg = region.ravel()
    down_in = np.where(recv >= 0, reg[np.clip(recv, 0, None)], False)
    ends = (order_flat > 0) & reg & ((down_order != order_flat) | ~down_in)
    return ends.reshape(dem.shape)


# Perimeter from simplified polygons (km).
perim_km = sub_gdf.set_index("sub_id").geometry.simplify(CELL).length / 1000.0

records = []
for i in analysis_ids:
    m = sub == i
    A = m.sum() * CELL_KM2  # km2
    P = float(perim_km.loc[i])  # km
    Lb = np.nanmax(flow_len[m]) / 1000.0  # km, longest flow path
    z = dem[m]
    H = float(np.nanmax(z) - np.nanmin(z))  # m
    st = m & streams
    L = float(np.nansum(step_km[st]))  # km of channel
    seg = segment_ends(m)
    n_by_order = {int(u): int((seg & (order == u)).sum()) for u in np.unique(order[st])}
    N = sum(n_by_order.values())
    orders = sorted(n_by_order)
    ratios = [n_by_order[u] / n_by_order[u + 1] for u in orders[:-1] if n_by_order.get(u + 1, 0) > 0]
    Dd = L / A
    records.append(
        {
            "sub_id": i,
            "area_km2": A,
            "perimeter_km": P,
            "basin_length_km": Lb,
            "relief_m": H,
            "max_order": max(orders),
            "n_segments": N,
            "stream_length_km": L,
            "form_factor": A / Lb**2,
            "circularity_ratio": 4 * np.pi * A / P**2,
            "elongation_ratio": 2 * np.sqrt(A / np.pi) / Lb,
            "compactness_coeff": P / (2 * np.sqrt(np.pi * A)),
            "relief_ratio": (H / 1000.0) / Lb,
            "drainage_density": Dd,
            "stream_frequency": N / A,
            "bifurcation_ratio": float(np.mean(ratios)) if ratios else np.nan,
            "drainage_texture": N / P,
            "ruggedness_number": (H / 1000.0) * Dd,
            "overland_flow_length_km": 1 / (2 * Dd) if Dd > 0 else np.nan,
        }
    )
morph = pd.DataFrame(records).set_index("sub_id")

Reading the tables.

Shape. Every unit has an elongation ratio below 0.7 and a form factor below 0.35, so all are elongated. That is expected where sub-basins follow long, straight through valleys, and it is reinforced by using the longest flow path, which is longer than the straight-line basin length, as \(L_b\). Elongated basins deliver runoff over a longer time and tend to have lower, broader flood peaks than compact ones of the same area.
Relief. Relief and relief ratio separate the plateau headwaters from the lake-plain units near Syracuse.
Network. For the whole watershed, segment counts fall roughly geometrically with order and mean segment length rises through order 4, as Horton’s laws predict. The single order-5 segment is short because it forms only where the two main creeks meet inside the lake. Bifurcation ratios between 3 and 5 indicate a network that is not strongly controlled by geological structure; values outside that range in individual sub-basins mostly reflect the low segment counts at this resolution.

Indices built on stream counts are unstable in units with only a handful of segments. Treat differences between small sub-basins with caution.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Hypsometric analysis
The hypsometric curve plots the share of basin area lying above each relative height. Its integral,
\[
HI = \frac{\bar z - z_{min}}{z_{max} - z_{min}},
\]
summarises how much of the original land mass remains. In Strahler’s interpretation, \(HI > 0.6\) indicates a youthful, actively eroding basin, \(0.35\) to \(0.6\) a mature one, and \(HI < 0.35\) a subdued, old-stage landscape. In glaciated terrain such as this, the curve also reflects valley filling by glacial sediment.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab20")
hi = {}
for k, i in enumerate(analysis_ids):
    z = np.sort(dem[sub == i])[::-1]  # elevations from high to low
    rel_h = (z - z.min()) / (z.max() - z.min())  # relative height h/H
    rel_a = np.arange(1, z.size + 1) / z.size  # relative area a/A above that height
    hi[i] = float((z.mean() - z.min()) / (z.max() - z.min()))
    ax.plot(rel_a, rel_h, color=cmap(k % 20), label=f"{i} (HI={hi[i]:.2f})")
z = np.sort(dem[in_ws])[::-1]
ax.plot(np.arange(1, z.size + 1) / z.size, (z - z.min()) / (z.max() - z.min()), color="black", linewidth=2.5,
        label=f"Whole watershed (HI={(z.mean() - z.min()) / (z.max() - z.min()):.2f})")
ax.set_xlabel("Relative area above height (a / A)")
ax.set_ylabel("Relative height (h / H)")
ax.set_title("Hypsometric curves by sub-basin")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2, title="Sub-basin")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

morph["hypsometric_integral"] = pd.Series(hi)









Reading the curves. The whole watershed has a hypsometric integral near 0.3, and no sub-basin exceeds 0.5. Most of the area lies low relative to the relief, the signature of broad valley floors and a wide lake plain beneath a narrow band of plateau upland. The lowest integrals belong to the lake-plain units around Syracuse; the highest belong to the plateau headwater units. In this glaciated landscape the low values record valley widening and filling by ice and sediment more than long fluvial erosion.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Hydrologic response
How quickly does a sub-basin respond to a storm? A first estimate is the time of concentration, the travel time from the most distant point to the outlet. The Kirpich (1940) formula needs only the length and slope of the main flow path:
\[
t_c = 0.0195\; L^{0.77}\; S^{-0.385}
\]
with \(t_c\) in minutes, \(L\) in metres and \(S\) the mean slope of the path (m/m). It was derived for small agricultural basins, so values for large or urban units are indicative only and are best used to compare sub-basins.


Code
resp = []
profiles = {}
for i in analysis_ids:
    m = sub == i
    d = np.where(m, flow_len, np.nan)
    r0, c0 = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(d), d.shape)  # most distant cell
    # Walk downstream to the sub-basin outlet, recording distance and elevation.
    dist, elev = [0.0], [dem[r0, c0]]
    idx = r0 * dem.shape[1] + c0
    while True:
        r, c = divmod(idx, dem.shape[1])
        if targets[r, c] or recv[idx] < 0:
            break
        dist.append(dist[-1] + step[idx] * CELL)
        idx = recv[idx]
        elev.append(dem[divmod(idx, dem.shape[1])])
    L = dist[-1]
    S = max((elev[0] - elev[-1]) / L, 1e-4)  # mean slope of the main flow path
    tc_min = 0.0195 * L**0.77 * S**-0.385
    profiles[i] = (np.array(dist) / 1000.0, np.array(elev))
    resp.append({"sub_id": i, "flow_path_km": L / 1000.0, "flow_path_slope_pct": 100 * S, "tc_kirpich_hr": tc_min / 60.0})
response = pd.DataFrame(resp).set_index("sub_id")
morph = morph.join(response)
display(response)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for k, i in enumerate(analysis_ids):
    x, y = profiles[i]
    ax.plot(x.max() - x, y, color=cmap(k % 20), label=str(i))  # distance upstream of the outlet
ax.set_xlabel("Distance upstream of sub-basin outlet (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("Elevation (m)")
ax.set_title("Longitudinal profiles along the longest flow path")
ax.legend(title="Sub-basin", ncol=3, fontsize=8)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

text:
Land cover and soils (optional external data)
Runoff depends on what covers the ground as much as on its shape. Two layers complete a characterization, and neither ships with the repository:








Layer
Expected file (under Data/03_spatial_analysis/capstone_spatial_analysis/)
Source




Land cover
onondaga/nlcd_landcover.tif
NLCD (USGS / MRLC)


Hydrologic soil group
onondaga/soil_hydrologic_group.tif
gSSURGO (USDA NRCS), coded A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4



When both files are present, the cell below resamples them to the analysis grid, reports land-cover composition per sub-basin and computes an area-weighted SCS curve number. When they are missing, the cell reports that and the notebook continues with terrain-only indicators.


Code
ext = dp.check_external_data(ROOT, ["onondaga_nlcd", "onondaga_hsg"])
HAVE_LANDCOVER = all(p is not None for p in ext.values())

if not HAVE_LANDCOVER:
    missing = [dp.EXTERNAL_DATA[k]["file"] for k, p in ext.items() if p is None]
    print("Optional layers not found, section skipped:")
    for f in missing:
        print(f"  Data/03_spatial_analysis/capstone_spatial_analysis/{f}")
else:
    from geolattice.raster import warp  # resample onto the analysis grid

    def to_grid(src, name):
        """Nearest-neighbour resample of a categorical raster onto the DEM grid."""
        dst = OUT / name
        warp(src, dst, dst_crs=dp.ONONDAGA_CRS, resample="near", xRes=CELL, yRes=CELL,
             outputBounds=(EXTENT[0], EXTENT[2], EXTENT[1], EXTENT[3]), overwrite=True)
        return dp.read_band(dst)[0]

    nlcd = to_grid(ext["onondaga_nlcd"], "nlcd_grid.tif")
    hsg = to_grid(ext["onondaga_hsg"], "hsg_grid.tif")

    # NLCD classes grouped into broad covers.
    groups = {"water_wetland": [11, 90, 95], "developed": [21, 22, 23, 24], "forest": [41, 42, 43],
              "shrub_grass": [52, 71], "pasture": [81], "cropland": [82], "barren": [31]}
    # Curve numbers (antecedent condition II) by cover group and soil group A-D.
    cn_table = {"water_wetland": (98, 98, 98, 98), "developed": (77, 85, 90, 92), "forest": (36, 60, 73, 79),
                "shrub_grass": (39, 61, 74, 80), "pasture": (49, 69, 79, 84), "cropland": (67, 78, 85, 89),
                "barren": (77, 86, 91, 94)}
    cn = np.full(dem.shape, np.nan)
    for g, codes in groups.items():
        for s in (1, 2, 3, 4):
            cn[np.isin(nlcd, codes) & (hsg == s)] = cn_table[g][s - 1]

    lc_rows = []
    for i in analysis_ids:
        m = sub == i
        row = {"sub_id": i, "curve_number": np.nanmean(cn[m])}
        for g, codes in groups.items():
            row[f"pct_{g}"] = 100 * np.mean(np.isin(nlcd[m], codes))
        lc_rows.append(row)
    landcover = pd.DataFrame(lc_rows).set_index("sub_id")
    morph = morph.join(landcover)
    display(landcover)

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Sub-basin prioritisation
Morphometric prioritisation ranks sub-basins by how strongly their form favours rapid runoff and erosion. The usual scheme is a compound ranking:

Linear and relief parameters (drainage density, stream frequency, bifurcation ratio, drainage texture, relief ratio, mean slope) are positively related to runoff and erosion: the largest value receives rank 1.
Shape parameters (form factor, circularity ratio, elongation ratio) are ranked the other way, following the convention of Biswas, Sudhakar and Desai (1999): the smallest value receives rank 1.

The compound value is the mean of the ranks; the lowest compound value is the highest priority. The method is a screening tool. It says where terrain form warrants a closer look, not where erosion is actually occurring.


Code
direct = ["drainage_density", "stream_frequency", "bifurcation_ratio", "drainage_texture", "relief_ratio", "mean_slope_deg"]
inverse = ["form_factor", "circularity_ratio", "elongation_ratio"]
if HAVE_LANDCOVER:
    direct.append("curve_number")  # more runoff-prone cover and soil -> higher priority

ranks = pd.DataFrame(index=morph.index)
for col in direct:
    ranks[col] = morph[col].rank(ascending=False, na_option="bottom")  # largest value -> rank 1
for col in inverse:
    ranks[col] = morph[col].rank(ascending=True, na_option="bottom")  # smallest value -> rank 1

morph["compound_value"] = ranks.mean(axis=1)
morph["priority_rank"] = morph["compound_value"].rank(method="min").astype(int)
morph["priority_class"] = pd.qcut(morph["compound_value"].rank(method="first"), 3, labels=["High", "Medium", "Low"])

display(ranks.assign(compound_value=morph["compound_value"], priority=morph["priority_class"]).sort_values("compound_value"))

Reading the map. The high-priority units form a band across the middle of the watershed, where plateau tributaries drop into the valleys: they combine high drainage density or strong branching with elongated, irregular outlines. The lake-plain units in the north rank low on every relief parameter. Note that the steepest headwater unit in the south-east ranks low overall, because its compact outline scores poorly on the three shape parameters and outweighs its high relief and slope. That is a property of equal-weight compound ranking, and a reason to read the result together with the slope and relief columns of the table, not in place of them.

title: Watershed Characterization of the Onondaga Lake Watershed
text:
Limitations

Resolution. A 100 m DEM cannot resolve small urban catchments or channels narrower than a cell. Harbor Brook is the clear failure in the validation table. Repeating the analysis with the 10 m USGS 3DEP DEM would improve small-basin divides and raise drainage density.
Engineered drainage. Storm sewers, culverts and the Onondaga Creek flood-control dam are not represented. In Syracuse the real drainage network departs from the terrain surface.
County clip. The DEM stops at the county line. The lake watershed fits almost entirely inside it, but any study of the Seneca or Oneida rivers would need a wider DEM.
Threshold dependence. Drainage density, stream frequency and everything derived from them depend on the 1 km² stream threshold.
Lakes. Onondaga and Otisco lakes are treated as flat land that drains across its surface. Flow lengths across them are geometric, not hydraulic.
Kirpich times. The formula is outside its calibration range for the large units; use the values to compare sub-basins, not as design numbers.
Prioritisation. Compound ranking weights all parameters equally and uses terrain form only. It screens for where to look; it does not measure erosion or runoff.

title: Spatial Causal Discovery
text:
Overview
The earlier notebooks assumed a causal structure (treatment → outcome) and estimated its strength. Causal discovery tries to learn the structure from data. It needs strong assumptions, and its output is a set of hypotheses to be tested with designs like those in notebooks 01-07, never a conclusion.
Spatial panel Granger causality is fit to the simulated panel, where the direction is known. Geographical convergent cross mapping (GCCM) and NOTEARS with spatial-lag nodes are applied to real CHR 2024 county measures, where no ground truth exists.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal._utils import as_sparse_weights
ts.use()

g = cc.build_county_frame()
w = cc.queen_weights()
xy = cc.coords_km(g)
n = len(g)

title: Spatial Causal Discovery
text:
Spatial Granger causality
\(x\) Granger-causes \(y\) if past \(x\) improves the prediction of \(y\) beyond \(y\)’s own past. With county panels and neighbours:
\[y_{it}=a_i+l_t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Big[\rho_\ell\,y_{i,t-\ell}+\gamma_\ell\,(Wy)_{i,t-\ell}
+\beta_\ell\,x_{i,t-\ell}+\eta_\ell\,(Wx)_{i,t-\ell}\Big]+e_{it}.\]
\(H_0^{\text{local}}:\beta=0\) (own past \(x\)) and \(H_0^{\text{spillover}}:\eta=0\) (neighbours’ past \(x\)) are tested with cluster-robust Wald statistics and a Hotelling-type \(F(q,G-q)\) reference.
Two traps, both handled by SpatialGranger:

Nickell bias. With unit fixed effects and lagged regressors, the within transformation correlates the demeaned error with the demeaned lags: the bias is of order \(1/T\) (Nickell, 1981). In a large panel this small bias becomes “significant” and produces spurious Granger causality. The half-panel jackknife (Dhaene & Jochmans, 2015) removes the \(O(1/T)\) term: \(\hat\beta_{\text{HJ}}=2\hat\beta-\tfrac12(\hat\beta_{\text{first half}}+\hat\beta_{\text{second half}})\).
Cross-sectional dependence. Shocks hitting neighbouring counties in the same year make unit-clustered SEs too small; we cluster on spatial blocks of counties.

Why not the CHR panel? CHR offers six annual releases (2020-2025), many measures pool several data years, and adjacent releases overlap. That is too few, too smooth time points for dynamic models (the jackknife needs at least three periods per half). We therefore simulate a 24-year panel on the real county map: \(x\) is a spatially autocorrelated AR(1) process, and \(y_{it}=0.4y_{i,t-1}+0.5x_{i,t-1}+0.4(Wx)_{i,t-1}+a_i+e_{it}\), so \(x\to y\) and not \(y\to x\).


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
Wr = as_sparse_weights(w, n, row_standardize=True)
T_, burn = 24, 20
x = np.zeros((n, T_ + burn)); y = np.zeros((n, T_ + burn)); a = rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
for t in range(1, T_ + burn):
    shock = rng.normal(size=n)
    x[:, t] = 0.5 * x[:, t - 1] + 0.5 * (Wr @ shock) + 0.5 * shock
    y[:, t] = 0.4 * y[:, t - 1] + 0.5 * x[:, t - 1] + 0.4 * (Wr @ x[:, t - 1]) + a + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n)
x, y = x[:, burn:], y[:, burn:]
panel = sc.SpatialPanel(np.repeat(g.fips, T_), np.tile(np.arange(T_), n), y.ravel(), g.fips, xy, X=x.ravel()[:, None])

fwd = sc.SpatialGranger(lags=1, w=w).fit(panel, cause=0)
print(fwd.summary())
