In the reverse regression (does \(y\) Granger-cause \(x\)?), Nickell bias pulls \(x\)’s own persistence down from 0.5 to 0.43 and pushes the coefficient on lagged \(y\) away from 0. With about 71,500 observations that small bias is “significant” (\(p<0.0001\)): a spurious causal finding. The half-panel jackknife restores both coefficients and the test no longer rejects. In this simulation the shocks’ spatial correlation is mild, so clustering matters less than the bias correction.

title: Spatial Causal Discovery
section: Geographical convergent cross mapping (GCCM) on real data
text:
Geographical convergent cross mapping (GCCM) on real data
CCM (Sugihara et al., 2012) comes from dynamical systems. If \(x\) drives \(y\), then \(y\)’s state carries an imprint of \(x\), so \(x\) can be cross-mapped (predicted) from a reconstruction of \(y\)’s state space. GCCM (Gao et al., 2023) replaces time delays with spatial lags:
\[M_y(i)=\Big(y_i,\ \bar y^{(1)}_i,\ \dots,\ \bar y^{(E-1)}_i\Big),\qquad \bar y^{(k)}_i=\text{mean of }y\text{ over the }k\text{-th ring of neighbours}.\]
To predict \(x_i\), find the \(E+1\) nearest neighbours of \(M_y(i)\) among a library of \(L\) counties and average their \(x\) with weights \(w_k\propto\exp(-d_k/d_1)\) (simplex projection). The cross-map skill is \(\rho(L)=\operatorname{corr}(\hat x,x)\). Evidence for \(x\to y\) is skill that rises and converges as \(L\) grows, not merely high skill.
A spatial exclusion zone is essential. Neighbouring counties share neighbour rings, so their embeddings are similar by construction. Using them as “nearest neighbours” lets ordinary spatial autocorrelation masquerade as cross-map skill. geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal excludes every county within \(2(E-1)\) rings of the target, a spatial analogue of the Theiler window. (In package tests, two independent smooth fields showed skill ≈ 0.5 without it.)


Code
pairs = [("inactivity_pct", "diabetes_pct"), ("obesity_pct", "diabetes_pct"), ("broadband_pct", "diabetes_pct")]
fits = {}
for xa, ya in pairs:
    fits[(xa, ya)] = sc.GCCM(E=3, n_rep=8, random_state=0).fit(g[xa].to_numpy(), g[ya].to_numpy(), w=w)
leak = sc.GCCM(E=3, n_rep=8, exclusion=0, random_state=0).fit(g["inactivity_pct"].to_numpy(), g["diabetes_pct"].to_numpy(), w=w)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 3.8), sharey=True)
for a, (xa, ya) in zip(ax, pairs):
    sk = fits[(xa, ya)].skill_
    a.plot(sk.index, sk["x_causes_y"], "o-", color=ts.BLUE, ms=4, label=f"{xa.replace('_pct','')} → diabetes")
    a.plot(sk.index, sk["y_causes_x"], "s-", color=ts.ORANGE, ms=4, label=f"diabetes → {xa.replace('_pct','')}")
    a.set_xlabel("library size L"); a.set_title(f"{cc.LABELS[xa]} vs diabetes")
    a.legend(fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel("cross-map skill ρ(L)")
plt.tight_layout()
tests = pd.DataFrame({f"{xa} | {k}": v for (xa, ya), f in fits.items() for k, v in f.tests_.items()}).T

      {k: round(v["skill"], 3) for k, v in fits[("inactivity_pct", "diabetes_pct")].tests_.items()})


inactivity vs diabetes, no exclusion zone: {'x_causes_y': 0.841, 'y_causes_x': 0.84}
inactivity vs diabetes, exclusion zone:    {'x_causes_y': 0.822, 'y_causes_x': 0.823}


Reading these results:

Skill is high for every pair (0.5-0.8), including broadband access, which nobody would argue causes diabetes. High skill alone reflects shared socioeconomic structure, not causation.
Convergence is the CCM criterion. Inactivity and diabetes converge in both directions, which CCM cannot separate from a common driver (income, rurality, regional culture, or county estimates modelled from the same surveys). Obesity → diabetes converges and the reverse is borderline (p ≈ 0.07). Broadband shows no clear convergence in either direction.
On these real data the exclusion zone lowers skill only slightly (0.84 → 0.82), so the patterns are not mainly neighbour leakage; on smooth simulated fields it removed most of the skill.

GCCM was designed for coupled nonlinear dynamics. Cross-sections of socially patterned county statistics violate its assumptions, so treat these patterns as descriptive.

title: Spatial Causal Discovery
section: NOTEARS with spatial-lag nodes on real data
text:
NOTEARS with spatial-lag nodes on real data
A linear structural equation model writes the variables as \(\mathbf X=\mathbf X\mathbf W+\mathbf E\), where \(W_{jk}\ne0\) means \(x_j\to x_k\). Learning \(W\) is a search over directed acyclic graphs, which is combinatorial. NOTEARS (Zheng et al., 2018) replaces it with a smooth constraint:
\[\min_W\ \frac{1}{2n}\lVert\mathbf X-\mathbf X W\rVert_F^2+\lambda\lVert W\rVert_1
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad h(W)=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(e^{W\circ W}\big)-d=0,\]
where \(h(W)=0\) exactly when the graph has no cycles (the trace counts weighted closed walks). It is solved by an augmented Lagrangian with L-BFGS, then small weights are thresholded.
Spatial version. We add nodes \((Wx)_j\), the neighbours’ average of each variable, and forbid any edge into them. Learned edges are then either local (\(x_j\to x_k\)) or spillover (\(Wx_j\to x_k\): the neighbours’ level of \(x_j\) affects a county’s \(x_k\)).
Identifiability and scale. Linear-Gaussian structure is only identified up to an equivalence class, and NOTEARS partly exploits differences in marginal variance (“varsortability”, Reisach et al., 2021). Results on raw and standardised data can differ, so we standardise (comparable penalties) and check stability with a spatial block bootstrap.


Code
V = ["inactivity_pct", "obesity_pct", "diabetes_pct", "smoking_pct", "food_env", "log_income", "child_poverty_pct"]
short = ["inactivity", "obesity", "diabetes", "smoking", "food_env", "log_income", "child_pov"]
nt = sc.SpatialNOTEARS(lambda1=0.05, w_threshold=0.3, standardize=True).fit(g[V].to_numpy(), w=w, names=short)
print(nt.summary())

# spatial block bootstrap: lag nodes are computed on the full map, then whole blocks of counties are resampled
Z = g[V].to_numpy(); Z = (Z - Z.mean(0)) / Z.std(0)
L = np.asarray(Wr @ Z)
data = np.hstack([Z, L])
d = len(V)
mask = np.ones((2 * d, 2 * d), bool); mask[:, d:] = False
blocks = sc.SpatialBlockKFold(n_splits=2, n_blocks=150, random_state=0).make_blocks(xy)
members = [np.flatnonzero(blocks == b) for b in np.unique(blocks)]
B = 30
freq = np.zeros((2 * d, d))
rngb = np.random.default_rng(1)
for _ in range(B):
    idx = np.concatenate([members[i] for i in rngb.integers(0, len(members), len(members))])
    Wb = sc.notears_linear(data[idx], lambda1=0.05, w_threshold=0.3, mask=mask)
    freq += (Wb[:, :d] != 0)
freq /= B
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.2))
im = ax.imshow(freq, cmap=ts.SEQ, vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(d), short, rotation=40, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(2 * d), short + [f"W.{s}" for s in short])
ax.axhline(d - 0.5, color=ts.INK2, lw=1)
for i in range(2 * d):
    for j in range(d):
        if freq[i, j] >= 0.1:
            ax.text(j, i, f"{freq[i, j]:.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                    color="white" if freq[i, j] > 0.6 else ts.INK)
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_title("Edge frequency over 30 spatial block bootstraps\n(rows cause columns; below the line: neighbours' values)")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="share of bootstrap fits with the edge")
plt.tight_layout()









How to read the graph:

The strongest and most stable edges are spillover self-edges (\(W.x\to x\)): every measure resembles its neighbours’ values. That is spatial autocorrelation, which this model can only represent as “neighbours cause”.
Among local edges, inactivity → diabetes (80% of fits) agrees with clinical knowledge, and so does log income → child poverty (90%).
Stability is not correctness. Diabetes → child poverty appears in all 30 fits, a perfectly stable edge whose direction is implausible. The bootstrap measures robustness to sampling; it says nothing about whether NOTEARS oriented the edge correctly. In linear models with roughly Gaussian errors, orientation rests largely on variance patterns (varsortability), not on causal information.
Edges present in fewer than about 70% of fits (smoking → log income, 60%) should not be interpreted.

title: Spatial Causal Discovery
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Discovery methods generate hypotheses. Their assumptions (no hidden common causes, correct functional form, acyclicity, deterministic coupling for CCM) are rarely met by county statistics.
Spatial data create spurious “discoveries” unless handled: Nickell bias and cross-sectional dependence in Granger tests, spatial autocorrelation in cross mapping, neighbour similarity in structure learning.
Report stability (bootstrap edge frequencies, convergence in both directions), not a single graph.
Take a stable discovered edge, such as inactivity → diabetes, back to a design: a quasi-experiment or trial in which the direction is identified by the intervention, not by the data’s correlations.

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
text:
Overview
Bayesian hierarchical models handle areal data naturally: a spatial random effect absorbs smooth unexplained variation, and the posterior gives full uncertainty for every quantity, including direct, spillover and total effects and the probability that an effect is beneficial.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal.bayes import _icar_eigen
ts.use()

gA, w, truth = cc.scenario_program()
X = gA[cc.COVARIATES].to_numpy()
xy = cc.coords_km(gA)
data = sc.SpatialCausalData(X, gA["T"], gA["y"], xy, w=w)

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
text:
Conditional autoregressive priors
A CAR prior specifies each area’s effect given its neighbours. The intrinsic CAR (Besag, 1974) is
\[u_i\mid u_{-i}\sim\mathcal N\!\Big(\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j\sim i}u_j,\ \frac{1}{\tau_u\,n_i}\Big),\]
with \(n_i\) neighbours: an area resembles the average of its neighbours, more tightly when it has many. The implied joint density is
\[p(\mathbf u\mid\tau_u)\propto\tau_u^{(n-c)/2}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\tau_u}{2}\mathbf u^\top Q\mathbf u\Big)
=\tau_u^{(n-c)/2}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\tau_u}{2}\sum_{i\sim j}(u_i-u_j)^2\Big),\qquad Q=D-A,\]
with \(A\) the binary adjacency, \(D=\operatorname{diag}(n_i)\) and \(c\) the number of connected components. \(Q\) is singular (\(Q\mathbf 1=0\) on each component), so the prior is improper: it fixes differences between neighbours but not the overall level. The standard fix is a sum-to-zero constraint per component, with the intercept carrying the mean.
BYM (Besag, York & Mollié, 1991) adds unstructured heterogeneity, \(u_i+v_i\) with \(v_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1/\tau_v)\), so the data decide how much variation is spatially structured. For a Gaussian outcome \(v\) is not identifiable separately from the noise, so we use ICAR + noise:
\[Y_i=\alpha+\tau T_i+\delta\,(WT)_i+X_i^\top\beta+u_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).\]
Priors: \(\beta\sim\mathcal N(0,10^2)\) on the standardised outcome scale, flat intercept, and \(\tau_u,\ \sigma^{-2}\sim\text{Gamma}(1,0.01)\).

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
section: An exact collapsed sampler in the eigenbasis of \(Q\)
text:
An exact collapsed sampler in the eigenbasis of \(Q\)
Diagonalise once: \(Q=V\Lambda V^\top\). Keep the \(n-c\) eigenvectors with \(\lambda_k>0\); the sum-to-zero constraint simply removes the null directions. Writing \(\mathbf u=V_+\mathbf c\), the ICAR prior becomes independent normals, \(c_k\sim\mathcal N\big(0,1/(\tau_u\lambda_k)\big)\), and everything becomes cheap:

Variance components, field integrated out. In the eigenbasis the residual \(\mathbf r=\mathbf y-A\boldsymbol\beta\) has independent components, \((V_+^\top\mathbf r)_k\sim\mathcal N\big(0,\ \sigma^2+1/(\tau_u\lambda_k)\big)\), while its part in the null space is \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I)\). This marginal likelihood is \(O(n)\) to evaluate, so \((\log\sigma^2,\log\tau_u)\) are updated jointly by several random-walk Metropolis steps per iteration. The two variances trade off strongly, and one-at-a-time Gibbs updates mix very slowly.
Coefficients, field integrated out. \(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2,\tau_u,\mathbf y\) is Gaussian with precision \(A^\top\Sigma^{-1}A/\ldots\) obtained via a Schur complement in the eigenbasis (only \(p\times p\) matrices). Drawing \(\beta\) without conditioning on \(\mathbf u\) keeps mixing fast even when treatment and the spatial field are correlated, which is the spatial-confounding case.
Field. \(c_k\mid\cdot\sim\mathcal N\!\Big(\frac{(V_+^\top\mathbf r)_k/\sigma^2}{D_k},\ \frac1{D_k}\Big)\) with \(D_k=\tau_u\lambda_k+\sigma^{-2}\).

Because \(\mathbf u\) is drawn last and not used by steps 1-2, this is a valid partially collapsed Gibbs sampler (van Dyk & Park, 2008). The smallest positive eigenvalues belong to the smoothest patterns:


Code
V, lam, n_null = _icar_eigen(w, len(gA))
print(f"Q has {n_null} null directions (one per connected component: mainland + 3 islands)")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 3.6))
ax[0].plot(np.sort(lam), color=ts.BLUE, lw=1.6)
ax[0].set_xlabel("index k"); ax[0].set_ylabel("eigenvalue λ_k of Q"); ax[0].set_title("ICAR spectrum")
for a, k in zip(ax[1:], (0, 25)):
    ts.county_map(gA, V[:, np.argsort(lam)[k]], a, cmap=ts.DIV, center=0, title=f"eigenvector with the {k+1}st smallest λ" if k == 0 else f"eigenvector with the {k+1}th smallest λ")

Convergence. \(\hat R\) compares between-chain and within-chain variance of split chains; values above 1.05 mean the chains have not mixed. The effective sample size (ESS) is the number of independent draws carrying the same information. The regression coefficients have ESS close to the 2,000 draws. Interpreting the effects. With heterogeneous \(\tau_i\) the coefficient on \(T\) is a variance-weighted average, like the PLM estimand (−0.907). The spillover coefficient \(\delta\) (truth −0.4) is the effect of moving from no treated neighbours to all treated, and the posterior directly gives \(P(\text{effect}<0\mid\text{data})\).

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
text:
Spatial confounding in Bayesian models
A spatial random effect is not automatically a confounding adjustment (Hodges & Reich, 2010; Khan & Calder, 2022). The posterior of \(\tau\) depends on how the prior apportions shared spatial variation between \(T\) and \(\mathbf u\). Bayesian spatial+ first residualises treatment (and its spatial lag) on the leading Moran eigenvectors, as in notebook 01.


Code
rows = {}
for name, kw in [("no spatial effect", dict(spatial="none")), ("ICAR", dict()), ("ICAR + spatial+", dict(adjust="spatial+"))]:
    m = sc.BayesianSpatialCausal(spillover=True, draws=600, tune=300, seed=2, **kw).fit(data)
    for eff in ("direct", "spillover"):
        lo, hi = m.result_._stats["credible_95"][eff]
        rows[(name, eff)] = {"posterior mean": m.effect(eff), "95% lower": lo, "95% upper": hi}
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
tab["truth"] = [truth["plm_estimand"], truth["delta"]] * 3

The ICAR field removes most of the bias here, because the confounder is smooth on the scale the field represents, and spatial+ moves both estimates a little closer to the truth. In other settings (penalised fields competing with a smooth treatment) the two can diverge, so it is good practice to fit both.

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
section: Counts: Poisson BYM for premature deaths
text:
Counts: Poisson BYM for premature deaths
For count outcomes, \(O_i\sim\text{Poisson}(E_i\,\theta_i)\) with expected counts \(E_i\) (population × a reference rate) and
\[\log\theta_i=\alpha+\tau T_i+\delta\,(WT)_i+X_i^\top\beta+u_i+v_i,\qquad
\mathbf u\sim\text{ICAR}(\tau_u),\ v_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1/\tau_v).\]
Effects are log rate ratios: \(e^{\tau}\) is the multiplicative change in the premature-death rate. This model runs through geolattice.spatial_statistics.bayes.BYM (built-in Gibbs/Metropolis sampler; PyMC NUTS with backend="pymc"). Scenario D simulates counts from the real CHR premature-death ratios with a program effect \(\tau=-0.10\) (rate ratio 0.905) and spillover \(\delta=-0.06\). The built-in sampler updates one area at a time and mixes slowly with many covariates, so we use five states (449 counties), three covariates and long, thinned chains.


Code
gD, wD, tD = cc.scenario_counts(states=["AL", "MS", "GA", "TN", "SC"])
cov = ["child_poverty_pct", "smoking_pct", "obesity_pct"]

pois = sc.BayesianSpatialCausal(family="poisson", spillover=True, draws=3000, tune=2000, thin=10, seed=3).fit(
    dD, expected=gD["expected"].to_numpy())
out = pois.result_.to_frame()[["estimate", "se"]]
out["rate ratio"] = np.exp(out.estimate)
out["truth (log RR)"] = [tD["direct"], tD["spillover"], tD["total"]]

title: Bayesian Spatial Causal Models (ICAR and BYM)
text:
Summary and Conclusions

ICAR priors encode “neighbours are similar”. Their impropriety is handled by a sum-to-zero constraint, which in the eigenbasis of \(Q=D-A\) amounts to dropping the null directions.
Collapsing the field out of the coefficient and variance updates gives fast, exact mixing for Gaussian outcomes.
A spatial random effect may or may not remove spatial confounding; compare with spatial+.
Posterior draws give interpretable statements such as “P(effect < 0)”, but only after convergence is checked.

text:
Overview
State borders are natural experiments: a state policy switches on abruptly at the border, while geography, climate and most social conditions change smoothly across it. Comparing counties just on either side identifies the policy’s effect at the border.
Scenario B. A hypothetical state policy whose map follows the 2024 Medicaid-expansion map: 41 jurisdictions (including DC) had adopted expansion and 10 had not (AL, FL, GA, KS, MS, SC, TN, TX, WI, WY) (KFF). The assignment is real; the effect on diabetes is simulated:
\[Y_i=Y_i(0)+\big(-0.6+0.3\cos(2\pi p_i)\big)\,T_i^{\text{state}},\]
where \(p_i\in[0,1]\) is the position of county \(i\)’s nearest border point along the border, so the jump varies along the border. \(Y_i(0)\) is the real 2024 diabetes prevalence plus the smooth \(U\).
At the end we analyse a real outcome, the uninsured share, for which no ground truth exists.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geopandas as gpd
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal import viz
ts.use()

gB, border, tb = cc.scenario_state_policy()
xy = cc.coords_km(gB)
T = gB["T_state"].to_numpy()
print(f"border length: {border.length:,.0f} km;  counties in expansion states: {T.sum()} of {len(T)}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.6))
ts.county_map(gB, "T_state", ax, categorical=True, colors=["#f2a8a3", "#9ec5f4"],
              legend_labels=["non-expansion state", "expansion state"],
              title="Treatment switches at state borders (border shown in black)")
gpd.GeoSeries([border], crs=None).scale(1000, 1000, origin=(0, 0)).plot(ax=ax, color="black", lw=1.4)
plt.tight_layout()

title: Geographic Regression Discontinuity
text:
The sharp RDD
Let the running variable be the signed distance to the border,
\[r_i=\begin{cases}+\,d(s_i,\mathcal B) & T_i=1\\ -\,d(s_i,\mathcal B) & T_i=0,\end{cases}\]
so treatment is a deterministic function of location, \(T_i=\mathbb 1\{r_i\ge 0\}\) (a sharp design). If both potential-outcome regressions \(\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid r]\) are continuous at \(r=0\), then
\[\tau_{\text{RD}}=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\mathbb E[Y\mid r]-\lim_{r\uparrow0}\mathbb E[Y\mid r]=\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid r=0].\]
Estimation: local linear regression. With a kernel \(K\) and bandwidth \(h\), solve
\[\min_{\alpha,\tau,\beta_0,\beta_1}\sum_i K\!\Big(\frac{r_i}{h}\Big)\Big(Y_i-\alpha-\tau T_i-\beta_0r_i-\beta_1r_iT_i\Big)^2,\]
a separate line on each side. \(\hat\tau\) is the gap between the two intercepts. The triangular kernel \(K(u)=(1-|u|)_+\) is optimal for estimation at a boundary point.
Bandwidth. Imbens & Kalyanaraman (2012) minimise the asymptotic MSE,
\[h_{\text{IK}}=C_K\left[\frac{\sigma^2_-+\sigma^2_+}{f(0)\,\big\{(m''_+-m''_-)^2+r_++r_-\big\}}\right]^{1/5}n^{-1/5},\]
with \(f(0)\) the density of \(r\) at the border, \(\sigma^2_\pm\) the conditional variances, \(m''_\pm\) the curvatures of each side and \(r_\pm\) regularisation terms. (\(C_K=3.44\) for the triangular kernel.)
Inference. \(\hat\tau\) is a weighted least-squares coefficient with influence contributions \(\psi_i=n\,[(A^\top WA)^{-1}a_i]_\tau\,w_i\hat e_i\), so heteroskedasticity-robust and Conley standard errors follow as in notebook 01.

Geography-specific additions

Segment fixed effects (Dell, 2010): cut the border into \(S\) segments and add a dummy for each county’s nearest segment, so treated and control counties are compared only along the same stretch of border, not Texas against Wisconsin.
Boundary-point effects (Keele & Titiunik, 2015): at a point \(b\) on the border, fit a local linear regression in the two coordinates on each side, with weights in the Euclidean distance to \(b\); the effect at \(b\) is the difference of the intercepts. This traces how the effect varies along the border.

title: Geographic Regression Discontinuity
section: A pre-existing discontinuity in the real data
text:
A pre-existing discontinuity in the real data
Before adding any simulated effect, run the RDD on the real 2024 diabetes prevalence. State borders bundle many differences (other state policies, how survey-based county estimates are produced), so real outcomes can already jump.


Code
def fit(yv, **kw):
    return sc.GeographicRDD(border, se="conley", cutoff=100, **kw).fit(None, T, gB[yv].to_numpy(), xy)

rows = {}
for name, col in [("real diabetes (no simulated effect)", "diabetes_pct"), ("Y(0) = real + smooth U", "y0"),
                  ("simulated outcome Y", "y_rdd")]:
    for seg in (None, 20):
        r = fit(col, n_segments=seg)
        e = r.result_["effect_at_boundary"]
        rows[(name, "none" if seg is None else "20 segments")] = {"jump": e.estimate, "se (Conley)": e.se,
                                                                     "bandwidth km": r.bandwidth_,
                                                                     "counties in bandwidth": r.result_._stats["n_in_bandwidth"]}

The real data show a small negative jump that is not statistically significant (and smaller with segment fixed effects). The simulated outcome’s jump combines that pre-existing discontinuity with the simulated effect.

What is the true estimand?
The simulated jump varies along the border, so the RDD estimand is a weighted average of \(-0.6+0.3\cos(2\pi p_i)\) over the counties that drive the estimate: those near the border, weighted by the kernel. A difference in discontinuities, the jump in \(Y\) minus the jump in \(Y(0)\) at the same bandwidth, removes the pre-existing discontinuity. This is only possible in a simulation; with real data one would use pre-policy outcomes instead.


Code
r_y = fit("y_rdd", n_segments=20)
h = r_y.bandwidth_
r0 = sc.GeographicRDD(border, bandwidth=h, n_segments=20, se="conley", cutoff=100).fit(None, T, gB["y0"].to_numpy(), xy)
k = np.clip(1 - np.abs(r_y.running_) / h, 0, None)
true_jump = tb["jump_at"](gB["border_pos"].to_numpy())
target = np.sum(k * true_jump) / np.sum(k)
did = r_y.effect() - r0.effect()
print(f"jump in Y: {r_y.effect():.3f}   jump in Y(0): {r0.effect():.3f}   difference: {did:.3f}")
print(f"kernel-weighted true jump among counties near the border: {target:.3f}")

title: Geographic Regression Discontinuity
section: How the effect varies along the border
text:
How the effect varies along the border
Boundary-point estimates at 12 points along the border, compared with the true simulated jump (plus the pre-existing local discontinuity, which this method cannot separate). Points are ordered by position along the border geometry.


Code
ab = r_y.along_boundary(12, bandwidth=2.5 * h)
ab["true simulated jump"] = tb["jump_at"](ab["position"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1]})
ok = ab.estimate.notna()
ax[0].errorbar(ab.position[ok], ab.estimate[ok], yerr=1.96 * ab.se[ok], fmt="o", capsize=3, color=ts.BLUE, label="boundary-point estimate")
pp = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
ax[0].plot(pp, tb["jump_at"](pp), "--", color=ts.TRUTH, lw=1.2, label="true simulated jump")
ax[0].set_xlabel("position along the border (0-1)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("jump"); ax[0].legend()
ax[0].set_title("Effect along the border")
ts.county_map(gB, "T_state", ax[1], categorical=True, colors=["#f2a8a3", "#9ec5f4"], legend_labels=["non-exp.", "exp."])
ax[1].scatter(ab.x * 1000, ab.y * 1000, c=ts.INK, s=30, zorder=5)
for _, r in ab.iterrows():
    ax[1].annotate(f"{r.position:.2f}", (r.x * 1000, r.y * 1000), fontsize=7.5, xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points")
ax[1].set_title("Boundary points")
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"correlation of boundary-point estimates with the true jump: "
      f"{np.corrcoef(ab.estimate[ok], ab['true simulated jump'][ok])[0, 1]:.2f}")


correlation of boundary-point estimates with the true jump: 0.33









Boundary-point estimates are noisy: each uses only the counties near one point, and real discontinuities in \(Y(0)\) vary along the border too. They are useful for spotting where an effect concentrates, not for precise local claims.

title: Geographic Regression Discontinuity
section: Real-data application: uninsurance at expansion borders
text:
Real-data application: uninsurance at expansion borders
Now a real outcome with no simulated effect: the share of the population without health insurance (CHR 2024; small-area estimates). Medicaid expansion is designed to reduce uninsurance, so we expect a negative jump entering expansion states.

out = {}
for seg in (None, 20):

            gB[pre].to_numpy(), T, gB["uninsured_pct"].to_numpy(), xy)
        e = r.result_["effect_at_boundary"]
        out[f"segments={seg or 0}, donut={donut} km"] = {"jump (points)": e.estimate, "se": e.se, "bandwidth km": r.bandwidth_}

Uninsurance is about 1.3-1.5 percentage points lower just inside expansion states (relative to a mean of about 5.3%), stable across segment fixed effects and a 25 km “donut” that drops the counties closest to the border.
Caveats before reading this causally:

Compound treatment. Expansion and non-expansion states differ in many other policies at the same border.
Measurement. County uninsurance in CHR comes from model-based small-area estimates, which can borrow strength within states and so may sharpen jumps at state lines.
County size. Counties are large and their centroids are a coarse running variable.

It is a well-posed descriptive discontinuity consistent with the expected direction, not a definitive estimate of the expansion effect.

title: Geographic Regression Discontinuity
text:
Summary and Conclusions

A border RDD compares like with like, but only at the border, and only for the bundle of everything that changes there.
Check the outcome for discontinuities that exist without the policy (placebos, pre-period data) and use segment fixed effects to compare along the same stretch of border.
Exclude post-treatment variables from covariates and balance tests.
Report bandwidth sensitivity. Effects along the border are informative but noisy.

title: Interference and Spillovers
text:
Overview
Health programs rarely stop at county lines: outreach workers, clinics and media reach neighbouring counties. Then a county’s outcome depends on its neighbours’ treatment as well as its own, which violates SUTVA.
Scenario A with spillovers: \(Y_i=Y_i(0)+\tau_iT_i+\delta\,(WT)_i\) with \(\delta=-0.4\) and \((WT)_i\) the share of treated Queen neighbours. The confounder \(U(s)\) is still present.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal._utils import as_sparse_weights
ts.use()

gA, w, truth = cc.scenario_program()
X = gA[cc.COVARIATES].to_numpy()
xy = cc.coords_km(gA)
T, y, tau, share = gA["T"].to_numpy(), gA["y"].to_numpy(), gA["tau"].to_numpy(), gA["share_treated"].to_numpy()
delta = truth["delta"]

title: Interference and Spillovers
text:
Potential outcomes under interference
With interference each county has a potential outcome for every assignment vector, \(Y_i(\mathbf t)\), \(\mathbf t\in\{0,1\}^n\), which is far too many to learn anything. An exposure mapping (Aronow & Samii, 2017) reduces \(\mathbf t\) to a few conditions,
\[f_i(\mathbf t)=\Big(t_i,\ \mathbb 1\big\{(W\mathbf t)_i\ge c\big\}\Big)\in\{00,\,01,\,10,\,11\},\]
own treatment × “high” neighbourhood exposure (share of treated neighbours at least \(c=0.5\)). The mapping is correct if \(Y_i(\mathbf t)=Y_i(\mathbf t')\) whenever \(f_i(\mathbf t)=f_i(\mathbf t')\). Then \(Y_i(c)\) is well defined and the estimands are averages \(\mu(c)=\frac1n\sum_iY_i(c)\):
\[\underbrace{\mu(10)-\mu(00)}_{\text{direct}},\quad
\underbrace{\mu(01)-\mu(00)}_{\text{spillover on controls}},\quad
\underbrace{\mu(11)-\mu(10)}_{\text{spillover on treated}},\quad
\underbrace{\mu(11)-\mu(00)}_{\text{total}}.\]
Neighbourhoods come from any geolattice.spatial_statistics weights object; here the Queen weights.


Code
exposure = sc.ExposureMapping(w, kind="share", threshold=0.5)
C = exposure.conditions(T)
counts = pd.Series(np.bincount(C, minlength=4), index=["c00 control/low", "c01 control/high",
                                                       "c10 treated/low", "c11 treated/high"])
print(counts.to_string())
gA["condition"] = C
ts.county_map(gA, "condition", categorical=True, colors=["#d9d8d3", "#86b6ef", ts.ORANGE, "#9b1c1c"],
              legend_labels=list(counts.index), title="Exposure conditions (Queen neighbours, threshold 0.5)")
plt.tight_layout()


c00 control/low     1355
c01 control/high     508
c10 treated/low      474
c11 treated/high     772










Our mapping is deliberately coarse
The true spillover is linear in the continuous share, so the binary mapping is misspecified: a county in condition 01 can have any share between 0.5 and 1. What an inverse-probability or AIPW estimator of \(\mu(c)\) then targets is the county average of \(\mathbb E[Y_i\mid C_i=c]\), which involves each county’s expected share given its condition:
\[\text{spillover}_{\text{target}}=\frac1n\sum_i\delta\,\Big(\mathbb E\big[(WT)_i\mid C_i=01\big]-\mathbb E\big[(WT)_i\mid C_i=00\big]\Big).\]
These expectations depend on the assignment mechanism. Because we know it (the true propensities \(e_i\)), cc.implied_exposure_contrasts computes the targets exactly by redrawing treatment 2,000 times. A naive shortcut, comparing average shares within observed conditions, gets them wrong: inverse-probability weights up-weight counties for which high exposure is rare (many neighbours), and those counties’ shares sit just above the threshold.


Code
implied, _ = cc.implied_exposure_contrasts(gA["e_true"].to_numpy(), w, tau, delta, n_sims=2000, seed=1)
pd.Series(implied, name="target (exact, by simulation)").round(3).to_frame()

title: Interference and Spillovers
section: Observational estimation: AIPW with generalised propensities
text:
Observational estimation: AIPW with generalised propensities
In observational data treatment is not randomised, and a county’s exposure depends on its neighbours’ covariates as well as its own. Let \(Z_i=(X_i,(WX)_i,S_i)\) collect own covariates, neighbours’ average covariates and location features. The generalised propensity is \(\pi_i(c)=P(C_i=c\mid Z_i)\) (multinomial logistic), and \(m_c(Z)=\mathbb E[Y\mid C=c,Z]\) is an outcome model per condition. The doubly robust estimator of \(\mu(c)\) is
\[\hat\mu_{\text{AIPW}}(c)=\frac1n\sum_i\Big[\hat m_c(Z_i)+\frac{\mathbb 1\{C_i=c\}\,\big(Y_i-\hat m_c(Z_i)\big)}{\hat\pi_i(c)}\Big].\]
It is consistent if either the propensity or the outcome model is correct, and nuisance models are cross-fitted on spatial blocks. The per-unit terms are influence contributions, so contrast SEs use the same iid / Conley / block machinery as notebook 01.
First, AIPW without location features, so \(U\) is not adjusted for.


Code
d_plain = sc.SpatialCausalData(X, T, y, xy, w=w)
aipw_plain = sc.InterferenceEstimator(exposure, learner="ridge", propensity_learner="logistic").fit(d_plain)

The spillover and total contrasts have the wrong sign, and the direct effect is unusable (its standard error exceeds 1): without location information some counties get extreme generalised propensities. High-exposure counties sit in clusters of treated counties, which is where \(U\) is high, and \(U\) raises diabetes. This is spatial confounding of the spillover contrast. As in notebook 01, the fix is a basis rich enough to represent \(U\): we add 155 radial basis functions. We compare two feature sets, with and without the neighbours’ average covariates \(WX\), and trim generalised propensities at 0.05.

title: Interference and Spillovers
section: A linear-in-means model for the spillover slope
text:
A linear-in-means model for the spillover slope
When spillovers plausibly scale with the share of treated neighbours, model the share directly:
\[Y_i=\alpha+\tau\,T_i+\delta\,(WT)_i+X_i^\top\beta+S_i^\top\theta+\varepsilon_i .\]
Here \(\delta\) is the effect of moving from no treated neighbours to all neighbours treated. With heterogeneous \(\tau_i\) the coefficient \(\tau\) is a variance-weighted average (as in notebook 01). \(\delta\) is identified from variation in neighbours’ treatment given own treatment, covariates and the smooth basis. We estimate it by OLS and use Conley standard errors from the OLS influence function \(\psi_i=n\,(A^\top A)^{-1}a_i\hat\varepsilon_i\).


Code
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), T, share, X, S])
beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)
resid = y - A @ beta
Ainv = np.linalg.pinv(A.T @ A / len(y))

                    "se (Conley 150 km)": [sc.standard_error(psi[:, j], xy, "conley", cutoff=150) for j in (1, 2)],
                    "truth": [truth["plm_estimand"], delta]}, index=["tau (own treatment)", "delta (share of neighbours)"])

title: Interference and Spillovers
section: Design-based estimation in a randomised experiment
text:
Design-based estimation in a randomised experiment
If the program were assigned at random with a known design, no outcome or propensity model would be needed. The design fixes each county’s probability \(\pi_i(c)\) of landing in each exposure condition, which we compute by simulating the design (exposure_probabilities). The Horvitz-Thompson and Hájek estimators are
\[\hat\mu_{\text{HT}}(c)=\frac1n\sum_i\frac{\mathbb 1\{C_i=c\}Y_i}{\pi_i(c)},\qquad
\hat\mu_{\text{Hájek}}(c)=\frac{\sum_i \mathbb 1\{C_i=c\}Y_i/\pi_i(c)}{\sum_i \mathbb 1\{C_i=c\}/\pi_i(c)} .\]
Hájek is slightly biased but far more stable. Note that \(\pi_i(c)\) differs across counties even under simple Bernoulli assignment: a county with 2 neighbours reaches “≥50% treated neighbours” much more easily than one with 10.
We re-run history: assign the program by Bernoulli(0.4) instead of self-selection and generate the outcomes with the same effects.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
design = sc.BernoulliDesign(0.4)
T_r = design.sample(len(gA), rng)
share_r = np.asarray(Wr @ T_r).ravel()
y_r = gA["y0"].to_numpy() + tau * T_r + delta * share_r
d_rct = sc.SpatialCausalData(X, T_r, y_r, xy, w=w)
hajek = sc.InterferenceEstimator(exposure, method="hajek", design=design, n_sims=2000,
                                 se="conley", cutoff=150).fit(d_rct)
implied_r, _ = cc.implied_exposure_contrasts(0.4, w, tau, delta, n_sims=2000, seed=2)
hres = hajek.result_.to_frame()[["estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"]]
hres["target"] = pd.Series(implied_r)
print("range of P(control, high exposure) across counties:",
      np.round(np.percentile(hajek.propensity_[:, 1], [5, 50, 95]), 3))
hres.round(3)

title: Interference and Spillovers
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Interference needs an explicit exposure mapping. The estimands are contrasts between exposure conditions, not a single “treatment effect”.
Spillover contrasts are also spatially confounded: high-exposure areas are treated clusters. Location features that represent the confounder are essential in observational data.
A coarse mapping is misspecified when exposure acts continuously. The estimand silently becomes a contrast between typical exposure levels, and power is lost. A linear-in-means model recovers the slope when its functional form is right.
Under a known randomised design, Hájek estimation needs no outcome model and is centred on its target. The exposure probabilities vary with each county’s number of neighbours and must be computed from the design.
With a misspecified mapping the estimand depends on the assignment mechanism. Compute it explicitly (here by simulation) rather than by averaging observed shares.

title: Spatial Causal Inference
text:
Overview
Spatial causal inference asks what would have happened to an outcome in a place if a treatment there, or in the places around it, had been different. The units in this chapter are counties. The outcome is adult diabetes prevalence. The treatment, in the worked examples, is a hypothetical community-health-worker program. The effect in a county is the difference between the prevalence that county would have had with the program and the prevalence it would have had without it. Only one of those two prevalences is ever observed. The other has to be constructed from other counties, other years, or a model of how the program was assigned.
A non-spatial analysis can already do that construction when three things hold. A county’s outcome depends only on its own treatment. Every common cause of the program and of diabetes is measured. Treated and untreated counties both appear at every combination of those measured causes. County data break all three, because the counties sit on a map.
A treated neighbour changes your outcome. A program, a clinic, or a pollutant does not stop at the county line. People commute, share a media market, and use services in the next county. The usual assumption that unit \(i\) responds only to its own treatment then fails. The effect splits. The direct effect is the change in county \(i\) from treating county \(i\). The spillover is the change in county \(i\) from treating its neighbours. The total effect is the sum. Notebooks 02 and 05 estimate those pieces. Notebook 07 designs a trial so the spillover can be measured on purpose, with buffers and saturation, rather than discovered after the fact.
The reasons a county is treated are themselves a map. Poverty, rurality, and state policy vary smoothly. Two counties with the same measured covariates can still differ by an unmeasured surface \(U(s)\): a regional climate of policy, an environmental exposure, a labour market. If that surface also raises diabetes, a plain comparison of counties with and without the program attributes the geography to the program. That is spatial confounding. Adjusting for a list of covariates does not remove a surface that was never measured. Notebook 01 fits the smooth part of the map and then estimates the program in what remains, with spatial+, spatial double machine learning, and standard errors that allow neighbouring residuals to be correlated. Notebook 06 puts a prior on that surface with an intrinsic CAR or a BYM model.
The effect need not be one number. A program can matter more where child poverty is high, or only in the Deep South, or only in the strip of counties that touch a state border. Notebook 03 maps the effect. Notebook 04 uses a real policy border, the 2024 Medicaid-expansion line, as a geographic regression discontinuity: counties just inside and just outside the line are compared, and the bandwidth decides how far “just” reaches. Notebook 05 follows the same counties from 2014 to 2025, so a county can be its own comparison across years, including when adoption is staggered and when neighbours are treated later.
Neighbouring counties are not separate draws. Even after the effect is identified, the residuals of adjacent counties move together. A standard error that treats 3,109 counties as independent observations is too small, and a confidence interval built from it is too narrow. Conley standard errors and spatial-block resampling keep clusters of neighbours together. The same dependence is what notebook 08 tries to learn rather than adjust away: which county health measures point at which, using spatial Granger causality, geographical convergent cross mapping, and a NOTEARS model with spatial-lag nodes.
Section 1 writes the two potential outcomes, the average effect, and the three assumptions in notation. The semi-synthetic design later in this notebook keeps the real county covariates, the real boundaries, and the real 2024 diabetes map, and lays a known program effect on top, so each of those methods can be checked against a number we chose.

title: Spatial Causal Inference
text:
Potential outcomes
For county \(i\) with binary treatment \(T_i \in \{0,1\}\) we imagine two potential outcomes: \(Y_i(1)\) (outcome if treated) and \(Y_i(0)\) (outcome if not). The unit-level effect is \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\), but only one potential outcome is ever observed:
\[Y_i = T_i\,Y_i(1) + (1-T_i)\,Y_i(0).\]
Common estimands:
\[\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)], \qquad
\text{ATT} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1], \qquad
\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]\ \text{(CATE)}.\]
Identification from observational data rests on three assumptions:

SUTVA: no interference (\(Y_i\) depends only on \(T_i\), not on \(T_j\)) and one version of treatment.
Unconfoundedness: \(\{Y(0),Y(1)\} \perp T \mid X\): all common causes of \(T\) and \(Y\) are measured.
Positivity: \(0 < e(x) = P(T=1\mid X=x) < 1\).

Then \(\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1,X] - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0,X]\big]\).

How space breaks each assumption








Assumption
Spatial violation
Notebook




SUTVA
a program in one county also helps its neighbours (interference)
02, 05


Unconfoundedness
an unmeasured, spatially smooth factor \(U(s)\) (regional policy climate, environment) drives both treatment and outcome (spatial confounding)
01, 06


Independence for inference
outcomes of neighbouring counties are correlated, so i.i.d. standard errors are too small
01

title: Spatial Causal Inference
text:
Spatial weights and spatial autocorrelation
A spatial weights matrix \(W\) encodes who neighbours whom. With Queen contiguity \(w_{ij}=1\) if counties \(i\) and \(j\) share a boundary point. Row-standardising, \(\tilde w_{ij} = w_{ij}/\sum_k w_{ik}\), turns the spatial lag
\[(Wy)_i = \sum_j \tilde w_{ij}\, y_j\]
into the average of the neighbours’ values. Moran’s I measures global spatial autocorrelation:
\[I = \frac{n}{S_0}\,\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(y_i-\bar y)(y_j-\bar y)}{\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2},
\qquad S_0=\sum_{ij} w_{ij}.\]
\(I>0\) means similar values cluster. Inference uses random permutations of \(y\) over locations. Weights and Moran’s I come from geolattice.spatial_statistics.


Code
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.esda import Moran

w = cc.queen_weights()
card = w.cardinalities if not callable(w.cardinalities) else w.cardinalities()
isl = w.islands if not callable(w.islands) else w.islands()
print(f"Queen weights: mean {np.mean(card):.2f} neighbours; islands: "
      f"{gdf.loc[isl, 'county'].tolist()} ({gdf.loc[isl, 'state_abbr'].tolist()})")

rows = []
for v in ["diabetes_pct", "obesity_pct", "inactivity_pct", "child_poverty_pct", "log_income", "uninsured_pct"]:
    m = Moran(gdf[v].to_numpy(), w, permutations=199, seed=1)
    rows.append({"variable": v, "Moran's I": round(m.I, 3), "z": round(m.z_score, 1), "p (perm.)": m.p_value})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable")

title: Spatial Causal Inference
text:
The semi-synthetic causal design (Scenario A)
We imagine a county community health worker (CHW) diabetes program. Counties choose to run it; we observe \(T_i\) and adult diabetes prevalence \(Y_i\) (percentage points).
Unmeasured confounder. \(U(s)\) is a smooth random surface (length scale 350 km, standardised) standing for an unobserved “regional health-policy climate”. It is not among the covariates.
Treatment assignment (logistic):
\[e_i = P(T_i=1\mid X_i,U_i)=\operatorname{expit}\!\big(-0.55+0.5\,z(\text{child pov.})_i+0.4\,z(\text{uninsured})_i
-0.3\,z(\text{rural})_i+0.3\,z(\log\text{PCP})_i+1.0\,U_i\big).\]
Potential outcomes. With \(D_i\) the real 2024 diabetes prevalence,
\[Y_i(0) = D_i + 0.9\,U_i, \qquad
\tau_i = -0.8-0.35\,z(\text{child pov.})_i-0.6\,\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{\lVert s_i-s_{\text{Jackson,MS}}\rVert^2}{2\cdot 400^2}\Big),\]
so the program lowers diabetes prevalence more in poorer counties and in the Deep South.
Spillover. Outreach crosses county lines: each county also gains \(\delta\cdot\bar T_{N(i)}\) with \(\delta=-0.4\) and \(\bar T_{N(i)}=(WT)_i\) the share of treated Queen neighbours:
\[Y_i = Y_i(0)+\tau_i T_i+\delta\,(WT)_i.\]
We store both y (with spillover) and y_noint (without), so notebook 01 can study confounding alone and notebook 02 adds interference.

text:
The naive comparison
The simple difference in means compares treated with untreated counties: \(\hat\Delta = \bar Y_{T=1}-\bar Y_{T=0}\). Because \(U\) raises both the chance of treatment and the outcome, \(\hat\Delta\) is pushed upward, away from the (negative) true effect.

title: Inference for segregation indices
text:
Overview
Notebook 03_07_05 built the null models. This notebook uses them, and the bootstrap, for the three inferential questions applied segregation studies need to answer:

Single value. Is Buffalo’s index larger than chance would produce?
Comparison. Is the index different between two census years?
Uncertainty. What is a credible range for the index, given that neighbouring tracts are not independent?

It follows the PySAL tutorial on single value and comparative inference, using seg.single_value_test, seg.two_value_test, seg.spatial_block_bootstrap, and seg.panel_trend_test. The main difference from PySAL is the bootstrap: resampling individual tracts treats neighbours as independent draws, which understates uncertainty when compositions are spatially autocorrelated. Resampling spatial blocks keeps neighbours together. Buffalo, where most Black residents live in one contiguous area, shows both the value and the pitfalls of doing this.
Topics:

Single-value tests against the evenness and systematic nulls
Two-sample permutation tests between years
Unit bootstrap vs. spatial block bootstrap
Choosing the number of blocks when one group is concentrated
Paired block bootstrap for change between years
Trend tests across a short census panel and their power

Tract boundaries change between censuses. To compare years on the same units, the 2000 and 2010 counts have been moved onto the 323 tracts of 2020 with dasymetric interpolation weighted by 2020 housing units; notebook 03_07_07 shows how. title: Inference for segregation indices
section: Part A: Is the index larger than chance?
text:
Part A: Is the index larger than chance?
seg.single_value_test(gdf, groups, index_fn, null=...) computes the observed index, simulates n_sims metro areas under the chosen null, recomputes the index on each, and returns a one-sided permutation p-value with the usual \(+1\) correction, \(p = (\#\{\text{null} \ge \text{obs}\} + 1)/(n_{sims} + 1)\).

For aspatial indices use null="evenness". Under null="systematic" an aspatial index never changes, so the test is meaningless.
For spatial indices null="systematic" asks whether the arrangement of tracts matters.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Part A: Is the index larger than chance?.
# `seg.single_value_test(gdf, groups, index_fn, null=...)` computes the observed index, simulates
# ===================================================================

pair = ["black", "white"]  # focal two-group pairing for D / Gini
rows, store = [], {}
for y in YEARS:  # loop over panel years
    for name, fn, grp in [("dissimilarity", seg.dissimilarity, pair), ("gini", seg.gini, pair),  # loop over group pairs
                          ("theil_h", seg.theil_h, GROUPS)]:  # run this analysis or plotting step
        r = seg.single_value_test(tracts[y], grp, fn, null="evenness", n_sims=499, seed=y)  # compute() result with value and CI
        store[(y, name)] = r  # assign a derived column or cell
        rows.append({"year": y, "index": name, "observed": r["statistic"], "null mean": r["null_mean"],  # append this year/group record
                     "null sd": r["null_std"], "p-value": r["p_value"]})

All observed values are far above the evenness null, and the p-values are at the floor \(1/500 = 0.002\), the smallest value 499 simulations can report. With tracts of a few thousand people, significance against evenness is almost guaranteed for any real pattern. The informative quantities are the effect size (observed minus null mean) and the comparisons below.

A1. Spatial index against the systematic null
single_value_test passes each simulated count table back to index_fn as a GeoDataFrame with the original geometry, so any spatial statistic works. Here, dissimilarity after pooling counts with a 2 km Gaussian kernel.


Code
# ===================================================================
# A1. Spatial index against the systematic null.
# All observed values are far above the evenness null, and the p-values are at the floor
# ===================================================================

def spatial_dissimilarity(gdf, groups, bandwidth=2000):
    nb = seg.kernel_weights(gdf, bandwidth=bandwidth)  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights
    pooled = gdf.copy()  # tract table with kernel-pooled group counts
    pooled[groups] = nb.pooled_counts(gdf[groups].to_numpy(float))  # assign a derived column or cell
    return seg.dissimilarity(pooled, groups)  # two-group dissimilarity index D

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for y in YEARS:  # loop over panel years
    r = seg.single_value_test(tracts[y], pair, spatial_dissimilarity, null="systematic", n_sims=299, seed=y)  # compute() result with value and CI
    rows.append({"year": y, "spatial D (2 km)": r["statistic"], "systematic null mean": r["null_mean"],  # append this year/group record
                 "observed / null mean": r["statistic"] / r["null_mean"], "p-value": r["p_value"]})

section: Part B: Did segregation change between two years?
text:
Part B: Did segregation change between two years?
seg.two_value_test(gdf_a, gdf_b, groups, index_fn) pools the tracts of both datasets, randomly re-splits them into two groups of the original sizes, and recomputes the difference each time. If the two datasets came from the same distribution of tract compositions, the observed difference should look like one of these random splits.

Only the 20-year comparison is clearly significant for dissimilarity (p = 0.005); the decade-by- decade declines of about 0.04 each have p-values of 0.09 and 0.11. Theil’s \(H\) falls more and its decade changes reach p < 0.05. With a decline this gradual, a test that ignores the pairing of tracts has little power, which the next caveat explains.

Caveat. This test treats the two datasets as independent samples of tracts. Here the same 323 tracts appear in both years, so the units are paired, and the test ignores that pairing as well as spatial dependence. It is the test PySAL implements, and a reasonable screen, but the paired block bootstrap in Part D is a better match for a same-tract panel.

title: Inference for segregation indices
section: Part C: Confidence intervals that respect space
text:
Part C: Confidence intervals that respect space

C1. Unit bootstrap vs. block bootstrap
A unit bootstrap resamples the 323 tracts with replacement. A spatial block bootstrap (seg.spatial_block_bootstrap) first groups tracts into spatial blocks, then resamples whole blocks. Because tract compositions are strongly autocorrelated, neighbouring tracts carry overlapping information; the unit bootstrap counts them as independent and produces intervals that are too narrow.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part C: Confidence intervals that respect space.
# Only the 20-year comparison is clearly significant for dissimilarity (p = 0.005); the decade-by-
# ===================================================================

def unit_bootstrap(gdf, groups, index_fn, n_boot=999, ci=0.95, seed=0, **kw):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # reproducible random generator
    n = len(gdf)  # define n
    vals = np.array([index_fn(gdf.iloc[rng.integers(0, n, n)], groups, **kw) for _ in range(n_boot)])  # define vals
    lo, hi = np.quantile(vals, [(1 - ci) / 2, 1 - (1 - ci) / 2])  # run this analysis or plotting step
    return {"estimate": index_fn(gdf, groups, **kw), "ci_lower": lo, "ci_upper": hi, "boot_distribution": vals}  # return the computed result

y = 2020  # panel year
ub = unit_bootstrap(tracts[y], pair, seg.dissimilarity, seed=3)  # define ub
bb = seg.spatial_block_bootstrap(tracts[y], pair, seg.dissimilarity, n_boot=999, n_blocks=30, seed=3)  # define bb

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.8, 1.3]})  # create figure and axes
tracts[y].assign(b=bb["blocks"]).plot(column="b", categorical=True, cmap="tab20", ax=axes[0], edgecolor="white", lw=0.3)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
tracts[y].dissolve(by=bb["blocks"]).boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="k", lw=0.8)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
add_context(axes[0], labels=False); axes[0].set_title("30 k-means blocks")  # county outlines and optional city zoom
axes[1].hist(ub["boot_distribution"], bins=40, alpha=0.6, label=f"unit bootstrap [{ub['ci_lower']:.3f}, {ub['ci_upper']:.3f}]")  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[1].hist(bb["boot_distribution"], bins=40, alpha=0.6, label=f"block bootstrap [{bb['ci_lower']:.3f}, {bb['ci_upper']:.3f}]")  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[1].axvline(bb["estimate"], color="k", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"estimate {bb['estimate']:.3f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[1].set(xlabel="bootstrap D(Black, white), 2020", title="Resampling tracts vs resampling blocks"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)  # add a legend
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
print(f"interval width ratio (block / unit): {(bb['ci_upper'] - bb['ci_lower']) / (ub['ci_upper'] - ub['ci_lower']):.2f}")  # status line for the notebook reader
print(f"bootstrap medians: unit {np.median(ub['boot_distribution']):.3f}, block {np.median(bb['boot_distribution']):.3f} (estimate {bb['estimate']:.3f})")  # status line for the notebook reader










interval width ratio (block / unit): 2.67
bootstrap medians: unit 0.685, block 0.678 (estimate 0.687)


The block-bootstrap interval is about 2.7 times wider than the unit-bootstrap interval. Resampling a block pulls in a whole run of similarly composed tracts, which is how the real uncertainty behaves when the pattern is spatially smooth. Both bootstrap distributions are centred close to the estimate here, but they are skewed to the left: replicates that happen to include few East Side tracts produce a much lower \(D\).


C2. How many blocks?
Fewer, larger blocks preserve more dependence but leave few resampling units. In Buffalo there is a second issue: if the blocks are large, one block may hold most of a group. Replicates that leave that block out describe a different metro area altogether. The table reports, for each block count, the largest share of Black residents in any single block.


Code
# ===================================================================
# C2. How many blocks?.
# The block-bootstrap interval is about 2.7 times wider than the unit-bootstrap interval. Resampling
# ===================================================================

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for k in [5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 80, 160, 323]:  # iterate over the collection
    if k == 323:  # conditional branch
        r = unit_bootstrap(tracts[2020], pair, seg.dissimilarity, n_boot=499, seed=0)  # compute() result with value and CI
        top = tracts[2020].black.max() / tracts[2020].black.sum()  # sum the selected values
    else:

        top = (tracts[2020].black.groupby(r["blocks"]).sum() / tracts[2020].black.sum()).max()  # sum the selected values
    rows.append({"blocks": k, "largest block's share of Black residents": top,  # append this year/group record
                 "ci_lower": r["ci_lower"], "ci_upper": r["ci_upper"],
                 "width": r["ci_upper"] - r["ci_lower"], "boot median": np.median(r["boot_distribution"])})  # run this analysis or plotting step
blk = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("blocks")  # build table blk

Every replicate that draws that block zero times describes a metro area with almost no Black population, so the interval stretches far down and is lopsided. title: Inference for segregation indices
section: Part D: A paired block bootstrap for change
text:
Part D: A paired block bootstrap for change
When both years use the same tracts, resample the same blocks for both years in each replicate and compute the difference. This keeps the pairing (each tract compared with itself) and the spatial dependence, and gives a confidence interval for the change directly. Because the same tracts drop in or out of both years together, the “missing East Side” problem of Part C largely cancels.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: A paired block bootstrap for change.
# With 5 or 10 blocks, a single block holds 70% to 80% of the metro area's Black residents. Every
# ===================================================================

def paired_block_change(gdf_a, gdf_b, groups, index_fn, n_boot=999, n_blocks=30, seed=0, ci=0.95):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # reproducible random generator
    blocks = seg.spatial_blocks(gdf_a, n_blocks=n_blocks, seed=seed)  # define blocks
    ub = np.unique(blocks)  # define ub
    members = {b_: np.where(blocks == b_)[0] for b_ in ub}  # define members
    diffs = np.empty(n_boot)  # define diffs
    for i in range(n_boot):  # iterate over the collection
        rows_ = np.concatenate([members[b_] for b_ in rng.choice(ub, size=len(ub), replace=True)])  # define rows_
        diffs[i] = index_fn(gdf_b.iloc[rows_], groups) - index_fn(gdf_a.iloc[rows_], groups)  # absolute gap between group share schedules
    est = index_fn(gdf_b, groups) - index_fn(gdf_a, groups)  # define est
    lo, hi = np.quantile(diffs, [(1 - ci) / 2, 1 - (1 - ci) / 2])  # run this analysis or plotting step
    return {"change": est, "ci_lower": lo, "ci_upper": hi, "share of replicates < 0": (diffs < 0).mean()}  # return the computed result

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for a, b in comparisons:  # iterate over the collection
    for name, fn, grp in [("D Black-white", seg.dissimilarity, pair), ("D Asian-white", seg.dissimilarity, ["asian", "white"]),  # loop over group pairs
                          ("Theil H", seg.theil_h, GROUPS)]:  # run this analysis or plotting step
        r = paired_block_change(tracts[a], tracts[b], grp, fn, n_blocks=30, seed=0)  # compute() result with value and CI
        rows.append({"index": name, "period": f"{a} to {b}", **r})  # append this year/group record

title: Inference for segregation indices
text:
Summary

Single-value tests compare an index with a null. Use the evenness null for aspatial indices and the systematic null for spatial ones; with tracts of thousands of people, focus on the effect size rather than the (always tiny) p-value.
Two-sample permutation tests compare two datasets but ignore pairing and spatial dependence.
The unit bootstrap understates uncertainty when compositions are spatially autocorrelated; the spatial block bootstrap gives wider, more honest intervals. When one group lives in a small part of the map, large blocks give unstable, skewed intervals. Report the number of blocks and how much of each group the largest block holds.
For a fixed-boundary panel, a paired block bootstrap of the change is the most direct way to show that segregation moved.
Mann-Kendall trend tests have almost no power with three or four census years. Report the Sen slope and bootstrap evidence, and extend the panel where possible.

Next: 03_07_07 harmonizes census boundaries across years and decomposes change into spatial and compositional parts.

title: Multiscale segregation profiles
text:
Overview
Every segregation index answers “how segregated?” at one scale: the scale of the tract or of the chosen neighbourhood. Segregation is not scale-free. Two metro areas with the same tract-level index can differ completely in how far their segregation extends: one may have a few homogeneous blocks scattered through a mixed city, the other a single large divide between city and suburbs.
A multiscale segregation profile (Reardon et al., 2008; Olteanu et al., 2019) follows each tract’s local environment outward. At radius \(r\) it pools the population of every tract within \(r\) and measures how far that pooled composition is from the metro composition. As \(r\) grows the environment eventually becomes the whole metro area and the divergence falls to zero; the speed of that fall describes the scale of segregation.
This notebook follows the PySAL tutorials on multiscalar profiles and the KL divergence profile using seg.compute_profile on Buffalo’s census tracts (four named groups).
Topics:

Divergence measures: Kullback-Leibler (KL) and L1
Profile curves for individual tracts
Mappable summaries: segregation scale, area under the curve, distortion
Sensitivity to the threshold and divergence choice
A metro-wide profile, and what it says about Theil’s \(H\)
Computational scaling with a KD-tree

title: Multiscale segregation profiles
section: Part A: Profiles for individual tracts
text:
Part A: Profiles for individual tracts
For tract \(i\) and radius \(r\), let \(\tilde{p}_{ik}(r)\) be group \(k\)’s share among everyone living in tracts whose centroid is within \(r\) of tract \(i\) (including \(i\) itself). Two divergences from the metro composition \(P_k\) are available:
\[\text{KL}_i(r) = \sum_k \tilde{p}_{ik}(r)\,\ln\frac{\tilde{p}_{ik}(r)}{P_k}, \qquad
\text{L1}_i(r) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_k |\tilde{p}_{ik}(r) - P_k|.\]
KL is the measure used in Reardon’s profiles and in PySAL’s kl_divergence_profile; it is the same entropy logic as Theil’s \(H\). L1 is bounded in \([0, 1]\) and reads as “the share of the local population that would need to change group for the environment to match the metro area”.
seg.compute_profile evaluates every tract at every radius in one pass. Radius 0 means the tract on its own. Buffalo’s tracts range from a few hundred metres across in the city to more than 10 km in rural Erie County, so the radii run to 30 km.

Reading the curves:

The East Side tract has by far the highest divergence at radius 0 and stays high out to 3 km, because its neighbours are also mostly Black. It drops sharply only between 3 and 8 km, once the ring crosses into the surrounding white neighbourhoods. The East Side cluster is about that wide.
The West Side tract also starts very high but falls by half within 1 to 2 km: the Hispanic concentration is a much smaller pocket. Its curve then rises again near 5 km as the ring reaches the East Side.
The Amherst tract starts moderately high and converges within about 5 km.
The outer suburb starts low (0.23) but stays above the metro mean out to 20 km: a low level of difference that extends a long way. The white suburban and rural ring is a very large homogeneous area.
The most diverse tract also starts high. Diverse is not the same as typical: in a metro area that is 73% white, a tract with four equal groups is far from the metro mix.

The radius-0 value alone does not predict any of these shapes, which is the information a single-scale index throws away.

title: Multiscale segregation profiles
text:
Part B: Mappable summaries
A curve per tract is hard to map. MultiscaleProfile stores three summaries, one value per tract:








Summary
Definition
Reads as




segregation_scale
smallest radius where divergence falls below a threshold
how far you must go before the environment looks like the metro (inf = beyond the largest radius)


auc
area under the divergence-radius curve
segregation integrated over all scales


distortion
divergence at the largest radius / divergence at radius 0
share of the tract’s segregation that persists at the metro scale

# ===================================================================
# Part B: Mappable summaries.
# Reading the curves:
# ===================================================================

def capped_scale(pr, cap):
    return np.where(np.isfinite(pr.segregation_scale), pr.segregation_scale, cap) / 1000  # return the computed result

cap = RADII[-1] * 1.2  # define cap
for y in (2000, 2020):  # iterate over the collection
    pr = prof[y]  # define pr

        (axes[1], pr.auc / 1000, f"{y}: area under profile (KL x km)", "PuRd", prof[2000].auc.max() / 1000),  # run this analysis or plotting step

section: Part D: A metro-wide profile, and a lesson about Theil’s \(H\)
text:
Part D: A metro-wide profile, and a lesson about Theil’s \(H\)
Averaging tract profiles with population weights gives one curve per year. At radius 0 this weighted mean has a precise meaning: it is the mutual information between tract and group, which equals \(H \times E\) (Theil’s \(H\) times the metro entropy). So the profile also shows why \(H\) changed.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: A metro-wide profile, and a lesson about Theil's $H$.
# KL and L1 order tracts similarly at any one radius, but KL falls faster with radius because it
# ===================================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))  # create figure and axes
rows = {}  # accumulate summary rows
for y, col in zip(YEARS, ["#3f007d", "#807dba", "#bcbddc"]):  # loop over panel years  # iterate paired sequences together
    wy = tracts[y][GROUPS].sum(axis=1).to_numpy()  # NumPy array view of the column
    metro = (prof[y].profile * wy[:, None]).sum(0) / wy.sum()  # sum the selected values
    axes[0].plot(np.array(RADII) / 1000, metro, marker="o", color=col, label=str(y))  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    axes[1].plot(np.array(RADII) / 1000, metro / metro[0], marker="o", color=col, label=str(y))  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    P = tracts[y][GROUPS].sum() / tracts[y][GROUPS].sum().sum()  # sum the selected values
    E = float(-(P * np.log(P)).sum())  # sum the selected values
    rows[y] = {"weighted KL at r = 0": metro[0], "metro entropy E": E, "KL / E": metro[0] / E,  # assign a derived column or cell
               "Theil H": seg.theil_h(tracts[y], GROUPS),  # run this analysis or plotting step
               **{f"share left at {r // 1000} km": metro[RADII.index(r)] / metro[0] for r in (5000, 12000, 20000)}}  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[0].set(xlabel="radius (km)", ylabel="population-weighted KL", title="Level")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
axes[1].set(xlabel="radius (km)", ylabel="relative to r = 0", title="Shape (macro share)", ylim=(0, 1.05))  # set labels, title, or axis limits
for a in axes: a.legend()  # iterate over the collection
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

Metro entropy \(E\) rose from 0.56 to 0.78 as the Hispanic and Asian populations grew. Because \(H = \text{KL}/E\), Theil’s \(H\) fell from 0.43 to 0.31 entirely through its denominator.

Which statement is “right” depends on the question: the normalized \(H\) answers “how segregated relative to how diverse”; the mutual information answers “how much does place predict group”. Report both when diversity is changing.

title: Multiscale segregation profiles
section: Part F: Scaling to many units
text:
Part F: Scaling to many units
Buffalo’s 323 tracts are small. Block groups or census blocks (about 15,000 populated blocks here) quickly make the problem large. A profile needs, for every unit, the cumulative population within each radius. The direct approach builds an \(n \times n\) distance matrix, which needs \(8n^2\) bytes: 800 MB at \(n = 10{,}000\) and 1.8 GB for Buffalo’s 15,000 populated blocks. compute_profile queries a cKDTree for each unit’s nearest neighbours in chunks, so memory grows with \(n \times\) (neighbours per unit). (Recent PySAL releases also fall back to streaming KD-tree queries when the dense matrix would not fit; older ones did not.)
The benchmark uses the real 2020 census blocks of Erie and Niagara counties (block internal points with population; group counts are not published at block level in this file, so synthetic group labels are drawn from the metro shares, which affects only the values, not the cost). It compares compute_profile with a dense NumPy implementation on random subsets.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part F: Scaling to many units.
# Buffalo's 323 tracts are small. Block groups or census blocks (about 15,000 populated blocks here)
# ===================================================================

import time  # library import used below
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist  # library import used below

blocks = gpd.read_file(DATA / "blocks_2020_points.geojson")  # load vector features from disk
blocks = blocks[blocks.pop20 > 0].reset_index(drop=True)  # index rows for keyed lookup / display
print(f"{len(blocks):,} populated 2020 blocks, {blocks.pop20.sum():,.0f} people")  # status line for the notebook reader

def dense_profile(xy, counts, radii):
    D = cdist(xy, xy)  # define D
    P = counts.sum(0) / counts.sum()  # sum the selected values
    out = np.empty((len(xy), len(radii)))  # define out
    for j, r in enumerate(radii):  # iterate with a numeric index
        pooled = (D <= r).astype(float) @ counts  # tract table with kernel-pooled group counts
        q = pooled / pooled.sum(1, keepdims=True)  # define q
        out[:, j] = np.sum(np.where(q > 0, q * np.log(q / P), 0), axis=1)  # temporary plot column for the choropleth
    return out  # return the computed result

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # reproducible random generator
P20 = (tracts[2020][GROUPS].sum() / tracts[2020][GROUPS].sum().sum()).to_numpy()  # sum the selected values
bench, radii_b = [], [250, 500, 1000]
for n in [1000, 2500, 5000, 10000, len(blocks)]:  # iterate over the collection
    sub = blocks.sample(n, random_state=1) if n < len(blocks) else blocks  # define sub
    counts = np.array([rng.multinomial(int(t), P20) for t in sub.pop20]).astype(float)  # define counts
    pts = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.DataFrame(counts, columns=GROUPS), geometry=sub.geometry.values, crs=sub.crs)  # build table pts
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); kd = seg.compute_profile(pts, GROUPS, radii=radii_b, chunk_size=1000); t_kd = time.perf_counter() - t0  # define t0
    row = {"units": n, "KD-tree time (s)": t_kd, "dense matrix memory (GB)": 8 * n**2 / 1e9}  # define row
    if n <= 5000:  # conditional branch
        xy = np.c_[pts.geometry.x, pts.geometry.y]  # define xy
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); dn = dense_profile(xy, counts, radii_b); row["dense time (s)"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # define t0
        row["max abs diff"] = float(np.abs(dn - kd.profile).max())  # absolute gap between group share schedules
    bench.append(row)  # append this year/group record
bench = pd.DataFrame(bench).set_index("units")  # build table bench
bench.round(4)  # run this analysis or plotting step

Both approaches give the same numbers (maximum difference zero). For a few thousand units the dense method is faster, because a matrix product is very efficient. Its memory, however, grows with \(n^2\): 1.8 GB for all 15,076 populated blocks in Erie and Niagara counties, and 200 GB or more for a large metro area. The KD-tree approach handles all Buffalo blocks in about 3 seconds with memory that grows roughly linearly.
Two practical notes:

max_neighbors (default 2000) caps how many neighbours each unit can pool. If a unit has more units within the largest radius, compute_profile raises an error rather than silently truncating. Raise it, or shrink the largest radius.
Radii are Euclidean distances between centroids in the layer’s CRS, so use a projected CRS in metres (here NAD83 / UTM zone 17N).

title: Multiscale segregation profiles
text:
Summary

A multiscale profile tracks how a tract’s surrounding population converges to the metro composition as the radius grows. Level and reach of segregation are separate properties.
segregation_scale, auc, and distortion turn the profiles into maps; the scale depends on a threshold that should be reported and varied.
KL and L1 rank tracts alike but decay at different rates, so thresholds are measure-specific.
The population-weighted profile at radius 0 is the mutual information \(H \times E\). Comparing it with \(H\) separates a change in sorting from a change in diversity.
compute_profile matches PySAL’s KL profile and handles block-level data without an \(n \times n\) matrix.

Next: 03_07_05 builds the null models that tell us which of these patterns could arise by chance.

title: Multigroup segregation indices
text:
Overview
Buffalo has more than two groups, and running a separate two-group index for every pair quickly becomes hard to read (four groups already give six pairs). Multigroup indices answer one question for all groups at once: how much does the composition of each tract differ from the composition of the metro area?
This notebook follows the PySAL segregation tutorial on multigroup indices using geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation. Multigroup indices here use the four named groups (GROUPS: white, Black, Hispanic, Asian); the heterogeneous other category is left out.
Topics:

Diversity is not integration: metro-wide Simpson and entropy
Theil’s information theory index \(H\) and each tract’s share of it
Multigroup dissimilarity and its link to the two-group index
Pairwise dissimilarity matrices
Local diversity maps
Spatial (kernel-pooled) multigroup indices
Validation against PySAL and confidence intervals

Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo, imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation as seg, and loads the data.
Study area and data. The Buffalo-Cheektowaga metropolitan area: Erie and Niagara counties, New York (about 1.17 million people in 2020). Counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau decennial censuses of 2000, 2010, and 2020, by census tract, for five mutually exclusive groups:



Column
Census definition

hispanic

asian

other
Everyone else (other single races and two or more races)



Tract boundaries change between censuses. To compare years on the same units, the 2000 and 2010 counts have been moved onto the 323 tracts of 2020 with dasymetric interpolation weighted by 2020 housing units; notebook 03_07_07 shows how. Tracts with fewer than 100 residents (water, parks, the airport) are dropped. Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/make_buffalo_data.py rebuilds everything from the Census files in Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/.
Two map helpers keep every map in the same frame: add_context(ax) draws the county outlines, and metro_and_core(...) shows the whole metro area next to a 30 km window centred on the City of Buffalo, where most tracts are small.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

title: Multigroup segregation indices
section: Part A: Diversity of the metro area
text:
Part A: Diversity of the metro area
Let \(P_k\) be group \(k\)’s share of the whole region. Two standard summaries of how mixed the region is:

Simpson diversity: the probability two random residents belong to different groups, \(I = 1 - \sum_k P_k^2\).
Shannon entropy: \(E = -\sum_k P_k \ln P_k\), maximal (\(\ln K\)) when all \(K\) groups are equal in size.

These describe the region, not how its residents are sorted. A metro area can be diverse and segregated at the same time.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part A: Diversity of the metro area.
# Let $P_k$ be group $k$'s share of the whole region. Two standard summaries of how mixed the region
# ===================================================================

def regional_entropy(g, groups):
    P = g[groups].sum() / g[groups].sum().sum()  # sum the selected values
    return float(-(P * np.log(P)).sum())  # return the computed result

div = pd.DataFrame({  # build table div
    y: {"Simpson diversity I": seg.simpson_diversity(g, GROUPS),  # run this analysis or plotting step
        "entropy E": regional_entropy(g, GROUPS),  # run this analysis or plotting step
        "entropy / ln K": regional_entropy(g, GROUPS) / np.log(len(GROUPS)),  # run this analysis or plotting step
        "Theil H": seg.theil_h(g, GROUPS)}  # run this analysis or plotting step
    for y, g in tracts.items()  # loop over each year and its tract GeoDataFrame
}).T
