title: Multigroup segregation indices
section: Part B: Theil’s information theory index \(H\)
text:
Part B: Theil’s information theory index \(H\)
Each tract \(i\) has its own entropy \(E_i = -\sum_k p_{ik}\ln p_{ik}\). If people were sorted randomly, every tract would look like the region and \(E_i \approx E\). Theil’s \(H\) (Theil and Finizza, 1971; Reardon and Firebaugh, 2002) is the population-weighted average loss of entropy:
\[H = \sum_i \frac{t_i}{T}\,\frac{E - E_i}{E}.\]
\(H = 0\) when every tract has the regional mix; \(H = 1\) when every tract contains a single group. Because \(H\) is a weighted sum over tracts, each tract’s term \(h_i = \frac{t_i (E - E_i)}{T E}\) is its contribution to metro-wide segregation and can be mapped.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part B: Theil's information theory index $H$.
# The metro area has become much more diverse: Simpson diversity rises from 0.28 to 0.39 and
# ===================================================================

def theil_contributions(g, groups):
    c = g[groups].to_numpy(float)  # NumPy array view of the column
    t = c.sum(1); T = t.sum()  # sum the selected values
    P = c.sum(0) / T  # define P
    E = -(P * np.log(P)).sum()  # sum the selected values
    p = c / t[:, None]  # tract share of the focal group within the pair
    Ei = -np.sum(np.where(p > 0, p * np.log(p), 0), axis=1)  # define Ei
    return t * (E - Ei) / (T * E), Ei  # return the computed result

for y in YEARS:  # loop over panel years
    h_i, _ = theil_contributions(tracts[y], GROUPS)  # run this analysis or plotting step
    assert np.isclose(h_i.sum(), seg.theil_h(tracts[y], GROUPS))  # sanity-check an invariant
    print(f"{y}: H = {h_i.sum():.3f}; {(h_i < 0).sum()} of {len(h_i)} tracts are more diverse than the metro (h_i < 0)")  # status line for the notebook reader

h20, E20 = theil_contributions(tracts[2020], GROUPS)  # run this analysis or plotting step
lim = np.abs(h20).max()  # define lim
metro_and_core(tracts[2020], h20, title="2020: tract contribution to Theil H", cmap="PuOr_r",  # side-by-side metro and city-window choropleths
               norm=plt.matplotlib.colors.TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-lim / 4, vcenter=0, vmax=lim),  # define norm
               label="$h_i$ (negative = more diverse than the metro)")  # define label
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook



2000: H = 0.434; 66 of 323 tracts are more diverse than the metro (h_i < 0)
2010: H = 0.368; 81 of 323 tracts are more diverse than the metro (h_i < 0)
2020: H = 0.306; 92 of 323 tracts are more diverse than the metro (h_i < 0)









The map is the opposite of what many people expect. The largest positive contributions come from the white suburban and rural ring, not from the East Side. \(H\) measures departure from the metro mix, and in 2020 that mix is about 73% white. A 97% white suburban tract therefore departs from it almost as much as an 85% Black city tract does, and there are many more such tracts with large populations. East Side tracts contribute modestly, while the West Side and the areas around downtown, where four groups live together, are more diverse than the metro and pull \(H\) down (purple). Segregation is a property of the whole region: the homogeneity of the suburbs is as much part of it as the concentration of Black residents in the city.
How concentrated is segregation? Sorting tracts by \(h_i\) shows what share of \(H\) the most segregated tracts account for.

Part C: Multigroup dissimilarity
Sakoda’s (1981) generalization of \(D\) sums each tract’s absolute deviation from the regional composition over all groups and normalizes by the region’s own Simpson interaction \(I_s = \sum_k P_k(1-P_k)\):
\[D_{multi} = \frac{\sum_i \sum_k t_i\,|p_{ik} - P_k|}{2\,T\,I_s}.\]
With only two groups this reduces to ordinary \(D\) exactly, which the cell verifies.

Part D: The pairwise matrix
A multigroup index compresses six pairwise contrasts into one number. Showing the full pairwise dissimilarity matrix alongside it tells the reader which groups drive it.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: The pairwise matrix.
# $H$ is always smaller than $D_{multi}$ for the same data; they use different scales (entropy vs.
# ===================================================================

def pairwise_matrix(g, groups, index_fn=seg.dissimilarity):
    M = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=groups, columns=groups)  # build table M
    for a in groups:  # loop over demographic groups
        for b in groups:  # loop over demographic groups
            if a != b:  # conditional branch
                M.loc[a, b] = index_fn(g, [a, b])  # assign a derived column or cell
    return M  # return the computed result

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, y in zip(axes, YEARS):  # loop over panel years
    M = pairwise_matrix(tracts[y], GROUPS)  # define M
    im = ax.imshow(M, cmap="Purples", vmin=0.3, vmax=0.8)  # define im
    ax.set_xticks(range(4), GROUPS, rotation=30); ax.set_yticks(range(4), GROUPS)  # label years on the x-axis
    for i in range(4):  # iterate over the collection
        for j in range(4):  # iterate over the collection
            if i != j:  # conditional branch
                ax.text(j, i, f"{M.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,  # run this analysis or plotting step
                        color="white" if M.iloc[i, j] > 0.6 else "black")  # define color
    ax.set_title(f"{y}: pairwise D")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










In 2000 the matrix is dominated by the Black row: Black residents are highly separated from every other group (0.64 to 0.77). By 2020 the Black-Hispanic and Black-Asian contrasts have fallen to about 0.46 and 0.50, while the Asian-white contrast has risen to 0.59. Black-white remains the largest pair, and the Asian row is the only one that grows. The multigroup indices hide these opposing movements.

title: Multigroup segregation indices
text:
Part F: Spatial multigroup segregation
As with the single-group indices, pool each tract’s counts over a kernel neighbourhood and recompute \(H\). The ratio \(H(\text{bandwidth})/H(\text{aspatial})\) reads as “the share of segregation that is still visible at that scale”, the core idea behind Reardon et al.’s (2008) macro/micro segregation comparison.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part F: Spatial multigroup segregation.
# Entropy and Simpson rank tracts almost identically (Spearman 0.998). The most diverse tracts are
# ===================================================================

def pooled(g, groups, bandwidth):
    nb = seg.kernel_weights(g, bandwidth=bandwidth, kernel="gaussian")  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights
    out = g.copy()  # mutable copy so originals stay unchanged
    out[groups] = nb.pooled_counts(g[groups].to_numpy(float))  # assign a derived column or cell
    return out  # return the computed result

bws = [500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000, 12000, 20000]  # define bws
spatial_H = pd.DataFrame({y: [seg.theil_h(pooled(g, GROUPS, b), GROUPS) for b in bws]  # build table spatial_H
                          for y, g in tracts.items()}, index=bws)  # loop over each year and its tract GeoDataFrame
ratio = spatial_H / pd.Series({y: seg.theil_h(g, GROUPS) for y, g in tracts.items()})  # define ratio

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))  # create figure and axes
for y, col in zip(YEARS, ["#3f007d", "#807dba", "#bcbddc"]):  # loop over panel years  # iterate paired sequences together

    axes[1].plot(np.array(bws) / 1000, ratio[y], marker="o", color=col, label=str(y))  # draw geometries or a series on the axes

title: Multigroup segregation indices
text:
Summary

Diversity is not integration. Metro-wide diversity rises as the population changes, while Theil’s \(H\) falls; the two answer different questions.
Theil’s \(H\) is a population-weighted entropy loss. Its tract contributions sum exactly to the metro value, so they can be mapped to show where segregation is produced.
Multigroup dissimilarity reduces to the two-group \(D\) for two groups. Report the pairwise matrix alongside any multigroup index so readers can see which contrasts drive it.
Local entropy and Simpson map diversity; the most diverse tracts are not the same as the least segregated region.
Kernel-pooled \(H\) shows how much segregation survives at larger scales, separating macro-scale divides from local patchiness.

Next: 03_07_03 moves from region-wide numbers to local measures with significance tests.
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Decennial Census 2000, 2010, 2020, tract level, Erie and Niagara counties, NY.

title: Multigroup segregation indices

Reardon, S. F., & Firebaugh, G. (2002). Measures of multigroup segregation. Sociological Methodology, 32(1), 33-67.
Reardon, S. F., Matthews, S. A., O’Sullivan, D., Lee, B. A., Firebaugh, G., Farrell, C. R., & Bischoff, K. (2008). The geographic scale of metropolitan racial segregation. Demography, 45(3), 489-514.
Sakoda, J. M. (1981). A generalized index of dissimilarity. Demography, 18(2), 245-250.

title: Segregation Analysis
text: Banner

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
The core idea
Dimensions. Segregation is not one quantity. Massey and Denton (1988) described five dimensions, and most indices in the package measure one of them:








Dimension
Question it answers
Example indices




Evenness
Are groups spread evenly across units?
Dissimilarity (D), Gini, Theil entropy (H), Atkinson


Exposure
How often do groups share units?
Isolation, Interaction


Concentration
How much physical space does a group occupy?
Delta, Absolute/Relative Concentration


Centralization
Is a group near the urban core?
Absolute/Relative Centralization


Clustering
Do a group’s units sit next to each other?
Absolute/Relative Clustering, Spatial Proximity



Aspatial vs spatial. Classic indices treat tracts as unconnected bins. That creates the checkerboard problem: a perfect checkerboard of all-Black and all-White tracts gets the same D as a city split into two halves, even though the lived experience is very different. Spatial indices fix this in one of two ways:

Spatially explicit indices include distance or adjacency in the original formula (Centralization, Clustering, Spatial Proximity).
Generalized (spatially implicit) indices, following Reardon and O’Sullivan, first smooth each unit’s population over its neighborhood, then compute the ordinary index on the smoothed data. The neighborhood can be defined by a kernel bandwidth, a libpysal.W weights object, or a pandana.Network of travel distance.

“Over time and space.” Space means comparing places, scales, and local patterns. Time means computing the same index for several census years and asking two questions: is the change real (inference), and why did it happen (decomposition)?

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Single-group indices (segregation.singlegroup)
These measure one focal group against everyone else, for example Black vs. non-Black.
Key formulas, with group count \(x_i\) and total \(t_i\) in unit \(i\), regional group total \(X\), and regional total \(T\):

Dissimilarity: \(D = \tfrac12 \sum_i \left| \frac{x_i}{X} - \frac{t_i - x_i}{T - X} \right|\). This is the share of the group that would have to move for an even distribution.
Isolation: \(xPx = \sum_i \frac{x_i}{X}\cdot\frac{x_i}{t_i}\). Interaction is \(1 - xPx\) for two groups.

The usage pattern is the same for every index:
from segregation.singlegroup import Dissim, Gini
d = Dissim(sacramento, group_pop_var="BLACK", total_pop_var="TOT_POP")
d.statistic   # 0.488
d.data        # data used in the computation
Results for Black residents in Sacramento:



Version
Gini




Aspatial
0.636


Generalized spatial, 2 km Euclidean kernel (distance=2000)
0.537


2 km network distance (network=net, decay='linear')
0.585



Smoothing lowers the index, because segregation between adjacent tracts partly cancels out. Network distance gives a higher value than straight-line distance, because people travel on roads, not “as the crow flies.” Barriers like freeways and rivers keep neighborhoods apart. batch_compute_singlegroup() returns all 27 single-group indices in one table.

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Multi-group indices (segregation.multigroup)
These measure segregation among several groups at once (White, Black, Hispanic) instead of one group against the rest.
The most widely used is Theil’s information theory index \(H\):
\[E = -\sum_m \pi_m \ln \pi_m, \qquad H = \sum_i \frac{t_i\,(E - E_i)}{T\,E}\]
Here \(E\) is regional entropy (diversity) and \(E_i\) is the entropy of unit \(i\). \(H = 0\) when every unit is as diverse as the region. \(H = 1\) when every unit holds only one group.

text:
Local measures (segregation.local)
Global indices give one number per region. Local measures give one value per tract, so you can map where segregation happens. With \(\pi_{im}\) = share of group \(m\) in unit \(i\):








Measure
Formula
Reading




Location Quotient
\(LQ_{im} = \dfrac{x_{im}/t_i}{X_m/T}\)
Greater than 1 means the group is over-represented relative to the region. Returns an n × M array, one column per group.


Local Diversity
\(-\sum_m \pi_{im}\ln\pi_{im}\)
Higher means more mixed.


Local Entropy
Diversity divided by \(\ln M\)
Same as diversity, scaled to 0-1. In Sacramento, 0.343 / ln 4 = 0.248.


Local Simpson Interaction
\(\sum_m \pi_{im}(1-\pi_{im})\)
Probability that two random residents belong to different groups.


Local Simpson Concentration
\(\sum_m \pi_{im}^2\)
Probability that they belong to the same group. It equals 1 - interaction.


Local Relative Centralization
Single-group, nearest-neighbor based
Ranges from -1 to +1. Shows whether the group is closer to each tract’s local center than the rest of the population.



Classes whose names start with Multi take a list of groups. The others take a single group and a total. These maps are the natural input for LISA or hot-spot analysis.

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Multiscalar segregation profiles (segregation.dynamics)
This approach comes from Reardon et al. (2008). You compute an index, widen the neighborhood radius, recompute, and repeat. The result is a curve of segregation against scale.
from segregation.dynamics import compute_multiscalar_profile
prof = compute_multiscalar_profile(sacramento, segregation_index=Gini,
        group_pop_var="BLACK", total_pop_var="TOT_POP",
        distances=range(500, 5500, 500))
For Black residents in Sacramento, Gini falls from 0.636 at 0 m to 0.537 at 2 km and 0.413 at 5 km.
Reading a profile:

Steep early drop: segregation is micro-scale. Pockets disappear once you look a little wider.
Flat curve: segregation is macro-scale. Large contiguous areas stay homogeneous even at wide radii.
Network vs. Euclidean: the network-based D profile falls more slowly. Travel infrastructure keeps segregation in place at larger distances.

Any of the 23 generalized indices (single or multi-group) can be profiled. The functions batch_multiscalar_singlegroup and batch_multiscalar_multigroup compute them all. For time analysis, plotting profiles for 1990, 2000, and 2010 on one chart shows whether segregation is fading at fine scales while persisting at coarse ones.

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Simulating random populations (null models)
A key point from Boisso et al. (1994) is that “no segregation” does not give an index of 0. Random allocation still produces some unevenness, especially for small groups. So you need a simulated reference distribution. The package offers three randomization schemes:









Function
What is randomized
What is preserved
What varies




simulate_evenness
Each resident in each unit is drawn as the focal group with probability equal to the regional share (6.8% for Black residents)
Unit totals
Group totals vary slightly (121,457 vs. 122,022)


simulate_systematic_randomization
Each group member is placed in a unit with probability equal to the unit’s share of total population
Group totals
Unit totals vary


simulate_person_permutation
Individuals are shuffled among units
Both group totals and unit totals
Neither



The notebook’s summary is: evenness includes group-level variation, systematic includes unit-level variation, and permutation includes neither. simulate_null(seg_class, sim_func) runs these in parallel to build the null distribution. For Sacramento, all three give similar distributions that are not centered on zero. The schemes can diverge when minority groups are very small or very unbalanced.

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Single-value and comparative inference (segregation.inference)

Single-value test: is this place segregated at all?
SingleValueTest(index, null_approach=...) compares the observed index with a simulated null distribution.

Evenness null. Hispanic D = 0.322, while the null mean is about 0.016, so p ≈ 0 and segregation is real. This null fits evenness indices.
Bootstrap. This simulates the sampling distribution of D itself, then tests it against 0 or against the evenness null mean. Both give the same conclusion here.
Geographic permutation. This shuffles where whole tracts sit, keeping their contents. It is the right test for spatial indices. Relative Concentration = 0.126 with p = 0.54, so it is not significant. The Hispanic population is uneven across tracts, but not unusually concentrated in space.
even_permutation. This generates an evenness population first, then permutes it geographically.

The point is to match the null to the dimension you are measuring.


Two-value test: are two places or two years different?
TwoValueTest(index1, index2, null_approach=...) handles both space (City A vs. City B) and time (Year 1 vs. Year 2). The notebook splits Sacramento into west (D = 0.277) and east (D = 0.258):

random_label (Rey & Sastré-Gutiérrez, 2010) shuffles units between the two contexts and builds a distribution of differences. p = 0.43.
bootstrap (Davidson, 2009) bootstraps each index and runs a means test. p = 0.43. Use it only for aspatial indices: it ignores spatial autocorrelation, and resampling duplicates units, which breaks the geometry.

Conclusion: the 0.02 gap is not significant. For time comparisons, the same tract geography must be used in both years, which means harmonizing boundaries first (for example with PySAL’s geosnap).

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Decomposition: why do two values differ?
text:
Decomposition: why do two values differ?
DecomposeSegregation(index1, index2, counterfactual_approach=...) follows Rey et al., “Comparative Spatial Segregation Analytics.” It uses a Shapley decomposition to split the difference between two indices into two parts:
\[S_A - S_B = c_s + c_a\]

\(c_a\) (attribute component): the part due to different population composition, such as how large the group is and how its tract shares are distributed.
\(c_s\) (spatial component): the part due to how those compositions are arranged in space.

The method builds counterfactuals: City A’s spatial layout with City B’s composition distribution, matched by quantiles (CDFs), and the reverse. It then averages the effects. There are three counterfactual approaches: composition (default), share, and dual_composition.
Sacramento, Black Gini, west minus east:




Difference
\(c_s\)
\(c_a\)




Composition approach
-0.150
-0.004
-0.146


Share approach
-0.150
-0.048
-0.101


Relative Concentration
-0.074
+0.035
-0.108



Almost all of the Gini gap comes from attributes, not spatial arrangement. For the spatial index, the spatial component carries more weight and points the opposite way. Use .plot(plot_type="cdfs") or "maps" to see the counterfactuals.
For time analysis, this is the most useful tool. It tells you whether segregation rose because the group’s composition changed (growth, immigration) or because people sorted differently in space.

title: Segregation Analysis
section: kl_divergence_profile: the Olteanu et al. (2019) multiscalar view
text:
kl_divergence_profile: the Olteanu et al. (2019) multiscalar view
This is a different multiscalar method, based on Olteanu et al., “Segregation through the multiscalar lens,” PNAS. For every unit, it grows a neighborhood outward one nearest neighbor at a time and measures how far the accumulated population mix is from the city-wide mix, using Kullback-Leibler divergence:
\[d_{KL}(q \,\|\, r) = \sum_{m=1}^{k} q_m \ln\frac{q_m}{r_m}\]
Here \(q\) is the cumulative group proportions around the focal unit and \(r\) is the regional proportions.
Algorithm:

Compute centroids and a full pairwise distance matrix with pdist. The metric is configurable.
For each unit, sort all units by distance and take cumulative group counts.
Convert to proportions \(q\) and compute divergence from \(r\) using scipy.special.rel_entr. This function treats \(0\ln 0 = 0\), which is why it is used instead of kl_div.
Return a row for each step with four columns: observation, distance, divergence, population_covered.

The output is large: n² rows (457² = 208,849 for Cincinnati).
Reading the profile:

At distance 0, divergence is local segregation: how unlike the city that unit is.
Divergence always converges to 0 once the whole city is included.
How far you must go before divergence becomes small is the “segregation scale” for that location. Large distances mean the unit sits inside a big homogeneous area.
Taking .groupby('observation').first() gives a local divergence map.

The “invalid value in divide” warnings in the notebook come from units with zero population and are harmless.
Inputs can be a GeoDataFrame containing only count columns plus geometry, or separate populations and coordinates objects. Use raw counts, not percentages.

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Putting it together for space and time
text:
Putting it together for space and time

Harmonize geography across census years so units are comparable.
Global indices for each year, single and multi-group, aspatial and spatial (network if possible).
Single-value test for each year: is segregation above what random allocation gives?
Two-value test between Year 1 and Year 2, or between cities: is the change real?
Decomposition of the change: composition shift or spatial re-sorting?
Multiscalar or KL profiles for each year: did segregation shift between micro and macro scale?
Local maps (LQ, entropy, local KL) for each year: where did it intensify or ease?

This pipeline would fit well alongside your spatial causal package. Local segregation surfaces can serve as exposures or confounders in a spatial causal model of health outcomes.
Sources: - Single-group Segregation Indices - Multi-group Segregation Indices - Local Measures of Segregation - Multiscalar Segregation Profiles - Simulating Population Groups Distributed Randomly in Space - Single Value and Comparative Inference - Segregation Index Decomposition - kl_divergence_profile walkthrough
geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation is a lighter, faster, time-series-aware alternative to PySAL’s segregation package, built around three gaps in it:

Scale. PySAL’s spatial (KL-divergence) profile builds a dense n x n distance matrix and an n^2-row table – it runs out of memory well before a few thousand units. This module’s multiscale.compute_profile uses a scipy.spatial.cKDTree and never materializes either.
Time. PySAL only ever compares two values at a time. This module accepts a whole panel of years, harmonizes boundaries across them (areal or dasymetric interpolation), tests the resulting trend (Mann-Kendall), and chains the spatial-vs-composition decomposition across every consecutive pair of periods instead of just one.
Inference. PySAL’s bootstrap resamples individual units, which is only valid if neighboring units are independent – exactly what spatial autocorrelation violates. This module resamples whole spatial blocks instead, and adds permutation significance with false-discovery-rate correction for local (LISA-style) maps.

This notebook is a hands-on tour of the whole module on one synthetic city. Every single- and multi-group index it computes is checked in tests/test_segregation.py against PySAL’s own segregation package values, so the numbers below are not just internally consistent – they agree with the field’s existing reference implementation wherever the two overlap.

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Setup and the synthetic study city
text:
Setup and the synthetic study city
The data below (Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/make_data.py) is a fictional ~14 km x 14 km city with four population groups across three census years (2000, 2010, 2020) on one shared set of 92 Voronoi “tracts”, plus a fourth, older year (1990) deliberately built on a different, coarser set of 18 tract boundaries – the real-world problem every multi- decade segregation panel has, since census geography gets redrawn almost every decade. A built-up-intensity raster is also provided, for the dasymetric boundary-harmonization example later on.
The city’s demographic pattern is not random: it starts as a sharp east/west divide in 1990 and partially integrates by 2020, so every index, map, trend test, and decomposition below has a real, interpretable signal to recover.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup and warning control.
# Areal interpolation can warn on zero-area slivers; geolattice already silences the expected case.

import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame I/O for tract panels

import pandas as pd  # tabular display of results

# Hide UserWarnings so notebook output stays readable.

# ===================================================================
# Setup for the segregation overview notebook.

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Region-wide indices, with a spatial-block bootstrap confidence interval
text:
Region-wide indices, with a spatial-block bootstrap confidence interval
seg.compute() is the single entry point: name an index, name the group columns, and optionally ask for a confidence interval. ci=True calls inference.spatial_block_bootstrap under the hood, which resamples whole spatial blocks of tracts together (so spatially correlated neighbors move together in each replicate) rather than resampling individual tracts as if they were independent – the assumption a plain unit-level bootstrap makes, and spatial autocorrelation violates.

Dissimilarity ("dissimilarity"): the share of either group that would have to move for every tract to match the city’s overall composition. 0 = no segregation, 1 = complete segregation.
Gini ("gini"): like dissimilarity, but weighted so larger tracts count more.
Theil’s H ("theil_h"): the multigroup information-theory index – how much of the city’s overall racial/ethnic diversity is “explained away” by which tract people live in, across all four groups at once (not just white/black).



Code
# ===================================================================
# Region-wide indices for 2020 with spatial-block-bootstrap CIs.
# n_blocks=8 keeps neighbouring tracts' dependence in the resampling.
# ===================================================================

# Dissimilarity and Gini for the white-black pair.
for index_name, pair in [("dissimilarity", ("white", "black")), ("gini", ("white", "black"))]:  # loop over group pairs
    result = seg.compute(  # define result
        tracts[2020],
        index=index_name,  # define index
        groups=list(pair),  # define groups
        ci=True,  # define ci
        n_boot=299,  # bootstrap replicates
        n_blocks=8,  # spatial blocks for dependence-preserving CI
        seed=0,  # define seed
    )
    print(result.summary())  # run this analysis or plotting step

# Theil's H uses all four groups at once, not just one pair.
theil_result = seg.compute(  # define theil_result
    tracts[2020],
    index="theil_h",  # define index
    groups=GROUPS,  # define groups
    ci=True,  # define ci
    n_boot=299,  # define n_boot
    n_blocks=8,  # define n_blocks
    seed=0,  # define seed
)
print(theil_result.summary())  # run this analysis or plotting step


dissimilarity(white, black) = 0.1383 (95% CI [0.0866, 0.1749])
gini(white, black) = 0.1881 (95% CI [0.1247, 0.2213])
theil_h(white, black, hispanic, asian) = 0.0187 (95% CI [0.0117, 0.0238])

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Local measures and permutation significance (a LISA-style map)
text:
Local measures and permutation significance (a LISA-style map)
A single region-wide number hides where segregation is concentrated. local_quotient computes each tract’s location quotient for one group: LQ = (tract's share of the group) / (city-wide share of the group). LQ > 1 means that group is over-represented in that tract.
But some of that variation is just noise from small tract populations. local_significance tests every tract’s LQ against an “evenness” null (each tract’s population redrawn from the city-wide proportions, keeping its own total fixed) with 999 permutations, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all 92 simultaneous tests – the same multiple-comparisons problem a local Moran’s I cluster map has. Only tracts whose LQ survives that correction are shown as significant.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Local quotient for 'black' with FDR-corrected permutation significance,
# then map LQ and hatch tracts that fail FDR 0.05.
# ===================================================================

# Permute each tract's 4-group composition under the city proportions.
sig = seg.local_significance(  # define sig
    tracts[2020],
    GROUPS,
    seg.local_quotient,
    group="black",  # define group
    permutations=999,  # define permutations
    alpha=0.05,  # define alpha
    seed=0,  # define seed
)
print(sig.describe())  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(f"\n{sig.significant_fdr.sum()} of {len(sig)} tracts are significant at FDR 0.05")  # run this analysis or plotting step

# Colour by LQ; hatch tracts that did not survive FDR correction.
ax = seg.plot_local_map(  # axes handle for drawing
    tracts[2020],
    sig["statistic"],
    significant=sig["significant_fdr"],  # define significant
    title="Local quotient for 'black' (2020), hatched = not significant",  # define title
    cmap="RdBu_r",  # define cmap
)
plt.show()  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Segregation Analysis
section: The multiscale segregation profile (fast, KD-tree based)
text:
The multiscale segregation profile (fast, KD-tree based)
How far does a tract’s segregation reach before it blends into the city’s overall composition? multiscale.compute_profile pools each tract’s composition within growing radii and measures its KL divergence from the city-wide composition at each one – Reardon et al.’s “spatial segregation profile” idea, but computed by querying a scipy.spatial.cKDTree for each tract’s own (typically small) neighbor list, never building the dense n x n distance matrix PySAL’s own implementation does. That is the difference between this running in milliseconds on 92 tracts (and staying linear-ish out to thousands) and running out of memory.
Three compact, mappable outputs come out of the profile instead of a raw curve per tract:

segregation_scale: the radius at which a tract’s divergence first drops below a threshold (small = a short-range, very local pattern; large/inf = persists broadly).
auc: area under the divergence-vs-radius curve (one number for “how segregated, integrated over scale”).
distortion: the fraction of a tract’s own-unit divergence still left at the largest radius queried (near 0 = decays away quickly with pooling; near 1 = barely decays over the measured range).



Code
# ===================================================================
# Multiscale KL divergence profiles and segregation-scale map.
# Radii span from a single tract (~250 m) to most of the city (~6000 m).
# ===================================================================

profile = seg.compute_profile(  # define profile
    tracts[2020],
    GROUPS,
    radii=[250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 6000],  # metres
    divergence="kl",  # Reardon KL divergence
    scale_threshold=0.05,  # converge when divergence falls below this
)
# Cap non-finite scales at the largest radius for mapping.
tracts[2020]["segregation_scale"] = np.where(  # assign a derived column or cell
    np.isfinite(profile.segregation_scale),  # run this analysis or plotting step
    profile.segregation_scale,
    6000.0,
)
tracts[2020]["profile_auc"] = profile.auc  # area under the divergence-radius curve

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))  # run this analysis or plotting step
seg.plot_local_map(  # run this analysis or plotting step
    tracts[2020], tracts[2020]["segregation_scale"], ax=axes[0],
    title="Segregation scale (m)", cmap="viridis",  # define title
)
seg.plot_profile(profile, ax=axes[1])  # highlight the most persistent tracts
axes[1].set_title("Divergence-vs-radius for the 5 most persistently segregated tracts")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
plt.tight_layout()  # run this analysis or plotting step
plt.show()  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Segregation Analysis
section: Spatial neighborhoods: pooling composition across nearby tracts
text:
Spatial neighborhoods: pooling composition across nearby tracts
A tract’s own population can be small enough that its composition is noisy. Pooling in nearby tracts first – building a “generalized spatial” version of any local measure – is what the neighborhoods module is for. kernel_weights gives every tract within a bandwidth a smooth (Gaussian) or hard-cutoff weight; knn_weights instead uses libpysal’s k-nearest-neighbor graph. Pass either into any local function’s neighborhood= argument.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Compare unpooled LQ with LQ pooled over a ~1200 m Gaussian kernel.
# knn_weights is built as the alternative neighbourhood constructor.
# ===================================================================

kernel_nb = seg.kernel_weights(tracts[2020], bandwidth=1200, kernel="gaussian")  # define kernel_nb
knn_nb = seg.knn_weights(tracts[2020], k=5)  # k-nearest tracts alternative

lq_unpooled = seg.local_quotient(tracts[2020], GROUPS, "black")  # own tract only
lq_pooled = seg.local_quotient(tracts[2020], GROUPS, "black", neighborhood=kernel_nb)  # define lq_pooled
print(f"std(LQ) unpooled: {lq_unpooled.std():.3f}   std(LQ) kernel-pooled: {lq_pooled.std():.3f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))  # run this analysis or plotting step
seg.plot_local_map(tracts[2020], lq_unpooled, ax=axes[0], title="LQ, unpooled (own tract only)")  # run this analysis or plotting step
seg.plot_local_map(tracts[2020], lq_pooled, ax=axes[1], title="LQ, pooled over a 1200 m Gaussian kernel")  # run this analysis or plotting step
plt.tight_layout()  # run this analysis or plotting step
plt.show()  # run this analysis or plotting step
_ = knn_nb  # constructed above to show the alternative; not plotted separately



std(LQ) unpooled: 0.177   std(LQ) kernel-pooled: 0.164

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Harmonizing boundaries across census years
1990’s 18 coarse tracts do not line up with the 92 tracts used from 2000 onward – exactly the boundary-redrawing problem every real multi-decade segregation panel runs into. data.areal_interpolate splits each 1990 tract’s counts across the 2000-vintage tracts it overlaps, in proportion to overlap area; data.dasymetric_interpolate instead weights by a raster’s mass inside each overlap piece (here, a synthetic built-up- intensity grid), so population lands preferentially on the land that could plausibly hold it rather than being spread uniformly across a large tract’s open space too.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Harmonise coarse 1990 tracts onto the 2000 geography two ways:
# areal (overlap area) vs dasymetric (built-up intensity weights).
# ===================================================================

# Area-weighted split of 1990 group counts onto 2000 tracts.
harmonized_areal = seg.areal_interpolate(tracts_1990_coarse, tracts[2000], GROUPS)  # define harmonized_areal
# Same split, but weighted by built-up intensity inside each overlap.
harmonized_dasymetric = seg.dasymetric_interpolate(  # define harmonized_dasymetric
    tracts_1990_coarse,
    tracts[2000],
    GROUPS,
    raster_path=DATA / "builtup_intensity.tif",  # define raster_path
)

# Total population is conserved; compare D under each method.
print(f"Coarse 1990 D(white, black):            {seg.dissimilarity(tracts_1990_coarse, ['white', 'black']):.3f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(f"Harmonized (areal) D(white, black):      {seg.dissimilarity(harmonized_areal, ['white', 'black']):.3f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(f"Harmonized (dasymetric) D(white, black): {seg.dissimilarity(harmonized_dasymetric, ['white', 'black']):.3f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"\nPopulation conserved? coarse={tracts_1990_coarse[GROUPS].sum().sum():.0f}  "  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"areal={harmonized_areal[GROUPS].sum().sum():.0f}  "  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"dasymetric={harmonized_dasymetric[GROUPS].sum().sum():.0f}"  # run this analysis or plotting step
)

Harmonized (areal) D(white, black):      0.402
Harmonized (dasymetric) D(white, black): 0.402

title: Segregation Analysis
section: A full four-period panel: trend test and decomposition
text:
A full four-period panel: trend test and decomposition
With 1990 harmonized onto the same tracts as 2000/2010/2020, all four years can be analyzed as one panel. temporal.trend computes an index for every period and runs a Mann-Kendall trend test across them (non-parametric, appropriate for a handful of census years rather than assuming a linear, normally-distributed trend).
decomposition.chain_decomposition then splits the change between every consecutive pair of periods into a spatial component (people’s arrangement across tracts changing) and a composition component (the city’s overall group mix changing), using a two-player Shapley value that is exactly additive by construction – the two components always sum to the observed change, which tests/test_segregation.py checks directly.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Build a consistent panel, test the Mann-Kendall trend in D, and chain
# spatial-vs-composition decompositions across consecutive periods.
# ===================================================================

# Harmonized 1990 plus the three shared-boundary years.
panel_gdfs = {  # define panel_gdfs
    1990: harmonized_areal,
    2000: tracts[2000],
    2010: tracts[2010],
    2020: tracts[2020],
}

# Mann-Kendall trend on dissimilarity(white, black) across the panel.
trend_result = seg.trend(panel_gdfs, ["white", "black"], seg.dissimilarity)  # define trend_result
print(trend_result["panel"])  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"\ntrend: {trend_result['trend']}  (p={trend_result['p_value']:.4f}, "  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"Sen slope={trend_result['sen_slope']:.5f} per period)"
)

ax = seg.plot_trend(trend_result["panel"], trend_result=trend_result)  # axes handle for drawing
ax.set_title("Dissimilarity(white, black) across the panel")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
plt.show()  # run this analysis or plotting step

# Spatial vs composition change for every consecutive pair of years.
chain = seg.chain_decomposition(panel_gdfs, ["white", "black"])  # define chain
print(chain[["period_from", "period_to", "total_change", "spatial_component", "composition_component"]])  # run this analysis or plotting step
ax2 = seg.plot_decomposition(chain)  # axes handle for drawing
plt.show()  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Segregation Analysis
text:
Summary

Region-wide indices (indices / report.compute) summarize a city in one number per group pairing, with a spatially-aware bootstrap confidence interval.
Local measures (local) and FDR-corrected permutation significance turn that one number into a LISA-style map of where segregation is concentrated.
The multiscale profile (multiscale) answers how far that segregation reaches, using a KD-tree instead of a dense pairwise-distance table – the specific scaling limit that motivated rewriting this instead of calling PySAL directly.
neighborhoods, data (boundary harmonization), temporal (panels and trend tests), and decomposition (chained, exactly-additive spatial-vs-composition splits) extend every one of those ideas across space, across boundary changes, and across time – the three gaps a two-values-at-a-time, unit-level-bootstrap tool cannot close.
report.export_for_causal is the hook back out to geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal and PyCausalML: a measured segregation surface, ready to use as an exposure or confounder rather than an assumption.

text:
Overview
Spatial accessibility asks how easily people can reach services. This notebook works through the standard toolkit on the synthetic region in Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/, using geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis for snapping, coverage, 2SFCA / E2SFCA, and Lorenz-Gini summaries.

Nearest-facility travel time (network vs straight line)
Network service areas (multi-source Dijkstra)
Coverage of total and older (65+) population within time thresholds
2SFCA and enhanced distance-decay E2SFCA
Hospital-closure scenario
Location-allocation ideas (p-median / maximal coverage)

Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at data/data_spatial_net, and imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis as sna.

section: Part A: Snap demand and supply to the network
text:
Part A: Snap demand and supply to the network
Demand points are tract centroids (population-weighted centroids from block data are better when available). We also record the snapping distance: the leg from the centroid to the road, which we convert to time at an assumed 30 km/h access speed.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Snap tract centroids and hospitals to the road network.
# Centroid-to-road legs become access_min at an assumed 30 km/h.
# ===================================================================

cent = tracts.geometry.centroid  # demand points (centroids as a proxy)
cent_gdf = tracts.copy()  # mutable copy stored as cent_gdf
cent_gdf.geometry = cent  # GeoDataFrame of centroid points for snapping
tracts["node"], snap_m = sna.snap_points_to_nodes(cent_gdf, G, return_dist=True)  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
# Convert snap distance (m) to minutes at 30 km/h = 500 m/min.
tracts["access_min"] = np.asarray(snap_m) / (30_000 / 60)  # run this analysis or plotting step
hosp["node"] = sna.snap_points_to_nodes(hosp, G)  # supply nodes
print(f"median centroid-to-road leg: {np.median(snap_m):.0f} m ({tracts.access_min.median():.1f} min)")  # status line for the notebook reader

section: Part B: Nearest hospital for everyone in one pass
text:
Part B: Nearest hospital for everyone in one pass
Running Dijkstra once per tract would work, but nx.multi_source_dijkstra is far more efficient: it starts from all hospitals at once and labels every node with the time to the nearest one. Because our roads are two-way, time from hospital to node equals time from node to hospital. (For networks with one-way streets, run it on G.reverse().)


Code
# ===================================================================
# Multi-source Dijkstra from all hospitals: nearest facility time/path.
# Compare network nearest hospital with Euclidean nearest hospital.
# ===================================================================

# One Dijkstra from every hospital node labels each network node.
dist, paths = nx.multi_source_dijkstra(G, set(hosp.node), weight="minutes")  # multi-source Dijkstra distances and paths
node2hosp = hosp.set_index("node")["hospital"]  # node id -> hospital name
# First node on each path is the source hospital that won the race.
nearest = {n: node2hosp[p[0]] for n, p in paths.items()}  # network node -> nearest hospital name

# Network minutes = on-network time + off-network access leg.
tracts["net_min"] = tracts.node.map(dist) + tracts.access_min  # run this analysis or plotting step
tracts["nearest_net"] = tracts.node.map(nearest)  # run this analysis or plotting step

# Straight-line comparison: min Euclidean distance to any hospital.
hx, hy = hosp.geometry.x.values, hosp.geometry.y.values  # hospital x/y coordinate arrays
D = np.hypot(cent.x.values[:, None] - hx, cent.y.values[:, None] - hy)  # pairwise distance matrix
tracts["euclid_km"] = D.min(axis=1) / 1000  # run this analysis or plotting step
tracts["nearest_euclid"] = hosp.hospital.values[D.argmin(axis=1)]  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Service-area and Facility Accessibility
text:
Part C: Service areas
The set of network locations closer (in time) to one facility than to any other is its network service area, the network analogue of a Voronoi polygon. Colouring every road segment by its nearest hospital and dissolving tracts by nearest hospital gives two views of it.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Map network service areas on roads and tract catchments by travel time.
# ===================================================================

nodes, edges = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G)  # convert MultiDiGraph to node/edge GeoDataFrames
# Colour each edge by the nearest hospital of its u-node.
edges["hospital"] = [nearest[u] for u, v, k in edges.index]  # notebook step
palette = dict(zip(hosp.hospital, ["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"]))  # hospital name -> display colour

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6.2))  # create a grid of subplot axes
# Left: roads coloured by nearest hospital (network Voronoi).
for h, sub in edges.groupby("hospital"):  # iterate over the collection
    sub.plot(ax=axes[0], color=palette[h], lw=1, label=h)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
hosp.plot(ax=axes[0], color="k", marker="P", markersize=120, zorder=3)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left")  # add a legend
axes[0].set_title("Network service areas (roads)")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
axes[0].set_axis_off()  # configure this subplot's labels or title

# Right: tract travel times with dissolved catchment boundaries.
tracts.plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax=axes[1],  # draw into these axes
    column="net_min",  # attribute used for the choropleth
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # colormap for continuous / categorical values

    lw=0.3,  # line width

tracts.dissolve("nearest_net").boundary.plot(ax=axes[1], color="k", lw=1.4)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
hosp.plot(ax=axes[1], color="k", marker="P", markersize=120, zorder=3)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
axes[1].set_title("Travel time and tract-level catchments")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
axes[1].set_axis_off()  # configure this subplot's labels or title

plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

title: Service-area and Facility Accessibility
section: Part E: Two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA)
text:
Part E: Two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA)
Luo & Wang (2003):

For each hospital j, compute a supply-to-demand ratio using all population within threshold \(d_0\) (we use 20 minutes): \(R_j = \dfrac{S_j}{\sum_{i:\, t_{ij} \le d_0} P_i}\)
For each tract i, sum the ratios of all hospitals it can reach: \(A_i = \sum_{j:\, t_{ij} \le d_0} R_j\)

The enhanced version (E2SFCA, Luo & Qi 2009) replaces the hard cutoff with a distance-decay weight \(f(t_{ij})\) in both steps. \(A_i\) is in beds per person; we report beds per 1,000.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Build tract-by-hospital travel-time matrix, then 2SFCA and E2SFCA.
# Accessibility reported as beds per 1,000 people.
# ===================================================================

# Tract-by-hospital travel-time matrix (minutes), including access legs.
H = []  # infection / prevalence trajectories
for r in hosp.itertuples():  # iterate GeoDataFrame rows as named tuples
    d = nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, r.node, weight="minutes")  # d argument
    H.append(tracts.node.map(d).values + tracts.access_min.values)  # append this record
T = np.array(H).T  # shape (tracts, hospitals), minutes
P = tracts.population.values.astype(float)  # demand vector
S = hosp.beds.values.astype(float)  # supply vector

# Hard 20-minute cutoff 2SFCA vs Gaussian-decay E2SFCA.
tracts["A_2sfca"] = sna.two_sfca(T, P, S)  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
tracts["A_e2sfca"] = sna.two_sfca(T, P, S, decay=lambda t: sna.gaussian_distance_decay(t, d0=20))  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
print(f"Region-wide supply: {S.sum() / P.sum() * 1000:.2f} beds per 1,000")  # status line for the notebook reader
tracts[["A_2sfca", "A_e2sfca"]].describe().round(2)  # run this analysis or plotting step

Both reveal something the nearest-facility map did not: tracts near small, crowded community hospitals can have lower effective supply than more distant tracts that also reach the large medical center.

Inequality in access
A Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient summarise how evenly access is distributed across the population.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients for 2SFCA vs E2SFCA accessibility.
# Population weights come from the demand vector P.
# ===================================================================

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))  # create figure and primary axes
for col, lab in [("A_2sfca", "2SFCA"), ("A_e2sfca", "E2SFCA")]:  # iterate over the collection
    x, y, g = sna.lorenz_curve_gini(tracts[col].values, P)  # cumulative shares + Gini
    ax.plot(x, y, label=f"{lab} (Gini = {g:.2f})")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=0.8)  # equality reference
ax.set(  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    xlabel="cumulative share of population",  # x-axis label
    ylabel="cumulative share of accessibility",  # y-axis label

title: Service-area and Facility Accessibility
section: Part F: Scenario: a hospital closes
text:
Part F: Scenario: a hospital closes
Rural hospital closures are a real and recurring policy issue. Remove the Lakeview Community Hospital and recompute nearest-facility times, coverage, and E2SFCA.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Closure scenario: remove Lakeview and recompute times / E2SFCA / coverage.
# ===================================================================

closed = "Lakeview Community Hospital"  # name of the hospital closed in the scenario
keep = hosp.hospital != closed  # boolean mask of hospitals that remain open
# Nearest-facility times without the closed hospital.
dist_c, _ = nx.multi_source_dijkstra(G, set(hosp.loc[keep, "node"]), weight="minutes")  # run this analysis or plotting step
tracts["net_min_closed"] = tracts.node.map(dist_c) + tracts.access_min  # run this analysis or plotting step
# E2SFCA with the closed hospital's column removed from T and S.
tracts["A_e2sfca_closed"] = sna.two_sfca(  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    T[:, keep.values],  # notebook step
    P,  # notebook step
    S[keep.values],  # notebook step
    decay=lambda t: sna.gaussian_distance_decay(t, d0=20),  # distance-decay function for E2SFCA
)
tracts["added_min"] = tracts.net_min_closed - tracts.net_min  # delay vs baseline

# Side-by-side coverage tables before and after the closure.

    {  # notebook step

Notice what does not change: the ratios of the remaining hospitals. In 2SFCA each \(R_j\) depends only on the population inside hospital j’s own catchment, so Lakeview’s former patients are not “pushed” onto Northfield or Eastbrook. Capturing that spillover requires models with facility choice or competition, such as 3SFCA (Wan et al., 2012) or Huff-model-weighted variants, a good extension exercise.

title: Service-area and Facility Accessibility
section: Part G: Location-allocation: where should a new facility go?
text:
Part G: Location-allocation: where should a new facility go?
Two classic objectives, evaluated over the 20 towns as candidate sites:

p-median: minimise total population-weighted travel time.
Maximal coverage: maximise population within a threshold (here 15 minutes).

With one new site we can evaluate every candidate exhaustively. For several sites, greedy addition or integer programming (e.g., spopt.locate) is used.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Exhaustive one-site location search over towns without a hospital.
# Compare p-median (min mean time) vs maximal coverage (<= 15 min).
# ===================================================================

# Candidate towns that do not already host a hospital.
cand = towns[~towns.town.isin(hosp.town)].copy()  # candidate facility sites without an existing hospital
cand["node"] = sna.snap_points_to_nodes(cand, G)  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
cur = tracts.net_min.values  # baseline nearest-facility minutes
rows = []  # accumulate one record per edge / pair / scenario
for r in cand.itertuples():  # iterate GeoDataFrame rows as named tuples
    # Minutes from the candidate site to every tract (plus access leg).
    d = nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, r.node, weight="minutes")  # d argument
    t_new = np.minimum(cur, tracts.node.map(d).values + tracts.access_min.values)  # t_new argument
    rows.append({  # append this record
        "candidate": r.town,  # continue string literal
        "pop-weighted mean min": np.average(t_new, weights=P),  # continue multi-line call
        "% pop <= 15 min": 100 * P[t_new <= 15].sum() / P.sum(),  # continue multi-line call
        "% 65+ <= 15 min": 100 * tracts.pop65.values[t_new <= 15].sum() / tracts.pop65.sum(),  # continue multi-line call
    })
loc = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # location-allocation evaluation table
# Baseline row with no new site for comparison.
base = {  # define base
    "candidate": "(no new site)",  # continue multi-line call
    "pop-weighted mean min": np.average(cur, weights=P),  # continue multi-line call
    "% pop <= 15 min": 100 * P[cur <= 15].sum() / P.sum(),  # continue multi-line call
    "% 65+ <= 15 min": 100 * tracts.pop65.values[cur <= 15].sum() / tracts.pop65.sum(),  # continue multi-line call
}
loc = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame([base]), loc]).set_index("candidate").round(2)  # location-allocation evaluation table
print("p-median best        :", loc["pop-weighted mean min"].iloc[1:].idxmin())  # status line for the notebook reader
print("maximal coverage best:", loc["% pop <= 15 min"].iloc[1:].idxmax())  # status line for the notebook reader
loc.sort_values("pop-weighted mean min").head(6)  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Service-area and Facility Accessibility
text:
Summary

multi_source_dijkstra gives nearest-facility time and allocation for every node in one pass.
Network service areas and coverage tables are the core descriptive outputs; always report vulnerable subgroups too.
Euclidean distance misallocates some tracts and misstates times; use the network.
2SFCA / E2SFCA account for capacity and competition; Lorenz curves and Gini summarise equity.
Closure and siting scenarios turn the same machinery into a decision-support tool.


Exercises

Repeat Part E with \(d_0\) = 15 and 30 minutes (at 30 minutes almost every tract reaches every hospital in this compact region; what happens to the map?). How does the Gini coefficient respond?
Weight demand by population aged 65+ instead of total population in 2SFCA. Which tracts change most?
Extend Part G greedily to add two new sites. Is the best pair the same as the best single site plus the next best?
Model winter conditions by slowing residential roads to 30 km/h. Which tracts drop below the 20-minute standard?

title: Road networks with OSMnx: Routing and Accessibility
text:
Overview
OSMnx downloads, models, and analyses street networks from OpenStreetMap as NetworkX MultiDiGraphs with geometry. This notebook runs offline on the synthetic GraphML in Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/ and uses geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis for travel times, snapping, routing summaries, OD matrices, and closure impact.
Topics:

Network statistics and edge speeds / travel times
Snap towns to the network and route by distance vs time
Town-to-town travel-time matrix
Isochrones and cumulative-opportunity accessibility
Critical segments and a road-closure scenario

title: Road networks with OSMnx: Routing and Accessibility
text:
Getting real data from OpenStreetMap (reference)
The notebook runs offline on the synthetic network, but the code below is all you need to repeat every step on a real place. The download functions return an unprojected graph (lon/lat); project it before measuring areas or buffers.
import osmnx as ox

# by place name (geocoded boundary)
G = ox.graph_from_place("Ithaca, New York, USA", network_type="drive")

# by point + distance, or by bounding box (left, bottom, right, top)
G = ox.graph_from_point((42.4440, -76.5019), dist=15_000, network_type="drive")
G = ox.graph_from_bbox((-76.60, 42.38, -76.40, 42.50), network_type="drive")

G = ox.project_graph(G)                # to the local UTM zone
ox.save_graphml(G, "ithaca_drive.graphml")

# points of interest (hospitals, schools, markets ...)
hospitals = ox.features_from_place(
    "Tompkins County, New York, USA", tags={"amenity": "hospital"}
)
network_type can be "drive", "walk", "bike", "all", or a custom Overpass filter. Everything after Setup works identically on a downloaded graph.

Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at data/data_spatial_net, and imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis as sna.

section: Part B: Speeds and travel times
text:
Part B: Speeds and travel times
Shortest distance is rarely what people care about; shortest time is. OSMnx imputes speeds in two steps:

add_edge_speeds reads the OSM maxspeed tag; where missing, it fills the mean observed speed of that highway class (or values you pass with hwy_speeds).
add_edge_travel_times computes travel_time (seconds) = length ÷ speed.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Impute highway-class speeds and edge travel times (seconds).
# prepare_travel_times wraps OSMnx add_edge_speeds + add_edge_travel_times.
# ===================================================================

# Default speeds (km/h) by highway class when maxspeed tags are missing.
HWY_SPEEDS = {"residential": 50, "tertiary": 60, "secondary": 70, "primary": 90}  # default speeds (km/h) by highway class
# Attach speed_kph and travel_time attributes on every edge.
G = sna.prepare_travel_times(G, hwy_speeds=HWY_SPEEDS, minutes_attr=None)  # impute speeds and edge travel times
# Edge GeoDataFrame for grouped mean speed / length / time by class.
edges = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G, nodes=False)  # edge GeoDataFrame (LineStrings)
edges.groupby("highway")[["speed_kph", "length", "travel_time"]].mean().round(1)  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Road networks with OSMnx: Routing and Accessibility
text:
Part D: Isochrones
An isochrone is the area reachable within a time budget. Two steps:

nx.ego_graph(G, center, radius=t, distance="travel_time") returns every node reachable within t.
Turn the reachable network into a polygon. A convex hull is fast but overstates coverage; buffering the reachable edges and dissolving them is more faithful to the network.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Build nested isochrones from Centerville for 8 / 15 / 22 minute budgets.
# Compare convex-hull area with a network-buffer polygon area.
# ===================================================================

center = towns.set_index("town").loc["Centerville", "node"]  # isochrone seed node
budgets = [8, 15, 22]  # minutes
colors = ["#fee391", "#fe9929", "#cc4c02"]  # light -> dark for increasing time
iso = []  # accumulate one record per time budget
# Draw largest budget first so smaller fills sit on top in the map cell.
for t in sorted(budgets, reverse=True):  # iterate over the collection
    # Nodes reachable within t minutes (radius is in seconds).
    sub = nx.ego_graph(G, center, radius=t * 60, distance="travel_time")  # sub argument
    e = ox.graph_to_gdfs(sub, nodes=False)  # reachable edge geometries
    # Fast but optimistic coverage: convex hull of reachable nodes.
    hull = MultiPoint([Point(G.nodes[n]["x"], G.nodes[n]["y"]) for n in sub.nodes]).convex_hull  # hull argument
    # Network-faithful outline: buffer edges, dissolve, then erode slightly.
    buff = unary_union(e.geometry.buffer(1500)).buffer(-700)  # dilate then erode = smoother outline
    iso.append({  # append this record
        "minutes": t,  # continue string literal
        "nodes": sub.number_of_nodes(),  # continue multi-line call
        "hull_km2": hull.area / 1e6,  # continue string literal
        "network_km2": buff.area / 1e6,  # continue string literal
        "geometry": buff,  # continue string literal
        "hull": hull,  # continue string literal
    })
iso = gpd.GeoDataFrame(iso, crs=G.graph["crs"])  # isochrone records / GeoDataFrame
iso[["minutes", "nodes", "hull_km2", "network_km2"]].round(1)  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Road networks with OSMnx: Routing and Accessibility
text:
Part E: Accessibility surface
Cumulative-opportunity accessibility counts the opportunities (here, town population as a proxy for jobs and services) reachable within a time threshold:
\[A_i = \sum_j O_j \cdot \mathbb{1}(t_{ij} \le T)\]
Computing it for every node gives a continuous accessibility surface.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Cumulative-opportunity accessibility within 25 minutes of each node.
# Opportunity proxy: town population snapped onto network nodes.
# ===================================================================

T = 25 * 60  # accessibility time budget in seconds
# Population mass at each snapped town node (sum if duplicates share a node).
town_nodes = towns.set_index("node")["population"].groupby(level=0).sum()  # population mass at snapped town nodes
acc = {}  # node id -> reachable population
for n in G.nodes:  # iterate over the collection
    # All nodes reachable from n within the time cutoff.
    reach = nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, n, cutoff=T, weight="travel_time")  # reach argument
    acc[n] = town_nodes.reindex(list(reach)).sum()  # sum population at reached town nodes
nodes = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G, edges=False)  # node GeoDataFrame (Points)
nodes["access_25min"] = pd.Series(acc)  # attach accessibility to the node gdf

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7))  # create figure and primary axes
ox.graph_to_gdfs(G, nodes=False).plot(ax=ax, color="#dddddd", lw=0.4)  # faint road backdrop
nodes.sort_values("access_25min").plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax=ax,  # draw into these axes
    column="access_25min",  # attribute used for the choropleth
    cmap="viridis",  # colormap for continuous / categorical values
    markersize=14,  # marker area or size
    legend=True,  # show a legend or colour bar
    legend_kwds={"label": "population reachable in 25 min", "shrink": 0.7},  # legend / colour-bar styling
)
towns.plot(ax=ax, color="red", markersize=8)  # opportunity locations
ax.set_title("Cumulative-opportunity accessibility")  # panel / map title
ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

Part F: Critical segments and a road closure
Edge betweenness weighted by travel time estimates how many fastest paths use each segment; high values mark corridors whose disruption would affect many trips. On large graphs use k sampled sources for speed.

title: Road networks with OSMnx: Routing and Accessibility
text:
Summary

graph_from_place / point / bbox → project_graph → save_graphml is the standard OSMnx data pipeline.
add_edge_speeds + add_edge_travel_times turn a geometric network into a time network.
nearest_nodes snaps places to the network; shortest_path and Dijkstra give routes and OD matrices.
Isochrones = ego_graph with a travel-time radius, then a polygon (prefer network buffers to convex hulls).
Cumulative accessibility and travel-time betweenness reveal who is well connected and which roads matter most.


Exercises

Reduce all residential speeds to 30 km/h (a snowstorm) and recompute the 25-minute accessibility surface. Which towns lose the most?
Replace the cumulative measure with a gravity accessibility \(A_i = \sum_j O_j e^{-\beta t_{ij}}\) and compare maps for β = 0.05 and 0.15.
Close the five highest-betweenness segments at once. Does any town pair now exceed 60 minutes?
Download a real drive network for your own county and reproduce Parts B-D.

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text: Banner

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text:
Overview
A network is a set of nodes (also called vertices) joined by edges (also called links). A spatial network gives every node a location, and it gives every edge a geographic meaning: a road segment, a shared boundary, a volume of trips, or a social tie whose chance of existing falls with distance.
The same object appears under several names. Transport planners say network. Graph theory says graph. Spatial statistics says weights matrix. An origin-destination table is a flow network written as a matrix. All four are the same idea: who is connected to whom, and what that connection costs or carries.
Three ingredients turn an ordinary graph into a spatial one:

Locations. Each node has coordinates and a coordinate reference system (longitude/latitude, or a projected CRS such as a UTM zone).
A connection rule. Edges exist because a road was built, two polygons touch, two points fall inside a distance, or a survey recorded a tie.
A weight. The edge stores a length, a travel time, a count of commuters, or a binary “linked / not linked”.

Once the graph exists, analysis is a shortest-path, a neighbour list, a flow balance, or a diffusion process on those weights. The map is how you read the result; the graph is how you compute it.

A small vocabulary







Term
Meaning in this chapter




Node
A junction, town, tract, hospital, or farmer


Edge
A road segment, shared border, trip, or advice tie


Weight
Length (km), travel time (minutes), or volume (commuters)


Directed edge
A one-way street, a commute from home to work, or “A seeks advice from B”


Path
A sequence of edges from an origin to a destination


Component
A set of nodes that can reach one another


Embedding
The coordinates that place the graph on the Earth


Impedance
The cost minimised by a route (distance or time)

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text:
Measuring a spatial network

Length and travel time
Edge length has to respect the CRS.

On longitude/latitude, length is the haversine (great-circle) distance. One degree of longitude is shorter than one degree of latitude, so treating degrees as flat x/y stretches east-west distances.
On a projected metric CRS (metres), length is ordinary Euclidean distance between the endpoints.

Travel time then follows from length and speed:
\[t = \frac{\text{length}}{\text{speed}}\]
OSMnx fills speeds from the highway class (or from an observed maxspeed tag) and stores travel_time in seconds. Shortest-distance routes and shortest-time routes diverge wherever fast roads are longer than slow ones.


Circuity
Circuity compares the route you can actually travel with the straight line between the same two points:
\[\text{circuity} = \frac{\text{network distance}}{\text{straight-line distance}}\]
A value of 1 is a perfectly direct link. Urban street grids often fall around 1.2-1.4; mountainous or river-cut regions run higher. Circuity is why a 5 km buffer around a hospital overstates who can reach it: people travel along roads.


How connected is the network?
Kansky indices summarise a planar network with three ratios. With (v) nodes, (e) edges, and (p) components:
\[
\beta = \frac{e}{v}, \qquad
\alpha = \frac{e - v + p}{2v - 5}, \qquad
\gamma = \frac{e}{3(v - 2)}
\]

β is the average number of edges per node. A tree has β just under 1; a dense street grid is higher.
α (the redundancy index) is the share of the maximum number of cycles a planar graph can hold. α near 0 is a branching tree; α near 1 is as looped as a planar graph can be.
γ is the share of the maximum number of edges in a connected planar graph.

Alongside those indices, a description of a spatial graph usually reports the number of components, the share of nodes in the largest component, average clustering, and mean path length. A road network that looks connected on a map can still have a bridge whose removal splits it in two.


Distance decay
Across roads, trips, and social ties, interaction thins out as separation grows. A random geometric graph links every pair of points closer than a threshold. A Waxman graph links them with probability
\[P(\text{link}) \propto \exp(-d / d_0)\]
Empirical link rates, the chance two tracts touch, two towns exchange commuters, or two farmers name each other, follow the same shape. Distance decay is the reason a neighbour graph, a gravity model, and an advice network belong in one chapter.

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text:
Types of spatial networks
The connection rule, more than the software, decides which network you have. This chapter works through four types. The same GeoLattice functions serve all of them; what changes is how edges are defined.










Type
Nodes
Edges
Weight
Leading question




Transportation and infrastructure
Junctions, stops, towns
Road, rail, pipe, or stream segments
Length, minutes
What is the best route, and who is cut off if a link fails?


Proximity and contiguity
Polygons or points
Shared border, or nearness in space
Binary, or inverse distance
Who counts as a neighbour?


Flow and interaction
Places or zones
Origin-destination pairs
Trips, tonnes, migrants
Where does volume go, and which places form a region?


Spatially embedded social networks
People, farms, firms
Advice, kinship, collaboration
Binary or frequency
Who should be reached first so something spreads?




Transportation and infrastructure networks
Edges are physical objects. A street, a rail line, a water main, or a channel is a linestring with a length. Nodes are intersections, stops, or the places snapped onto that network. These graphs are embedded: you can draw every edge on a map, and most of them are planar or nearly so (bridges and tunnels are the usual exceptions).
Typical products:

a shortest path by distance or by time
an origin-destination matrix of travel times
an isochrone, the set of nodes reachable within 10, 20, or 30 minutes
the edges whose removal adds the most travel time (a closure scenario)

Notebooks 03_06_01 and 03_06_02 build this type. 03_06_04 uses the same road graph to measure access to hospitals.


Proximity and contiguity networks
Many GIS layers have no built links. Counties, tracts, farms, and sample points become a network only after you choose a neighbour rule.








Rule
Two units are linked when…
Geometry




Rook
They share a boundary of positive length
Polygons


Queen
They share any point, including a corner
Polygons


k-nearest neighbours
One is among the k closest of the other
Points


Distance band
They lie inside a threshold distance
Points


Delaunay
Their Voronoi cells touch
Points


Gabriel / relative neighbourhood (RNG)
The empty-region test of that graph family holds
Points


Shared endpoints
Line ends meet, after snapping
Lines



Rook and Queen are the standard contiguity rules for a spatial weights matrix (W). Queen has at least as many links as Rook; on a regular grid the corner contacts are the difference. k-NN graphs keep every unit connected (each has k neighbours) and are directed until you symmetrise them. A distance band can leave islands, units with no neighbour, until the threshold reaches the minimum that connects the nearest isolated pair.
These graphs are the neighbour structure for spatial lag, Moran’s I, and regionalisation. Notebook 03_06_03 builds all of them from a GeoDataFrame with libpysal.


Flow and interaction networks
A flow network records movement between places. The natural storage is an origin-destination (OD) table: one row per pair, with a volume. As a graph, the same table is directed and weighted. The edge i → j carries commuters, freight, migrants, or trade, and it is a different edge from j → i.
Standard summaries:

inflow, outflow, and net flow at each place
a gravity model, which predicts volume from the size of the two places and the cost of separating them

\[F_{ij} = k \, O_i^{\alpha} \, D_j^{\beta} \, c_{ij}^{\gamma}\]
Here (O_i) and (D_j) are origin and destination mass (population, jobs), (c_{ij}) is impedance (minutes or kilometres), and () is negative: longer separations carry less flow. The chapter fits this both by ordinary least squares on the logarithms and by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML), which keeps the zero flows that a log transform drops.

a dominant-flow hierarchy (Nystuen-Dacey): each place points to the larger place that receives its single biggest outflow, which draws a tree of central places
functional regions from community detection on the symmetrised flows
a metapopulation model in which infection (or information) moves with the commuting matrix

Notebook 03_06_05 works this type on a synthetic commuting table, with travel time taken from the road network.


Spatially embedded social networks
People and organisations have coordinates too. An advice network, a kinship network, or a collaboration network is spatial when ties are more common at short distances and still exist, more rarely, across long ones. The edges are choices, recorded in a survey or inferred from interaction, and direction matters: if farmer i seeks advice from farmer j, information flows from j to i. In-degree (how often someone is named) is a simple measure of opinion leadership.
Two diffusion rules sit on the same adjacency matrix:

Simple contagion. One contact with an adopter is enough to adopt. Disease and many rumours behave this way.
Complex contagion. Adoption needs several adopting neighbours. Practices that are costly, unfamiliar, or socially risky often behave this way, so a single well-connected outsider may fail to spark a village while a pair of local leaders succeeds.

Distance still structures the graph: most ties stay inside a village, and a few bridges join villages. Those bridges, and farmers with high participation (ties spread across communities) or high diffusion centrality, are the people an extension service wants to train. Notebook 03_06_06 is the case study.

Accessibility in one formula
Service-area work in this chapter uses the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA). Supply at facility (j) is shared across the demand that can reach it, then each demand location (i) sums the supply ratios it can reach:
\[
R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_k P_k \, W(d_{kj})}, \qquad
A_i = \sum_j R_j \, W(d_{ij})
\]
(S_j) is supply (beds, clinics), (P_k) is demand (population), and (d) is network time. In classic 2SFCA the weight (W) is 1 inside a time threshold and 0 outside. Enhanced 2SFCA replaces that step with a smooth decay, such as a Gaussian, so a facility 5 minutes away counts more than one 25 minutes away. A Lorenz curve and a Gini coefficient then show whether those scores are shared evenly across the population.
The same travel times feed location-allocation sketches: the p-median idea (place facilities to reduce population-weighted travel time) and maximal coverage (place them so more people fall inside a time budget).
