section: A workflow that fits every type
text:
A workflow that fits every type
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  1. STATE THE QUESTION AND THE NODES                                |
|     Routes, neighbours, flows, or diffusion?                         |
|     Junctions, zones, facilities, or people?                         |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  2. CHOOSE THE CONNECTION RULE                                      |
|     Physical links  |  contiguity / k-NN / distance  |  OD table    |
|     or a recorded social tie                                         |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  3. SET THE CRS AND THE WEIGHT                                      |
|     Haversine or a projected CRS for length; speed to travel time;  |
|     volume for flows; binary or distance-decay for social ties      |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  4. DESCRIBE THE GRAPH                                              |
|     Components, degree, circuity, Kansky α/β/γ, distance decay      |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  5. COMPUTE THE QUANTITY THE QUESTION ASKS FOR                     |
|     Shortest paths, isochrones, 2SFCA, gravity fit, communities,    |
|     or a contagion run                                               |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  6. MAP A SCENARIO                                                  |
|     A closed road, a new clinic, a different neighbour rule,        |
|     or a different set of people trained first                      |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
Steps 1-3 are the modelling choices. Steps 4-6 are what the notebooks compute. Changing the neighbour rule or the time threshold and watching the map change is part of the analysis, in the same spirit as a sensitivity test in suitability modelling.

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text:
Network analysis with GeoLattice
The hands-on notebooks call one module:
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import network_analysis as sna
Graphs are NetworkX objects (Graph, DiGraph, or MultiDiGraph). Road networks are OSMnx graphs stored as GraphML. Polygon and point neighbours are libpysal weights converted to NetworkX. Tables of places and flows stay in GeoPandas and pandas, so a result can be mapped with the same .plot calls as the rest of this course.

title: Spatial Network Analysis
text:
The four types, drawn small
The next cell draws a schematic of each type. Edges in the transportation panel are street segments; the dashed line is the straight-line comparison used for circuity. The contiguity panel links tract centroids that share a border. The flow panel draws commuting arrows, with width proportional to volume. The social panel clusters advice ties inside villages and keeps a few bridges between them.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Numeric and plotting stack for the four schematic panels.
import numpy as np  # random village points and array arithmetic
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes for the 2x2 schematic
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Circle  # arrows, tracts, nodes

# Fixed seed so the social-panel village scatter is reproducible.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)  # reproducible random generator

# ===================================================================
# Draw a 2x2 schematic of the four spatial network types used in this
# chapter: transportation, contiguity, flow, and social embedding.
# ===================================================================

# Create a 2x2 grid of axes for the four network-type panels.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12.2, 10.2))  # create a grid of subplot axes


def style(ax, title):
    """Apply a shared title, hide ticks, and lighten spines for schematic panels."""
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontweight="bold", fontsize=12, pad=8)  # left-aligned panel title
    ax.set_xticks([])  # hide x tick labels on schematic axes
    ax.set_yticks([])  # hide y tick labels on schematic axes
    for spine in ax.spines.values():  # iterate over the collection
        spine.set_color("#d0d5dd")  # soft grey frame around each panel
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # keep street / tract geometry undistorted


# --- A. Transportation: street grid, route, and straight line -------------
ax = axes[0, 0]  # top-left panel
cols, rows = np.arange(5), np.arange(4)  # 5 vertical and 4 horizontal grid lines
# Draw horizontal street segments across each row.
for y in rows:  # iterate over the collection
    ax.plot([cols[0], cols[-1]], [y, y], color="#b7c3d0", lw=3, zorder=1, solid_capstyle="round")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
# Draw vertical street segments across each column.
for x in cols:  # iterate over the collection
    ax.plot([x, x], [rows[0], rows[-1]], color="#b7c3d0", lw=3, zorder=1, solid_capstyle="round")  # draw lines or edges on the axes

# Network route that follows the grid from origin to destination.
route = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3)]  # ordered route vertices for the schematic
rx, ry = zip(*route)  # unzip route vertices into x and y sequences
ax.plot(rx, ry, color="#c0392b", lw=3.2, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="round", label="Network route")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
# Straight-line chord used in the circuity ratio (network / Euclidean).
ax.plot([0, 3], [0, 3], color="#1f4e79", lw=1.6, ls="--", zorder=2, label="Straight line")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
# Scatter all grid junctions as small nodes.
ax.scatter(cols.repeat(len(rows)), np.tile(rows, len(cols)), s=28, c="#1f4e79", zorder=3)  # plot point markers
# Highlight origin and destination nodes.
ax.scatter([0, 3], [0, 3], s=90, c="#c0392b", zorder=4)  # plot point markers
ax.annotate("origin", (0, 0), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-28, -14), fontsize=8, color="#c0392b")  # label a feature near its coordinates
ax.annotate("destination", (3, 3), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 6), fontsize=8, color="#c0392b")  # label a feature near its coordinates
# Caption explaining the circuity definition shown in the panel.
ax.text(0.02, 0.98, "circuity = route / straight line", transform=ax.transAxes,  # caption or note in axes / figure coordinates
        va="top", fontsize=8, color="#344054")  # vertical alignment
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right")  # route vs straight-line legend
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 4.8)  # pad around the street grid
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 3.7)  # pad or zoom the y extent
style(ax, "A   Transportation")  # apply shared schematic panel styling

# --- B. Contiguity: tracts and shared borders -----------------------------
ax = axes[0, 1]  # top-right panel
nrow, ncol = 2, 3  # 2x3 tract grid
# Draw tract polygons and label each cell.
for i in range(nrow):  # loop over an integer range
    for j in range(ncol):  # loop over an integer range
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j, i), 1, 1, facecolor="#e8f1fb", edgecolor="#1f4e79", lw=1.2))  # add a shape / arrow patch to the axes
        ax.text(j + 0.5, i + 0.78, f"T{i * ncol + j + 1}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color="#1f4e79")  # caption or note in axes / figure coordinates

def centroid(i, j):
    """Return the centroid (x, y) of tract cell (row i, column j)."""
    return j + 0.5, i + 0.5  # return the computed result

# Rook neighbours: draw an edge only when two tracts share a full border.
for i in range(nrow):  # loop over an integer range
    for j in range(ncol):  # loop over an integer range
        for di, dj in ((0, 1), (1, 0)):  # right neighbour and upper neighbour
            ni, nj = i + di, j + dj  # notebook step
            if ni < nrow and nj < ncol:  # conditional branch
                x0, y0 = centroid(i, j)  # run this analysis or plotting step
                x1, y1 = centroid(ni, nj)  # run this analysis or plotting step
                ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color="#1a7a4c", lw=1.8, zorder=2)  # draw lines or edges on the axes
# Plot tract centroids as graph nodes.
for i in range(nrow):  # loop over an integer range
    for j in range(ncol):  # loop over an integer range
        ax.add_patch(Circle(centroid(i, j), 0.06, facecolor="#1a7a4c", edgecolor="none", zorder=3))  # add a shape / arrow patch to the axes
ax.text(0.02, 0.98, "Rook: centroids join across a shared border", transform=ax.transAxes,  # caption or note in axes / figure coordinates
        va="top", fontsize=8, color="#344054")  # vertical alignment
ax.set_xlim(-0.15, 3.15)  # pad or zoom the x extent
ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 2.35)  # pad or zoom the y extent
style(ax, "B   Contiguity")  # apply shared schematic panel styling

# --- C. Flow: commuting arrows --------------------------------------------
ax = axes[1, 0]  # bottom-left panel
# Town locations (x, y) and marker size proxy (population).
towns = {  # schematic town locations and sizes
    "North": (1.6, 2.6, 42),  # continue multi-line call
    "West": (0.2, 1.2, 18),  # continue multi-line call
    "East": (3.0, 1.3, 22),  # continue multi-line call
    "South": (1.5, 0.15, 12),  # continue multi-line call
    "Hub": (1.6, 1.35, 55),  # continue multi-line call
}
# Directed commuting volumes (origin, destination, volume).
flows = [  # town in-/out-/net-flow balance table
    ("West", "Hub", 8),  # continue multi-line call
    ("East", "Hub", 9),  # continue multi-line call
    ("South", "Hub", 5),  # continue multi-line call
    ("North", "Hub", 11),  # continue multi-line call
    ("Hub", "North", 4),  # continue multi-line call
    ("West", "South", 1.5),  # continue multi-line call
    ("East", "North", 2),  # continue multi-line call
]
# Draw each OD flow as an arrow whose width scales with volume.
for a, b, vol in flows:  # iterate over the collection
    x0, y0, _ = towns[a]  # notebook step
    x1, y1, _ = towns[b]  # notebook step
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(  # add a shape / arrow patch to the axes
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1),  # origin and destination coordinates
        arrowstyle="-|>",  # filled arrow head
        mutation_scale=10 + vol,  # head size grows with volume
        lw=0.4 + 0.28 * vol,  # stroke width proportional to volume
        color="#1a7a4c",  # artist colour
        alpha=0.85,  # regularisation strength (0 = unpenalised PPML)
        connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.12",  # slight curve so overlapping OD pairs separate
        shrinkA=14, shrinkB=14,  # keep arrow tips clear of town markers
    ))
# Offset each town label so it does not cover the marker.
label_at = {  # label offsets so text clears markers
    "North": (0, 14, "center"),  # continue multi-line call
    "West": (-12, 2, "right"),  # continue multi-line call
    "East": (12, 2, "left"),  # continue multi-line call
    "South": (0, -16, "center"),  # continue multi-line call
    "Hub": (14, 6, "left"),  # continue multi-line call
}
for name, (x, y, pop) in towns.items():  # iterate key/value pairs
    ax.scatter([x], [y], s=8 * pop, c="#1f4e79", zorder=3)  # marker area scales with population
    dx, dy, ha = label_at[name]  # notebook step
    ax.annotate(name, (x, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),  # label a feature near its coordinates
                ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=8, color="#1f4e79",  # horizontal alignment
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))  # bbox argument
ax.text(0.02, 0.98, "Arrow width is commuting volume", transform=ax.transAxes,  # caption or note in axes / figure coordinates
        va="top", fontsize=8, color="#344054")  # vertical alignment
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 3.6)  # pad or zoom the x extent
ax.set_ylim(-0.35, 3.15)  # pad or zoom the y extent
style(ax, "C   Flow")  # apply shared schematic panel styling

# --- D. Social: villages, local ties, bridges -----------------------------
ax = axes[1, 1]  # bottom-right panel
centers = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [2.7, 0.25], [1.35, 2.35]])  # three village centres
village_color = ["#1f4e79", "#1a7a4c", "#b86e00"]  # one colour per village
points = []  # will hold the farmer point clouds
# Scatter farmers around each village and link nearby pairs (local ties).
for c, col in zip(centers, village_color):  # iterate paired sequences together
    pts = c + rng.normal(scale=0.28, size=(8, 2))  # 8 farmers per village
    points.append(pts)  # append this record
    for i in range(len(pts)):  # loop over an integer range
        for j in range(i + 1, len(pts)):  # loop over an integer range
            if np.hypot(*(pts[i] - pts[j])) < 0.55:  # link only close farmers
                ax.plot([pts[i, 0], pts[j, 0]], [pts[i, 1], pts[j, 1]],  # draw lines or edges on the axes
                        color="#9bb0c3", lw=0.8, zorder=1)  # artist colour
# Two between-village bridges that let practices leave a village.
bridges = [(points[0][2], points[1][5]), (points[1][1], points[2][4])]  # between-village bridge endpoints
for p, q in bridges:  # iterate over the collection
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color="#c0392b", lw=1.6, zorder=2)  # draw lines or edges on the axes
# Plot farmers coloured by village membership.
for pts, col in zip(points, village_color):  # iterate paired sequences together
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=36, c=col, zorder=3)  # plot point markers
ax.text(0.02, 0.98, "Most ties stay inside a village; a few bridges cross",  # caption or note in axes / figure coordinates
        transform=ax.transAxes, va="top", fontsize=8, color="#344054")  # coordinate transform for text placement
ax.set_xlim(-0.9, 3.7)  # pad or zoom the x extent
ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 3.3)  # pad or zoom the y extent
style(ax, "D   Social")  # apply shared schematic panel styling

# Shared figure title and tight layout before display.
fig.suptitle("Four kinds of spatial network", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", y=1.01)  # shared figure title above all panels
fig.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the schematic in the notebook










Reading the figure

A: Transportation. The red path is a legal route along street segments. The dashed line is the straight-line distance used in the circuity ratio. Service areas and hospital access in this chapter follow the red kind of path.
B: Contiguity. Tract polygons become nodes at their centroids. A Rook edge exists only where two tracts share a boundary segment. Queen contiguity would add the corner contacts this panel leaves out.
C: Flow. Each arrow is a directed commuting volume. The largest arrows point toward the hub, which is the pattern a dominant-flow hierarchy and a gravity model both try to summarise.
D: Social. Advice ties cluster inside villages because farmers talk to people nearby. The red bridges are the between-village ties that let a new practice leave the village where it started.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text: Banner

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
section: Comparing maps: the Jaccard index of top areas
text:
Comparing maps: the Jaccard index of top areas
Suitability values from different model variants are not on comparable scales. Product values, for example, are always lower than Sum values. A fairer comparison asks whether two variants identify the same best land.

Take the top 20% of feasible cells from each map.
Compute the Jaccard index, |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. It is 1 when the two sets are identical and 0 when they are disjoint.

Spearman’s ρ over all feasible cells complements Jaccard by measuring agreement in the overall ordering.


Code
# Helpers to compare an alternate map against the baseline (Jaccard + Spearman).
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # reproducible sampler
SAMPLE = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(feasible), 20_000, replace=False)  # subsample for fast Spearman


def compare(arr, ref=baseline):
    """Return (Jaccard of top-20% masks, Spearman rho on a feasible subsample)."""
    rho = spearmanr(np.ravel(arr)[SAMPLE], np.ravel(ref)[SAMPLE], nan_policy="omit")[0]  # rank agreement
    return jaccard_index(top_quantile_mask(arr, mask=feasible), top_quantile_mask(ref, mask=feasible)), rho  # overlap + rho


BASE_TOP = top_quantile_mask(baseline, mask=feasible, q=0.80)  # top 20% of baseline scores
print("Baseline top-20% area (km²):", round(BASE_TOP.sum() * 0.81 / 100, 1))  # 90 m cells -> 0.81 ha each



Baseline top-20% area (km²): 170.0

# Sweep gamma and measure agreement of each map with the gamma=0.8 baseline.
rows = []  # one row per gamma value
for g in [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 1.0]:
    arr = fz.overlay(MUS, "gamma", gamma=g)  # suitability at this gamma
    j, rho = compare(arr)  # agreement with baseline
    rows.append({"gamma": g, "Jaccard vs gamma=0.8": j, "Spearman rho": rho,
                 "area >= 0.85 (km2)": (np.nan_to_num(np.where(feasible, arr, np.nan)) >= 0.85).sum() * 0.0081})  # high-mu area

Code
# Plot Jaccard / Spearman agreement and high-suitability area against gamma.
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))  # dual-axis sensitivity figure
ax1.plot(gsens["gamma"], gsens["Jaccard vs gamma=0.8"], marker="o", label="Jaccard (top 20%)")  # set overlap
ax1.plot(gsens["gamma"], gsens["Spearman rho"], marker="s", label="Spearman rho")  # rank agreement
ax1.set(xlabel="gamma", ylabel="Agreement with gamma = 0.8", ylim=(0, 1.05))  # left axis
ax2 = ax1.twinx()  # right axis for area
ax2.plot(gsens["gamma"], gsens["area >= 0.85 (km2)"], color="tab:green", ls="--", marker="^",
         label="Area with mu >= 0.85")  # high-mu area curve
ax2.set_ylabel("km2")  # area axis label
h1, l1 = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels(); h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()  # combine legends
ax1.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2, loc="lower left", fontsize=8)  # unified legend
ax1.set_title("Sensitivity of the suitability map to gamma")  # panel title
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)  # light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure










Two lessons:

The ranking is unchanged for every γ below about 0.95 (Jaccard and ρ ≈ 1). With four criteria, the fuzzy Sum is close to 1 almost everywhere, so Gamma ≈ Product^(1-γ). That is a monotonic transformation of Product, so the order of cells cannot change. Only at γ = 1, the saturated Sum, does the ranking collapse.
The amount of land above a fixed threshold changes greatly with γ, from about 20 km² at γ = 0 to about 350 km² at γ = 0.9. Any absolute threshold, like the 0.85 used in Module 7, must therefore be reported together with the γ used, or replaced by a relative rule such as “top 20%”.

In practice, then, γ calibrates the values, while the membership functions determine the ranking. The next section tests those functions.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text:
Sensitivity to membership parameters
Membership midpoints and spreads come from expert judgment, so each one is tested one at a time (OAT) by varying it ±25% while holding the others at baseline. The result is recomputed with Gamma 0.8 and compared with the baseline using Jaccard.


Code
# Rebuild memberships from parameters so OAT +/-25% perturbations are easy.
def memberships(slope_mid=4, slope_sp=4, south_mu90=0.3, tpi_lo=-6, tpi_hi=4, stream_mid=300, stream_sp=3):
    """Return the four membership rasters under the given parameterisation."""
    asp_sp = -np.log(south_mu90) / 90 ** 2  # Gaussian spread from mu(90 deg)
    mu_exp = np.maximum(fz.gaussian(dev_south, 0, asp_sp), fz.small(slope_pct, 1, 6))  # exposure OR flat
    return [fz.small(slope_pct, slope_mid, slope_sp), mu_exp,
            fz.linear(tpi, tpi_lo, tpi_hi), fz.large(dist_stream, stream_mid, stream_sp)]  # four criteria


BASE = dict(slope_mid=4, slope_sp=4, south_mu90=0.3, tpi_lo=-6, tpi_hi=4, stream_mid=300, stream_sp=3)  # baseline params
# Confirm the parametric memberships match the saved Module 7 arrays.
assert np.allclose(np.nan_to_num(fz.overlay(memberships(), "gamma", gamma=0.8)),
                   np.nan_to_num(fz.overlay(MUS, "gamma", gamma=0.8)))  # sanity check

rows = []  # one row per parameter x direction
for p, v in BASE.items():
    for f in (0.75, 1.25):
        new = v * f  # +/-25% perturbation
        if p == "south_mu90":
            new = min(new, 0.95)  # keep membership parameter in (0, 1)
        arr = fz.overlay(memberships(**{**BASE, p: new}), "gamma", gamma=0.8)  # perturbed map
        j, rho = compare(arr)  # agreement with baseline
        rows.append({"parameter": p, "change": f"{'-' if f < 1 else '+'}25%", "value": round(new, 3),
                     "Jaccard": j, "Spearman rho": rho})  # record row
psens = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # parameter sensitivity table

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text:
Weighting fuzzy criteria
Standard fuzzy overlay treats every criterion as equally important. Three common ways to add importance weights \(w_i\) (with \(\sum w_i = 1\)) are listed below. Each reduces to its unweighted version when all weights are equal, with the inputs raised to \(n w_i\):







Weighted operator
Formula




Weighted product (geometric mean)
\(\prod \mu_i^{\,w_i}\)


Weighted sum
\(1 - \prod (1 - \mu_i)^{w_i}\)


Weighted gamma
\((\text{W-Sum})^{\gamma} \cdot (\text{W-Product})^{1-\gamma}\)



Raising a membership to a power above 1 acts like the very hedge, making that criterion more demanding. A criterion with a larger weight therefore has more influence on the result. This approach follows the importance-weighting method of Yager (1978).


Code
# Confirm equal-weight weighted_fuzzy_overlay matches unweighted Gamma 0.8.
eq = weighted_fuzzy_overlay(MUS, [1, 1, 1, 1])  # equal weights
print("Equal weights reproduce Gamma 0.8:",
      np.allclose(np.nan_to_num(eq), np.nan_to_num(fz.overlay(MUS, "gamma", gamma=0.8))))  # should be True



Equal weights reproduce Gamma 0.8: True


Two stakeholder views are compared:

An engineering view, where grading cost (slope) and flood risk (streams) dominate: weights 0.35, 0.15, 0.15, 0.35.
An energy-yield view, where sun exposure dominates: weights 0.2, 0.5, 0.1, 0.2.



Code
# Compare equal, engineering, and energy-yield weight vectors under weighted fuzzy overlay.
W = {"Equal": [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25],  # uniform importance
     "Engineering": [0.35, 0.15, 0.15, 0.35],  # emphasise slope + stream distance
     "Energy yield": [0.20, 0.50, 0.10, 0.20]}  # emphasise exposure / aspect

wres = {k: weighted_fuzzy_overlay(MUS, w) for k, w in W.items()}  # one map per weight vector

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5.5), layout="constrained")  # three stakeholder maps
for ax, (k, arr) in zip(axes, wres.items()):
    im = show(arr, f"Weighted Gamma 0.8: {k}", ax)  # suitability under this weighting
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.6, label="mu")  # shared colourbar
plt.show()  # render the figure

pd.DataFrame({k: dict(zip(["Jaccard vs equal", "Spearman rho vs equal"], compare(v, wres["Equal"])))
              for k, v in wres.items()}).T.round(3)  # agreement vs equal weights

Raising the weight on exposure moves the best land toward south-facing ground, while the engineering weights favor gentle land far from streams. Making these weightings explicit and visible helps a group reach agreement, because the disagreement becomes something on the map that everyone can look at.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
section: Rule-based suitability: a Mamdani fuzzy inference system
text:
Rule-based suitability: a Mamdani fuzzy inference system
Fuzzy overlay combines criteria with one operator everywhere. A fuzzy inference system (FIS) instead uses expert rules expressed in words:

IF slope is gentle AND aspect is south AND streams are far, THEN suitability is high.

A Mamdani FIS has four steps:

Fuzzify the inputs with linguistic terms, such as slope = {flat, gentle, moderate, steep}.
Evaluate the rules. Each rule’s firing strength is the minimum (AND) or maximum (OR) of its antecedent memberships.
Implication and aggregation. Each rule’s output set is clipped at its firing strength, and the clipped sets are combined with max.
Defuzzify. The centroid of the aggregated output set gives a crisp score from 0 to 100.

The advantage is interpretability and flexibility. Rules can express interactions that a single operator cannot, for example aspect only matters on sloping land.

Defining linguistic terms


Code
# Define linguistic universes and trapezoid/triangle membership terms for the FIS.
U = {
    "slope":  np.linspace(0, 15, 301),  # slope (%) universe
    "dev":    np.linspace(0, 180, 181),  # south-deviation (deg) universe
    "stream": np.linspace(0, 3000, 301),  # stream distance (m) universe
    "out":    np.linspace(0, 100, 101),  # suitability output (0-100)
}

TERMS = {
    "slope": {"flat":     skf.trapmf(U["slope"], [0, 0, 0.8, 1.5]),  # nearly level
              "gentle":   skf.trapmf(U["slope"], [0.8, 1.5, 3, 5]),  # easy to grade
              "moderate": skf.trimf(U["slope"], [3, 5.5, 8]),  # transitional
              "steep":    skf.trapmf(U["slope"], [6, 9, 15, 15])},  # costly / unsuitable
    "dev":   {"south":    skf.trapmf(U["dev"], [0, 0, 45, 90]),  # favourable aspect
              "eastwest": skf.trimf(U["dev"], [45, 90, 135]),  # intermediate aspect
              "north":    skf.trapmf(U["dev"], [90, 135, 180, 180])},  # unfavourable aspect
    "stream": {"near":    skf.trapmf(U["stream"], [0, 0, 150, 400]),  # flood / setback risk
               "far":     skf.trapmf(U["stream"], [150, 400, 3000, 3000])},  # safer setback
    "out":   {"low":      skf.trapmf(U["out"], [0, 0, 20, 45]),  # low suitability
              "medium":   skf.trimf(U["out"], [30, 50, 70]),  # medium suitability
              "high":     skf.trapmf(U["out"], [55, 80, 100, 100])},  # high suitability
}

# Plot the linguistic terms for each variable.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.4))  # four variable panels
for ax, (var, label) in zip(axes, [("slope", "Slope (%)"), ("dev", "Deviation from south (deg)"),
                                   ("stream", "Distance to stream (m)"), ("out", "Suitability (0-100)")]):
    for term, mf in TERMS[var].items():
        ax.plot(U[var], mf, lw=2, label=term)  # membership curve for this term
    ax.set(xlabel=label, ylim=(-0.05, 1.05))  # axis limits
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)  # term legend
axes[0].set_ylabel("mu")  # membership axis
plt.suptitle("Linguistic terms (trapezoidal and triangular membership functions)")  # figure title
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure

Rule 1 encodes the flatness override from Module 7 directly in words. TPI is left out to keep the rule base readable, and adding it is an exercise.


Vectorized evaluation over the raster
skfuzzy.interp_membership accepts whole arrays, so every rule is evaluated for all cells at once. Aggregation creates an array of shape (cells × 101 output points), which is about 10 million values and fits easily in memory.


Code
# Evaluate a vectorised Mamdani FIS on all feasible cells using eight IF-THEN rules.
idx = np.flatnonzero(feasible)  # flat indices of feasible cells
x_slope = np.clip(np.ravel(slope_pct)[idx], 0, 15)  # slope inputs clipped to universe
x_dev = np.ravel(dev_south)[idx]  # aspect-deviation inputs
x_stream = np.clip(np.ravel(dist_stream)[idx], 0, 3000)  # stream-distance inputs clipped


def m(var, term, x):
    """Interpolate a linguistic membership for array-valued inputs x."""
    return skf.interp_membership(U[var], TERMS[var][term], x)  # membership of x in term


S = {t: m("slope", t, x_slope) for t in TERMS["slope"]}  # slope-term memberships
A = {t: m("dev", t, x_dev) for t in TERMS["dev"]}  # aspect-term memberships
D = {t: m("stream", t, x_stream) for t in TERMS["stream"]}  # stream-term memberships

RULES = [  # (firing strength, output term)
    (np.minimum(S["flat"], D["far"]), "high"),  # flat + far -> high
    (np.minimum.reduce([S["gentle"], A["south"], D["far"]]), "high"),  # gentle south far -> high
    (np.minimum.reduce([S["gentle"], A["eastwest"], D["far"]]), "medium"),  # gentle E/W far -> medium
    (np.minimum.reduce([S["gentle"], A["north"], D["far"]]), "medium"),  # gentle north far -> medium
    (np.minimum.reduce([S["moderate"], A["south"], D["far"]]), "medium"),  # moderate south far -> medium
    (np.minimum(S["moderate"], np.maximum(A["eastwest"], A["north"])), "low"),  # moderate non-south -> low
    (S["steep"], "low"),  # steep anywhere -> low
    (D["near"], "low"),  # near stream anywhere -> low
]

fis_vals = mamdani(RULES, TERMS["out"], U["out"])  # vectorised centroid defuzzification
fis = np.full(feasible.shape, np.nan)  # map-shaped FIS output
fis.ravel()[idx] = fis_vals  # scatter FIS values onto feasible cells

print(f"FIS output: {np.nanmin(fis_vals):.1f}-{np.nanmax(fis_vals):.1f} | "
      f"cells with no rule firing: {np.isnan(fis_vals).sum()}")  # completeness check



FIS output: 16.8-83.2 | cells with no rule firing: 0


Checking that every cell fires at least one rule confirms that the rule base is complete, meaning the terms cover every combination of inputs. Cells where no rule fires would have no defined output.


Validating against scikit-fuzzy’s control API
The control API (skfuzzy.control) builds the same Mamdani system with objects and evaluates one cell at a time. It is too slow for full rasters, but it is a good independent check of the vectorized code. Small differences come from how the two discretize the output universe.


Code
# Spot-check the vectorised FIS against skfuzzy.control on eight random feasible cells.
from skfuzzy import control as ctrl  # classical FIS control API

# Build Antecedent/Consequent objects and attach the same linguistic terms.
slope_v = ctrl.Antecedent(U["slope"], "slope")  # slope input
dev_v = ctrl.Antecedent(U["dev"], "dev")  # aspect-deviation input
stream_v = ctrl.Antecedent(U["stream"], "stream")  # stream-distance input
out_v = ctrl.Consequent(U["out"], "out", defuzzify_method="centroid")  # suitability output
for var, obj in [("slope", slope_v), ("dev", dev_v), ("stream", stream_v), ("out", out_v)]:
    for term, mf in TERMS[var].items():
        obj[term] = mf  # attach membership function

# Encode the same eight rules in skfuzzy.control syntax.
rules = [
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["flat"] & stream_v["far"], out_v["high"]),  # rule 1
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["gentle"] & dev_v["south"] & stream_v["far"], out_v["high"]),  # rule 2
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["gentle"] & dev_v["eastwest"] & stream_v["far"], out_v["medium"]),  # rule 3
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["gentle"] & dev_v["north"] & stream_v["far"], out_v["medium"]),  # rule 4
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["moderate"] & dev_v["south"] & stream_v["far"], out_v["medium"]),  # rule 5
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["moderate"] & (dev_v["eastwest"] | dev_v["north"]), out_v["low"]),  # rule 6
    ctrl.Rule(slope_v["steep"], out_v["low"]),  # rule 7
    ctrl.Rule(stream_v["near"], out_v["low"]),  # rule 8
]
sim = ctrl.ControlSystemSimulation(ctrl.ControlSystem(rules))  # reusable simulator

# Compare outputs on eight randomly chosen feasible cells.
check = []  # rows of side-by-side results
for i in np.random.default_rng(1).choice(len(idx), 8, replace=False):
    sim.inputs({"slope": x_slope[i], "dev": x_dev[i], "stream": x_stream[i]})  # set inputs
    sim.compute()  # run skfuzzy.control
    check.append({"slope %": x_slope[i], "dev deg": x_dev[i], "stream m": x_stream[i],
                  "vectorized": fis_vals[i], "skfuzzy.control": sim.output["out"]})  # compare
pd.DataFrame(check).round(2)  # display agreement table

FIS vs. fuzzy overlay


Code
# Side-by-side maps: fuzzy gamma overlay vs Mamdani FIS (scaled to 0-1).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6), layout="constrained")  # two-method comparison
im = show(baseline, "Fuzzy overlay: Gamma 0.8 (4 criteria)", axes[0])  # overlay map
show(fis / 100, "Mamdani FIS: 8 rules, 3 inputs (scaled 0-1)", axes[1])  # FIS map on [0, 1]
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.6, label="Suitability")  # shared colourbar
plt.show()  # render the figure

j, rho = compare(fis, baseline)  # note: compare uses top_quantile on raw values; FIS scale differs but ranks matter
print(f"FIS vs Gamma 0.8: Jaccard (top 20%) = {j:.3f} | Spearman rho = {rho:.3f}")  # agreement summary










FIS vs Gamma 0.8: Jaccard (top 20%) = 0.476 | Spearman rho = 0.803




Code
# Histogram of FIS suitability scores on feasible cells (0-100 scale).
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # FIS output distribution
ax.hist(fis_vals, bins=60, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")  # score histogram
ax.set(xlabel="FIS suitability (0-100)", ylabel="Cells", title="FIS output distribution")  # labels
plt.show()  # render the figure










The FIS output is clustered around the centroids of the output terms (low, medium, high). This is typical of Mamdani systems with few rules: the result behaves like an ordinal classification with smooth transitions, while Gamma overlay gives a more continuous surface.
The two maps agree on the broad pattern (ρ ≈ 0.8), but only about half of their top-20% areas coincide. There are three reasons:

The FIS uses three inputs and ignores topographic position.
Its output is clustered, so many cells share the same “high” value and the top-20% cutoff falls among tied values.
Its rules encode different logic. Gentle north-facing slopes are medium under the rules, while the overlay penalizes them more smoothly through the exposure criterion.

Disagreement between two reasonable models is useful information. It shows where the result depends on modeling choices rather than on the data.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text:
Choosing a method










Method
Logic
Weights
Strengths
Limitations




Boolean (Module 3)
Crisp AND
None
Simple, transparent
Hard edges, no ranking


WLC (Module 4)
Fully compensatory
Explicit
Intuitive, easy to weight
Strengths mask weaknesses


Fuzzy overlay (Modules 6-7)
Graded, adjustable from strict to lenient
Optional (4)
Removes hard edges, few parameters
One operator for all interactions


Weighted fuzzy (4)
Graded + importance
Explicit
Combines both ideas
More parameters to justify


Fuzzy inference (5)
Expert IF-THEN rules
Implicit in rules
Interpretable, captures interactions
Rule base grows quickly with inputs



Practical recommendation: start with constraints plus fuzzy Gamma or AND overlay. Add weights when stakeholders clearly disagree about importance, and move to a FIS when experts describe suitability as conditional rules rather than independent criteria.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text:
Exercises

Add TPI to the FIS with terms valley, mid-slope, and ridge, and add two rules that use it. How many rules would a complete rule base with four inputs need?
Replace centroid defuzzification with mean of maximum (skf.defuzz(..., "mom")) on the validation cells. How do the results differ?
Repeat the OAT analysis in 8.3 with the AND operator. Which operator is more sensitive to the parameters?
Search for weights that maximize the Jaccard agreement between weighted Gamma and the FIS. What do those weights reveal about the implicit priorities in the rule base?

title: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: Sensitivity, Weighting, and Rule-based Inference
text:
Key takeaways

Report fuzzy results with their γ and parameters, and prefer relative thresholds (top k%) over absolute ones.
OAT sensitivity with Jaccard agreement shows which expert parameters drive the result.
Weighted fuzzy operators add explicit importance while keeping the fuzzy logic.
A Mamdani FIS turns expert rules into a suitability map, can be vectorized for rasters, and should be validated against a reference implementation.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup.
import warnings  # silence benign RuntimeWarnings
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for MCSM sample data

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack used throughout this notebook.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for membership maps
import numpy as np  # array ops for membership curves
import pandas as pd  # tabular previews of memberships and ranks

# ===================================================================
# Locate the repository root, import fuzzy helpers, load criteria + WLC results.
# ===================================================================
# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.
import geolattice

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if not (ROOT / "Data").is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

DATA_DIR = ROOT / "Data" / "03_spatial_analysis" / "MCSM_data"  # shared MCSM sample-data folder
DATA_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if missing

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)  # quiet numeric warnings
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider DataFrame previews
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = [9, 6]  # default figure size for maps

# Import the fuzzy MCSM module and the named helpers used below / in exercises.
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis as fz  # fuzzy API alias
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis import (
    SuitabilityAnalysisError,  # typed error for invalid overlay / FIS inputs
    categorical_and,  # Boolean AND (for comparisons)
    categorical_or,  # Boolean OR (for comparisons)
    criteria_count,  # k-of-n counts (for comparisons)
    hybrid_suitability,  # constrained continuous scores
    jaccard_index,  # set similarity for top-quantile agreement
    limiting_criterion,  # weakest membership name under AND
    mamdani,  # rule-based FIS (used in later notebooks / exercises)
    minmax_normalize,  # min-max standardisation helper
    monte_carlo_weights,  # weight uncertainty helper
    overlay,  # fuzzy overlay operators
    percentile_rank_normalize,  # rank-based standardisation
    perturb_weights,  # OAT weight perturbation
    spread_for_small,  # calibrate Small-function spread
    top_quantile_mask,  # top-q Boolean mask from a score
    trapezoidal_mf,  # trapezoid membership for FIS
    triangular_mf,  # triangle membership for FIS
    weighted_fuzzy_overlay,  # weighted fuzzy operators
    weighted_linear_combination,  # WLC for comparisons
)

import geopandas as gpd  # vector GeoDataFrames for counties / hubs

# Load criteria layers and Part I weighted results for side-by-side comparison.

def fuzzy_map(gdf, column, title, ax=None, cmap="RdYlGn"):
    """Plot a continuous membership choropleth (0-1) with a state outline."""
    ax = gdf.plot(column, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=1, legend=ax is None, ax=ax,
                  edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3,  # county edges
                  legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6, "label": "Membership mu"} if ax is None else None)  # colourbar
    state.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#00000080", linewidth=0.8)  # state outline
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)  # panel title
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide axis ticks
    return ax  # return axes for overlays

The maps show the operator spectrum from Module 5:

Sum and OR are close to 1 almost everywhere. Every county is strong on something, so these operators discriminate poorly here.
Product is low almost everywhere. Four memberships multiplied together shrink quickly, which makes Product a very strict screen.
AND highlights counties where every criterion is at least moderately satisfied.
Gamma (0.9) keeps more variation than Sum while being less harsh than Product.

Every metro county scores 0 under Product and Gamma, because μ_rural = 0 makes the product zero. A single zero membership vetoes a location under any operator except Sum and OR.
For a siting decision where every criterion matters, AND or Gamma with a moderate γ are the most useful operators.

Choosing γ
Statistics alone cannot pick γ, but a simple diagnostic shows how much each choice spreads the counties apart. A spread that is too small cannot tell counties apart.
The diagnostic below plots the mean result and the coefficient of variation (CV) against γ. All metro counties have μ_rural = 0, which makes Product, and therefore every Gamma with γ < 1, equal to 0 for them. The CV is therefore computed only over counties with a non-zero result, the ones actually in contention.


Code
# Diagnose gamma: mean level vs coefficient of variation across gamma in [0, 1].
gammas = np.round(np.arange(0, 1.01, 0.05), 2)  # gamma grid
res = pd.DataFrame({g: fz.overlay(mus, "gamma", gamma=g).values for g in gammas})  # one column per gamma

pos = res[res.iloc[:, 0] > 0]  # counties with non-zero Product (eligible for CV)
stats = pd.DataFrame({"mean": pos.mean(), "cv": pos.std() / pos.mean()})  # level vs discrimination
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # gamma diagnostic figure
ax.plot(stats.index, stats["mean"], marker="o", label="Mean combined mu (eligible counties)")  # mean curve
ax.plot(stats.index, stats["cv"], marker="s", label="Coefficient of variation (eligible counties)")  # CV curve
ax.set(xlabel="gamma", title="Gamma overlay: level vs. discrimination")  # labels
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # legend and light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure










As γ rises, the mean combined membership increases and the CV falls. For the eligible counties, the CV drops from about 1.1 at γ = 0 to about 0.4 at γ = 0.7 and 0.15 at γ = 0.9, so near 0.9 the counties become hard to tell apart. Values between about 0.5 and 0.8 keep a useful spread for this dataset. The rest of this module uses γ = 0.7 alongside AND.


Code

Several patterns stand out:

Chautauqua gets μ_capacity = 0.50 rather than a fail, and its strong need keeps it competitive.
Sullivan gets μ_access just under 0.5 at 106 km, so it is penalized slightly rather than eliminated.
Hamilton, ranked 1st by WLC, drops to 8th. Its distance to a hub (μ_access = 0.38) can no longer be offset by its excellent need and capacity scores.

text:
Key takeaways

Crisp thresholds become midpoints of membership functions, which removes hard edges.
With four or more criteria, Sum and OR saturate and Product collapses, so AND and moderate Gamma are usually the most informative operators.
Fuzzy AND is non-compensatory but graded, and its limiting criterion map is a useful diagnostic.
Fuzzy and WLC rankings largely agree on the top counties but differ where compensation matters, such as the Bronx.

title: Weighted Suitability Analysis
text:
Overview
Weighted suitability analysis is a powerful spatial decision-making method used when multiple criteria must be considered to identify optimal locations for interventions or resources.
In this notebook, we illustrate how to synthesize a range of county-level indicators, such as healthcare need, ICU capacity, rurality, and access to critical care hubs, into a single composite suitability score for each county in New York State.
This approach enables us to: - Standardize factors measured on different scales, making them directly comparable - Assign different weights to each criterion to reflect their relative importance - Generate objective, reproducible rankings for data-driven support, resource allocation, or further analysis
Common applications of weighted suitability analysis include: - Planning and prioritizing health resource deployment (e.g., siting new clinics or outreach) - Emergency service siting and optimization - Environmental risk or vulnerability assessments - Site selection for infrastructure projects
In this analysis, our chief aim is to identify which counties are most in need of additional critical care capacity, using a transparent and reproducible weighting process.
Categorical (Boolean) analysis can tell us which counties meet a threshold, but not which is most in need. Weighted suitability analysis produces a continuous score for every location, enabling nuanced prioritization:
\[S_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j \, x_{ij}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j = 1, \qquad 0 \le x_{ij} \le 1\]

\(S_i\) is the suitability score for county \(i\), ranging from 0 (least suitable) to 1 (most suitable).
\(x_{ij}\) represents the standardized value of criterion \(j\) for county \(i\).
\(w_j\) denotes the weight (importance) of criterion \(j\), chosen based on expert judgment or policy priorities.

Although the equation closely resembles a linear regression model, there is a key difference: in regression, we estimate weights from the data to predict an outcome; in suitability analysis, we define weights based on expert knowledge and then calculate the outcome (suitability).
The weighted linear combination (WLC) model is compensatory: a lower score in one criterion can be balanced by higher scores in others. This is fundamentally different from a Boolean AND logic, which requires all criteria to be met and is covered elsewhere in Module 3.
Standardize criteria and combine them with a weighted linear combination (WLC) using minmax_normalize, percentile_rank_normalize, weighted_linear_combination, and hybrid_suitability from geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis.
Inputs and outputs live under Data/03_spatial_analysis/MCSM_data/.

Overview
Identifying Priority Counties for Critical Care Expansion

2.2 Assigning weights

title: Weighted Suitability Analysis
section: Identifying Priority Counties for Critical Care Expansion
text:
Identifying Priority Counties for Critical Care Expansion
In this analysis, our goal is to identify which counties could benefit most from increased critical care capacity, using a transparent and reproducible weighting process.

Standardizing criteria
Weights are only meaningful if the criteria share a scale. Min-max normalization rescales each criterion to the range 0-1, and its direction depends on whether the criterion is a benefit or a cost:








Criterion type
Formula
Used for




Benefit (higher is better)
\(x' = \dfrac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}\)
need index, rurality


Cost (lower is better)
\(x' = \dfrac{x_{max} - x}{x_{max} - x_{min}}\)
ICU-bed LQ, distance to hub



For an ordinal code with a known range, such as RUCC 1-9, it is better to scale against the theoretical range (1 and 9) than the observed one, so a score of 1 means completely rural and not just the most rural county in this sample.


Code
# Min-max standardise each criterion to [0, 1] with the correct benefit/cost direction.
counties["need_s"] = minmax_normalize(counties["need_index"], benefit=True)  # higher need -> higher score
counties["capacity_s"] = minmax_normalize(counties["icu_lq"], benefit=False)  # lower LQ -> higher score
counties["rural_s"] = minmax_normalize(counties["rucc"], benefit=True, lo=1, hi=9)  # fixed RUCC bounds
counties["access_s"] = minmax_normalize(counties["hub_km"], benefit=False)  # shorter distance -> higher score

STD = ["need_s", "capacity_s", "rural_s", "access_s"]  # standardized column names
counties[STD].describe().round(3)  # confirm all lie in [0, 1]

describe() confirms that every standardized criterion lies within 0-1. The distributions differ, though, and the histograms below show how.


Code
# Histograms of the four standardized criteria (shared y-axis for comparison).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3), sharey=True)  # four side-by-side panels
for ax, col in zip(axes, STD):
    ax.hist(counties[col], bins=12, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")  # score distribution
    ax.set_title(col)  # criterion name
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)  # standardized domain
axes[0].set_ylabel("Counties")  # shared count axis label
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure











The outlier problem
Min-max scaling depends entirely on the two most extreme values. Manhattan’s ICU-bed LQ (2.31) is far above the rest, which compresses the remaining counties into the upper part of the capacity_s scale. Distance has a similar long tail in the North Country.
Percentile-rank normalization avoids this problem by scoring each county by its position in the distribution rather than its distance from the extremes:


Code
# Compare min-max vs percentile-rank normalisation for the two skewed cost criteria.
counties["capacity_r"] = percentile_rank_normalize(counties["icu_lq"], benefit=False)  # rank-based capacity
counties["access_r"] = percentile_rank_normalize(counties["hub_km"], benefit=False)  # rank-based access

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))  # two scatter panels
for ax, (mm, pr, name) in zip(axes, [("capacity_s", "capacity_r", "ICU-bed LQ (cost)"),
                                     ("access_s", "access_r", "Distance to hub (cost)")]):
    ax.scatter(counties[mm], counties[pr], s=18)  # each county as a point
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=0.8)  # 1:1 reference line
    ax.set(xlabel="Min-max score", ylabel="Percentile-rank score", title=name)  # axis labels
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure










Neither method is “correct”:

Min-max preserves the magnitude of differences. A county twice as far from a hub loses proportionally more.
Percentile rank preserves only order. It is robust to outliers, but it treats a 1 km gap and a 50 km gap the same if they separate neighboring ranks.

The main analysis uses min-max scaling. Section 2.6 checks whether the choice changes the ranking.



Assigning weights
The weights express the program’s priorities and must sum to 1. They are set before looking at the results, which guards against tuning the weights to favor a preferred outcome.

Weight
Rationale

0.25

0.25

0.15
Important, but telehealth reduces its role



Module 6 replaces these direct-rating weights with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP).

Why does a county score highly? Criterion contributions
Each county’s score is a sum of weighted parts, \(w_j x_{ij}\). Plotting those parts shows why a county ranks where it does. This makes the model transparent and easy to explain to stakeholders.


Code
# Decompose each top-12 county's score into weighted criterion contributions.
contrib = pd.DataFrame({c.replace("_s", ""): counties[c] * w for c, w in WEIGHTS.items()})  # w_j * x_ij
contrib.index = counties["county"].str.replace(" County", "")  # shorter row labels
contrib = contrib.loc[counties.sort_values("rank")["county"].str.replace(" County", "").head(12)]  # top 12 order

# Stacked horizontal bars: each segment is one criterion's contribution.

                                  color=["#d95f02", "#7570b3", "#1b9e77", "#e7298a"])  # criterion colours

       title="Score decomposition: top 12 counties")  # axis labels / title

Counties that enter the weighted top 12 without passing the categorical screen are the compensation effect in action. Each fails one threshold: distance to a hub for Hamilton and Essex, ICU capacity for Otsego, and rurality for the Bronx. Each is strong enough on the other criteria to rank highly anyway. The Bronx, a fully metropolitan county, reaches the top 12 on need alone. Whether that is acceptable is a policy question, not a technical one. If the 100 km referral limit is non-negotiable, it should be a constraint rather than a weighted factor.


Hybrid model: constraints + weighted ranking
Most real suitability models are hybrids:

Hard constraints (Boolean) remove infeasible locations.
Soft factors (weighted) rank the locations that remain.

In this example, eligibility (non-metro) and the referral limit (≤ 100 km) are treated as constraints, while need, capacity, and rurality are weighted factors.


Code
# Hybrid model: hard Boolean constraints, then WLC ranking among feasible counties.
constraint = counties["ok_rural"] & counties["ok_access"]  # must be non-metro and within 100 km

HYBRID_W = {"need_s": 0.45, "capacity_s": 0.30, "rural_s": 0.25}  # weights among constrained counties
# Score unconstrained counties as NaN/masked via hybrid_suitability.
counties["score_hybrid"] = hybrid_suitability(
    weighted_linear_combination({c: counties[c] for c in HYBRID_W}, HYBRID_W),  # WLC among hybrid weights
    constraint,  # Boolean mask of feasible counties
)

# Grey out excluded counties; colour constrained counties by hybrid score.
ax = counties.plot(color="#e0e0e0", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)  # excluded = grey base

state.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#00000080", linewidth=0.8)  # state outline
hubs.plot(ax=ax, marker="*", color="black", markersize=100)  # hubs

Is the ranking robust?
Weights and normalization choices are judgments, so a credible analysis shows how much the results depend on them. The analysis below compares four weighting scenarios and the alternative normalization, using Spearman’s rank correlation with the baseline and the rank range of the leading counties.

# Rank stability across weight scenarios and an alternate normalisation choice.
scenarios = {
    "Baseline":        WEIGHTS,  # original expert weights
    "Equal weights":   {"need_s": .25, "capacity_s": .25, "rural_s": .25, "access_s": .25},  # uniform
    "Need-focused":    {"need_s": .55, "capacity_s": .15, "rural_s": .15, "access_s": .15},  # emphasise need
    "Access-focused":  {"need_s": .25, "capacity_s": .20, "rural_s": .20, "access_s": .35},  # emphasise access
}

ranks = pd.DataFrame(index=counties["county"])  # one column per scenario
for name, w in scenarios.items():
    # Rank counties under this weight vector (1 = best score).
    ranks[name] = pd.Series(weighted_linear_combination({c: counties[c] for c in w}, w), index=counties.index).rank(ascending=False, method="min").values  # scenario ranks

# Alternative normalisation: swap in percentile-rank versions of the two cost criteria.
alt = counties.assign(capacity_s=counties["capacity_r"], access_s=counties["access_r"])  # replace columns
ranks["Pct-rank normalization"] = pd.Series(weighted_linear_combination({c: alt[c] for c in WEIGHTS}, WEIGHTS), index=alt.index).rank(ascending=False, method="min").values  # alt ranks

ranks.corr(method="spearman")["Baseline"].round(3).to_frame("Spearman rho vs baseline")  # rank agreement

title: Weighted Suitability Analysis
text:
Key takeaways

WLC computes \(S = \sum w_j x_j\) on standardized criteria, and it is compensatory.
Standardization must account for direction (benefit or cost), and min-max scaling is sensitive to outliers.
Score decomposition makes the model transparent.
Hybrid models (constraints + weighted factors) usually reflect real decision rules best.
Always report how robust the ranking is to weights and normalization choices.

title: Deriving Criteria for Clinic Site Selection
text:
Overview
In spatial analysis, deriving criteria refers to the process of establishing measurable variables or indicators that reflect the goals and constraints of a site selection task. Theory underlying this process emphasizes identifying factors that are relevant, quantifiable, and spatially explicit so that locations can be compared objectively. In this context, criteria such as health-need indices, healthcare capacity, rurality, and proximity to hubs are chosen to reflect real-world priorities and disparities in service access. By clearly defining and deriving these criteria, spatial analysts ensure the analysis is systematic, transparent, and can be justified using both empirical evidence and policy rationale.
Build the four clinic-siting criteria from Data/03_spatial_analysis/MCSM_data/ny_counties.gpkg: a health-need index, ICU-bed location quotient, RUCC rurality, and distance to a referral hub.

Overview
Driving Criteria

2.1 Criterion 1: Health-care need index
2.2 Criterion 2: Hospital capacity gap (ICU-bed location quotient)
2.3 Criterion 3: Rurality from the RUCC
2.4 Criterion 4: Proximity to a referral hub
2.5 Checking criteria for redundancy
2.6 Save the criteria layer

Exercises
Key takeaways

Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup.
import warnings  # silence benign RuntimeWarnings during criterion math
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for MCSM sample data

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack used throughout this notebook.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for choropleths
import numpy as np  # array ops kept available for later criterion math
import pandas as pd  # tabular operations on county attributes

# ===================================================================

title: Deriving Criteria for Clinic Site Selection
text:
Driving Criteria
Raw counts are rarely good criteria. Kings County has more ICU beds than Hamilton County simply because it has about 580 times as many people. Criteria should describe a condition of a place, and that usually means one of the following:

a rate (per capita, per 10,000),
a relative index (local value ÷ reference value), or
a distance or accessibility measure.

Relative indices are especially useful in suitability analysis because the value 1 (or 100) has a clear meaning: the same as the reference area

Criterion 1: Health-care need index
The need index combines two indicators of primary-care demand: the share of residents aged 65+ and the poverty rate. Each is divided by its statewide value, the two ratios are averaged, and the result is multiplied by 100:
\[\text{Need}_i = 100 \times \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\%65^+_i}{\%65^+_{NY}} + \frac{\text{Poverty}_i}{\text{Poverty}_{NY}}\right)\]
An index of 100 means need equal to the state average, values above 100 mean higher need, and values below 100 mean lower need.
The state reference values should be population-weighted. The share of people aged 65+ in New York is total 65+ ÷ total population, not the unweighted mean of 62 county percentages.


Code
# Compute statewide baselines for elderly share and poverty (population-weighted).
state_pct65 = 100 * counties["pop65"].sum() / counties["pop"].sum()  # NY % aged 65+
state_poverty = (counties["poverty_pct"] * counties["pop"]).sum() / counties["pop"].sum()  # NY poverty %

print(f"NY % aged 65+   : {state_pct65:.1f}")  # statewide elderly share
print(f"NY poverty rate : {state_poverty:.1f}")  # statewide poverty rate

# Equal-weight composite of relative elderly share and relative poverty (NY = 100).
counties["need_index"] = 100 * 0.5 * (counties["pct65"] / state_pct65 +
                                      counties["poverty_pct"] / state_poverty)  # need index

# Preview the five highest-need counties.
counties.sort_values("need_index", ascending=False)[["county", "pct65", "poverty_pct", "need_index"]].head()  # top need

Criterion 2: Hospital capacity gap (ICU-bed location quotient)
A location quotient (LQ) compares a local share with a reference share:
\[LQ_i = \frac{\text{ICU beds}_i / \text{Population}_i}{\text{ICU beds}_{NY} / \text{Population}_{NY}}\]







LQ
Interpretation




1
ICU beds per capita equal to the state rate


< 1
Fewer beds than expected, so the county is under-served


> 1
More beds than expected, so the county is a regional hospital center



For this problem, a lower LQ is better, because it signals a capacity gap a clinic could help fill through prevention and earlier referral. Counties with no ICU beds have LQ = 0, which is a valid observation, not missing data.


Code
# ICU-bed location quotient: local beds/pop divided by the statewide beds/pop rate.
state_icu_rate = counties["icu_beds"].sum() / counties["pop"].sum()  # statewide ICU beds per person
counties["icu_lq"] = (counties["icu_beds"] / counties["pop"]) / state_icu_rate  # LQ; 1 = state rate

print("Counties with zero ICU beds:", (counties["icu_beds"] == 0).sum())  # absolute zero capacity
print("Counties with LQ < 1       :", (counties["icu_lq"] < 1).sum())  # below state average
counties.sort_values("icu_lq", ascending=False)[["county", "icu_beds", "icu_lq"]].head()  # highest LQ

counties["rurality_class"] = pd.cut(counties["rucc"], bins=[0, 3, 7, 9],

Distance to the nearest hub with sjoin_nearest()
sjoin_nearest() finds the nearest feature in another layer and can report the distance. What you measure from matters:

Polygon → point: distance from the nearest edge of the county. A large county touching a hub city gets distance 0, even if most of its residents live far away.
Centroid → point: distance from the county’s center, which better represents a typical trip for its residents.

Both are computed so they can be compared. When two hubs are equally near, sjoin_nearest() returns duplicate rows, so drop_duplicates() keeps one row per county.


Code
# Measure proximity to the nearest referral hub two ways: edge vs centroid.
# (a) Edge-based distance: nearest hub to the county polygon boundary.
edge = gpd.sjoin_nearest(counties[["GEOID", "geometry"]], hubs[["hub", "geometry"]],
                         how="left", distance_col="dist_m").drop_duplicates("GEOID")  # one row/county

# (b) Centroid-based distance: nearest hub to the county centroid.
centroids = counties[["GEOID", "county"]].copy()  # start from county ids/names
centroids = centroids.set_geometry(counties.geometry.centroid)  # replace geometry with centroids
cent = gpd.sjoin_nearest(centroids, hubs[["hub", "geometry"]],
                         how="left", distance_col="dist_m").drop_duplicates("GEOID")  # one row/county

# Attach distances (km) and nearest-hub name back onto the counties table.
counties["hub_km_edge"] = counties["GEOID"].map(edge.set_index("GEOID")["dist_m"] / 1000)  # edge km
counties["hub_km"] = counties["GEOID"].map(cent.set_index("GEOID")["dist_m"] / 1000)  # centroid km
counties["nearest_hub"] = counties["GEOID"].map(cent.set_index("GEOID")["hub"])  # nearest hub name

title: Deriving Criteria for Clinic Site Selection
text:
Key takeaways

Express criteria as rates, relative indices, or distances, not raw counts.
A location quotient (local share ÷ reference share) gives a natural threshold at 1.
Spatial joins link layers by location. Use sjoin() for containment or intersection and sjoin_nearest() for proximity.
The geometry you measure from (edge or centroid) can change distances dramatically.
Check criteria correlations to avoid double-counting.

Next: Module 3: Categorical (Boolean) Suitability Analysis.

title: Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
text: Banner

title: Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
text:
Overview
Suitability analysis asks where an activity, facility, or land use is most appropriate by measuring how well every location satisfies a collection of criteria. It is the spatial expression of Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA):







MCDA concept
Spatial equivalent




Alternative
A location: a raster cell, a polygon, a site


Criterion
A spatial layer (distance, slope, population density)


Weight
Relative importance of each criterion


Composite score
A suitability surface or ranked map



Suitability maps are not predictions: they are ranked evidence summaries. They make assumptions explicit (which factors matter, how they are combined, what thresholds or weights are used) and must be validated against independent observations or expert judgement.

Why is it challenging?
Several challenges make MCSM more than simple map overlay:

Commensurability: criteria come in different units (km, %, persons/km2) and must be standardised before combination.
Directionality: some criteria are “higher is better” (population need), others “lower is better” (slope, distance).
Threshold uncertainty: crisp Boolean cuts (e.g. slope < 5 degrees) ignore the fact that a site at 5.1 degrees is nearly as good as one at 4.9 degrees.
Weight elicitation: weights reflect value judgements; different stakeholders prefer different emphases.
Sensitivity: the top-ranked sites may change dramatically if a weight or threshold shifts slightly.

This chapter addresses all five, moving from the simplest (Boolean) through to probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

title: Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
text:
General MCSM Workflow
Every suitability model, regardless of technique, follows the same logical arc:
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  1. DEFINE THE GOAL AND DECISION UNIT                                |
|     What are we siting / ranking?  What is the spatial unit?         |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  2. ASSEMBLE CRITERIA                                                |
|     Collect raw layers (census, DEM, land cover, road network)       |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  3. DERIVE AND STANDARDISE CRITERIA                                  |
|     Indices, location quotients, distance transforms;                |
|     min-max / percentile / fuzzy normalisation                       |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  4. COMBINE CRITERIA                                                 |
|     Boolean (AND / OR / k-of-n)  -->  Part I                        |
|     Weighted Linear Combination  -->  Part I                        |
|     Fuzzy overlay                -->  Part II                       |
|     Rule-based (Mamdani FIS)     -->  Part II                       |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  5. VALIDATE AND TEST SENSITIVITY                                    |
|     Rank stability, OAT perturbation, Monte Carlo, SALib             |
+---------------------------+------------------------------------------+
                            |
                            v
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  6. COMMUNICATE AND DECIDE                                           |
|     Maps, ranked lists, scenario comparisons, equity summaries       |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
Network analysis (Part IV) enters the workflow at Steps 2-3: travel time to the nearest facility, isochrone coverage, or 2SFCA accessibility scores become suitability criteria just like any other spatial variable.

title: Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
text:
Methods at a Glance

Boolean (Categorical) Suitability
Each criterion becomes a binary mask: a location either passes or fails a hard threshold. Masks are combined with logical AND (must satisfy all), OR (must satisfy at least one), or k-of-n (must satisfy at least k out of n criteria).

Pros: Transparent and easy to explain to non-technical audiences.
Cons: Sensitive to threshold choice; discards all information within each category.



Weighted Linear Combination (WLC)
Criteria are standardised to a common scale and summed with expert-assigned weights:
\[S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot x_i, \quad \sum w_i = 1, \quad w_i \geq 0\]
WLC allows full trade-off: a weak score on one criterion can be compensated by a strong score on another. Hard constraints (Boolean masks applied after scoring) prevent physically impossible combinations from appearing in the final result.

Pros: Continuous output; easy to adjust weights.
Cons: Full compensation may let poor-performing locations score highly overall.



Fuzzy Logic Suitability
Instead of binary pass/fail, each location receives a membership value in [0, 1] indicating its degree of suitability for each criterion. Membership functions replace crisp thresholds:








Function
Shape
Best for




large / ms_large
S-shaped
“More is better” (need, demand)


small / ms_small
Reversed S
“Less is better” (distance, slope)


near
Symmetric bell
“Close to a target value is best”


gaussian
Gaussian bell
Smooth, symmetric preference


linear
Trapezoid / ramp
Simple linear transition



Memberships are combined with fuzzy overlay operators (AND = min, OR = max, PRODUCT, SUM, GAMMA) that trade off between full-conjunction and full-disjunction strategies.

Pros: Handles boundary uncertainty; eliminates abrupt threshold effects.
Cons: Requires more parameter choices (function type, spread, crossover point).



Rule-Based Inference (Mamdani FIS)
A Fuzzy Inference System (FIS) encodes expert knowledge as IF-THEN rules over fuzzy sets:
IF   health_need IS high   AND   icu_gap IS large
THEN suitability IS very_high
The vectorised Mamdani FIS in geolattice evaluates all rules simultaneously for every spatial unit and defuzzifies the result to a numeric suitability score.

Pros: Expert-interpretable; captures non-linear interactions between criteria.
Cons: Rule base grows large with many criteria; requires careful validation.



Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis







Technique
What it tests




OAT (One-at-a-time) perturbation
Impact of changing a single weight by delta while others are fixed


Dirichlet Monte Carlo
Distribution of rank outcomes over randomly drawn weight vectors


SALib Sobol / Morris
Global variance-based sensitivity indices


Data uncertainty
Propagation of input measurement error into the suitability surface

title: Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
text:
Conceptual Overview: MCSM Techniques Compared
The cell below draws a compact visual comparison of the three main combination strategies on a toy two-criterion example, alongside a plot of the most common fuzzy membership functions.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack for the method-comparison figure.
import numpy as np  # array ops for toy criteria and membership curves
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches  # legend patches for Boolean classes
from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec  # 2x3 layout for comparison panels

# ===================================================================
# Toy data: 200 random locations with two criteria on a 0-1 scale.
# Used only to illustrate Boolean AND, WLC, and fuzzy GAMMA visually.
# ===================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)  # reproducible RNG for the scatter demo
n = 200  # number of synthetic locations
c1 = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)  # criterion 1 (e.g. normalised need)
c2 = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)  # criterion 2 (e.g. normalised rurality)

# Boolean AND: a location is suitable only if both criteria are at least 0.5.
bool_mask = (c1 >= 0.5) & (c2 >= 0.5)  # crisp pass/fail mask

# Weighted linear combination with equal weights (full trade-off).
wlc = 0.5 * c1 + 0.5 * c2  # continuous suitability score in [0, 1]

# Fuzzy GAMMA overlay: blend fuzzy AND (min) and fuzzy OR (max).
fuzzy_and = np.minimum(c1, c2)  # fuzzy AND = element-wise minimum
fuzzy_or = np.maximum(c1, c2)  # fuzzy OR = element-wise maximum
gamma = 0.5  # 0 -> pure AND, 1 -> pure OR; 0.5 balances both
fuzzy_gamma = (fuzzy_and ** (1 - gamma)) * (fuzzy_or ** gamma)  # gamma product blend

# ===================================================================
# Membership function definitions (pure NumPy, matching ArcGIS-style shapes).
# ===================================================================
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)  # dense x-grid for plotting membership curves


# Membership: larger values score closer to 1 (S-curve).
def ms_large(x, mid=0.5, spread=5):
    """S-curve: 'larger is better'."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-spread * (x - mid)))  # logistic rising through midpoint


# Membership: smaller values score closer to 1 (reversed S-curve).
def ms_small(x, mid=0.5, spread=5):
    """Reversed S-curve: 'smaller is better'."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(spread * (x - mid)))  # logistic falling through midpoint


# Membership: values near the midpoint score closest to 1 (bell).
def near(x, mid=0.5, spread=5):
    """Symmetric bell: 'close to midpoint is best'."""
    return np.exp(-spread * (x - mid) ** 2)  # Gaussian-like peak at midpoint


# ===================================================================
# Build the 2-row comparison figure: Boolean / WLC / GAMMA + memberships.
# ===================================================================
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 10))  # wide canvas for three scatters + one curve panel
gs = GridSpec(2, 3, figure=fig, hspace=0.42, wspace=0.35)  # 2 rows, 3 columns with spacing
cmap_suit = 'RdYlGn'  # red-yellow-green colormap for continuous scores
scatter_kw = dict(alpha=0.55, edgecolors='none', s=35)  # shared scatter style

# --- Boolean AND panel (top-left) ---
ax0 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])  # first panel in the top row
colors0 = np.where(bool_mask, '#2ca02c', '#d62728')  # green = pass, red = fail
ax0.scatter(c1, c2, c=colors0, **scatter_kw)  # plot locations coloured by pass/fail
ax0.axvline(0.5, color='k', lw=1, ls='--')  # vertical threshold line for criterion 1
ax0.axhline(0.5, color='k', lw=1, ls='--')  # horizontal threshold line for criterion 2
ax0.set_title('Boolean AND\n(both criteria >= 0.5)', fontweight='bold')  # panel title
ax0.set_xlabel('Criterion 1'); ax0.set_ylabel('Criterion 2')  # axis labels
patch_s = mpatches.Patch(color='#2ca02c', label='Suitable')  # legend patch for suitable
patch_n = mpatches.Patch(color='#d62728', label='Not suitable')  # legend patch for unsuitable
ax0.legend(handles=[patch_s, patch_n], fontsize=8)  # show Boolean class legend

# --- WLC panel (top-centre) ---
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])  # second panel in the top row
sc1 = ax1.scatter(c1, c2, c=wlc, cmap=cmap_suit, vmin=0, vmax=1, **scatter_kw)  # colour by WLC score
fig.colorbar(sc1, ax=ax1, label='WLC score')  # continuous score colourbar
ax1.set_title('Weighted Linear Combination\n(equal weights)', fontweight='bold')  # panel title
ax1.set_xlabel('Criterion 1'); ax1.set_ylabel('Criterion 2')  # axis labels

# --- Fuzzy GAMMA panel (top-right) ---
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])  # third panel in the top row
sc2 = ax2.scatter(c1, c2, c=fuzzy_gamma, cmap=cmap_suit, vmin=0, vmax=1, **scatter_kw)  # colour by gamma score
fig.colorbar(sc2, ax=ax2, label='Fuzzy gamma score')  # gamma score colourbar
ax2.set_title(f'Fuzzy GAMMA overlay (gamma={gamma})', fontweight='bold')  # panel title with gamma
ax2.set_xlabel('Criterion 1'); ax2.set_ylabel('Criterion 2')  # axis labels

# --- Membership function panel (bottom row, full width) ---
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])  # span all three columns on the bottom row
ax3.plot(x, ms_large(x, 0.5, 8), lw=2.5, color='#1f77b4',
         label='large  -- larger is better (S-curve, midpoint=0.5)')  # rising S-curve
ax3.plot(x, ms_small(x, 0.5, 8), lw=2.5, color='#d62728',
         label='small  -- smaller is better (reversed S, midpoint=0.5)')  # falling S-curve
ax3.plot(x, near(x, 0.5, 15), lw=2.5, color='#2ca02c',
         label='near   -- close to midpoint is best (bell, midpoint=0.5)')  # peaked near mid
ax3.plot(x, ms_large(x, 0.3, 8), lw=1.5, color='#1f77b4', ls='--',
         label='large  -- shifted midpoint (midpoint=0.3)')  # same shape, lower midpoint
ax3.axhline(0.5, color='grey', lw=0.8, ls=':')  # crossover reference at mu = 0.5
ax3.text(0.01, 0.52, 'crossover (mu = 0.5)', fontsize=8, color='grey')  # label the crossover
ax3.set_xlabel('Standardised criterion value', fontsize=11)  # x-axis: raw criterion
ax3.set_ylabel('Fuzzy membership mu', fontsize=11)  # y-axis: membership in [0, 1]
ax3.set_title('Common fuzzy membership functions used in MCSM', fontweight='bold')  # panel title
ax3.legend(fontsize=9, loc='center right')  # place legend away from the curves
ax3.set_xlim(0, 1); ax3.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)  # keep membership curves fully visible

# Figure-level title spanning all panels.
fig.suptitle('Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling -- Method Comparison',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)  # title styling
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing between panels
plt.show()  # render the comparison figure in the notebook











Reading the figure:

Boolean AND (top-left): produces a hard split. Only the upper-right quadrant is suitable; a location at (0.49, 0.99) is treated identically to one at (0.0, 0.0) - both fail.
WLC (top-centre): assigns a continuous score. The colour gradient shows full trade-off: a high score on criterion 1 compensates for a low score on criterion 2.
Fuzzy GAMMA (top-right): behaves similarly to WLC but score variation near the boundary is shaped by membership functions rather than raw values. Setting gamma -> 0 approaches fuzzy AND, gamma -> 1 approaches fuzzy OR.
Membership functions (bottom): show how raw criterion values map to memberships. The crossover point (mu = 0.5) is the value where a location is equally inside and outside the suitable set.
