section: Network Analysis and MCSM: The Connection
text:
Network Analysis and MCSM: The Connection
Network analysis enters suitability modeling in two main ways:

As a criterion-generation tool
Travel time to the nearest hospital, the number of facilities reachable within 30 minutes, or a 2SFCA accessibility score are all spatially varying quantities that can be normalised and used as suitability criteria exactly like slope or population density.
Road network
    +--> shortest_path / od_matrix
              +--> travel_time_to_hub  (criterion 3 in the NY clinic case study)
                        +--> minmax_normalize
                                  +--> weighted_linear_combination


As a post-selection evaluation tool
After a suitability model identifies top candidate locations, network analysis can evaluate how accessible each candidate is from the demand population and compare candidates on equity grounds using Lorenz-Gini analysis.
Suitability surface
    +--> top-k candidates
              +--> isochrone / two_sfca
                        +--> coverage assessment
                                  +--> lorenz_gini (equity summary)
Part IV covers both pathways in detail.

title: Multidimensional Trend Analysis
text:
Overview
Three complementary approaches were employed to quantify long-term trends in groundwater levels/storage using the bi-weekly raster time series (2000-2020). All approaches applied pixel-wise ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression but differed in the temporal grouping of observations. This multi-scale framework enabled assessment of the overall trend as well as intra-annual (monthly and seasonal) variations in groundwater dynamics.

title: Multidimensional Trend Analysis
text:
Core concepts
The input dataset consists of bi-weekly GeoTIFF rasters named according to the convention watertable_YYYY_JJJ.tif (equivalent to gw_YYYY_JJJ.tif in the methods note), where YYYY denotes the year and JJJ is the Julian day of the year (1-366). All raster files are parsed for date information using the Julian day to generate accurate datetime objects and sorted chronologically. A continuous time axis is created in decimal years as:
\[
t = \text{year} + \frac{\text{day of year} - 1}{\text{days in year}}
\]
accounting for leap years. This formulation ensures that regression slopes represent the rate of change in groundwater units per year. All rasters are stacked into a three-dimensional array of dimensions (n_time, height, width). NoData values are masked consistently using the native NoData flag of the input rasters (or NaN where applicable).

Pixel-wise linear regression
For each pixel and each temporal subset independently, a simple linear model is fitted:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_i + \epsilon_i
\]
where \(y_i\) is the groundwater value at time \(t_i\), \(\beta_1\) is the slope (trend magnitude), \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, and \(\epsilon_i\) is the random error term. In this notebook the regression is performed by generate_trend_raster(..., trend_type="LINEAR") (equivalent to scipy.stats.linregress per pixel). Pixels with fewer than three valid (non-NoData) observations in a given subset are masked as NaN in the output rasters. The analysis returns three raster outputs per temporal subset:

Slope raster: rate of groundwater change (units per year).
P-value raster: two-tailed statistical significance of the slope.
R² raster: coefficient of determination (goodness-of-fit).

All output GeoTIFFs inherit the original spatial properties (CRS, resolution, extent, and transform) of the input rasters.


Overall (full-period) trend analysis
The overall trend is computed using the complete set of bi-weekly observations spanning 2000-2020. This provides a baseline assessment of the long-term linear change across the entire study period without seasonal partitioning.


Monthly trend analysis
To examine intra-annual variability, observations are grouped by calendar month (January through December). For each month, bi-weekly rasters falling within that month across all years (2000-2020) are retained (here as yearly monthly means), and linear regression is applied independently to each monthly subset. This results in 12 sets of output rasters (slope, p-value, and R² for each month), revealing which months exhibit the strongest or most significant trends.


Seasonal trend analysis
Three hydrologically relevant seasons are defined based on regional water-cycle patterns:

Pre-monsoon: 15 March to 15 July
Monsoon: 16 July to 15 November
Winter: 16 November to 14 March (of the following year)

Each bi-weekly raster is assigned to one season according to its acquisition date. Winter spans the calendar-year boundary; the decimal-year time axis ensures correct temporal spacing. Linear regression is performed separately on the observations within each season, producing nine output rasters (three per season). This captures trend behavior during distinct hydrological periods while maintaining sufficient sample sizes for robust statistical inference.


Implementation in this notebook
Analyses use Python 3 with geolattice.spatial_analysis (MultidimensionalRaster, generate_trend_raster, predict_using_trend_raster, raster_to_netcdf), plus rasterio, xarray, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, and scipy. An optional Mann-Kendall / Theil-Sen overall trend is also demonstrated.

title: Multidimensional Trend Analysis
text:
Helpers
Parse watertable_YYYY_DOY.tif, stack into a MultidimensionalRaster, assign Bangladesh seasons, and convert timestamps to decimal years so LINEAR slopes are in units per year (as in R_Code/00_methods_trend_analysis.ipynb).


Code
# The following helper functions are used to process and analyze water table raster time series
# as part of a multidimensional trend analysis. These helpers handle file name parsing, time
# conversion, seasonal assignment, raster stacking, exporting geotiffs, and plotting results.

def parse_doy_filename(path: Path, prefix: str = "watertable") -> datetime:
    """
    Parse filenames like '{prefix}_YYYY_DOY.tif' into Python datetime objects.

    - Extracts the year and day-of-year (DOY) from the file name.
    - Converts to a datetime representing that day in the specified year.

    Used to get the observation date for each raster file.

    Example:
        watertable_2017_174.tif  =>  datetime(2017, 6, 23)
    """

    m = re.match(rf"{re.escape(prefix)}_(\d{{4}})_(\d{{1,3}})$", path.stem, re.IGNORECASE)  # m
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected filename: {path.name}")  # fail with a clear error message
    year, doy = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))  # year
    if not 1 <= doy <= 366:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid DOY {doy} in {path.name}")  # fail with a clear error message
    return datetime(year, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=doy - 1)  # return the computed result

def decimal_year(dt: datetime) -> float:
    """
    Convert a datetime object to a decimal year (e.g., 2017.5 for mid-2017).

    - Accounts for leap years.
    - The fraction is days elapsed divided by total days in the year.

    Useful for fitting linear trends in 'units per year' with irregular time steps.
    """

    year_start = datetime(dt.year, 1, 1)  # year_start
    day_of_year = (dt - year_start).days  # day_of_year
    days_in_year = 366 if (dt.year % 4 == 0 and (dt.year % 100 != 0 or dt.year % 400 == 0)) else 365  # days_in_year
    return dt.year + day_of_year / days_in_year  # return the computed result

def get_bangladesh_season(dt: datetime):
    """
    Assign a Bangladesh hydrological season to a given date.

    Seasons are:
      - 'Premonsoon': roughly mid-March to mid-July
      - 'Monsoon': roughly mid-July to mid-November
      - 'Winter': roughly mid-November to mid-March

    Returns one of the above season names or None if the date does not fit.
    Used for summarizing seasonal trends.

    """
    m, d = dt.month, dt.day  # m
    if (m == 3 and d >= 15) or (4 <= m <= 6) or (m == 7 and d <= 15):
        return "Premonsoon"  # return the computed result
    if (m == 7 and d >= 16) or (8 <= m <= 10) or (m == 11 and d <= 15):
        return "Monsoon"  # return the computed result
    if (m == 11 and d >= 16) or (m == 12) or (1 <= m <= 2) or (m == 3 and d <= 14):
        return "Winter"  # return the computed result
    return None  # return the computed result

def stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(paths, times, variable_name: str = "watertable") -> MultidimensionalRaster:
    """
    Read a series of GeoTIFF raster files (one per time step) and stack into an
    xarray-based MultidimensionalRaster.

    - Reads each raster as a 2D array, replacing nodata values with np.nan.
    - Calculates spatial coordinates using the GeoTIFF's affine transform.
    - Stacks the arrays on a new 'time' dimension with user-supplied coordinates.

    Returns a MultidimensionalRaster ready for analysis.
    """

    arrays = []  # arrays
    xs = ys = None  # xs
    for path in paths:  # iterate over items
        with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
            data = src.read(1).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
            nodata = src.nodata  # nodata
            if nodata is not None:
                data = np.where(data == nodata, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            data = np.where(np.abs(data) > 1e30, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            transform = src.transform  # transform
            height, width = data.shape  # height
            xs = transform.c + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * transform.a  # compute xs
            ys = transform.f + (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * transform.e  # compute ys
            arrays.append(data)

    da = xr.DataArray(  # da
        np.stack(arrays, axis=0),  # set np.stack(arrays
        dims=("time", "y", "x"),  # dims
        coords={  # coords
            "time": np.asarray(times, dtype="datetime64[ns]"),  # set "time": np.asarray(times
            "y": ys,
            "x": xs,
        },
        name=variable_name,  # name
    )
    return MultidimensionalRaster(da)  # return the computed result

def with_decimal_year_time(mdr: MultidimensionalRaster, variable: str = "watertable") -> MultidimensionalRaster:
    """
    Replace the datetime-based 'time' coordinate in a MultidimensionalRaster with a
    decimal year float coordinate for trend fitting.

    - Retains the original datetime coordinate as 'date'.
    - Updates attributes to describe the new coordinate.

    Allows regression/trend analysis in year-based units.
    """

    da = mdr.dataset[variable]  # da
    dates = pd.to_datetime(da.time.values)  # parse timestamps
    t_dec = np.array([decimal_year(d.to_pydatetime()) for d in dates], dtype=np.float64)  # compute t_dec
    da2 = da.assign_coords(date=("time", dates), time=("time", t_dec))  # da2
    da2.time.attrs.update(units="decimal_year", long_name="Decimal year")  # set da2.time.attrs.update(units
    return MultidimensionalRaster(da2)  # return the computed result

def write_geotiff_from_array(array: np.ndarray, out_path: Path, profile_src: Path, nodata=np.nan):
    """
    Write a single-band array to a GeoTIFF file, copying metadata (CRS, affine, etc.)
    from a reference GeoTIFF.

    - Converts the array to float32.
    - Sets compression (LZW) and nodata value.
    - Ensures parent directory exists.

    Used to save processed or derived raster outputs for mapping or further analysis.
    """
    with rasterio.open(profile_src) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
        profile = src.profile.copy()  # profile
    profile.update(dtype="float32", count=1, nodata=nodata, compress="LZW")  # set profile.update(dtype
    out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # set out_path.parent.mkdir(parents
    with rasterio.open(out_path, "w", **profile) as dst:  # open a context-managed resource
        dst.write(np.asarray(array, dtype=np.float32), 1)  # compute dst.write(np.asarray(array

def export_trend_bands(trend: MultidimensionalRaster, out_dir: Path, stem: str, profile_src: Path):
    """
    Save multiple trend result layers (slope, p-value, R²) as GeoTIFF files using
    write_geotiff_from_array.

    - Exports each trend output (if present) with a standardized filename.
    - Returns list of written filenames for reference/logging.
    """
    ds = trend.dataset  # ds
    mapping = {  # mapping
        "slope": f"{stem}_slope.tif",
        "p_value": f"{stem}_pvalue.tif",
        "r2": f"{stem}_R2.tif",
    }
    written = []  # written
    for var, fname in mapping.items():  # iterate over items
        if var not in ds:
            continue  # skip this candidate
        path = out_dir / fname  # path
        write_geotiff_from_array(ds[var].values, path, profile_src)
        written.append(path.name)
    return written  # return the computed result

def plot_trend_triplet(trend: MultidimensionalRaster, title: str, cmap_slope="RdBu_r"):
    """
    Display quicklook maps of the spatial patterns in trend results:
    - Slope (rate of change, units/year)
    - p-value (statistical significance)
    - R² (coefficient of determination)

    Uses matplotlib with side-by-side subplots for compact visualization.
    Color scales are automatically set for robust and interpretable display.
    """
    ds = trend.dataset  # ds
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.2))  # create the figure and axes
    slope = ds["slope"]  # slope
    vmax = np.nanpercentile(np.abs(slope.values), 98)  # compute vmax
    vmax = max(float(vmax), 1e-6)  # vmax
    im0 = axes[0].imshow(slope.values, cmap=cmap_slope, vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, origin="upper")  # show a 2-D array as an image
    axes[0].set_title("Slope (units/year)")  # panel title
    fig.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046)  # add a colorbar

    im1 = axes[1].imshow(ds["p_value"].values, cmap="viridis_r", vmin=0, vmax=0.1, origin="upper")  # show a 2-D array as an image
    axes[1].set_title("p-value")  # panel title
    fig.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.046)  # add a colorbar

    im2 = axes[2].imshow(ds["r2"].values, cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1, origin="upper")  # show a 2-D array as an image
    axes[2].set_title("R2")  # panel title
    fig.colorbar(im2, ax=axes[2], fraction=0.046)  # add a colorbar

    for ax in axes:  # iterate over items
        ax.set_xticks([])  # configure tick labels
        ax.set_yticks([])  # configure tick labels
    fig.suptitle(title, y=1.02)  # set fig.suptitle(title
    plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
    plt.show()  # render the figure

print("Helpers ready.")  # status / summary print

Optional: Mann-Kendall / Theil-Sen
The Mann-Kendall test and Theil-Sen estimator provide non-parametric methods for detecting monotonic trends in time series data.
Mann-Kendall trend test:

For a time series \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\), compute the Mann-Kendall statistic \(S\):

\[
S = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \mathrm{sgn}(x_j - x_i)
\]
where the sign function \(\mathrm{sgn}(x)\) is defined as:
\[
\mathrm{sgn}(x) = \begin{cases}
  +1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\
  0  & \text{if } x = 0 \\
  -1 & \text{if } x < 0
\end{cases}
\]

The normalized value of \(S\) gives Kendall’s tau (\(\tau\)), a correlation between time and the variable.
A p-value is computed to test the null hypothesis of no trend.

Theil-Sen slope estimator:

For all \(i < j\), compute all pairwise slopes:
\[
  m_{ij} = \frac{x_j - x_i}{t_j - t_i}
  \]
where \(t_i\) and \(t_j\) are the time points.
The Theil-Sen slope is the median of all \(m_{ij}\).
The intercept is estimated as the median of \([x_i - (\text{slope} \times t_i) ]\).

This method is more robust to outliers than ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.
Setting trend_type="MANN_KENDALL" returns the following statistics: Kendall’s tau (τ), p-value, Theil-Sen slope (per year), and intercept.

title: Multidimensional Trend Analysis
text:
Monthly trend analysis

Average bi-weekly slices into year-month means.

For each calendar month (Jan-Dec), fit a LINEAR trend across years.

Slope = groundwater change per year for that calendar month (R_Code/02_monthly_trend.ipynb).


Code
# Work from datetime-indexed cube for groupby
da = wt_mdr.dataset["watertable"]  # da

print("Computing year-month means...")  # status / summary print
monthly_avg = da.groupby("time.year").map(  # monthly_avg
    lambda x: x.groupby("time.month").mean("time", skipna=True)
)
print(monthly_avg)  # status / summary print

monthly_trends = {}  # monthly_trends
for month in range(1, 13):  # iterate over items
    month_name = calendar.month_name[month]  # month_name
    try:  # attempt optional or version-sensitive call
        month_da = monthly_avg.sel(month=month)  # select along coordinates or indices
    except Exception:  # handle the failure path
        print(f"  skip {month_name}: month not in dataset")  # status / summary print
        continue  # skip this candidate

    if "year" in month_da.dims:
        month_da = month_da.dropna("year", how="all")  # month_da
        years = month_da["year"].values.astype(np.float64)  # cast to the target dtype
        if len(years) < 3:
            print(f"  skip {month_name}: only {len(years)} years")  # status / summary print
            continue  # skip this candidate
        month_da = month_da.assign_coords(time=("year", years)).swap_dims({"year": "time"})  # month_da
    else:
        print(f"  skip {month_name}: unexpected dims {month_da.dims}")  # status / summary print
        continue  # skip this candidate

    drop_coords = [c for c in ("month", "year") if c in month_da.coords]  # drop_coords
    if drop_coords:
        month_da = month_da.drop_vars(drop_coords)  # month_da
    month_da.name = "watertable"  # set month_da.name
    mdr_m = MultidimensionalRaster(month_da)  # mdr_m

    print(f"-> {month_name}: {len(years)} yearly means ({int(years.min())}-{int(years.max())})")  # status / summary print
    tr = generate_trend_raster(  # tr
        mdr_m, variable="watertable", dimension="time", trend_type="LINEAR"  # mdr_m
    )
    monthly_trends[month] = tr  # set monthly_trends[month]
    stem = f"watertable_{month_name}"  # stem
    written = export_trend_bands(tr, MONTHLY_DIR, stem, REF_TIF)  # written
    print(f"   wrote {', '.join(written)}")  # status / summary print

print(f"\nMonthly trend sets: {len(monthly_trends)} / 12")  # status / summary print

text:
Multidimensional Raster Creation from ERA NetCDF
This notebook demonstrates the full processing pipeline for handling 2 m air temperature (t2m) data from the ECMWF ERA merged NetCDF (Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/t2m_2000_2018.nc).

Extract annual temperature: Selects data for a target year (e.g., 2018) from the multiyear NetCDF.
Temporal aggregation to daily means: Converts 3-hourly (sub-daily) values to daily average temperature in Celsius.
Spatial transformation: Constructs spatial point features for temperature values and reprojects them to the Bangladesh Transverse Mercator (BUTM) coordinate system.
Boundary masking: Clips the points to the Bangladesh official boundary using a shapefile mask.
16-day MODIS-style temporal aggregation: Aggregates daily temperature values into 16-day means, matching MODIS NDVI temporal granularity (output format: CSV columns like D_YYYY_017, D_YYYY_033 …).
Spatial interpolation and rasterization: Applies thin-plate spline interpolation over the entire Bangladesh domain at 1000 m spatial resolution, and exports the results as a multi-band GeoTIFF (one band per 16-day period).


Output products







Output type
Path location




16-day mean temperature CSV (all years)
Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/Tabular_Data/t2m_YYYY_mean_16days.csv


Multi-band raster (GeoTIFF) for all years
Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/Raster_Data/t2m_YYYY_16day_1000m.tif




Note: The available years in t2m_2000_2018.nc are 2000-2003, 2007-2018 (years 2004-2006 are absent).



Dependencies

netCDF data I/O and manipulation: xarray, netCDF4
Vector GIS operations: geopandas
Raster creation and export: rasterio
Geometric and spatial transformation: shapely
Interpolation: scipy.interpolate
Data handling: numpy, pandas

text:
Helper functions
Shared utilities for daily averaging, clipping, 16-day composites, TPS, and GeoTIFF writing.


Code
# --- Helper functions for multidimensional temperature data processing ---
# Each function includes comments explaining its role and main steps.

def load_year_t2m_celsius(nc_path: Path, year: int) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Load temperature (t2m) data for a given year from a NetCDF file and convert from Kelvin to Celsius.
    
    Steps:
    1. Open the NetCDF dataset.
    2. Select temperature values (t2m) for the specified year only.
    3. Check if data exists for this year.
    4. Convert temperature from Kelvin to Celsius.
    5. Attach relevant attributes and load data into memory.
    6. Close the dataset and return the result.
    """
    ds = xr.open_dataset(nc_path)  # open the NetCDF dataset
    t2m = ds["t2m"].sel(time=slice(f"{year}-01-01", f"{year}-12-31"))  # select one calendar year of t2m
    if t2m.sizes.get("time", 0) == 0:  # abort if the year has no timesteps
        ds.close()  # close the NetCDF handle
        raise ValueError(f"No t2m timesteps found for year {year}")  # fail with a clear error message
    t2m_c = (t2m - 273.15).astype("float32")  # Kelvin to Celsius as float32
    t2m_c.attrs.update({"units": "degC", "long_name": "2 metre temperature"})  # attach CF-style units metadata
    out = t2m_c.load()  # load the array into memory
    ds.close()  # close the NetCDF handle
    return out  # return the result

def to_daily_mean(t2m_3h: xr.DataArray) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Convert 3-hourly temperature data into daily averages.
    
    Steps:
    1. Use xarray's resample to average all 3-hourly values within each calendar day.
    2. Update metadata for clarity.
    3. Return the daily mean DataArray.
    """
    daily = t2m_3h.resample(time="1D").mean(skipna=True)  # average 3-hourly values to daily means
    daily.name = "t2m"  # set the DataArray name
    daily.attrs.update({"units": "degC", "long_name": "Daily mean 2 metre temperature"})  # attach CF-style units metadata
    return daily  # return the result

def daily_to_points(daily: xr.DataArray) -> gpd.GeoDataFrame:
    """
    Convert daily gridded temperature to a GeoDataFrame with a row per 2D grid point and columns for each date.
    
    Steps:
    1. Generate 2D longitude and latitude arrays representing each grid node.
    2. Flatten arrays to build table rows; assign unique station ids.
    3. Move daily temp values into a (points x time) table.
    4. Build a pandas DataFrame for values and locations.
    5. Convert to GeoDataFrame with geometry column (EPSG:4326).
    """
    lon2d, lat2d = np.meshgrid(daily.longitude.values, daily.latitude.values)  # 2-D lon/lat grids for each cell
    n_pts = lon2d.size  # n_pts
    station_id = [f"S{i:04d}" for i in range(n_pts)]  # stable point identifiers

    vals = np.moveaxis(daily.values, 0, -1).reshape(n_pts, daily.sizes["time"])  # reshape cube to points x time
    dates = pd.to_datetime(daily.time.values).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")  # date strings as column labels
    df = pd.DataFrame(vals, columns=dates)  # build the attribute table
    df.insert(0, "station_id", station_id)  # prepend id / coordinate columns
    df.insert(1, "lon", lon2d.ravel().astype("float64"))  # prepend id / coordinate columns
    df.insert(2, "lat", lat2d.ravel().astype("float64"))  # prepend id / coordinate columns

    geometry = gpd.points_from_xy(df["lon"], df["lat"], crs="EPSG:4326")  # build point geometries in WGS84
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=geometry, crs="EPSG:4326")  # return the result

def reproject_and_clip(gdf: gpd.GeoDataFrame, bd: gpd.GeoDataFrame) -> gpd.GeoDataFrame:
    """
    Reproject the points to the coordinate reference system (CRS) of `bd` and clip them to Bangladesh's boundary.
    
    Steps:
    1. Project all point geometries into the same CRS as the Bangladesh boundary (BUTM).
    2. Clip points to those inside the boundary polygon.
    3. Reset the index for a clean output.
    """
    proj = gdf.to_crs(bd.crs)  # reproject to the boundary CRS
    clipped = gpd.clip(proj, bd)  # keep points inside Bangladesh
    return clipped.reset_index(drop=True)  # return the result

def modis_16day_means(clipped: gpd.GeoDataFrame, year: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Average daily columns into MODIS-like 16-day intervals for each point.
    
    Output table columns: station_id, lon, lat, and one column per 16-day composite (D_{year}_{start_DOY}).
    
    Steps:
    1. Identify which columns are dates (exclude id/lon/lat/geometry).
    2. Convert column headers to datetime to extract day-of-year.
    3. Prepare output DataFrame for ids and point locations (in WGS84).
    4. For each 16-day MODIS interval, calculate the mean across all matching days per row.
    5. Assign results to output table.
    """
    date_cols = [c for c in clipped.columns if c not in {"station_id", "lon", "lat", "geometry"}]  # daily value columns only
    dates = pd.to_datetime(date_cols)  # daily value columns only
    doys = dates.dayofyear.to_numpy()  # DOY for each daily column

    wgs = clipped.to_crs("EPSG:4326")  # reproject to the boundary CRS
    out = pd.DataFrame({  # build the attribute table
        "station_id": clipped["station_id"].values,
        "lon": wgs.geometry.x.values,
        "lat": wgs.geometry.y.values,
    })

    starts = MODIS_DOYS  # 16-day composite start DOYs
    for i, start in enumerate(starts):  # iterate over items
        end = starts[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(starts) else 367  # end
        mask = (doys >= start) & (doys < end)  # mask
        cols = [date_cols[j] for j, m in enumerate(mask) if m]  # daily value columns only
        name = f"D_{year}_{start:03d}"  # name
        if cols:
            out[name] = clipped[cols].mean(axis=1, skipna=True).astype("float32").values  # mean of days in this 16-day window
        else:
            out[name] = np.nan  # no days in this window
    return out  # return the result

def make_target_grid(bd: gpd.GeoDataFrame, resolution_m: float = 1000.0):
    """
    Create a regular raster grid (width x height, meters per pixel) covering the extent of Bangladesh.
    
    Steps:
    1. Compute the full bounding box (total_bounds) for bd.
    2. Convert to integer grid width/height using resolution.
    3. Calculate affine transform mapping pixel to map coordinates.
    4. Generate evenly spaced grid points for X/Y pixel centers.
    5. Stack to Nx2 array of coordinates for interpolation.
    6. Create a mask so only grid cells inside bd geometry are True.
    7. Return all grid-related parameters.
    """
    bounds = bd.total_bounds  # boundary extent in projected metres
    width = int(np.ceil((bounds[2] - bounds[0]) / resolution_m))  # grid size from extent and resolution
    height = int(np.ceil((bounds[3] - bounds[1]) / resolution_m))  # grid size from extent and resolution
    transform = from_bounds(bounds[0], bounds[1], bounds[2], bounds[3], width, height)  # affine transform for the target grid
    xs = bounds[0] + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * resolution_m  # pixel-centre coordinates
    ys = bounds[3] - (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * resolution_m  # pixel-centre coordinates
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)  # 2-D lon/lat grids for each cell
    grid_xy = np.column_stack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel()])  # Nx2 array of grid centres for RBF
    mask = geometry_mask(  # True inside the Bangladesh polygon
        bd.geometry, out_shape=(height, width), transform=transform, invert=True  # GeoTIFF creation option
    )
    return width, height, transform, grid_xy, mask  # return the result

def tps_interpolate_band(coords_xy, values, grid_xy, height, width, mask):
    """
    Interpolate scattered point data onto a raster grid using Thin Plate Spline (RBF).
    
    Steps:
    1. Identify valid (not NaN) values among the points.
    2. If fewer than 3 valid points, output a raster of NaNs.
    3. Fit a thin-plate spline RBF interpolator to these points.
    4. Predict/interpolate values at all grid pixel centers.
    5. Mask out pixels falling outside the target boundary.
    6. Return the interpolated raster array.
    """
    valid = np.isfinite(values)  # valid-value mask
    if valid.sum() < 3:
        return np.full((height, width), np.nan, dtype="float32")  # return the result
    rbf = RBFInterpolator(  # fit thin-plate spline to valid points
        coords_xy[valid], values[valid], kernel="thin_plate_spline", smoothing=0.0  # set coords_xy[valid]
    )
    pred = rbf(grid_xy).reshape(height, width).astype("float32")  # reshape cube to points x time
    pred[~mask] = np.nan  # nodata outside the boundary
    return pred  # return the result

def write_multiband_geotiff(path: Path, bands, band_names, transform, crs):
    """
    Write several raster bands into a single (multi-band) GeoTIFF file.
    
    Steps:
    1. Use rasterio to open/create the output TIFF, specify shape/CRS/transform.
    2. Write each 2D array (one for each composite) as a new band.
    3. Save descriptive names for each band in the TIFF metadata.
    """
    height, width = bands[0].shape  # height
    with rasterio.open(  # write the multi-band GeoTIFF
        path,
        "w",
        driver="GTiff",  # driver
        height=height,  # height
        width=width,  # width
        count=len(bands),  # GeoTIFF creation option
        dtype="float32",  # GeoTIFF creation option
        crs=crs,  # GeoTIFF creation option
        transform=transform,  # GeoTIFF creation option
        nodata=np.nan,  # GeoTIFF creation option
        compress="lzw",  # GeoTIFF creation option
    ) as dst:
        for i, (arr, name) in enumerate(zip(bands, band_names), start=1):  # iterate over items
            dst.write(arr, i)  # write one band
            dst.set_band_description(i, name)

def process_year(nc_path, year, bd, tab_dir, ras_dir, grid_cache, resolution_m=1000.0):
    """
    Complete workflow for processing one year of temperature data:
        → Save Bangladesh-clipped, MODIS-16day mean temperatures (tabular and raster).
    
    Steps (with logging):
    1. Load temperature for one year and convert to Celsius.
    2. Average to daily means.
    3. Convert daily gridded data to spatial points.
    4. Reproject and clip to Bangladesh.
    5. Tabulate 16-day means, save to CSV.
    6. For each composite, interpolate to grid, stack results as raster bands.
    7. Write all bands to a single GeoTIFF (one band per composite).
    8. Return paths to output files.
    """
    print(f"\n=== Year {year} ===")  # status / summary print
    t2m = load_year_t2m_celsius(nc_path, year)  # t2m
    print(f"  3-hourly: {t2m.sizes['time']} steps")  # status / summary print
    daily = to_daily_mean(t2m)  # aggregate along time or groups
    print(f"  daily:    {daily.sizes['time']} days")  # status / summary print

    gdf = daily_to_points(daily)  # gdf
    clipped = reproject_and_clip(gdf, bd)  # reproject or clip geometries
    print(f"  points after clip: {len(clipped)}")  # status / summary print

    table = modis_16day_means(clipped, year)  # table
    csv_path = tab_dir / f"t2m_{year}_mean_16days.csv"  # csv_path
    table.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)  # set table.to_csv(csv_path
    print(f"  CSV → {csv_path.name}  ({table.shape[1] - 3} composites)")  # status / summary print

    width, height, transform, grid_xy, mask = grid_cache  # width
    coords_xy = np.column_stack([clipped.geometry.x.values, clipped.geometry.y.values])  # Nx2 array of grid centres for RBF
    band_cols = [c for c in table.columns if c.startswith(f"D_{year}_")]  # band_cols
    bands = []  # bands
    for col in band_cols:  # iterate over items
        arr = tps_interpolate_band(  # arr
            coords_xy, table[col].to_numpy(), grid_xy, height, width, mask
        )
        bands.append(arr)
        print(f"  TPS {col}")  # status / summary print

    tif_path = ras_dir / f"t2m_{year}_16day_1000m.tif"  # tif_path
    write_multiband_geotiff(tif_path, bands, band_cols, transform, bd.crs)
    print(f"  GeoTIFF → {tif_path.name}  ({len(bands)} bands, {width}×{height} @ {resolution_m:.0f} m)")  # status / summary print
    return csv_path, tif_path  # return the result

title: Multidimensional Data Management
text:
Raster to NetCDF
Convert the Bangladesh watertable GeoTIFF series under Data/00_shared/raster_data/Bangladesh/watertable/ into a multidimensional NetCDF with geolattice.spatial_analysis.multidimensional_raster (ArcGIS-style Raster to NetCDF).








Step
API / tool
Role




1
rasterio + MultidimensionalRaster
Read each watertable_YYYY_DOY.tif as a time slice


2
merge_multidimensional_rasters
Combine yearly cubes along time


3
raster_to_netcdf
Write the merged cube to NetCDF



Filenames encode MODIS 16-day composites (watertable_1985_001.tif -> 1985-01-01).
Output: Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/watertable_1985_2020.nc

Note: GeoTIFFs are opened with rasterio so this cell works in Jupyter without relying on the system osgeo/libgdal shared library. Re-run Setup first after a kernel restart.



Code
# Raster to NetCDF: watertable GeoTIFF series -> multidimensional NetCDF
#
# Reads GeoTIFFs with rasterio (reliable in Jupyter), then wraps with
# geolattice MultidimensionalRaster + raster_to_netcdf.
import re  # regular expressions for filename / DOY parsing
from datetime import datetime, timedelta  # parse and construct timestamps

def parse_watertable_time(path: Path) -> datetime:
    """Parse watertable_YYYY_DOY.tif -> datetime at that day-of-year."""
    m = re.match(r"watertable_(\d{4})_(\d{3})$", path.stem)  # m
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected watertable filename: {path.name}")  # fail with a clear error message
    year, doy = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))  # year
    return datetime(year, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=doy - 1)  # return the computed result


def stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(paths, times, variable_name="watertable"):
    """Build a MultidimensionalRaster from a GeoTIFF time series (rasterio)."""
    arrays = []  # arrays
    xs = ys = None  # xs
    for path in paths:  # iterate over items
        with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
            data = src.read(1).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
            nodata = src.nodata  # nodata
            if nodata is not None:
                data = np.where(data == nodata, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            # also mask extreme GDAL nodata sentinels
            data = np.where(np.abs(data) > 1e30, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            transform = src.transform  # transform
            height, width = data.shape  # height
            xs = transform.c + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * transform.a  # compute xs
            ys = transform.f + (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * transform.e  # compute ys
            arrays.append(data)

    da = xr.DataArray(  # da
        np.stack(arrays, axis=0),  # set np.stack(arrays
        dims=("time", "y", "x"),  # dims
        coords={"time": list(times), "y": ys, "x": xs},  # coords
        name=variable_name,  # name
    )
    return MultidimensionalRaster(da)  # return the computed result


# 1) List GeoTIFF slices
wt_tifs = sorted(WT_DIR.glob("watertable_*.tif"))  # collect matching files
print(f"Found {len(wt_tifs)} watertable GeoTIFFs in {WT_DIR}")  # status / summary print
if not wt_tifs:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"No watertable_*.tif under {WT_DIR}")  # fail with a clear error message

years = sorted({int(p.stem.split("_")[1]) for p in wt_tifs})  # years
print(f"Years: {years[0]}-{years[-1]} ({len(years)} years)")  # status / summary print

# 2) Build one cube per year, write yearly NetCDF (keeps memory bounded)
yearly_nc = []  # yearly_nc
wt_year_dir = NC_OUT_DIR / "watertable_yearly"  # build a filesystem path
wt_year_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # set wt_year_dir.mkdir(parents

for year in years:  # iterate over items
    paths = sorted(WT_DIR.glob(f"watertable_{year}_*.tif"))  # collect matching files
    times = [parse_watertable_time(p) for p in paths]  # times
    year_nc = wt_year_dir / f"watertable_{year}.nc"  # year_nc
    mdr_year = stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(paths, times, variable_name="watertable")  # build multidimensional layer
    raster_to_netcdf(
        mdr_year,
        year_nc,
        overwrite=True,  # overwrite
        encoding={"watertable": {"zlib": True, "complevel": 4, "dtype": "float32"}},  # encoding
    )
    yearly_nc.append(year_nc)
    print(f"  {year}: {len(paths)} slices -> {year_nc.name}")  # status / summary print

# 3) Merge along time and write combined NetCDF
WT_NC = NC_OUT_DIR / "watertable_1985_2020.nc"  # build a filesystem path
merged = merge_multidimensional_rasters(  # merged
    yearly_nc,
    dimension="time",  # dimension
    combine="by_coords",  # combine
)
ds = merged.dataset.copy(deep=False)  # ds
ds["watertable"] = ds["watertable"].astype("float32")  # set ds["watertable"]
ds["watertable"].attrs.update({
    "long_name": "Groundwater watertable depth / level",
    "units": "m",
})
ds.attrs.update({
    "title": "Bangladesh watertable 16-day series (1985-2020)",
    "source": str(WT_DIR),
    "Conventions": "CF-1.8",
})

raster_to_netcdf(
    MultidimensionalRaster(ds),
    WT_NC,
    overwrite=True,  # overwrite
    encoding={"watertable": {"zlib": True, "complevel": 4, "dtype": "float32"}},  # encoding
)

# 4) Verify 
chk = xr.open_dataset(WT_NC)  # open the NetCDF / dataset
print("\nWrote:", WT_NC)  # status / summary print
print(chk)  # status / summary print
print(f"size_mb={WT_NC.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f}")  # status / summary print
print("time:", chk.time.values[0], "->", chk.time.values[-1], f"(n={chk.sizes['time']})")  # status / summary print

title: Multidimensional Data Management
text:
Table to NetCDF
Export the 16-day t2m CSVs in Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/Tabular_Data/ to NetCDF with geolattice.spatial_analysis.table_to_netcdf (ArcGIS Table to NetCDF).
Each CSV has columns:
station_id, lon, lat, D_YYYY_001, D_YYYY_017, … D_YYYY_353
This section:

Loads one year (demo 2018) and all yearly CSVs from Tabular_Data
Writes a wide table NetCDF (one variable per 16-day column)
Melts to long form (station x time) and writes an analysis-friendly NetCDF
Optionally stacks every year into one multi-year long-form NetCDF

Outputs (under Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/):



File
Content




t2m_2018_table_wide.nc
Wide table via table_to_netcdf


t2m_2018_table_long.nc
Long station x time cube


t2m_all_years_table_long.nc
All years stacked





Code
# Table to NetCDF: use CSVs from Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/output/Tabular_Data
import re  # regular expressions for filename / DOY parsing
from datetime import datetime, timedelta  # parse and construct timestamps

csv_files = sorted(TAB_DIR.glob("t2m_*_mean_16days.csv"))  # collect matching files
print(f"Found {len(csv_files)} CSV files in {TAB_DIR}")  # status / summary print
for pth in csv_files:  # iterate over items
    print(" ", pth.name)  # status / summary print

demo_csv = TAB_DIR / f"t2m_{DEMO_YEAR}_mean_16days.csv"  # demo_csv
if not demo_csv.is_file():  # only when the path exists
    raise FileNotFoundError(  # fail with a clear error message
        f"Missing {demo_csv}. Run the 16-day CSV steps (section 5 / 7) first."
    )

table = pd.read_csv(demo_csv)  # compute table
print(f"\nDemo table {demo_csv.name}: {table.shape}")  # status / summary print
print(table.head(3))  # status / summary print


def composite_col_to_time(col: str) -> datetime:
    """D_2018_017 -> datetime for that year + DOY."""
    m = re.match(r"D_(\d{4})_(\d{3})$", col)  # m
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected composite column: {col}")  # fail with a clear error message
    year, doy = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))  # year
    return datetime(year, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=doy - 1)  # return the computed result


def wide_to_long(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Melt D_YYYY_DOY columns to station_id, lon, lat, time, t2m."""
    id_vars = ["station_id", "lon", "lat"]  # id_vars
    value_vars = [c for c in df.columns if re.match(r"D_\d{4}_\d{3}$", c)]  # value_vars
    long = df.melt(id_vars=id_vars, value_vars=value_vars, var_name="composite", value_name="t2m")  # long
    long["time"] = long["composite"].map(composite_col_to_time)  # set long["time"]
    return long.drop(columns=["composite"]).sort_values(["station_id", "time"]).reset_index(drop=True)  # return the computed result


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A) Wide table -> NetCDF (ArcGIS Table to NetCDF style)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
wide_nc = NC_OUT_DIR / f"t2m_{DEMO_YEAR}_table_wide.nc"  # wide_nc
# Keep a clean numeric index for the row dimension
wide_df = table.copy()  # wide_df
# station_id as a column variable; use RangeIndex as record dim
wide_df = wide_df.reset_index(drop=True)  # wide_df
table_to_netcdf(wide_df, wide_nc, row_dimension="record", overwrite=True)  # set table_to_netcdf(wide_df
print(f"\nWide NetCDF -> {wide_nc}")  # status / summary print
print(xr.open_dataset(wide_nc))  # status / summary print


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B) Long station x time cube (better for analysis)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
long_df = wide_to_long(table)  # long_df
print(f"\nLong table: {long_df.shape}")  # status / summary print
print(long_df.head(3))  # status / summary print

# Pivot to (time, station) DataArray, then write via MultidimensionalRaster helper path
stations = long_df["station_id"].astype(str)  # cast to the target dtype
lon_by_st = long_df.drop_duplicates("station_id").set_index("station_id")["lon"]  # lon_by_st
lat_by_st = long_df.drop_duplicates("station_id").set_index("station_id")["lat"]  # lat_by_st

pivot = long_df.pivot(index="time", columns="station_id", values="t2m").sort_index()  # pivot
da = xr.DataArray(  # da
    pivot.to_numpy(dtype="float32"),  # set pivot.to_numpy(dtype
    dims=("time", "station"),  # dims
    coords={  # coords
        "time": pivot.index.to_numpy(),
        "station": pivot.columns.astype(str).to_numpy(),
        "lon": ("station", lon_by_st.loc[pivot.columns].to_numpy()),
        "lat": ("station", lat_by_st.loc[pivot.columns].to_numpy()),
    },
    name="t2m",  # name
    attrs={"units": "degC", "long_name": "16-day mean 2 metre temperature"},  # attrs
)
long_nc = NC_OUT_DIR / f"t2m_{DEMO_YEAR}_table_long.nc"  # long_nc
da.to_dataset().to_netcdf(
    long_nc,
    encoding={"t2m": {"zlib": True, "complevel": 4, "dtype": "float32"}},  # encoding
)
print(f"Long NetCDF -> {long_nc}")  # status / summary print
print(xr.open_dataset(long_nc))  # status / summary print


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# C) All years from Tabular_Data -> one long NetCDF
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
frames = []  # frames
for csv_path in csv_files:  # iterate over items
    frames.append(wide_to_long(pd.read_csv(csv_path)))
all_long = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)  # compute all_long
print(f"\nAll-years long table: {all_long.shape}")  # status / summary print

# Also export the concatenated long table with table_to_netcdf (record form)
all_table_nc = NC_OUT_DIR / "t2m_all_years_table_records.nc"  # build a filesystem path
table_to_netcdf(
    all_long.assign(time=all_long["time"].astype("datetime64[ns]")),  # set all_long.assign(time
    all_table_nc,
    row_dimension="record",  # row_dimension
    overwrite=True,  # overwrite
)
print(f"All-years record NetCDF -> {all_table_nc}")  # status / summary print

# Station x time cube for all years
pivot_all = all_long.pivot_table(index="time", columns="station_id", values="t2m", aggfunc="mean").sort_index()  # pivot_all
lon_all = all_long.drop_duplicates("station_id").set_index("station_id")["lon"]  # lon_all
lat_all = all_long.drop_duplicates("station_id").set_index("station_id")["lat"]  # lat_all
da_all = xr.DataArray(  # da_all
    pivot_all.to_numpy(dtype="float32"),  # set pivot_all.to_numpy(dtype
    dims=("time", "station"),  # dims
    coords={  # coords
        "time": pivot_all.index.to_numpy(),
        "station": pivot_all.columns.astype(str).to_numpy(),
        "lon": ("station", lon_all.loc[pivot_all.columns].to_numpy()),
        "lat": ("station", lat_all.loc[pivot_all.columns].to_numpy()),
    },
    name="t2m",  # name
    attrs={"units": "degC", "long_name": "16-day mean 2 metre temperature"},  # attrs
)
all_long_nc = NC_OUT_DIR / "t2m_all_years_table_long.nc"  # build a filesystem path
da_all.to_dataset().to_netcdf(
    all_long_nc,
    encoding={"t2m": {"zlib": True, "complevel": 4, "dtype": "float32"}},  # encoding
)
print(f"All-years long cube -> {all_long_nc}")  # status / summary print
chk = xr.open_dataset(all_long_nc)  # open the NetCDF / dataset
print(chk)  # status / summary print
print("time:", chk.time.values[0], "->", chk.time.values[-1], f"(n={chk.sizes['time']})")  # status / summary print
print("stations:", chk.sizes["station"])  # status / summary print

# Quick plot: one station time series
st0 = str(chk.station.values[0])  # st0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))  # create the figure and axes
chk["t2m"].sel(station=st0).plot(ax=ax)  # draw the map or chart
ax.set_title(f"t2m 16-day means: station {st0}")  # panel title
ax.set_ylabel("°C")  # y-axis label
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render the figure
chk.close()  # release the file handle

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Overview
Spatial hydrology analyses how water moves and accumulates across a land surface using a digital elevation model (DEM). It is one of the deepest specialisations in Whitebox-style terrain analysis and spans DEM conditioning, flow routing, watershed delineation, stream extraction, and connectivity / storage modelling.
This notebook uses geolattice.spatial_analysis.surface_hydrology with the entire Bangladesh hilly-district DEM (Data/00_shared/raster_data/Bangladesh/hilly_dem_BTM.tiff, Bangladesh Transverse Mercator, 250 m; ~521 × 1329 cells). The workflow follows the topics in the Whitebox Workflows Spatial Hydrology chapter and the R notes in R_Code/surface-hydrological-anlysis-whitbox-r.qmd.

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Core concepts

The hydrologic DEM problem
Most raw DEMs contain surface depressions: cells or groups of cells enclosed by higher neighbours. They may be real topographic basins, acquisition noise, or interpolation artefacts. Standard single-flow routing (D8) cannot route water out of closed sinks: the algorithm terminates where no downhill neighbour exists.
Before flow routing, the DEM must be conditioned so spurious depressions are removed while genuine basins (lakes, wetlands) can be preserved when desired.
Two principal strategies:

Filling: raise cells inside each depression up to the spill (pour-point) elevation. Guarantees a drained surface but can create large flats that need a secondary gradient (flat increment).
Breaching: cut a narrow least-cost channel through the barrier around a depression. Preserves more of the original elevation field and is preferred when barriers are road embankments or similar artefacts.

In practice a hybrid approach: breach where possible, fill remaining sinks, is often optimal (Whitebox breach_depressions_least_cost(..., fill_deps=True)).


Flow direction algorithms
After conditioning, a flow-direction raster encodes where water leaves each cell:








Algorithm
Flow type
Best use




D8
Single (deterministic)
Channel delineation, simple watersheds


Rho8
Single (stochastic)
Reduces D8 cardinal bias


D-infinity (Dinf)
Multiple (proportional split)
Hillslope flux, dispersive flow


FD8
Multiple (proportional)
Shallow overland flow


MD-infinity
Multiple
Subsurface / soil-moisture modelling


Quinn et al.
Multiple (FD8 variant)
Wetness index, slope-area workflows


Minimal dispersion
Adaptive
Balance between D8 and Dinf



See the Whitebox Spatial Hydrology manual for the same taxonomy.

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
DEM conditioning
Hydrology tools route water downhill based on cell elevations. If no neighbour is lower, flow stops: a sink, pit, or depression.

Filling vs breaching
For a depression with pour-point elevation \(z_p\) and interior cells \(z_i\):
\[
z_i^{\text{filled}} = \max(z_i,\, z_p)
\]
Priority-flood / Wang-Liu filling raises every interior cell to \(z_p\). Flats may need a tiny gradient \(\varepsilon\) so D8 has a unique direction:
\[
z^{\text{flat}} = z_p + k\,\varepsilon,\quad k = 0,1,2,\ldots
\]
Breaching instead lowers a path of cells through the barrier. A least-cost breach minimises cumulative vertical cost subject to maximum length / depth constraints (Whitebox breach_depressions_least_cost).
geolattice exposes:

breach_depressions: single-cell pits + priority breach / optional fill
fill_depressions: Wang-Liu-style priority flood with optional flat fix



Code
# Condition the DEM: breach depressions, then fill remaining sinks.
breached = OUT / "dem_breached.tif"  # DEM after depression breaching
filled = OUT / "dem_filled.tif"  # hydrologically conditioned DEM

breach_depressions(dem, breached, fill_pits=True, overwrite=True)  # carve outlets through sinks
fill_depressions(breached, filled, fix_flats=True, overwrite=True)  # raise leftover sinks / flats

# Visualise how conditioning changed the DEM.
with open_raster_data(dem) as ds:
    z0 = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # raw elevation array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
if nd is not None:
    z0 = np.where(z0 == nd, np.nan, z0)  # mask nodata as NaN

with open_raster_data(filled) as ds:
    z1 = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # filled elevation array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
if nd is not None:
    z1 = np.where(z1 == nd, np.nan, z1)  # mask nodata as NaN

diff = z1 - z0  # fill depth (positive where fill raised the surface)
diff = np.where(np.abs(diff) < 1e-6, np.nan, diff)  # hide near-zero differences

# Three-panel comparison: raw, filled, and fill depth.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 7))  # three-panel figure
im0 = axes[0].imshow(z0, cmap="terrain")  # raw DEM
axes[0].set_title("Raw DEM")  # left panel title
plt.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046)  # colorbar for raw elevations
im1 = axes[1].imshow(z1, cmap="terrain")  # conditioned DEM
axes[1].set_title("Breached + filled")  # middle panel title
plt.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.046)  # colorbar for filled elevations
im2 = axes[2].imshow(diff, cmap="RdBu_r")  # fill depth
axes[2].set_title("Filled - raw (m)\n(zeros hidden)")  # right panel title
plt.colorbar(im2, ax=axes[2], fraction=0.046)  # colorbar for fill depth
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([])  # hide x tick labels
    ax.set_yticks([])  # hide y tick labels
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render the comparison

print(f"Cells raised by fill: {int(np.nansum(diff > 0))}")  # count of filled cells
print(f"Max fill depth (m):   {float(np.nanmax(diff)) if np.isfinite(np.nanmax(diff)) else 0:.3f}")  # max fill

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Flow direction

D8 (O’Callaghan & Mark, 1984)
Each cell \(i\) sends all flow to the neighbour \(j\) with the steepest drop:
\[
S_j = \frac{z_i - z_j}{d_{ij}},\qquad
d_{ij} = \begin{cases}
\Delta x & \text{cardinal}\\
\sqrt{2}\,\Delta x & \text{diagonal}
\end{cases}
\]
\[
\text{receiver}(i) = \arg\max_{j \in N_8(i)} S_j
\]
Whitebox / this package store the direction as a pointer code (power of 2):



Code
1
2
4
8
16
32
64
128




Dir
E
SE
S
SW
W
NW
N
NE





Rho8 (Fairfield & Leymarie, 1991)
Same neighbourhood, but the receiver is drawn randomly with probability proportional to \(S_j\) among downslope neighbours: reducing D8’s preference for cardinal axes.


D-infinity (Tarboton, 1997)
Flow is split between two adjacent downslope neighbours according to the aspect angle of the steepest triangular facet. If the facet angle is \(\alpha\) and the facet spans \(0\ldots\alpha_{\max}\):
\[
p_{\text{card}} = 1 - \frac{\alpha}{\alpha_{\max}},\qquad
p_{\text{diag}} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha_{\max}}
\]
The pointer raster stores continuous direction (degrees clockwise from east in Whitebox style).


FD8 / Quinn / MDinf / minimal dispersion

FD8 (Freeman): weights \(\propto (S_j)^p\) to all downslope neighbours (default \(p \approx 1.1\)).
Quinn: FD8 variant with contour-length factor: common in wetness work.
MD-infinity: apportions flow among multiple triangular facets.
Minimal dispersion: blends D8 (channels) and Dinf (hillslopes) using a local convergence proxy.



Code
# Compute D8, D-infinity, and Rho8 flow-direction pointers from the filled DEM.
d8p = OUT / "d8_pointer.tif"  # D8 pointer codes
dinf_p = OUT / "dinf_pointer.tif"  # D-infinity flow direction
rho8_p = OUT / "rho8_pointer.tif"  # stochastic Rho8 pointer

d8_pointer(filled, d8p, overwrite=True)  # single-receiver D8 codes
dinf_pointer(filled, dinf_p, overwrite=True)  # continuous D-infinity directions
rho8_pointer(filled, rho8_p, seed=42, overwrite=True)  # Rho8 with fixed seed

# Optional multi-band MFD weights (8 bands: E..NE).
fd8_p = OUT / "fd8_weights.tif"  # FD8 fractional outflow stack
fd8_pointer(filled, fd8_p, exponent=1.1, overwrite=True)  # MFD weights with slope exponent

# Map the three single-band pointer surfaces.
plot_rasters(
    [d8p, dinf_p, rho8_p],  # pointer paths
    titles=["D8 pointer (codes)", "Dinf direction (deg CW from E)", "Rho8 pointer"],  # panel titles
    ncols=3,  # three columns
    cmap="twilight",  # cyclic-friendly colormap
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the pointer maps

with open_raster_data(fd8_p) as ds:
    print(f"FD8 weight stack: {ds.band_count} bands (fractional outflow to 8 neighbours)")  # confirm 8 bands

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Flow accumulation
Flow accumulation measures how much upslope area drains through each cell. It is the primary surface for extracting streams, delineating watersheds, and building wetness indices.

D8 cell-count accumulation
Process cells from high to low elevation. Let \(A_i\) be the accumulation at cell \(i\) (initialised to 1 = the cell itself):
\[
A_j \leftarrow A_j + A_i \quad\text{for receiver } j = \text{D8}(i)
\]
Optional output types:








out_type
Formula
Units




"cells"
\(A_i\)
cell count


"area"
\(A_i \,(\Delta x)^2\)
m²


"sca" / "catchment_area"
\(A_i \,\Delta x\)
m (specific catchment area)





Specific contributing area (D-infinity)
With Dinf proportional weights \(w_{ij}\) to downslope neighbours:
\[
A_j \leftarrow A_j + w_{ij}\, A_i
\]
Specific contributing area (SCA) normalises by cell width and is the \(a\) term in TWI and many erosion models (Whitebox SCA section):
\[
\mathrm{SCA}_i = a_i = A_i^{\text{cells}} \cdot \Delta x
\quad [\mathrm{m}]
\]
Log-transforming \(A\) or SCA helps visualisation because values span many orders of magnitude.


Code
# Compute D8 cell accumulation and D-infinity specific catchment area (SCA).
fa_cells = OUT / "d8_flow_accum_cells.tif"  # D8 accumulation in cells
sca = OUT / "dinf_sca.tif"  # D-infinity SCA in metres

d8_flow_accumulation(filled, fa_cells, out_type="cells", overwrite=True)  # upslope cell count
dinf_flow_accumulation(filled, sca, out_type="sca", overwrite=True)  # specific catchment area

# Log-transform accumulation for display (span many orders of magnitude).
with open_raster_data(fa_cells) as ds:
    fa = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # D8 accumulation array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
    gt = ds.geotransform  # keep geotransform for later outlet placement
if nd is not None:
    fa = np.where(fa == nd, np.nan, fa)  # mask nodata
fa_log = np.log10(np.maximum(fa, 1.0))  # log10 for visualization

with open_raster_data(sca) as ds:
    sca_arr = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # SCA array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
if nd is not None:
    sca_arr = np.where(sca_arr == nd, np.nan, sca_arr)  # mask nodata
sca_log = np.log10(np.maximum(sca_arr, 1.0))  # log10 for visualization

with open_raster_data(hs) as ds:
    hs_arr = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # hillshade backdrop

# Overlay log accumulation on hillshade.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))  # two-panel figure
for ax, arr, title in zip(
    axes,
    [fa_log, sca_log],  # log-transformed surfaces
    ["log10(D8 flow accumulation, cells)", "log10(Dinf SCA, m)"],  # panel titles
):
    ax.imshow(hs_arr, cmap="gray", alpha=0.85)  # hillshade base
    im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap="Blues", alpha=0.65)  # accumulation overlay
    ax.set_title(title)  # panel title
    ax.set_xticks([])  # hide x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # hide y ticks
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)  # colorbar for log values
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render both panels

print(f"D8 FA  min/max cells: {np.nanmin(fa):.0f} / {np.nanmax(fa):.0f}")  # D8 range
print(f"Dinf SCA min/max (m):   {np.nanmin(sca_arr):.1f} / {np.nanmax(sca_arr):.1f}")  # SCA range

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Topographic Wetness Index (TWI)
TWI is a terrain-based proxy for soil moisture and saturation potential (Beven & Kirkby; Quinn et al.). Areas with large upslope area and gentle slopes tend to stay wetter.
\[
\mathrm{TWI} = \ln\!\left(\frac{a}{\tan\beta}\right)
\]
where:

\(a\) = specific catchment area (m): preferably from Dinf SCA
\(\beta\) = local slope angle (radians)

Implementation notes:

Clamp \(\beta \ge \beta_{\min}\) (e.g. \(0.001°\)) to avoid \(\tan\beta = 0\).
Clamp \(a \ge a_{\min}\) to avoid \(\ln 0\).

wetness_index(..., method="dinf"|"d8") computes SCA and slope internally. Higher TWI -> greater wetness / runoff-generation potential.


Code
# Compute Topographic Wetness Index from the filled DEM using D-infinity SCA.
twi_path = OUT / "twi.tif"  # TWI output path
wetness_index(filled, twi_path, method="dinf", overwrite=True)  # TWI = ln(a / tan(beta))

# Map TWI with a blue-green colormap.
ax = plot_raster(
    twi_path,  # TWI GeoTIFF
    title="Topographic Wetness Index (Dinf SCA)",  # map title
    cmap="YlGnBu",  # wetness-friendly colormap
    kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the TWI map

stats = summarize_raster(twi_path, percentiles=(5, 25, 50, 75, 95))  # TWI percentiles
display(pd.Series(stats).to_frame("TWI"))  # show summary table

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Stream network extraction
Channel cells appear in the flow-accumulation surface as locations with very large contributing area. A simple threshold maps the network:
\[
\text{stream}_i =
\begin{cases}
1 & A_i \ge T\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
\(T\) depends on DEM resolution and landscape. For this full 250 m mosaic we use a threshold of 1000 cells (same order as the R Whitebox notes); lower it for a denser network.
Downstream tools:

stream_segmentation: unique IDs for links between junctions / heads / outlets
catchment_delineation / subbasins: upslope area of each link

Whitebox also converts raster streams to vectors with a D8 pointer (raster_streams_to_vector); here we stay in raster space for the notebook.


Code
# Threshold in cells: tune to landscape / resolution (full DEM).
STREAM_THRESHOLD = 1000  # minimum upslope cells to classify as stream

streams = OUT / "streams.tif"  # binary stream raster
extract_streams(fa_cells, streams, threshold=STREAM_THRESHOLD, overwrite=True)  # threshold FA

links = OUT / "stream_links.tif"  # unique stream-link IDs
stream_segmentation(streams, d8p, links, overwrite=True)  # segment the network

# Read stream and link arrays for plotting.
with open_raster_data(streams) as ds:
    st = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # stream mask values
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
if nd is not None:
    st = np.where(st == nd, np.nan, st)  # mask nodata

with open_raster_data(links) as ds:
    lk = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # link ID array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
if nd is not None:
    lk = np.where(lk == nd, np.nan, lk)  # mask nodata

# Overlay streams and link IDs on hillshade.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))  # two-panel figure
axes[0].imshow(hs_arr, cmap="gray")  # hillshade base
axes[0].imshow(np.ma.masked_where(~(st > 0), st), cmap="winter", alpha=0.9)  # stream cells
axes[0].set_title(f"Streams (A >= {STREAM_THRESHOLD} cells)")  # left title
axes[1].imshow(hs_arr, cmap="gray")  # hillshade base
axes[1].imshow(np.ma.masked_where(~np.isfinite(lk) | (lk <= 0), lk), cmap="tab20", alpha=0.9)  # links
axes[1].set_title("Stream link IDs")  # right title
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([])  # hide x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # hide y ticks
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render both panels

print(f"Stream cells: {int(np.nansum(st > 0))}")  # count of channel cells
print(f"Unique links: {len(np.unique(lk[np.isfinite(lk) & (lk > 0)]))}")  # number of link IDs

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Watershed delineation
A watershed (catchment, basin) is the set of cells that drain to a common outlet. Given D8 pointers, delineation is an upstream flood fill from one or more pour points.

Single / multiple outlets

Place outlet point(s) on or near the stream network.
Optionally snap each point to the nearest stream cell within distance \(d\) (Jenson snap: prefer high-\(A\) cells when a weight raster is supplied).
watershed(d8_pointer, pour_points, ...) labels every upslope cell with the outlet ID.

Multiple outlets produce nested or adjacent basins; each cell keeps the ID of the first seed reached when walking upstream (nested accounting is explicit in Whitebox unnest_basins).


Subbasins
subbasins(d8_pointer, streams) / catchment_delineation seed every stream-link outlet and label its upslope area: useful for distributed hydrologic modelling.


Whole DEM basins
basins(d8_pointer) treats DEM-edge and no-flow sinks as outlets and labels complete drainage basins.


Code
# Place pour points at high-accumulation stream cells (auto outlets).
with open_raster_data(fa_cells) as ds:
    fa2 = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)  # D8 accumulation array
    nd = ds.get_band(1).nodata  # nodata flag
    gt = ds.geotransform  # origin and pixel size for map coords
if nd is not None:
    fa2 = np.where(fa2 == nd, np.nan, fa2)  # mask nodata

stream_mask = np.isfinite(st) & (st > 0)  # True on channel cells
# Pick a few local FA maxima along streams as outlets.
fa_stream = np.where(stream_mask, fa2, np.nan)  # FA only on streams
# Sample top cells, then keep spatially separated outlets.
flat_idx = np.argsort(-np.nan_to_num(fa_stream, nan=-np.inf), axis=None)  # high FA first
outlets = []  # list of (x, y) map coordinates
chosen = []  # list of (row, col) already accepted
rows, cols = fa_stream.shape  # array dimensions
for idx in flat_idx[:2000]:  # scan the top FA candidates
    r, c = divmod(int(idx), cols)  # convert flat index to row/col
    if not np.isfinite(fa_stream[r, c]):  # skip non-stream / nodata
        continue
    # Keep outlets ~20 km apart on the full mosaic (80 cells x 250 m).
    if any(abs(r - rr) + abs(c - cc) < 80 for rr, cc in chosen):
        continue  # too close to an existing outlet
    x = gt[0] + (c + 0.5) * gt[1]  # map X of cell centre
    y = gt[3] + (r + 0.5) * gt[5]  # map Y of cell centre
    outlets.append((x, y))  # accept this outlet
    chosen.append((r, c))  # remember its pixel location
    if len(outlets) >= 8:  # stop after eight outlets
        break

print(f"Candidate outlets (map coords): {len(outlets)}")  # how many outlets we kept
for i, (x, y) in enumerate(outlets, 1):
    print(f"  {i}: ({x:.1f}, {y:.1f})")  # print each outlet coordinate

snapped = snap_pour_points(outlets, streams, snap_distance=5000.0)  # snap onto streams within 5 km
print("Snapped:", snapped)  # confirm snapped coordinates

ws = OUT / "watersheds.tif"  # watersheds for the snapped outlets
watershed(d8p, snapped, ws, overwrite=True)  # delineate pour-point watersheds

sub = OUT / "subbasins.tif"  # subbasins per stream link
subbasins(d8p, streams, sub, overwrite=True)  # one subbasin per link

whole = OUT / "basins.tif"  # whole-DEM basin IDs
basins(d8p, whole, overwrite=True)  # basins draining to the DEM edge

# Side-by-side watershed / subbasin / whole-basin maps.
plot_rasters(
    [ws, sub, whole],  # basin rasters
    titles=[
        f"Watersheds ({len(snapped)} outlets)",  # pour-point watersheds
        "Subbasins (stream links)",  # link-based subbasins
        "Whole DEM basins",  # edge-draining basins
    ],
    ncols=3,  # three columns
    cmap="tab20",  # categorical colormap
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the basin maps

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Terrain hydrologic indices

Elevation above stream (HAND-style)
Vertical height of each cell above the stream cell it drains to along the D8 path:
\[
\mathrm{EAS}_i = z_i - z_{s(i)}
\]
where \(s(i)\) is the first stream cell downstream of \(i\). Values near 0-2 m are often candidate floodplain / valley-bottom cells.


Downslope distance to stream
Path length following the flow network:
\[
D_i = \sum_{k \in \mathrm{path}(i \rightarrow s(i))} d_k
\]
with \(d_k = \Delta x\) (cardinal) or \(\sqrt{2}\,\Delta x\) (diagonal). Alternatively, set vertical=True to return drop \(z_i - z_{s(i)}\).


Code
# Compute HAND-style elevation above stream and downslope distance to stream.
eas = OUT / "elevation_above_stream.tif"  # height above nearest stream (m)
dds = OUT / "distance_to_stream.tif"  # along-flow distance to stream (m)

elevation_above_stream(filled, streams, d8p, eas, overwrite=True)  # vertical height above channel
downslope_distance_to_stream(streams, d8p, dds, overwrite=True)  # flow-path distance to channel

# Side-by-side HAND and distance-to-stream maps.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))  # two-panel figure
plot_raster(
    eas, ax=axes[0], title="Elevation above stream (m)", cmap="YlOrBr", robust=True, show=False
)  # left: HAND
plot_raster(
    dds, ax=axes[1], title="Downslope distance to stream (m)", cmap="PuBuGn", robust=True, show=False
)  # right: distance
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render both panels

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
Advanced analyses

Stochastic depression analysis
Real DEMs have vertical uncertainty \(\sigma\). A depression that appears once may vanish under a different noise realisation. Monte Carlo perturbation:
\[
z^{(m)} = z + \varepsilon^{(m)},\quad
\varepsilon^{(m)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
Fill each realisation and record the fraction of iterations where cell \(i\) was raised:
\[
P(\text{depression})_i = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[z_i^{(m,\text{filled})} > z_i^{(m)}\right]
\]
Cells with \(P > 0.5\) are more likely real basins than noise artefacts (Whitebox stochastic depression analysis).


Hydrologic connectivity
Binary (or probabilistic) indicator of whether a cell drains to the stream network along D8 within an optional maximum path distance: a simple proxy for runoff contribution and variable source areas.


Impoundment size index
For each potential dam cell, estimate the upslope volume (m³) or area (m²) impounded by a dam of given length / height: useful for small-reservoir screening.


Code
# Stochastic depression probability on the full DEM
# (fewer iterations than a research run so the notebook stays practical).
dep_prob = OUT / "depression_probability.tif"  # probability of being a depression
stochastic_depression_analysis(
    dem,  # raw DEM (uncertainty is on the observed surface)
    dep_prob,  # output probability raster
    n_iter=10,  # Monte Carlo iterations (small for a tutorial)
    error_magnitude=2.0,  # metres: illustrative for 250 m SRTM
    seed=7,  # reproducible random seed
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous probability file
)

conn = OUT / "hydrologic_connectivity.tif"  # connectivity to streams
hydrologic_connectivity(filled, streams, conn, overwrite=True)  # upslope connection strength

imp = OUT / "impoundment_volume.tif"  # impoundment size index
impoundment_analysis(
    filled,  # conditioned DEM
    imp,  # output index raster
    dam_length=750.0,  # ~3 cells at 250 m
    out_type="volume",  # report a volume-style size index
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous impoundment file
)

# Three-panel advanced hydrology products.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 7))  # three-panel figure
plot_raster(
    dep_prob,  # depression probability
    ax=axes[0],
    title="Depression probability (sigma=2 m, M=10)",  # left title
    cmap="magma",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
plot_raster(
    conn,  # hydrologic connectivity
    ax=axes[1],
    title="Hydrologic connectivity to streams",  # middle title
    cmap="Blues",
    show=False,
)
plot_raster(
    imp,  # impoundment index
    ax=axes[2],
    title="Impoundment size index (volume)",  # right title
    cmap="viridis",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render all three panels

title: Hydrology Modeling
text:
End-to-end pipeline (summary)
Hydrological analysis in this package follows the Whitebox preparation -> routing -> network -> delineation progression:

Condition the DEM (breach_depressions + fill_depressions).
Route flow with the algorithm that matches the question (D8 for channels, Dinf for hillslope flux / TWI).
Accumulate flow and extract streams by thresholding.
Delineate watersheds / subbasins from outlets or channel junctions.
Compute terrain hydrologic indices (TWI, height above stream, distance).
Advance to probabilistic depression analysis, connectivity, or impoundment modelling when uncertainty or storage matters.


Compact recipe
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import (
    breach_depressions,
    fill_depressions,
    d8_pointer,
    d8_flow_accumulation,
    dinf_flow_accumulation,
    extract_streams,
    snap_pour_points,
    watershed,
    wetness_index,
)

breach_depressions("dem.tif", "breached.tif", fill_pits=True)
fill_depressions("breached.tif", "filled.tif")
d8_pointer("filled.tif", "d8.tif")
d8_flow_accumulation("filled.tif", "fa.tif", out_type="cells")
dinf_flow_accumulation("filled.tif", "sca.tif", out_type="sca")
extract_streams("fa.tif", "streams.tif", threshold=1000)
snap_pour_points([(x, y)], "streams.tif", "outlets.shp", snap_distance=5000)
watershed("d8.tif", "outlets.shp", "watersheds.tif")
wetness_index("filled.tif", "twi.tif", method="dinf")

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
DEM, DTM, and DSM
These three terms are often used loosely. Keep the distinctions clear when you choose a product and when you interpret derivatives.








Surface
What it represents
Best for




DEM
Generic elevation raster; may be bare earth or mixed
Broad elevation context (check metadata)


DTM
Bare-ground surface only
Hydrology, geomorphometry, floodplain analysis


DSM
Uppermost surface including buildings and vegetation
Urban canopy, obstacle-aware viewsheds



A simplified relationship is:
\[DSM \approx DTM + \text{above-ground object heights}\]
Public “DEMs” such as SRTM often behave closer to a DSM in forested or built-up areas. For drainage and landform work, prefer a bare-earth DTM when one is available. Conceptual background is in 03_02_00_digital_terrain_modeling_introduction.ipynb.

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
Sources of elevation data
Global and near-global elevation products differ in resolution, vertical accuracy, void handling, and whether they lean toward DTM or DSM behaviour.









Product
Typical resolution
Coverage / notes
DTM vs DSM tendency




SRTM (NASA / NGA)
~30 m (1 arc-sec), also 90 m
~60°N-56°S; C-band radar (2000); voids filled in later releases
Mixed; canopy bias in forest


Copernicus DEM (ESA / Airbus)
30 m (GLO-30), 90 m (GLO-90)
Near-global; edited WorldDEM; good void handling
Closer to bare earth in many edited areas; still check docs


ASTER GDEM (NASA / METI)
~30 m
Near-global; stereo optical; more artefacts in steep / cloudy terrain
Mixed; often noisier than SRTM / Copernicus



Other common sources include national lidar DTMs (metre to sub-metre), TanDEM-X, ALOS World 3D, and ICESat-2 photon products. For Bangladesh regional work in this chapter we use a 250 m BTM mosaic derived from SRTM-class elevation over the hilly districts (hilly_dem_BTM.tiff). Finer products are better for local engineering; coarser grids are enough for regional morphometry and teaching.

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
Setup
Locate the repository root, import raster and terrain helpers, and create an output folder for preprocessing products.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for the DEM and outputs

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # maps, histograms, profiles, and 3D axes
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D  # noqa: F401  register 3D projection
import numpy as np  # array ops for profiles and the 3D surface
import pandas as pd  # tabular display of summarize_raster results
from IPython.display import display  # rich table preview

# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.
import geolattice

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if not (ROOT / "Data").is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

# Raster I/O and preprocessing helpers.
from geolattice.raster import (
    aggregate,  # coarsen by an integer factor
    clip,  # crop by projected bounds
    open_raster_data,  # open a GeoTIFF for metadata / arrays
    resample,  # warp to a target resolution
    summarize_raster,  # count/min/max/mean/percentiles
)
# Terrain helper used for shaded relief.
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import hillshade  # gdaldem-style hillshade
from geolattice.viz import apply_map_style, plot_raster, plot_raster_histogram, plot_rasters

apply_map_style()  # apply the GeoLattice tutorial matplotlib map defaults

# Bangladesh DEM and a dedicated preprocessing output folder.

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
Clipping and resampling
Clipping focuses later work on an area of interest (AOI). Resampling changes cell size: coarser grids run faster and match regional analyses; finer grids need a higher-resolution source (resampling alone does not invent true detail).
Here we:

Clip a central ~40 km × 60 km window (same idea as the terrain-analysis notebook).
Aggregate the AOI by factor 2 (~500 m) with averaging.
Resample that coarse grid back toward 250 m with bilinear interpolation for comparison.



Code
# Build a central analysis window (~40 km x 60 km) from the full DEM bounds.
with open_raster_data(DEM) as ds:
    b = ds.bounds  # full DEM extent in BTM metres
    mid_x = 0.5 * (b.minx + b.maxx)
    mid_y = 0.5 * (b.miny + b.maxy)
    half_x, half_y = 20000.0, 30000.0  # half-width / half-height in metres
    aoi_bounds = (mid_x - half_x, mid_y - half_y, mid_x + half_x, mid_y + half_y)

dem = OUT / "aoi_dem_250m.tif"
clip(DEM, dem, bounds=aoi_bounds, overwrite=True)
show_raster(dem, "Clipped AOI DEM (250 m)")

# Coarsen to ~500 m, then resample back toward the original 250 m grid.
agg_500 = OUT / "aoi_dem_500m.tif"
resamp_250 = OUT / "aoi_dem_resampled_250m.tif"
aggregate(dem, agg_500, factor=2, method="average", overwrite=True)
with open_raster_data(dem) as ds:
    xres, yres = abs(ds.geotransform[1]), abs(ds.geotransform[5])
resample(agg_500, resamp_250, resolution=(xres, yres), method="bilinear", overwrite=True)

for label, path in [
    ("250 m (clip)", dem),
    ("500 m (aggregate)", agg_500),
    ("~250 m (resampled from 500 m)", resamp_250),
]:
    print(f"\n=== {label} ===")
    show_raster(path)
