Elevation visualization and histograms
A continuous elevation map with a terrain colormap shows absolute height. A histogram shows how those heights are distributed and whether voids or spikes dominate the AOI. Use robust=True on plot_raster when a few extreme cells would otherwise crush the color stretch.


Code
# Map elevation for the clipped AOI.
ax = plot_raster(
    dem,
    title="AOI elevation (m)",
    cmap="terrain",
    kind="general",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
plt.show()

# Elevation histogram for the same AOI.
ax = plot_raster_histogram(
    dem,
    bins=40,
    title="AOI elevation distribution",
    show=False,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Elevation (m)")
plt.show()

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
Hillshade visualization
Hillshade simulates illumination of the terrain so ridges and valleys read as relief. A single sun direction (often azimuth 315°, altitude 45°) is the cartographic default; a multidirectional hillshade blends several azimuths and reduces directional bias. Hillshade is a visualization aid; slope and aspect remain the quantitative derivatives (next notebook).


Code
# Compute single-direction and multidirectional hillshade for the AOI.
hs = OUT / "aoi_hillshade.tif"
hs_md = OUT / "aoi_hillshade_multidirectional.tif"
hillshade(dem, hs, azimuth=315, altitude=45, overwrite=True)
hillshade(dem, hs_md, multidirectional=True, overwrite=True)

plot_rasters(
    [hs, hs_md],
    titles=["Hillshade (315 / 45)", "Multidirectional hillshade"],
    ncols=2,
    cmap="gray",
    figsize=(12, 5),
    show=False,
)
plt.show()

title: DEM Preprocessing
text:
3D terrain visualization and elevation profiles
A 3D surface plot makes relative relief obvious; elevation profiles quantify height along a transect. Both use the clipped AOI array. The 3D view is downsampled so the notebook stays responsive. Profiles are sampled along west-east and south-north lines through the AOI centre.


Code
# Read the AOI DEM into a masked NumPy array for 3D and profile work.
with open_raster_data(dem) as ds:
    gt = ds.geotransform
    nodata = ds.get_band(1).nodata
    elev = np.asarray(ds.read(bands=1), dtype=np.float64)
    xmin, xmax = ds.bounds.minx, ds.bounds.maxx
    ymin, ymax = ds.bounds.miny, ds.bounds.maxy

if nodata is not None:
    elev = np.where(elev == nodata, np.nan, elev)
elev = np.where(np.isfinite(elev), elev, np.nan)

# Downsample for a responsive 3D surface (every nth cell).
step = max(1, min(elev.shape) // 80)
z = elev[::step, ::step]
rows, cols = z.shape
x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, cols)
y = np.linspace(ymax, ymin, rows)  # north at top of the array
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
surf = ax.plot_surface(
    X, Y, z,
    cmap="terrain",
    linewidth=0,
    antialiased=True,
    rstride=1,
    cstride=1,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, BTM)")
ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, BTM)")
ax.set_zlabel("Elevation (m)")
ax.set_title("AOI DEM as a 3D surface (downsampled)")
fig.colorbar(surf, ax=ax, shrink=0.55, label="Elevation (m)")
ax.view_init(elev=35, azim=-60)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Code
# Sample west-east and south-north elevation profiles through the AOI centre.
nrows, ncols = elev.shape
xres, yres = abs(gt[1]), abs(gt[5])
row_c, col_c = nrows // 2, ncols // 2

# West-east profile: fixed row, all columns.
we_z = elev[row_c, :]
we_dist = np.arange(ncols) * xres / 1000.0  # distance along profile in km
# South-north profile: fixed column, all rows (top = north).
sn_z = elev[:, col_c]
sn_dist = np.arange(nrows) * yres / 1000.0

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
axes[0].plot(we_dist, we_z, color="#1f4e79", lw=1.4)
axes[0].set_title("West-east profile (through AOI centre)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Distance along profile (km)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Elevation (m)")
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

axes[1].plot(sn_dist, sn_z, color="#7a3e09", lw=1.4)
axes[1].set_title("South-north profile (through AOI centre)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Distance along profile (km)")
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
fig.suptitle("Elevation profiles", y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Show where the profiles cross the elevation map.
ax = plot_raster(
    dem,
    title="Profile lines on the AOI DEM",
    cmap="terrain",
    kind="general",
    robust=True,
    show=False,
)
# Convert pixel centres of the profile lines to map coordinates.
we_xs = xmin + (np.arange(ncols) + 0.5) * xres
we_ys = np.full(ncols, ymax - (row_c + 0.5) * yres)
sn_xs = np.full(nrows, xmin + (col_c + 0.5) * xres)
sn_ys = ymax - (np.arange(nrows) + 0.5) * yres
ax.plot(we_xs, we_ys, color="#1f4e79", lw=1.8, label="West-east")
ax.plot(sn_xs, sn_ys, color="#7a3e09", lw=1.8, label="South-north")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=True)
plt.show()

title: Raster Data Analysis
text:
Study data
We use the hilly-district DEM (BTM, 250 m) and clip a central AOI so focal, algebra, and proximity steps stay responsive. District polygons that intersect the full DEM provide zones and centroid hubs for proximity.


Code
# Clip a central AOI from the full DEM (preprocessing detail lives elsewhere).
with open_raster_data(DEM_FULL) as ds:
    b = ds.bounds
    mid_x = 0.5 * (b.minx + b.maxx)
    mid_y = 0.5 * (b.miny + b.maxy)
    half_x, half_y = 20000.0, 30000.0
    aoi_bounds = (mid_x - half_x, mid_y - half_y, mid_x + half_x, mid_y + half_y)
    dem_bounds = (b.minx, b.miny, b.maxx, b.maxy)

dem = OUT / "aoi_dem.tif"
clip(DEM_FULL, dem, bounds=aoi_bounds, overwrite=True)

# Keep districts that intersect the full hilly DEM, with a numeric zone_id for zonal_stats.
districts_all = gpd.read_file(DISTRICTS)
full_poly = box(*dem_bounds)
hill_districts = districts_all[districts_all.intersects(full_poly)].copy()
hill_districts = hill_districts.reset_index(drop=True)
hill_districts["zone_id"] = np.arange(1, len(hill_districts) + 1, dtype=int)
zones_path = OUT / "hill_districts.gpkg"
hill_districts.to_file(zones_path, layer="districts", driver="GPKG")

# Proximity hubs: representative points of each district clipped to the AOI
# (full district centroids often fall outside this window).
aoi_poly = box(*aoi_bounds)
pieces = hill_districts.copy()
pieces["geometry"] = pieces.geometry.intersection(aoi_poly)
pieces = pieces[~pieces.geometry.is_empty & pieces.geometry.is_valid].copy()
hubs = pieces.copy()
hubs["geometry"] = hubs.geometry.representative_point()
hubs_path = OUT / "aoi_hubs.gpkg"
hubs.to_file(hubs_path, layer="hubs", driver="GPKG")

print(f"AOI DEM: {dem.name}")
print(summarize_raster(dem))
print(f"Hill districts: {len(hill_districts)} -> {[n for n in hill_districts['ADM2_EN']]}")
print(f"AOI hubs: {len(hubs)}")

Local analysis: reclassify elevation
Local analysis assigns a new value to each cell from that cell alone. Reclassification turns continuous elevation into thematic bands used in land suitability, hazard screening, and map algebra.

# Reclassify AOI elevation into four bands (metres).

    dem,
    elev_class,
    mapping=[
        (0, 50, 1),       # low plains / valleys
        (50, 150, 2),     # foothills
        (150, 400, 3),    # hills
        (400, 2000, 4),   # high ridges

    default=0,
    overwrite=True,
)

ax = plot_raster(
    elev_class,
    title="Elevation classes (1=low ... 4=high)",
    cmap="YlOrBr",
    kind="unique",
    categories={1: "0-50 m", 2: "50-150 m", 3: "150-400 m", 4: ">=400 m"},

Neighborhood analysis: focal statistics
Focal analysis replaces each cell with a statistic of a moving window. A local mean smooths noise; a local range summarises short-range relief without computing full morphometric derivatives (those belong in 03.02.02).

focal_range = OUT / "focal_range_5x5.tif"

    titles=["Elevation", "Focal mean (5x5)", "Focal range (5x5)"],

text:
Map algebra: combine criteria
Map algebra combines rasters cell-by-cell. Here a simple binary screen keeps cells that are in the foothill / hill classes (2 or 3) and within a local-relief threshold from the focal range layer. Full multi-criteria weighting and fuzzy membership belong in Module 03.04 (MCSM); this cell only shows the raster-algebra pattern.


Code
# Binary mask: elevation class in {2, 3} AND focal range below 75 m.
suitable = OUT / "criteria_mask.tif"
calc(
    "((CLS == 2) | (CLS == 3)) & (RNG < 75)",
    suitable,
    inputs={"CLS": elev_class, "RNG": focal_range},
    dtype="float32",
    overwrite=True,
)

plot_rasters(
    [elev_class, focal_range, suitable],
    titles=["Elevation class", "Focal range (m)", "Criteria mask"],
    ncols=3,
    cmap="viridis",
    robust=True,
    figsize=(14, 4.5),
    show=False,
)
plt.suptitle("Map algebra combination", y=1.02)
plt.show()

mask_summary = summarize_raster(suitable)
print(f"Selected cells: {int(mask_summary['sum'])} / {mask_summary['count']}")

title: Raster Data Analysis
section: Proximity analysis: distance to AOI hubs
text:
Proximity analysis: distance to AOI hubs
Proximity turns feature locations into a continuous distance surface. District centroids often fall outside a clipped window, so this notebook burns representative points of each district’s intersection with the AOI, then computes distance to those hubs. The result supports accessibility screens and further map algebra (for example, “class 2-3 and within 10 km of a hub”).


Code
# Burn AOI hubs onto the DEM grid, then compute map-unit distance.
targets = OUT / "hub_targets.tif"
dist = OUT / "distance_to_hub.tif"
with open_raster_data(dem) as ds:
    aoi_extent = (ds.bounds.minx, ds.bounds.miny, ds.bounds.maxx, ds.bounds.maxy)

rasterize(
    hubs_path,
    targets,
    burn_value=1.0,
    template=dem,
    bounds=aoi_extent,
    overwrite=True,
)
proximity(
    targets,
    dist,
    target_values=[1],
    dist_units="GEO",  # metres in the DEM CRS
    overwrite=True,
)

# Accessibility-style screen: preferred elevation class and within 10 km of a hub.
access = OUT / "access_screen.tif"
calc(
    "((CLS == 2) | (CLS == 3)) & (DIST <= 10000)",
    access,
    inputs={"CLS": elev_class, "DIST": dist},
    dtype="float32",
    overwrite=True,
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5))
plot_raster(dist, ax=axes[0], title="Distance to hub (m)", cmap="plasma", robust=True, show=False)
hubs.plot(ax=axes[0], color="white", markersize=28, edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.6)
plot_raster(elev_class, ax=axes[1], title="Elevation class", cmap="YlOrBr", kind="unique", show=False)
plot_raster(access, ax=axes[2], title="Class 2-3 within 10 km", cmap="Greens", show=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Spatial Analysis
text:
What is Spatial Analysis?
Spatial analysis is the process of examining the locations, attributes, and relationships of features in spatial data to discover patterns, understand phenomena, and make decisions. It integrates principles from geography, mathematics, statistics, and computer science to answer questions such as:

Where are things located, and how do they cluster or disperse?
What is the relationship between spatial features (overlap, adjacency, proximity)?
How do terrain, hydrology, or land cover influence human and ecological processes?
Which areas are most suitable for a specific use?
How does a phenomenon change over space and time?

The term was popularised by geographers and quantitative researchers in the 1960s-70s (most notably by Cliff & Ord on spatial autocorrelation, and later by Anselin on exploratory spatial data analysis) and has since grown into a multidisciplinary field underpinning environmental science, urban planning, public health, logistics, remote sensing, and more.

title: Spatial Analysis
text:
Why Spatial Analysis Matters
Location matters in virtually every field of science and applied decision-making:

Environmental Science: Understanding erosion, flood risk, habitat connectivity, and climate change impacts.
Public Health: Mapping disease outbreaks, identifying underserved populations, optimizing clinic placement.
Urban Planning: Site selection, accessibility analysis, land-use zoning, infrastructure routing.
Agriculture: Precision farming, crop yield prediction, irrigation planning, soil variability mapping.
Disaster Management: Risk mapping, emergency routing, evacuation modelling, damage assessment.
Business & Logistics: Trade area analysis, optimal warehouse location, delivery routing.
Remote Sensing & Earth Observation: Multi-temporal change detection, time-series trend analysis, anomaly detection.

Python, through libraries such as GeoPandas, Rasterio, xarray, WhiteboxTools, OSMnx, NetworkX, and scikit-fuzzy, has become the dominant open-source platform for spatial analysis. GeoLattice unifies these tools behind a consistent, GIS-practitioner-friendly API organised around the workflows described in this module.

title: Spatial Analysis
text:
Core Concepts
Before diving into the notebooks, a few foundational concepts are worth reviewing:

Spatial Data Models








Model
Description
Typical Formats




Vector
Discrete objects: points, lines, polygons with attributes
Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, FlatGeobuf


Raster
Continuous grid of cells (pixels) with a value per cell
GeoTIFF, NetCDF, HDF5, Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF


Multidimensional raster
Raster with extra axes: time, depth, wavelength
NetCDF, HDF5, Zarr


Network / Graph
Nodes + edges with spatial embedding
GraphML, OSM, GeoPackage





Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
All spatial analysis must occur in a consistent CRS. Key distinctions: - Geographic CRS (lon/lat, e.g., WGS 84 / EPSG:4326): angles, not metres: avoid for distance/area calculations. - Projected CRS (e.g., UTM, BTM): metres/feet: required for accurate distance, area, and slope calculations. - GeoLattice uses pyproj and PROJ under the hood; always check .crs before running analysis.


Tobler’s First Law of Geography


“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”

Waldo Tobler, 1970



This principle motivates spatial autocorrelation analysis, kriging, and the spatial weight matrices used throughout this module.


Scale and Resolution
Results depend heavily on the spatial resolution of the input data and the analysis scale (the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem. MAUP). Always document data provenance and resolution.

Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM)
API modules: geolattice.spatial_analysis.suitability, geolattice.spatial_analysis.fuzzy
Multi-Criteria Suitability Modeling (MCSM) integrates multiple spatial criteria to identify optimal or suitable locations for a given objective. It is one of the most widely applied decision-support frameworks in GIS: used in site selection, land-use planning, conservation prioritisation, and infrastructure routing.
GeoLattice supports three complementary approaches, each covered by a dedicated notebook series:

Part II: Fuzzy Suitability Modeling
Classical suitability models use crisp Boolean thresholds: a location either meets a criterion or it does not. Fuzzy logic allows partial membership: a slope of 14° might be “somewhat suitable” (membership = 0.7) rather than simply suitable or not. This is more realistic and reduces the sensitivity to arbitrary threshold choices.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Spatial analysis turns layers into answers. It asks where water flows, which land is suitable for a crop or a clinic, how far people are from services, how groups are spread across a city and whether a policy changed outcomes in the places it reached. Every one of these questions starts from the vector and raster data of the first two chapters and adds a method built for space.
These 51 notebooks are chapter 03 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They cover terrain and hydrology, multidimensional data cubes, multi-criteria suitability, spatial networks, segregation and spatial causal inference, and finish with six capstone projects, using geolattice.spatial_analysis with real data from the United States and Bangladesh.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, xarray DataArrays, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.



Package
geolattice


Repository
github.com/zia207/GeoLattice


Python
3.10 or newer


License
MIT


Author
Zia Ahmed, Upatta Analytics



GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library (conda or your system package manager). Then install the spatial statistics option, which includes spatial analysis and the scikit-learn models that spatial causal inference needs:
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[statistics]"
The chapter uses four imports:
import geolattice.spatial_analysis as sa
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import network_analysis as sna, segregation as seg
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Terrain and hydrology
A digital elevation model (DEM) is a raster of heights. Its derivatives describe the shape of the land: slope, aspect and curvature, the position of a cell relative to its neighbours and how wet it is likely to be. Hydrology follows water over that surface: fill or breach the pits a DEM always has, give each cell a flow direction, accumulate the area that drains through it, and cut the network into streams and watersheds.







Task
Functions (sa)




Surface derivatives
slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, plan_curvature, profile_curvature


Position and ruggedness
tpi, tri, roughness, twi, landform_classification, multiscale_analysis


Visibility and contours
viewshed, contours


Condition the DEM
fill_depressions, breach_depressions


Flow direction and accumulation
d8_pointer, dinf_pointer, fd8_pointer, d8_flow_accumulation, dinf_flow_accumulation


Streams and watersheds
extract_streams, stream_segmentation, snap_pour_points, watershed, subbasins, basins


Height above drainage
elevation_above_stream, wetness_index



The terrain and hydrology tools read a DEM from a path and write their result to another path:
import geolattice.spatial_analysis as sa

sa.slope("dem.tif", "slope.tif")                                  # degrees
sa.hillshade("dem.tif", "hillshade.tif", azimuth=315, altitude=45)
sa.breach_depressions("dem.tif", "dem_breached.tif")              # condition the DEM
sa.d8_pointer("dem_breached.tif", "d8.tif")                       # flow direction
sa.d8_flow_accumulation("dem_breached.tif", "facc.tif")           # upslope cells
sa.extract_streams("facc.tif", "streams.tif", threshold=1000)     # cells draining > 1000 cells
sa.watershed("d8.tif", "outlets.shp", "watersheds.tif")           # watershed of each outlet

Multidimensional data

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Multi-criteria suitability
Suitability modelling ranks places against several criteria at once: slope, distance to roads, soil, rainfall and so on. Each criterion is put on a common scale, then the criteria are combined, either by hard rules (Boolean), by weights (weighted overlay or weighted linear combination) or by fuzzy membership, which lets a place be partly suitable. The last step tests how much the answer depends on the weights.







Task
Functions (sa)




Common scale
suitability_reclassify, minmax_normalize, percentile_rank_normalize, rescale_by_function


Boolean and categorical rules
categorical_and, categorical_or, criteria_count, limiting_criterion


Weighted overlay
weighted_overlay, weighted_sum, weighted_linear_combination, score_contributions


Fuzzy logic
fuzzy_membership, fuzzy_overlay, weighted_fuzzy_overlay, linear, gaussian, large, small, near


Sensitivity and sites
monte_carlo_weights, perturb_weights, locate_regions, top_quantile_mask



import geolattice.spatial_analysis as sa

# Fuzzy "small" membership: close to 1 for low values, 0.5 at the midpoint
sa.fuzzy_membership("slope.tif", "slope_fz.tif", membership_type="small", midpoint=8, spread=5)          # 8 degrees
sa.fuzzy_membership("dist_road.tif", "road_fz.tif", membership_type="small", midpoint=2000, spread=4)   # 2 km

# Combine: fuzzy AND keeps the weakest criterion; a weighted overlay trades them off
sa.fuzzy_overlay(["slope_fz.tif", "road_fz.tif"], "suit_fuzzy.tif", overlay_type="and")
sa.weighted_overlay(["slope_class.tif", "road_class.tif"], "suit_weighted.tif", weights=[0.6, 0.4])

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Network analysis
A road network is a graph: intersections are nodes and road segments are edges with a length and a travel time. Network analysis finds shortest routes, the area reachable within a time budget, how well each place is served by facilities and how goods, people or a disease move along the links.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Segregation analysis
Segregation measures describe how two or more groups are spread across the units of a city or region. Indices summarise the whole area, local measures map where groups are concentrated, multiscale profiles show how the answer changes with neighbourhood size, and null models and bootstraps say whether a value is larger than chance.

title: GeoLattice: Spatial Analysis
text:
Spatial causal inference
Correlation in space is easy to find and hard to interpret. Spatial causal inference estimates the effect of a treatment when nearby places share unmeasured causes (spatial confounding), when treating one place affects its neighbours (interference and spillovers) and when the effect itself varies over space. Quasi-experiments use borders and the timing of policies, and the last two notebooks design spatial experiments and learn causal graphs.

import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc

data = sc.datasets.simulate_spatial_confounding(n=400, random_state=0)
print(sc.diagnose_spatial_confounding(data))                 # Moran's I on treatment and outcome
print(sc.SpatialDML(se="conley", cutoff=0.2).fit(data).summary())

title: Vector Data Analysis
text:
Overview
Vector analysis tools summarize attribute tables, measure spatial relationships, and build new geometry from existing layers. GeoLattice implements them in geolattice.spatial_analysis.vector_analysis (also geolattice.vector.vector_analysis) and exports them from geolattice.vector. The API follows common desktop GIS vector analysis operations (QGIS Vector analysis) and attribute workflows from sf / dplyr.
The notebook is organized in two parts:

Part 1: Spatial / statistical analysis on shapefiles in Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA, grouped by five broader functions:

Attribute statistics
Distance and proximity
Clustering and spatial pattern
Overlay and aggregation
Geometry summary

Part 2: Attribute manipulation on Bangladesh rice districts, upazilas, and poverty tables in Data/00_shared/vector_data/Bangladesh and data/tabular_data

title: Vector Data Analysis
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, applies the tutorial map style, and defines helpers to open USA and Bangladesh layers.
Spatial tools come from geolattice.spatial_analysis.vector_analysis (also geolattice.vector.vector_analysis). Attribute tools come from the same geolattice.vector export surface. Maps use plot_layer and related helpers from geolattice.viz.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 1 (vector, raster, CRS and visualization): pip install "geolattice[core]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for time helpers.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta  # date helpers (available for temporal demos)
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample layers

# Third-party geospatial / plotting stack used throughout the notebook.
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame I/O and geometry helpers
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for maps
import numpy as np  # array ops for synthetic Z profiles and numeric transforms
import pandas as pd  # tabular display and attribute joins
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook
from shapely.geometry import LineString, Point  # build 3D lines for climb_along_line




Code
# ===================================================================
# Setup and helpers for vector analysis and attribute tools.
# Import GeoLattice, point DATA/BD/TABULAR at sample folders, and define
# read_layer() for opening shapefiles as GeoDataFrames.
# ===================================================================

# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.
import geolattice

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if not (ROOT / "Data").is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

# Import the vector analysis and attribute helpers used below.
from geolattice.vector import (
    aggregate_attributes,  # dissolve / group-by attribute aggregation
    basic_statistics_for_fields,  # min/max/mean/std for one field
    calculate_fields,  # derive new columns from expressions
    climb_along_line,  # elevation gain/loss along 3D line vertices
    count_points_in_polygon,  # point-in-polygon counts (optional weights)
    dbscan_clustering,  # density-based spatial clusters
    distance_matrix,  # origin-destination distance matrix
    distance_to_nearest_hub_lines,  # sample-to-hub connector lines
    distance_to_nearest_hub_points,  # sample-to-hub distance table
    drop_geometry,  # attribute table only (plain DataFrame)
    filter_features,  # query / subset rows by expression
    join_attributes,  # tabular join on a key field
    join_by_lines,  # hub-spoke lines for matching IDs
    kmeans_clustering,  # fixed-k centroid clusters
    list_unique_values,  # distinct values and frequencies
    mean_coordinates,  # center of mass of feature centroids
    nearest_neighbour_analysis,  # Clark-Evans nearest-neighbour index
    open_vectors_data,  # open a vector dataset path
    overlap_analysis,  # polygon overlap area and percent
    rename_fields,  # rename attribute columns
    reshape_attributes,  # long <-> wide reshape
    select_fields,  # keep a subset of columns
    shortest_line_between_features,  # shortest connector to nearest feature
    sort_features,  # sort rows by one or more fields
    statistics_by_categories,  # grouped stats by category field
    stdbscan_clustering,  # space-time DBSCAN clusters
    string_field,  # string case / slice helpers
    sum_line_lengths,  # total line length and count per polygon
    transform_field,  # apply a numeric transform to a column
    update_where,  # conditional field updates
)
from geolattice.viz import apply_map_style, plot_layer, plot_pair, style_axes  # map styling helpers

# Paths to the USA, Bangladesh, and tabular sample data folders.
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA"  # USA shapefiles
BD = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "Bangladesh"  # Bangladesh shapefiles
TABULAR = ROOT / "Data" / "00_shared" / "tabular_data"  # CSV attribute tables
assert DATA.is_dir(), DATA  # fail early if USA data is missing
assert BD.is_dir(), BD  # fail early if Bangladesh data is missing
assert TABULAR.is_dir(), TABULAR  # fail early if tabular data is missing

# Compact pandas display defaults for notebook tables.
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)  # show up to 12 columns
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 48)  # truncate long cell text
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider text wrapping for prints
apply_map_style()  # apply the GeoLattice tutorial matplotlib map defaults


def read_layer(relative, base=DATA):
    """Open one shapefile and return a GeoDataFrame without the reader fid."""
    path = base / relative  # absolute path to the shapefile
    with open_vectors_data(path) as dataset:  # open via the GeoLattice vector reader
        frame = dataset.to_dataframe()  # materialize features as a table
        crs = frame.crs  # remember the layer CRS
    if "fid" in frame.columns:  # drop internal feature id if present
        frame = frame.drop(columns="fid")
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(frame, geometry="geometry", crs=crs)  # ensure GeoDataFrame type

title: Vector Data Analysis
text:
Available analysis tools
Each function below is imported from geolattice.vector. Distances and areas use the coordinate units of the layer unless a ground unit is requested for hub distances. Project geographic layers to a metre or foot CRS before using ground distances for clustering and neighbour tools.

Attribute statistics
Summarize field values, unique lists, and grouped stats.








Tool
Function
What it does




Basic statistics for fields
basic_statistics_for_fields()
Summarizes one attribute column. Numeric fields get count, unique, min, max, mean, median, quartiles, and related stats. Text fields get length statistics.


List unique values
list_unique_values()
Lists distinct attribute values (or combinations) and their counts.


Statistics by categories
statistics_by_categories()
Field statistics within category groups, or row counts when no value field is given.





Distance and proximity
Measure how far features are from each other, or link each feature to its nearest hub or destination.








Tool
Function
What it does




Distance matrix
distance_matrix()
Builds point-to-point distances. Output can be linear (one row per pair), standard (wide matrix), or summary (mean, min, max per origin).


Distance to nearest hub (lines)
distance_to_nearest_hub_lines()
Draws a line from each feature to its nearest hub and stores hub name and distance.


Distance to nearest hub (points)
distance_to_nearest_hub_points()
Keeps each feature location as a point with nearest hub name and distance.


Join by lines (hub lines)
join_by_lines()
Connects hubs and spokes that share an ID field. Alias: hub_lines. Optional geodesic lines and antimeridian splitting.


Shortest line between features
shortest_line_between_features()
Creates the shortest link from each source feature to nearest destinations (nearest point on geometry or centroid distance).





Clustering and spatial pattern
Group features in space (and time) or test whether points are clustered or dispersed.








Tool
Function
What it does




DBSCAN clustering
dbscan_clustering()
Clusters point features with DBSCAN. Parameters are minimum cluster size and neighbourhood radius (eps) in layer units.


K-means clustering
kmeans_clustering()
Partitions feature centroids into k clusters with farthest-point or k-means++ seeding.


ST-DBSCAN clustering
stdbscan_clustering()
Spatiotemporal DBSCAN: neighbours must be within eps in space and eps2 in time.


Nearest neighbour analysis
nearest_neighbour_analysis()
Clark-Evans nearest-neighbour index for a point layer (observed vs expected mean distance, Z-score). US spelling alias: nearest_neighbor_analysis.





Overlay and aggregation
Count, sum, or measure how features from one layer fall inside or across polygons of another.








Tool
Function
What it does




Count points in polygon
count_points_in_polygon()
Counts points inside each polygon. Optional weight field sums values; optional class field counts distinct classes.


Overlap analysis
overlap_analysis()
For each input polygon, measures overlap area and percentage covered by one or more overlay layers.


Sum line lengths
sum_line_lengths()
Sums line length and count of lines crossing each polygon.





Geometry summary
Derive representative locations or elevation change from feature geometry.








Tool
Function
What it does




Mean coordinates
mean_coordinates()
Computes center of mass of feature centroids, optionally weighted and grouped by an ID field.


Climb along line
climb_along_line()
Totals climb and descent along 3D line vertices and records minimum and maximum elevation per line.





Shared rules
Inputs can be a GeoDataFrame, a GeoSeries, a pandas DataFrame with a geometry column, Shapely geometry, WKT, GeoJSON geometry, sequences of those, VectorFeature objects, or an open vector layer from open_vectors_data(). Spatial results are GeoDataFrames when GeoPandas is installed; table-only tools return pandas DataFrames.
When two layers have different CRS definitions, the second layer is reprojected to the first. Geographic CRS layers trigger a warning when planar distance or area is used.

Part 1: Spatial analysis (USA)
Part 1 walks through the analysis tools in five functional groups: attribute statistics, distance and proximity, clustering and spatial pattern, overlay and aggregation, and geometry summary.

Load data
Layers come from Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA:

Colorado soil-sample points (CO_SOC_data.shp)
Colorado county polygons (US_COUNTY.shp, filtered to Colorado)
US state boundaries (US_STATE.shp) and Yellowstone (Yellow_Stone.shp) for overlap examples
Onondaga County street centerlines (Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp) and New York counties (NY_County_PROJ.shp) for line-length totals

Soil samples are rebuilt from the x and y fields in Albers metres, matching the other USA layers.


Code
# Load the USA layers used in Part 1 (states, counties, streets, park, soil samples).
states = read_layer("US_STATE.shp")  # US state polygons
counties = read_layer("US_COUNTY.shp")  # US county polygons
streets = read_layer("Ononda_Street_PROJ.shp")  # Onondaga County street centerlines (projected)
ny_counties = read_layer("NY_County_PROJ.shp")  # New York county polygons (same CRS as streets)
park = read_layer("Yellow_Stone.shp")  # Yellowstone park polygon for overlap demos
samples_raw = read_layer("CO_SOC_data.shp")  # Colorado soil organic carbon sample points

# Rebuild sample geometries from explicit x/y columns and match the states CRS.
samples = samples_raw.set_geometry(gpd.points_from_xy(samples_raw["x"], samples_raw["y"]))  # build points from x/y
samples = samples.set_crs(states.crs)  # align CRS with the state layer

# Subset states/counties used repeatedly below.
colorado = states.loc[states["STATE"] == "Colorado"].copy()  # Colorado state outline
co_counties = counties.loc[counties["STATE"] == "Colorado"].copy()  # Colorado counties only
wyoming = states.loc[states["STATE"] == "Wyoming"].copy()  # Wyoming for park overlap
montana = states.loc[states["STATE"] == "Montana"].copy()  # Montana for park overlap

# County seats as hubs: one representative point per county for hub-distance demos.
hub_points = co_counties.copy()  # copy county attributes onto hub points
hub_points["geometry"] = co_counties.geometry.representative_point()  # interior point per county

# Synthetic collection time for ST-DBSCAN (spread over one year by sample ID).
samples = samples.assign(
    collected=pd.to_datetime("2020-01-01")  # start date for the synthetic timeline
    + pd.to_timedelta(samples["ID"].astype(int), unit="D")  # offset each sample by its ID in days
)

print(f"Soil samples: {len(samples)}")  # number of Colorado soil points
print(f"Colorado counties: {len(co_counties)}")  # number of county polygons
print(f"Street segments (Onondaga): {len(streets)}")  # number of street features
print(f"New York counties: {len(ny_counties)}")  # number of NY counties
display(samples[["ID", "COUNTY", "SOC", "Longitude", "Latitude"]].head())  # preview key columns

Clustering and spatial pattern
Group features in space (and time) or test whether points are clustered or dispersed.

DBSCAN clustering
DBSCAN groups dense clusters of points. eps is in layer units (metres here). Noise points get a null cluster id.


Code

dbscan = dbscan_clustering(samples, min_size=4, eps=80_000)  # eps in layer units (metres)
print(dbscan["CLUSTER_ID"].value_counts(dropna=False).head())  # cluster sizes (NaN = noise)

# Map clusters colored by CLUSTER_ID.

fig.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render the map

# Map K-means labels over Colorado county boundaries.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))  # create the map figure
kmeans.plot(column="CLUSTER_ID", categorical=True, legend=True, ax=ax, markersize=8)  # color by cluster id

ST-DBSCAN adds a temporal threshold: points must be close in space and in time. The collected field was derived from sample ID for this demo.


Code
# Space-time DBSCAN: points must be close in space (80 km) and time (30 days).
st_clusters = stdbscan_clustering(
    samples,  # points with a synthetic collected timestamp
    "collected",  # datetime column for the temporal threshold
    min_size=4,  # minimum points to form a cluster
    eps=80_000,  # spatial neighbourhood radius in metres
    eps2=30,  # temporal neighbourhood in time_unit
    time_unit="days",  # interpret eps2 as days
)
print(st_clusters["CLUSTER_ID"].value_counts(dropna=False).head())  # cluster sizes

# Build a synthetic 3D profile on the longest street so climb_along_line has Z values.
road = streets.loc[[streets.geometry.length.idxmax()]].copy()  # longest street segment
coords = list(road.geometry.iloc[0].coords)  # 2D vertex list
z_profile = np.linspace(200, 260, len(coords))  # synthetic elevation ramp (m)
road_3d = road.copy()  # copy attributes onto the 3D version
road_3d["geometry"] = [
    LineString([(x, y, z) for (x, y), z in zip(coords, z_profile)])  # attach Z to each vertex
]

climbed = climb_along_line(road_3d)  # climb, descent, min/max elevation along the line
display(climbed[["CompleteSt", "climb", "descent", "minelev", "maxelev"]])  # climb metrics for the road
print(f"Layer total climb: {climbed.attrs['total_climb']:.1f} m")  # layer-level climb total

title: Digital Terrain Modeling (DTM)
text:
What is Digital Terrain Modeling?
Digital Terrain Modeling (DTM) represents, analyzes, and models the Earth’s bare-ground surface from digital elevation data. A DTM captures three-dimensional topographic structure, including:

Elevation and terrain morphology
Slopes and slope directions (aspect)
Ridges, valleys, hills, and depressions
Surface curvature and terrain ruggedness
Drainage patterns and potential water accumulation
Visibility and other topographic relationships

DTM sits at the intersection of GIS, remote sensing, hydrology, geomorphology, environmental modeling, and spatial analysis. Elevation measurements become terrain attributes that support environmental monitoring, watershed management, flood modeling, agricultural planning, and infrastructure development.

title: Digital Terrain Modeling (DTM)
section: DEM, DTM, and DSM: What is the difference?
text:
DEM, DTM, and DSM: What is the difference?
These three terms are closely related but describe different elevation surfaces.

Digital Elevation Model (DEM)
A DEM is a raster of elevation values. Depending on the dataset and how it was produced, it may represent bare earth or include surface objects. In practice, many public “DEMs” (for example SRTM products) behave closer to a DSM in vegetated or built-up areas, so always check the product documentation.


Digital Terrain Model (DTM)
A DTM represents the bare-earth terrain: buildings, trees, and other above-ground objects are removed. It is the preferred surface for geomorphological and hydrological analysis because flow and landform metrics should follow the ground, not rooftops or canopy.


Digital Surface Model (DSM)
A DSM represents the uppermost surface elevation, including buildings, trees, and other above-ground features. DSMs are useful for viewsheds that include canopy or built form, urban canopy studies, and change detection of surface objects.
A simplified relationship is:
\[DSM \approx DTM + \text{above-ground object heights}\]
The equality is approximate. Vegetation penetration, building footprints, interpolation, sensor geometry, and processing choices all introduce differences between products.

For Bangladesh, DTM analysis is especially useful for floodplain topography, river channels, coastal chars, seasonal inundation, drainage patterns, and agricultural land suitability. Low-relief floodplains and dense drainage networks reward careful DEM conditioning before flow routing; steeper hill tracts reward morphometric derivatives such as slope, TPI, and landform class.

title: Digital Terrain Modeling (DTM)
text:
A typical DTM workflow
Most terrain and hydrology studies follow the same sequence, whether the study area is a Bangladesh upazila or a mountain catchment:

Acquire elevation data. Choose a DEM / DTM with a resolution and vertical accuracy that match the question (for example 30-90 m SRTM-class products for regional work; finer lidar DTMs for local engineering).
Reproject and clip. Work in a metric CRS so slope, distance, and accumulation have meaningful units. Clip to the area of interest to keep later steps responsive.
Inspect the surface. Plot elevation and hillshade; check nodata, voids, and vertical units.
Derive morphometric attributes. Slope, aspect, curvature, TRI / TPI / roughness, landforms, viewshed, and contours describe form and relative position.
Condition the DEM for hydrology. Breach or fill depressions so water can drain (covered in the hydrology notebook).
Route flow and extract networks. Flow direction, accumulation, streams, and watersheds turn elevation into drainage structure.
Compute terrain-hydrology indices. TWI, elevation above stream, and related indices connect form to wetness and floodplain context.

GeoLattice splits steps 4 and 5-7 across terrain_analysis and surface_hydrology so each notebook stays focused.

Overview
Digital terrain analysis (DTA) derives morphometric attributes from a digital elevation model (DEM). From a gridded surface you can measure steepness and orientation, summarize local relief, describe curvature and relative position, estimate wetness, classify landforms, and map visibility and contours. Those products support erosion and landslide studies, site suitability, hydrologic context, and cartographic relief.
This notebook works through the terrain products in geolattice.spatial_analysis.terrain_analysis, in the order used below:

Curvature surfaces

Viewshed and contours

Flow routing, watershed delineation, and multi-criteria suitability are covered in later Module 03 notebooks.

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Slope
Slope measures the steepness or gradient of the land surface at any location, representing how quickly elevation changes across a given horizontal distance. It is commonly expressed either in degrees or as a percentage, revealing whether terrain is steep or gentle.
Understanding slope is fundamental for terrain analysis because it directly affects water runoff, erosion potential, suitability for construction, agricultural planning, and assessment of natural hazards such as landslides. Accurate slope information is invaluable for fields like geography, geology, civil engineering, hydrology, and environmental science, guiding effective land management, risk mitigation, and infrastructure planning.
By quantifying how elevation changes over distance, slope analysis helps model landscape processes, informs decision-making, and supports evidence-based practices in a variety of land use and environmental applications.
Slope can be represented in three main ways: as a ratio, a percentage, or an angle. Here’s what each means:
Slope can be defined mathematically in several ways:

Slope Ratio: The slope ratio quantifies the steepness as the ratio of vertical change (“rise”) to horizontal distance (“run”):
\[
\text{Slope Ratio} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}
\] For example, if you ascend 1 meter (rise) over a horizontal distance of 2 meters (run), the slope ratio is \(1:2\).
Slope Percentage: Expresses the steepness as a percent, calculated by multiplying the slope ratio by 100:
\[
\text{Slope (\%)} = \left( \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} \right) \times 100
\] So a rise of 25 units over 100 units of run gives a slope of \((25/100) \times 100 = 25\%\).
Slope Angle (Degrees): The slope angle, typically denoted \(\theta\), is the angle between the horizontal and the slope. It can be calculated using the arctangent (inverse tangent) function:
\[
\theta = \arctan\left( \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} \right)
\] and is usually measured in degrees.

These three descriptions are mathematically equivalent, just expressed in different forms.

To convert from percentage or ratio to degrees: \(\theta = \arctan(\text{Slope Ratio})\)
To convert from degrees to percent: \(\text{Slope (\%)} = \tan(\theta) \times 100\)

Where “rise” denotes the change in elevation between two points, and “run” denotes the horizontal distance between them.
Slope analysis is important for a wide variety of applications:

Erosion and Sediment Control: Steeper slopes are more susceptible to erosion; understanding slope is vital for managing soil loss and sediment transport.
Land Use Planning: Identifying appropriate areas for agriculture, construction, and infrastructure often relies on slope assessment.
Hydrology: Slope determines the direction and speed of water flow, influencing drainage and runoff patterns.
Geological Studies: Slope measurements help in evaluating rock stability and the likelihood of landslides or related phenomena.
Environmental Management: Assessing the effects of land use changes on habitats and ecosystems involves understanding terrain slope.
Transportation Planning: Designers use slope information to establish safe, efficient routes for roads, railways, and other infrastructure.

Digital terrain models (DTMs) and geographic information systems (GIS) are essential tools for slope analysis, enabling the creation of slope maps, the visualization of terrain, and evidence-based decision-making about landscape management.
In summary, slope describes the steepness of a surface, typically in degrees (0-90) or percent rise (rise/run × 100). Steeper slopes are especially significant in the context of erosion, landslides, and routing.
The function slope(..., units="degrees"|"percent") provides a convenient interface to the gdaldem slope tool.


Code
# Compute slope in degrees and percent rise for the AOI DEM.
slope_deg = OUT / "slope_degrees.tif"  # output path for slope in degrees
slope_pct = OUT / "slope_percent.tif"  # output path for slope in percent
slope(dem, slope_deg, units="degrees", overwrite=True)  # gdaldem-style slope degrees
slope(dem, slope_pct, units="percent", overwrite=True)  # percent rise = 100 * rise/run

# Side-by-side slope maps.
plot_rasters(
    [slope_deg, slope_pct],  # input paths
    titles=["Slope (degrees)", "Slope (percent)"],  # panel titles
    ncols=2,  # two columns
    cmap="YlOrRd",  # warm colormap for steepness
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render both panels

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Aspect
Aspect is a key quantitative parameter in terrain analysis that describes the compass direction a slope faces. Mathematically, aspect is the azimuth angle (θ) of the gradient vector, measured in degrees clockwise from north (0°).
If the elevation \(z\) is given as a gridded surface \(z(x, y)\), then the aspect at any point is computed from the partial derivatives:
\[
\theta = \arctan2\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}, -\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)
\]
Where:
- \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\) and \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\) are the east-west and north-south slopes (rate of elevation change per unit distance). - The resulting θ is then converted to compass bearings (0° = north, 90° = east, 180° = south, 270° = west), and typically mapped into the range [0°, 360°).
Aspect is important because it affects the amount of sunlight, wind exposure, and precipitation a landscape receives. For example, a north-facing slope (aspect ≈ 0°) gets different solar radiation than a south-facing one (aspect ≈ 180°) in the Northern Hemisphere.
In more detail:

North (0°): North-facing slopes get less direct sunlight, staying cooler and moister, often affecting plant growth, snow retention, and even soil temperature.
East (90°): These slopes receive early morning sunlight, typically warming up earlier in the day, which can benefit plants that prefer cooler afternoons.
South (180°): In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes are sunniest and driest, favoring plants that need warmth and leading to faster snowmelt.
West (270°): Receive strong afternoon sun, often creating warmer late-day conditions.

Aspect analysis reveals critical spatial patterns and underpins decisions in:

Solar radiation modeling: Identifying warm and cold zones based on sun exposure, aiding in energy, agriculture, and climate models.
Ecosystem and vegetation studies: Understanding which plant communities are suited to specific slopes, as aspect shifts microclimates.
Snow distribution: Predicting where snow will melt first (south-facing) vs. linger longer (north-facing), important for hydrology and hazard assessment.
Hydrology: Mapping runoff patterns, water moves faster on sunny, drier slopes, helping with watershed management.
Soil moisture and erosion: Recognizing which slopes are at higher risk of drying and erosion, guiding land management.
Wildlife habitat: Many animal species choose habitats based on microclimate and shelter effects produced by aspect.
Land use planning: Guiding agriculture, forestry, and urban development by assessing suitability and risk tied to slope orientation.

Overall, aspect is integral to understanding landscape processes and making informed decisions in environmental science, resource management, and planning.
aspect wraps gdaldem aspect. Flat cells are typically nodata (-9999).

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Hillshade
Hillshade is a widely used cartographic and GIS technique for visually enhancing terrain maps by simulating the interplay of sunlight and shadow over elevation data. By creating the illusion of light striking the landscape’s surface, hillshading adds realistic depth, making it easier to interpret topography and spatial landforms on otherwise flat, two-dimensional maps.
Most often applied to digital elevation models (DEMs) or digital terrain models (DTMs), hillshading models how sunlight would illuminate the surface. It casts shadows across slopes and highlights ridges and valleys, resulting in maps that are both informative and visually appealing. This approach is invaluable in numerous applications, including land use planning, environmental assessment, natural resource management, and outdoor recreation mapping.
The hillshade process typically involves several steps:

Illumination Angle: A virtual sun position is selected (defined by azimuth and altitude angles), dictating the direction and height of the simulated light source relative to the terrain. Angles between 45° and 60° are frequently chosen for a natural balance of light and shadow.
Slope and Aspect Calculation: For each pixel in the elevation grid, the slope (steepness) and aspect (direction the slope faces) are computed.
Shading Calculation: Using these values, the intensity of light received by each pixel is determined. Slopes oriented away from the light source appear darker, simulating shadow, while those facing the sun appear brighter.
Grayscale Representation: The final output is a raster where pixel values correspond to illumination intensity, typically rendered in grayscale. Brighter areas indicate higher exposure to the simulated sunlight, and darker areas represent shadows.

By applying hillshading to elevation data, mapmakers can produce terrain visualizations that closely match how landscapes look under actual sunlight from various directions. These realistic relief maps help users perceive surface features, such as valleys, ridges, slopes, and escarpments, with greater clarity.
Hillshade rasters are often overlaid with additional geographic layers (e.g., land cover, hydrology, infrastructure) to produce multilayered, easily interpreted maps that support deeper spatial analysis and richer cartographic storytelling.


Code
# Compute single-direction and multidirectional hillshade for cartographic relief.
hs = OUT / "hillshade.tif"  # single illumination hillshade
hs_md = OUT / "hillshade_multidirectional.tif"  # multidirectional hillshade
hillshade(dem, hs, azimuth=315, altitude=45, overwrite=True)  # NW sun at 45 deg elevation
hillshade(dem, hs_md, multidirectional=True, overwrite=True)  # blend multiple sun angles

# Side-by-side hillshade comparison.
plot_rasters(
    [hs, hs_md],  # input paths
    titles=["Hillshade (315 deg / 45 deg)", "Multidirectional hillshade"],  # panel titles
    ncols=2,  # two columns
    cmap="gray",  # grayscale relief
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render both panels

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI)
The Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI) quantifies how much elevation changes between a grid cell and its surrounding neighbors, providing a measure of local topographic variability or roughness. This metric is especially valuable in landscape analysis, ecological modeling, geomorphology, and route planning, as it characterizes terrain complexity and heterogeneity.
How TRI is calculated: 1. Window Selection: Choose a window size (e.g., 3×3, 5×5, etc.) around each cell to define its neighborhood. Common sizes are 3×3 to 9×9 cells. 2. Elevation Differences: Compute the absolute elevation difference between the central cell and each neighboring cell within the window. 3. Aggregation: Sum (or average) these absolute differences across the window. 4. Normalization: Divide the total by the number of neighboring cells to standardize the result, making TRI values comparable across window sizes.
Mathematically, the commonly used formula is:
TRI Formula:
\[
\mathrm{TRI} = \frac{\sum \left| z_i - z_c \right|}{n}
\]
where:

\(z_i\) = elevation of a neighboring cell

\(z_c\) = elevation of the central (target) cell

\(n\) = number of neighboring cells (excluding the center)

Interpretation:
- Higher TRI values indicate steeper, more rugged, and variable terrain. - Lower TRI values reflect smoother, flatter, or more homogeneous landscapes.
Applications of TRI: - Ecology: Assessing habitat diversity and wildlife connectivity - Geomorphology: Identifying valleys, ridges, and highly variable landforms - Landscape Classification: Differentiating between plains, slopes, and mountainous regions - Environmental Modeling: Supporting models for erosion, hydrology, and sediment transport - Recreation & Planning: Aiding in hiking route selection and risk evaluation for outdoor activities
In summary, TRI is a robust tool for quantifying and visualizing variation in elevation, helping researchers and planners better understand the complexity and functional characteristics of land surfaces.


Code

tri_path = OUT / "tri.tif"  # output path for TRI

# Map TRI with a high-contrast inferno colormap.

    tri_path,  # TRI GeoTIFF
    title="Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI)",  # map title
    cmap="inferno",  # high-contrast colormap
    kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the TRI map

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Topographic Position Index (TPI)
The Topographic Position Index (TPI) quantifies how the elevation of a given cell compares to its neighboring landscape, making it easier to distinguish whether that location sits in a valley, on a ridge, or on flat ground. TPI is especially insightful for analyzing local terrain context and finds broad use in hydrology, ecological studies, landform classification, and beyond.
To calculate TPI, subtract the mean elevation of neighboring cells (within a defined window or radius) from the elevation of the central cell. The resulting value shows how much higher or lower the target cell is relative to its surroundings: - Positive TPI: Indicates the cell is elevated above its neighbors, such as on a ridge or hilltop. - Negative TPI: Indicates the cell is lower than neighbors, typically found in valleys or drainage areas. - Near-zero TPI: Suggests the cell sits on flat or gently sloping terrain.
Calculation steps: 1. Define a neighborhood (square or circular) around the target cell. 2. Compute the mean elevation of all neighboring cells within this window. 3. Subtract this mean value from the central cell’s elevation.
Mathematically:
\[\mathrm{TPI} = z_c - \left( \frac{\sum z_i}{n} \right)\]
where: - \(z_c\): elevation of the central (target) cell - \(z_i\): elevations of neighboring cells within the window - \(n\): number of neighboring cells
Key uses of TPI: - Hydrology: Identifying ridges, drainage lines, and watershed boundaries - Ecology: Mapping habitat variation, species distribution, and wildlife corridors - Geomorphology: Landform classification and landscape analysis - Soil and environmental sciences: Estimating potential wet areas and soil moisture patterns
By integrating TPI with other terrain metrics, you gain powerful insights into landscape structure, enabling more precise environmental modeling and landform interpretation at local scales.
TPI = elevation - mean of neighbours. Positive -> ridges / hilltops; negative -> valleys; near zero -> flats or mid-slopes. The default 3×3 uses gdaldem TPI; larger odd windows match the multi-scale TPI grids in the R notes.


Code
# Compute TPI at the default 3x3 window (gdaldem-style).
tpi3 = OUT / "tpi_3x3.tif"  # output path for 3x3 TPI

# Nested windows (odd sizes), as in the R tpiw() examples.
tpi_paths = []  # collect TPI paths for a multi-panel plot
tpi_titles = []  # matching panel titles
for size in (5, 15, 25, 35):  # odd window sizes in cells
    path = OUT / f"tpi_{size}x{size}.tif"  # output path for this window
    tpi(dem, path, window_size=size, overwrite=True)  # TPI at this scale
    tpi_paths.append(path)  # remember path
    tpi_titles.append(f"TPI {size}x{size}")  # remember title

# Map the default 3x3 TPI first.
ax = plot_raster(tpi3, title="TPI 3x3 (gdaldem)", cmap="RdBu_r", robust=True, show=False)
plt.show()  # render the 3x3 TPI map

# Multi-panel map of nested-window TPI surfaces.
plot_rasters(
    tpi_paths,  # nested TPI paths
    titles=tpi_titles,  # panel titles
    ncols=2,  # two columns
    cmap="RdBu_r",  # diverging colormap (ridges vs valleys)

    show=False,  # defer display

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Roughness
In terrain analysis, roughness describes the degree of unevenness or surface irregularity in the landscape. It quantifies how much elevations vary within a given area: highly rough terrain has sharp, frequent changes in elevation, while smooth terrain features gentle or gradual changes.
Several approaches are used to assess and represent terrain roughness; each method highlights different aspects of the landscape:

Standard Deviation of Elevation: Calculates the spread of elevation values within a neighborhood or window. Higher standard deviation signifies more elevation variability and thus rougher terrain.
Root Mean Square (RMS) Slope: Computes the square root of the mean of squared slope values in an area, capturing the average steepness. Higher RMS slope values reflect rougher, steeper terrain.
Slope Variance: Assesses the variability of slope values; greater variance points to a more irregular and complex surface.
Elevation Range: Measures the difference between the highest and lowest elevations in an area. A greater range indicates a wider span of elevation differences and increased roughness.
Texture Analysis: Applies image processing or remote sensing techniques to DEMs to derive texture metrics, which reveal spatial patterns of elevation fluctuation.
Fractal Dimension: Evaluates the complexity and scaling characteristics of terrain surfaces. Higher fractal dimensions indicate more intricate and rough landscapes.

Roughness metrics serve important roles in various disciplines:

Geomorphology: Identifying and classifying landforms, such as ridges, valleys, and escarpments.
Engineering: Informing the design and routing of infrastructure (e.g., roads, railways), as smoother terrain generally reduces construction complexity.
Environmental Science: Understanding how roughness impacts hydrology, erosion, sediment transport, and flood potential.
Ecology: Assessing habitat diversity and suitability, since terrain structure influences species distributions and biodiversity.
Land Use Planning: Aiding in the optimal allocation of land based on topographic constraints, accessibility, and environmental impacts.

Roughness is typically calculated using GIS software and DEM or DTM datasets, supporting a wide range of analyses that require insights into the complexity and variability of Earth’s surface.


Code
# Compute roughness as the elevation range within a local window.
rough_path = OUT / "roughness.tif"  # output path for roughness
roughness(dem, rough_path, overwrite=True)  # gdaldem-style roughness

# Map roughness with a magma colormap.
ax = plot_raster(
    rough_path,  # roughness GeoTIFF
    title="Roughness",  # map title
    cmap="magma",  # sequential colormap
    kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the roughness map

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Curvature
Curvature, in the context of terrain analysis, refers to the rate of change of slope or the change in slope along a surface. It provides information about the concavity or convexity of the terrain at a specific location. Curvature analysis helps in understanding the local shape of the landscape and can provide insights into landforms, erosion patterns, and hydrological behavior.
Curvature is the rate of change of slope (second derivatives). Zevenbergen & Thorne (1987) finite differences give:

Profile Curvature: Denoted as \(k_p\), the profile curvature is calculated in the direction of maximum slope (gradient), influencing flow acceleration/deceleration along a surface. It is mathematically given by:
\[
k_p = -\frac{z_{xx} p^2 + 2 z_{xy} p q + z_{yy} q^2}{(p^2 + q^2)^{3/2}}
\]
where \(p = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\), \(q = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\), \(z_{xx} = \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2}\), \(z_{yy} = \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2}\), and \(z_{xy} = \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x \partial y}\). Positive values indicate convexity (ridges), negative values concavity (valleys).
Plan Curvature: Denoted as \(k_{pl}\), plan curvature is measured perpendicular to the direction of slope (along contours), affecting the convergence or divergence of flow:
\[
k_{pl} = \frac{z_{xx} q^2 - 2 z_{xy} p q + z_{yy} p^2}{(p^2 + q^2)^{3/2}}
\]
Here, positive values indicate convexity (divergence, crests), negative values concavity (convergence, hollows).
Tangential Curvature: Often used interchangeably with plan curvature, but formally refers to curvature in the direction perpendicular to the slope (in the tangent plane to the surface):
\[
k_t = k_{pl}
\]
In most DEM analysis, “tangential” and “plan” curvature are computed using the same formula.
Mean Curvature: Mean curvature \(H\) at a surface point is the average of the principal curvatures (profile and plan):
\[
H = \frac{1}{2}(k_1 + k_2)
\]
In terrain analysis, it is commonly approximated as:
\[
H = \frac{k_p + k_{pl}}{2}
\]
It provides a general measure of how much the surface bends at that point.
Gaussian Curvature: Gaussian curvature \(K\) is the product of the principal curvatures:
\[
K = k_1 \cdot k_2
\]
For DEMs, \(K\) can be derived via the determinants of the first and second fundamental forms or by:
\[
K = \frac{z_{xx}z_{yy} - z_{xy}^2}{(1 + p^2 + q^2)^2}
\]
Negative \(K\) indicates a saddle, zero is flat, and positive values indicate peak or pit-like regions.



Code
# Compute five curvature surfaces commonly used in geomorphometry.
curv_paths = []  # collect output paths
curv_titles = []  # collect panel titles
for kind, fn in [
    ("profile", profile_curvature),  # curvature along the slope line
    ("plan", plan_curvature),  # curvature of contour lines
    ("tangential", tangential_curvature),  # curvature perpendicular to slope
    ("mean", mean_curvature),  # average of principal curvatures
    ("gaussian", gaussian_curvature),  # product of principal curvatures
]:
    path = OUT / f"curvature_{kind}.tif"  # output path for this curvature type
    fn(dem, path, overwrite=True)  # compute and write the surface
    curv_paths.append(path)  # remember path
    curv_titles.append(f"{kind.capitalize()} curvature")  # remember title

# First row: profile, plan, and tangential curvature.
plot_rasters(
    curv_paths[:3],  # first three curvature rasters
    titles=curv_titles[:3],  # matching titles
    ncols=3,  # three columns
    cmap="RdBu_r",  # diverging colormap
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the first curvature row

# Second row: mean and Gaussian curvature.
plot_rasters(
    curv_paths[3:],  # remaining curvature rasters
    titles=curv_titles[3:],  # matching titles
    ncols=2,  # two columns
    cmap="RdBu_r",  # diverging colormap
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the second curvature row

# Equivalent generic API for profile curvature (alias of profile_curvature).
curvature(dem, OUT / "curvature_profile_alias.tif", curvature_type="profile", overwrite=True)

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Topographic Wetness Index (TWI)
The Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) is a widely used hydrological index that quantifies the effect of local topography on the location and extent of soil moisture and potential saturation zones. It is calculated using the formula:
TWI = ln(a / tan β)
where: - a is the specific catchment area (the local upslope area draining through each point per unit contour length), typically derived from flow accumulation using the D8 algorithm. - β is the local slope angle (in radians) at each cell.
High TWI values indicate areas that are likely to be wetter or more saturated, such as valley bottoms, depressions, or zones where surface or subsurface water accumulates. Conversely, low TWI values correspond to ridges or well-drained slopes.
In this notebook, TWI is calculated using functions from the terrain_analysis module, which automates the computation of upslope area (flow accumulation) and local slope for each DEM cell. This is different from the approach in the referenced R notes, where flow direction is calculated explicitly as part of the process. Here, TWI acts as an integrative hydrological indicator, helpful for environmental modeling, hydrology, and land suitability studies.


Code
# Compute the Topographic Wetness Index (upslope area and local slope).
twi_path = OUT / "twi.tif"  # output path for TWI
twi(dem, twi_path, overwrite=True)  # write the TWI surface

# Map TWI with a blue sequential colormap.
ax = plot_raster(
    twi_path,  # TWI GeoTIFF
    title="Topographic Wetness Index (TWI)",  # map title
    cmap="Blues",  # wetness-friendly colormap
    kind="general",  # single-band continuous display
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the TWI map

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Landform classification
Landform classification identifies different geomorphic landforms (such as valleys, ridges, slopes, and flats) using a combination of the Topographic Position Index (TPI) calculated at multiple spatial scales and local slope. Specifically, the method computes TPI using both a small window and a large window for each cell in the DEM: - The small-window TPI highlights fine-scale landform features (e.g., small ridges or depressions). - The large-window TPI captures broader-scale terrain positions (e.g., major valleys or hilltops).
By comparing a cell’s elevation to its surroundings at both scales, and incorporating the local slope, this “nested TPI” method assigns each cell a landform class according to the Weiss (2001) scheme.
Typical classes produced include: Valley, Lower Slope, Flat, Middle Slope, Upper Slope, Local Ridge, and High Ridge.


Code
# Classify landforms from nested small/large TPI windows and a slope threshold.
lf = landform_classification(
    dem,  # AOI DEM
    OUT / "landforms.tif",  # categorical landform output
    small_window=3,  # fine-scale TPI window (cells)
    large_window=35,  # coarse-scale TPI window (cells)
    slope_threshold=5.0,  # degrees; separates flats from slopes
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous landform file
)
print("Classes:", lf["classes"])  # print the class name lookup

# Map categorical landforms with a diverging colormap.
ax = plot_raster(
    lf["path"],  # landform GeoTIFF path
    title="Landform classification (nested TPI)",  # map title
    cmap="RdYlBu_r",  # categorical-friendly colormap
    kind="general",  # display mode
    categories=lf["classes"],  # class labels for the legend
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render the landform map

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Multiscale analysis
Many geomorphic properties of terrain, such as topographic position, roughness, TRI (Terrain Ruggedness Index), and mean curvature, vary depending on the scale at which they are calculated. The multiscale_analysis function allows you to systematically analyze these metrics at multiple spatial scales by computing the chosen metric using several odd-sized window kernels (e.g., 3x3, 7x7, …, up to the maximum specified scale). For each cell in the DEM, the function calculates the metric at all these scales. The main result is typically: - a map of the maximum absolute value (|response|) of the metric across scales for each cell, - a corresponding “scale map” indicating at which window size this maximum response occurred, - or, if requested, a stack showing all computed bands (one per window size). This multiscale approach is valuable for detecting landforms and terrain features whose prominence depends on the spatial context, helping to reveal both small- and large-scale patterns in the landscape.


Code
# Compute TPI across multiple window sizes and keep the scale of maximum |TPI|.
ms = multiscale_analysis(
    dem,  # AOI DEM
    OUT / "ms_tpi.tif",  # base output path (value + scale companions)
    metric="tpi",  # geomorphometric metric to evaluate
    min_scale=3,  # smallest odd window size
    max_scale=21,  # largest odd window size
    step=4,  # step between window sizes
    output="max",  # keep the scale of maximum absolute TPI
    overwrite=True,  # replace previous multiscale outputs
)
print(ms)  # print the returned path dictionary

# Side-by-side: multiscale TPI value and the scale at which it peaks.
plot_rasters(
    [ms["value"], ms["scale"]],  # value and scale rasters
    titles=["Multiscale TPI (at scale of max |TPI|)", "Scale of maximum |TPI|"],  # panel titles
    ncols=2,  # two columns
    cmap="viridis",  # sequential colormap
    robust=True,  # percentile stretch
    show=False,  # defer display
)
plt.show()  # render both panels

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Viewshed
A viewshed identifies which locations (cells) in a DEM are visible from a specific observer position, based on line-of-sight analysis. For this example, we select an observer located near the center of the AOI, ideally placed on a ridge or high elevation point. The observer_height parameter lets you specify the height (in meters) of the observer above the DEM surface (e.g., the height of a person or structure). Every cell is checked to determine whether it is visible to this observer, taking terrain obstruction into account: areas blocked by intervening hills/mountains are not visible, and the result is a binary raster showing visible (1) and not visible (0) areas. This type of analysis is commonly used for applications like communication tower siting, landscape planning, or determining the visual impact of new developments.


Code
# Place an observer near the AOI centre and compute a binary viewshed.
with open_raster_data(dem) as ds:
    gt = ds.geotransform  # origin and pixel size
    # Map coordinates of a cell near the centre.
    row, col = ds.height // 2, ds.width // 2  # centre pixel indices
    obs_x = gt[0] + (col + 0.5) * gt[1]  # observer X (map units)
    obs_y = gt[3] + (row + 0.5) * gt[5]  # observer Y (map units)
    print(f"Observer pixel ({row}, {col}) -> ({obs_x:.1f}, {obs_y:.1f})")  # confirm location

vs_path = OUT / "viewshed.tif"  # output path for the viewshed mask
viewshed(
    dem,  # AOI DEM
    vs_path,  # binary visible/hidden output
    observer=(obs_x, obs_y),  # observer map coordinates
    observer_height=1.8,  # eye height in metres
    max_distance=15000,  # search radius in metres
    overwrite=True,  # replace any previous viewshed
)

# Side-by-side DEM and viewshed.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))  # two-panel figure
plot_raster(dem, ax=axes[0], title="DEM", cmap="terrain", robust=True, show=False)  # left: DEM
plot_raster(vs_path, ax=axes[1], title="Viewshed (1 = visible)", cmap="gray", show=False)  # right: viewshed
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce unused whitespace
plt.show()  # render both panels

title: Terrain Derivatives and Morphometric Analysis
text:
Contours
Elevation contours are vector lines that connect points of equal elevation on the terrain surface. These contours are generated from the DEM using the GDAL tool gdal_contour (accessible via ContourGenerateEx in the API). The process works by interpolating the raster elevation values and extracting continuous lines at set elevation intervals (e.g., every 50 meters). Contour lines provide an intuitive way to visualize topography, showing both the shape of the landscape and gradients: closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes, while widely spaced lines mark gentle or flat areas. These vectors are commonly used for topographic mapping, landscape analysis, and as overlays on maps to clarify elevation structure. Here, we generate a set of contours from the DEM in GeoPackage format, then overlay them on the raster DEM for visualization.


Code
# Extract 50 m elevation contours from the AOI DEM to a GeoPackage.
contour_path = OUT / "contours.gpkg"  # vector output path
contours(dem, contour_path, interval=50.0, overwrite=True)  # 50 m contour interval
print(f"Wrote {contour_path}")  # confirm write

# Overlay contours on the DEM (requires geopandas).
try:
    import geopandas as gpd  # vector overlay for contour lines

    lines = gpd.read_file(contour_path)  # load contour geometries
    ax = plot_raster(dem, title="Elevation contours (50 m)", cmap="terrain", robust=True, show=False)
    lines.plot(ax=ax, color="k", linewidth=0.4)  # black contour lines
    plt.show()  # render DEM + contours
except ImportError:
    print("Install geopandas (geolattice[viz] or [io]) to overlay contour lines.")  # optional dependency note

title: Spatial Analysis of Multidimensional Raster Data
text:
Overview
A conventional GeoTIFF raster typically represents data in 2 dimensions: rows × columns (or y × x), which describe spatial layout on the ground, essentially, images with pixels organized in a grid. These rasters might have a few bands, where each band is a separate 2D array (like RGB channels), but they are fundamentally flat in the sense of describing only one variable or acquisition at a time.
In contrast, multidimensional raster data (also called data cubes or “hyperstacks”) introduce one or more additional axes beyond just y and x. These new axes can represent time (e.g., repeated observations), depth or elevation (e.g., atmospheric/soil layers), or properties such as wavelength. With multidimensional data, every pixel location (a specific y, x point) can store not just one value, but a whole series or stack of values, for example, a temperature measurement every 6 hours over many years, or imagery from multiple satellite bands at each date. These extra axes unlock much richer analysis, letting you slice the dataset in time, extract profiles across depth, or compute changes and trends, all within a single, efficiently structured file.
2-D raster:     value[y, x]
3-D cube:       value[time, y, x]          ← common climate / remote-sensing case
4-D+ cube:      value[time, depth, y, x]   ← oceans, atmosphere, soil profiles

Building blocks








Concept
Meaning
Example in this tutorial




Variable
A measured or derived field
t2m (2 m air temperature)


Dimension
An axis of the array
time, latitude, longitude


Coordinate
Labels along a dimension
2000-01-01T03:00, 26.5°N, 90.0°E


Attribute
Metadata (units, CRS notes, history)
units = "K", CF conventions





Why it matters in GIS and Earth science

Store time series of maps (temperature, NDVI, groundwater) in one file instead of hundreds of GeoTIFFs.
Subset by date, depth, or region without rewriting the full archive.
Aggregate (daily -> monthly), compute anomalies, and find “date of maximum” along a dimension.
Interoperate with CF-compliant NetCDF used by climate models and reanalyses (ERA5, CMIP, …).


ArcGIS note: Esri’s Multidimensional Raster / Image Analyst tools map closely to geolattice.spatial_analysis.multidimensional_raster. This series uses the open-source API backed by xarray.

title: Spatial Analysis of Multidimensional Raster Data
text:
Common formats








Format
Typical use
Notes




NetCDF (.nc)
Climate / weather cubes
CF conventions; primary format in this series


Zarr (.zarr)
Cloud-friendly chunked arrays
Good for large remote datasets


GRIB / GRIB2
NWP model output
Often converted to NetCDF first


HDF4 / HDF5
Satellite products (MODIS, …)
Hierarchical groups / datasets


Multi-band GeoTIFF
Time or band stacks on disk
One band ≈ one time slice; weaker metadata than NetCDF


OPeNDAP / THREDDS
Remote streaming
Open subsets without downloading the full cube



Recommended analysis outputs in geolattice are NetCDF or Zarr. Multi-band GeoTIFF remains useful for mapping and for tools that expect classic raster bands.

Demo dataset
We use ECMWF ERA 2 m temperature merged for Bangladesh:
Data/03_spatial_analysis/NetCDF/t2m_2000_2018.nc

Variable: t2m (Kelvin)
Dimensions: time × latitude × longitude
Coverage: roughly 2000-2018 (years 2004-2006 missing), 3-hourly steps
