2-D vs multidimensional (same pixel)
Pick one grid cell near Dhaka and compare a single map slice with the temperature time series at that location.


Code
# Approximate Dhaka coordinates for a point sample.
LAT, LON = 23.81, 90.41  # approximate Dhaka latitude / longitude

# One time slice -> behaves like a classic 2-D raster map.
slice_2d = ds["t2m"].isel(time=0) - 273.15  # Kelvin -> deg C for the first time step

# Full series at nearest grid point -> 1-D time series.
series = ds["t2m"].sel(latitude=LAT, longitude=LON, method="nearest") - 273.15  # nearest cell to Dhaka

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))  # map panel + time-series panel

im = axes[0].imshow(
    slice_2d.values,  # 2-D temperature field
    origin="upper",  # match NetCDF row order
    extent=[
        float(ds.longitude.min()),  # west
        float(ds.longitude.max()),  # east
        float(ds.latitude.min()),  # south
        float(ds.latitude.max()),  # north
    ],
    aspect="auto",  # stretch to the axes
    cmap="RdYlBu_r",  # temperature colormap
)
axes[0].set_title(f"2-D map @ {pd.to_datetime(ds.time.values[0])}")  # time stamp title
axes[0].set_xlabel("Longitude")  # x-axis label
axes[0].set_ylabel("Latitude")  # y-axis label
axes[0].plot(LON, LAT, "k*", markersize=12, label="Dhaka")  # mark Dhaka
axes[0].legend(loc="lower left")  # show the Dhaka marker legend
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], label="t2m (deg C)", fraction=0.046)  # temperature colorbar

# Plot a manageable window (first year of data) for readability.
t0 = pd.to_datetime(series.time.values[0])  # first timestamp in the series
mask = (series.time >= np.datetime64(f"{t0.year}-01-01")) & (

Key takeaways

Multidimensional rasters are variables + dimensions + coordinates, not just pixels.
Prefer NetCDF / Zarr when time (or depth) metadata must travel with the data.
xarray is the engine; MultidimensionalRaster and the functions in §5 are the ArcPy-style facade used throughout pyGeoSpatial.
Always subset early: full reanalysis cubes are large; work on the years / regions you need.

Overview
This section provides a detailed overview of Multidimensional Data Analysis, covering the core methodologies and applications for extracting meaningful insights from raster datasets with multiple dimensions such as time or depth. By leveraging analytical techniques available in geolattice.spatial_analysis, we demonstrate practical workflows for temporal aggregation, anomaly detection, and the identification of key statistics across spatial-temporal raster datasets.

Core concepts

Aggregate Multidimensional Data
Temporal aggregation reduces a dense time series into summary rasters that are easier to map and compare. We demonstrate two common workflows for Bangladesh:

section: Helpers: parse DOY filenames and stack GeoTIFFs
text:
Helpers: parse DOY filenames and stack GeoTIFFs
Both watertable and NDVI use MODIS-style day-of-year naming (*_YYYY_DOY.tif). NDVI DOY values are sometimes unpadded (ndvi_2024_1.tif), so the parser accepts 1-3 digit DOY.


Code
def parse_doy_filename(path: Path, prefix: str) -> datetime:
    """Parse ``{prefix}_YYYY_DOY.tif`` -> datetime at that day-of-year."""
    m = re.match(rf"{re.escape(prefix)}_(\d{{4}})_(\d{{1,3}})$", path.stem, re.IGNORECASE)  # m
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected filename: {path.name} (expected {prefix}_YYYY_DOY.tif)")  # fail with a clear error message
    year, doy = int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))  # year
    if not 1 <= doy <= 366:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid DOY {doy} in {path.name}")  # fail with a clear error message
    return datetime(year, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=doy - 1)  # return the computed result


def stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(
    paths, times, variable_name: str, scale: float = 1.0  # paths
) -> MultidimensionalRaster:
    """Build a MultidimensionalRaster from a GeoTIFF time series (rasterio)."""
    arrays = []  # arrays
    xs = ys = None  # xs
    for path in paths:  # iterate over items
        with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
            data = src.read(1).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
            nodata = src.nodata  # nodata
            if nodata is not None:
                data = np.where(data == nodata, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            # Mask extreme GDAL nodata sentinels
            data = np.where(np.abs(data) > 1e30, np.nan, data)  # compute data
            if scale != 1.0:
                data = data * np.float32(scale)  # compute data
            transform = src.transform  # transform
            height, width = data.shape  # height
            xs = transform.c + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * transform.a  # compute xs
            ys = transform.f + (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * transform.e  # compute ys
            arrays.append(data)

    da = xr.DataArray(  # da
        np.stack(arrays, axis=0),  # set np.stack(arrays
        dims=("time", "y", "x"),  # dims
        coords={  # coords
            "time": np.array(times, dtype="datetime64[ns]"),  # set "time": np.array(times
            "y": ys,
            "x": xs,
        },
        name=variable_name,  # name
    )
    return MultidimensionalRaster(da)  # return the computed result


def write_geotiff_from_array(array: np.ndarray, out_path: Path, profile_src: Path, nodata=np.nan):
    """Write a 2-D array using georeferencing from a reference GeoTIFF."""
    with rasterio.open(profile_src) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
        profile = src.profile.copy()  # profile
    profile.update(dtype="float32", count=1, nodata=nodata, compress="LZW")  # set profile.update(dtype
    out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # set out_path.parent.mkdir(parents
    with rasterio.open(out_path, "w", **profile) as dst:  # open a context-managed resource
        dst.write(np.asarray(array, dtype=np.float32), 1)  # compute dst.write(np.asarray(array


def get_bangladesh_season(dt: datetime) -> str | None:
    """Assign Premonsoon / Monsoon / Winter (mid-Mar / mid-Jul / mid-Nov boundaries)."""
    m, d = dt.month, dt.day  # m
    if (m == 3 and d >= 15) or (4 <= m <= 6) or (m == 7 and d <= 15):
        return "Premonsoon"  # return the computed result
    if (m == 7 and d >= 16) or (8 <= m <= 10) or (m == 11 and d <= 15):
        return "Monsoon"  # return the computed result
    if (m == 11 and d >= 16) or (m == 12) or (1 <= m <= 2) or (m == 3 and d <= 14):
        return "Winter"  # return the computed result
    return None  # return the computed result


print("Helpers ready.")  # status / summary print


Helpers ready.

    WT_DIR.glob(f"watertable_{YEAR_WT}_*.tif"),
    key=lambda p: parse_doy_filename(p, "watertable"),  # key

    raise FileNotFoundError(f"No watertable_{YEAR_WT}_*.tif under {WT_DIR}")  # fail with a clear error message

wt_times = [parse_doy_filename(p, "watertable") for p in wt_paths]  # timestamps parsed from filenames
wt_mdr = stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(wt_paths, wt_times, variable_name="watertable")  # build multidimensional layer

for i, dt in enumerate(wt_times):  # iterate over items

    )

title: Multidimensional Data Analysis
text:
Multidimensional Anomaly
In this section, we will compute vegetation anomalies using NDVI data, specifically measuring how much the NDVI for each month in a target year (e.g., 2024) deviates from the “normal” value for that same month, based on a historical baseline.
This is accomplished by comparing recent NDVI observations to a month-of-year climatology: that is, long-term average NDVI values for each calendar month, calculated from several years of past data.
To do this, we use the function generate_multidimensional_anomaly (ArcGIS Generate Multidimensional Anomaly tool). This tool allows us to: - Stack multiple years of NDVI data to build up a climatology for each month (e.g., average all Januarys, all Februarys, etc., across many years) - Calculate, for each month in a given year, how different the observed NDVI is from its long-term monthly average - Express this anomaly as either the absolute difference, percent difference, or standardized z-score
This workflow enables us to spot unusually green or brown months and detect significant changes in vegetation conditions.
Workflow 1. Stack 16-day NDVI for a baseline window (2015-2024) 2. Aggregate to monthly means 3. Compute anomalies with calculation_interval="BY_MONTH": - DIFFERENCE_FROM_MEAN: NDVI units above/below the month mean - PERCENT_DIFFERENCE_FROM_MEAN: relative (%) departure - Z_SCORE: standardized departure 4. Map and export 2024 monthly anomalies
Positive values = greener / denser vegetation than the month climatology; negative = browner.


Code
# Build multi-year NDVI cube (16-day -> monthly) for climatology + anomaly
NDVI_SCALE = 1e-4  # tutorial parameter
ANOM_YEARS = range(2015, 2025)  # 2015-2024 baseline window
TARGET_ANOM_YEAR = 2024  # TARGET_ANOM_YEAR

ndvi_paths_clim = []  # ndvi_paths_clim
for year in ANOM_YEARS:  # iterate over items
    ndvi_paths_clim.extend(NDVI_DIR.glob(f"ndvi_{year}_*.tif"))
ndvi_paths_clim = sorted(ndvi_paths_clim, key=lambda p: parse_doy_filename(p, "ndvi"))  # ndvi_paths_clim
if not ndvi_paths_clim:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"No NDVI GeoTIFFs for {min(ANOM_YEARS)}-{max(ANOM_YEARS)} under {NDVI_DIR}")  # fail with a clear error message

ndvi_times_clim = [parse_doy_filename(p, "ndvi") for p in ndvi_paths_clim]  # ndvi_times_clim
print(  # status / summary print
    f"Loading {len(ndvi_paths_clim)} NDVI 16-day slices "
    f"({ndvi_times_clim[0].date()} -> {ndvi_times_clim[-1].date()})…"
)

ndvi_clim_mdr = stack_geotiffs_to_mdr(  # ndvi_clim_mdr
    ndvi_paths_clim, ndvi_times_clim, variable_name="ndvi", scale=NDVI_SCALE  # ndvi_paths_clim
)
ndvi_clim_da = ndvi_clim_mdr.dataset["ndvi"]  # ndvi_clim_da
ndvi_clim_da = ndvi_clim_da.where((ndvi_clim_da >= -0.2) & (ndvi_clim_da <= 1.0))  # ndvi_clim_da
ndvi_clim_mdr = MultidimensionalRaster(ndvi_clim_da.to_dataset(name="ndvi"))  # ndvi_clim_mdr

# Aggregate 16-day -> monthly means (required for BY_MONTH climatology)
ndvi_monthly_clim = aggregate_multidimensional_raster(  # ndvi_monthly_clim
    ndvi_clim_mdr,
    variable="ndvi",  # variable
    dimension="time",  # dimension
    aggregation_method="MEAN",  # aggregation_method
    aggregation_definition="INTERVAL_KEYWORD",  # aggregation_definition
    interval_keyword="MONTHLY",  # interval_keyword

)

title: Multidimensional Data Analysis
text:
Find Argument Statistics (NDVI)
In spatiotemporal raster analysis, it is often useful to determine when a particular statistic (e.g., a maximum or minimum value) occurs for each pixel over time. This is achieved by identifying, for each spatial location, the time index (or timestamp) at which a specified statistic (such as the maximum NDVI) is reached, rather than just reporting the value itself.
In this section, we use the function find_argument_statistics, which performs the so-called argument statistics commonly referred to in ArcGIS as Find Argument Statistics, to extract, for each pixel, the time-dimension value (e.g., date or index) at which the desired condition is satisfied (e.g., maximum or minimum NDVI).
For example, by applying find_argument_statistics to a time series of NDVI images, we can create a new raster layer where each pixel encodes the time (such as day-of-year or date) of peak greenness (NDVI maximum), lowest greenness (NDVI minimum), or first threshold crossing.
This approach enables spatial mapping of ecological timing metrics, such as: - Date of maximum NDVI (peak greenness) - Date of minimum NDVI (senescence or disturbance) - Duration and timing of greenness thresholds (e.g., number of time slices above NDVI = 0.5) - First date when a pixel reaches a certain NDVI threshold
These argument statistics provide valuable insight into seasonal vegetation dynamics and can reveal spatial patterns in phenology or environmental events.
We use the 2024 16-day NDVI stack from Data/00_shared/raster_data/Bangladesh/ndvi:







statistics_type
Result per pixel




ARGUMENT_OF_MAXIMUM
Date of maximum NDVI (peak greenness)


ARGUMENT_OF_MINIMUM
Date of minimum NDVI


DURATION + min_value
Number of 16-day composites with NDVI ≥ threshold


ARGUMENT_OF_MIN_VALUE

title: Multidimensional Principal Components Analysis
text:
Overview
Multidimensional Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is a statistical technique used to reduce the dimensionality of large datasets while preserving as much variance as possible. In the context of multidimensional raster data (such as climate model or remote sensing outputs), PCA helps identify key patterns and summarize the dominant modes of variability across both time and multiple variables.
Multidimensional PCA works by transforming correlated input variables (e.g., monthly surface temperature, solar radiation, heat flux, etc.) into a new set of uncorrelated variables called principal components. Each principal component represents a unique direction in the dataset’s multidimensional space, ordered by the amount of original variance they capture.
The main benefits of applying PCA to multidimensional raster data are: - Data Reduction: Compressing a large number of variables or time steps into a small set of informative patterns. - Pattern Extraction: Revealing underlying spatial and temporal structures not immediately apparent in the raw data. - Noise Reduction: Filtering out minor components that contribute less to overall variability.
In practical applications, such as climate analysis, multidimensional PCA can help distinguish between dominant climate drivers, seasonal cycles, and anomalies across regions or variables, facilitating improved visualization and further statistical modeling.

text:
Helper functions
Utilities adapted from 03_03_01_multidimensional_data_mangement.ipynb: unit conversion / deaccumulation, monthly aggregation, Bangladesh clip, thin-plate-spline interpolation, and multi-band GeoTIFF export.


Code
def deaccumulate_forecast(da: xr.DataArray) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Convert forecast accumulations that reset when a new forecast cycle starts
    into per-step increments (same units as the input accumulation).
    """
    vals = np.asarray(da.values, dtype=np.float64)  # compute vals
    out = np.empty_like(vals)  # compute out
    out[0] = vals[0]  # set out[0]
    # Vectorized reset detection along time for the full 3-D cube.
    prev = vals[:-1]  # prev
    cur = vals[1:]  # cur
    # Reset when magnitude drops sharply relative to the previous step.
    reset = np.abs(cur) < (0.5 * np.abs(prev))  # compute reset
    increments = np.where(reset, cur, cur - prev)  # compute increments
    out[1:] = increments  # set out[1:]
    return xr.DataArray(out, coords=da.coords, dims=da.dims, name=da.name, attrs=dict(da.attrs))  # return the computed result


def prepare_variable(da: xr.DataArray, kind: str) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Convert a raw ERA field to analysis units."""
    if kind == "temp_c":
        out = (da - 273.15).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
        out.attrs.update({"units": "degC"})
        return out  # return the computed result
    if kind == "flux_wm2":
        # Accumulated J m**-2 over each forecast step -> approximate W m**-2
        incr = deaccumulate_forecast(da)  # incr
        out = (incr / SECONDS_3H).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
        out.attrs.update({"units": "W m-2"})
        return out  # return the computed result
    if kind == "evap_mm":
        # Accumulated m of water -> mm over the step
        incr = deaccumulate_forecast(da)  # incr
        out = (incr * 1000.0).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
        out.attrs.update({"units": "mm"})
        return out  # return the computed result
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown kind: {kind}")  # fail with a clear error message


def to_monthly_mean(da: xr.DataArray) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Aggregate sub-daily values to calendar-month means."""
    monthly = da.resample(time="1MS").mean(skipna=True)  # temporally resample / aggregate
    # Keep only months inside the analysis year
    monthly = monthly.sel(time=slice(f"{YEAR}-01-01", f"{YEAR}-12-31"))  # select along coordinates or indices
    return monthly  # return the computed result


def monthly_to_points(monthly: xr.DataArray) -> gpd.GeoDataFrame:
    """One row per grid node; one column per month (YYYY-MM)."""
    lon2d, lat2d = np.meshgrid(monthly.longitude.values, monthly.latitude.values)  # build 2-D coordinate grids
    n_pts = lon2d.size  # n_pts
    station_id = [f"S{i:04d}" for i in range(n_pts)]  # station_id

    vals = np.moveaxis(monthly.values, 0, -1).reshape(n_pts, monthly.sizes["time"])  # compute vals
    months = pd.to_datetime(monthly.time.values).strftime("%Y-%m")  # parse timestamps
    df = pd.DataFrame(vals, columns=months)  # compute df
    df.insert(0, "station_id", station_id)
    df.insert(1, "lon", lon2d.ravel().astype("float64"))
    df.insert(2, "lat", lat2d.ravel().astype("float64"))

    geometry = gpd.points_from_xy(df["lon"], df["lat"], crs=WGS84)  # build point geometries from x/y
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=geometry, crs=WGS84)  # return the computed result


def reproject_and_clip(gdf: gpd.GeoDataFrame, bd: gpd.GeoDataFrame) -> gpd.GeoDataFrame:
    proj = gdf.to_crs(bd.crs)  # reproject to the target CRS
    clipped = gpd.clip(proj, bd)  # clip points to the boundary
    return clipped.reset_index(drop=True)  # return the computed result


def make_target_grid(bd: gpd.GeoDataFrame, resolution_m: float = 2000.0):
    bounds = bd.total_bounds  # bounds
    width = int(np.ceil((bounds[2] - bounds[0]) / resolution_m))  # compute width
    height = int(np.ceil((bounds[3] - bounds[1]) / resolution_m))  # compute height
    transform = from_bounds(bounds[0], bounds[1], bounds[2], bounds[3], width, height)  # affine transform from map bounds
    xs = bounds[0] + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * resolution_m  # compute xs
    ys = bounds[3] - (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * resolution_m  # compute ys
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)  # build 2-D coordinate grids
    grid_xy = np.column_stack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel()])  # stack coordinate columns
    mask = geometry_mask(  # mask
        bd.geometry, out_shape=(height, width), transform=transform, invert=True  # bd.geometry container
    )
    return width, height, transform, grid_xy, mask  # return the computed result


def tps_interpolate_band(coords_xy, values, grid_xy, height, width, mask):
    valid = np.isfinite(values)  # compute valid
    if valid.sum() < 3:
        return np.full((height, width), np.nan, dtype="float32")  # return the computed result
    rbf = RBFInterpolator(  # rbf
        coords_xy[valid], values[valid], kernel="thin_plate_spline", smoothing=0.0  # set coords_xy[valid]
    )
    pred = rbf(grid_xy).reshape(height, width).astype("float32")  # cast to the target dtype
    pred[~mask] = np.nan  # compute pred[~mask]
    return pred  # return the computed result


def write_multiband_geotiff(path: Path, bands, band_names, transform, crs):
    height, width = bands[0].shape  # height
    with rasterio.open(
        path,
        "w",
        driver="GTiff",  # driver
        height=height,  # height
        width=width,  # width
        count=len(bands),  # count
        dtype="float32",  # dtype
        crs=crs,  # crs
        transform=transform,  # transform
        nodata=np.nan,  # compute nodata
        compress="lzw",  # compress
    ) as dst:
        for i, (arr, name) in enumerate(zip(bands, band_names), start=1):  # iterate over items
            dst.write(arr, i)
            dst.set_band_description(i, name)


def stack_multiband_geotiff_to_mdr(path: Path, variable_name: str) -> MultidimensionalRaster:
    """Read a 12-band monthly GeoTIFF into MultidimensionalRaster(time, y, x)."""
    with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open a context-managed resource
        data = src.read().astype("float32")  # (bands, y, x)
        nodata = src.nodata  # nodata
        if nodata is not None:
            data = np.where(data == nodata, np.nan, data)  # compute data
        data = np.where(np.abs(data) > 1e30, np.nan, data)  # compute data
        transform = src.transform  # transform
        height, width = src.height, src.width  # height
        xs = transform.c + (np.arange(width) + 0.5) * transform.a  # compute xs
        ys = transform.f + (np.arange(height) + 0.5) * transform.e  # compute ys
        n_bands = src.count  # n_bands
        # Prefer band descriptions like 2018-01; fall back to month starts.
        times = []  # times
        for i in range(1, n_bands + 1):  # iterate over items
            desc = src.descriptions[i - 1]  # desc
            if desc:
                times.append(np.datetime64(desc + "-01" if len(desc) == 7 else desc))
            else:
                times.append(np.datetime64(f"{YEAR}-{i:02d}-01"))

    da = xr.DataArray(  # da
        data,
        dims=("time", "y", "x"),  # dims
        coords={"time": np.array(times, dtype="datetime64[ns]"), "y": ys, "x": xs},  # coords
        name=variable_name,  # name
    )
    return MultidimensionalRaster(da)  # return the computed result


def process_variable_monthly(nc_path, varname, meta, bd, grid_cache, ras_dir, tab_dir, year=YEAR):
    """
    Full monthly pipeline for one variable:
    load -> convert -> monthly mean -> points -> clip -> CSV -> TPS -> GeoTIFF.
    """
    alias = meta["alias"]  # alias
    print(f"\n=== {varname} ({alias}): {meta['long_name']} ===")  # status / summary print
    tif_path = ras_dir / f"{alias}_{year}_monthly_{int(RESOLUTION_M)}m.tif"  # tif_path
    csv_path = tab_dir / f"{alias}_{year}_monthly_means.csv"  # csv_path

    if tif_path.is_file() and csv_path.is_file():  # only when the path exists
        print(f"  skip (exists): {tif_path.name}")  # status / summary print
        return csv_path, tif_path  # return the computed result

    ds = xr.open_dataset(nc_path)  # open the NetCDF / dataset
    raw = ds[varname].sel(time=slice(f"{year}-01-01", f"{year}-12-31"))  # select along coordinates or indices
    if raw.sizes.get("time", 0) == 0:
        ds.close()  # release the file handle
        raise ValueError(f"No timesteps for {varname} in {year}")  # fail with a clear error message
    converted = prepare_variable(raw.load(), meta["kind"])  # converted
    ds.close()  # release the file handle

    monthly = to_monthly_mean(converted)  # aggregate along time or groups
    print(f"  monthly slices: {monthly.sizes['time']}")  # status / summary print

    gdf = monthly_to_points(monthly)  # gdf
    clipped = reproject_and_clip(gdf, bd)  # reproject or clip geometries
    print(f"  points after clip: {len(clipped)}")  # status / summary print

    month_cols = [c for c in clipped.columns if c not in {"station_id", "lon", "lat", "geometry"}]  # month_cols
    wgs = clipped.to_crs(WGS84)  # reproject to the target CRS
    table = pd.DataFrame(  # table
        {
            "station_id": clipped["station_id"].values,
            "lon": wgs.geometry.x.values,
            "lat": wgs.geometry.y.values,
        }
    )
    for col in month_cols:  # iterate over items
        table[col] = clipped[col].astype("float32").values  # cast to the target dtype
    table.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)  # set table.to_csv(csv_path
    print(f"  CSV -> {csv_path.name}")  # status / summary print

    width, height, transform, grid_xy, mask = grid_cache  # width
    coords_xy = np.column_stack([clipped.geometry.x.values, clipped.geometry.y.values])  # stack coordinate columns
    bands, band_names = [], []  # bands
    for col in month_cols:  # iterate over items
        arr = tps_interpolate_band(  # arr
            coords_xy, table[col].to_numpy(), grid_xy, height, width, mask
        )
        bands.append(arr)
        band_names.append(col)
        print(f"  TPS {col}")  # status / summary print

    write_multiband_geotiff(tif_path, bands, band_names, transform, bd.crs)
    print(f"  GeoTIFF -> {tif_path.name}  ({len(bands)} bands, {width}x{height})")  # status / summary print
    return csv_path, tif_path  # return the computed result

title: Multidimensional Principal Components Analysis
text:
Multivariate PCA across climate variables
Stack the annual mean of each monthly raster (7 variables) as a synthetic dimension named variable, standardize each field (zero mean / unit variance over land pixels), then run multidimensional_principal_components across that dimension. This highlights spatial co-variability among heat, moisture, and radiation fields.


Code
# Annual mean per variable (mean over 12 months)
annual_stack = []  # annual_stack
aliases = list(mdr_by_alias.keys())  # aliases
for alias in aliases:  # iterate over items
    annual = mdr_by_alias[alias].dataset[alias].mean(dim="time", skipna=True)  # aggregate along time or groups
    # Standardize over land pixels
    vals = annual.values.astype("float64")  # cast to the target dtype
    mu = np.nanmean(vals)  # aggregate along time or groups
    sigma = np.nanstd(vals)  # compute sigma
    if not np.isfinite(sigma) or sigma == 0:
        z = vals * np.nan  # compute z
    else:
        z = (vals - mu) / sigma  # z
    annual_stack.append(z)

arr = np.stack(annual_stack, axis=0)  # (variable, y, x)
y = mdr_by_alias[aliases[0]].dataset["y"].values  # y
x = mdr_by_alias[aliases[0]].dataset["x"].values  # x

mv_da = xr.DataArray(  # mv_da
    arr.astype("float32"),
    dims=("variable", "y", "x"),  # dims
    coords={"variable": aliases, "y": y, "x": x},  # coords
    name="climate_z",  # name
    attrs={"note": "annual-mean fields, standardized per variable"},  # attrs
)
mv_mdr = MultidimensionalRaster(mv_da)  # mv_mdr

title: Vector-based Suitability Analysis
text:
Overview
Vector-based suitability analysis is a geospatial technique used to determine the most appropriate locations for a particular activity or facility by systematically evaluating spatial units, such as polygons representing parcels, counties, or other administrative boundaries, against multiple criteria. This process is crucial in spatial planning and decision support scenarios where the “best” location depends on several, often competing, factors.
In this approach, each spatial unit (e.g., a county polygon) is considered an alternative, while each spatial dataset or variable (represented as a map layer) is treated as a criterion to evaluate. This method is a spatial implementation of Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA), which integrates multiple quantitative or qualitative criteria to provide an objective, reproducible ranking of locations.
The detailed workflow for vector-based suitability analysis typically includes:

Goal Definition and Spatial Units Selection: Clearly stating the objective (e.g., siting a new clinic) and specifying the spatial units of analysis (e.g., counties, zones, or parcels) that will be assessed for suitability.
Criteria Selection and Data Preparation: Identifying and collecting relevant spatial criteria as vector layers (such as population demographics, land use, access to services, etc.).
Criteria Derivation and Standardization: Processing and transforming criteria so that they are comparable, for example by reclassifying raw values into standard scores or normalizing data ranges.
Criteria Combination: Aggregating the standardized criteria for each spatial unit to compute an overall suitability score. This is commonly done using:

Boolean (categorical) methods: Where each location is assessed against fixed thresholds for all criteria; only those passing all conditions are deemed suitable.
Weighted scoring methods: Where criteria are assigned relative importance (weights), and a composite score is calculated for each location based on how well it meets each criterion.

Result Evaluation and Mapping: Interpreting, ranking, and visualizing the output by mapping suitability scores, identifying top-ranked sites, and possibly validating results with field data or expert input.

Within this notebook, the analysis focuses on polygon features (counties), utilizing geopandas for spatial operations and attribute analysis. In later, more advanced modules, the same concepts are extended to raster data, supporting additional techniques such as fuzzy logic, Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) weighting, and sensitivity analysis, culminating in robust site selection workflows.

Case study: where should a new rural health clinic go?
A regional health network in New York State wants to open a new primary-care and telehealth clinic. Planners want counties that:









#
Criterion
Rationale
Direction




1
Health-care need
Older and poorer populations use more primary care and face more access barriers
Higher is better


2
Hospital capacity gap
Counties with few ICU beds relative to the state average are underserved
Fewer beds per capita is better


3
Proximity to a referral hub
The clinic must refer complex cases to, and receive telehealth support from, an academic medical center
Closer is better

Rurality
The program targets non-metropolitan populations
More rural is better

Latitude/longitude degrees are not suitable for measuring distance or area. The data are reprojected to NAD83 / Conus Albers Equal Area (EPSG:5070), an equal-area projection in meters used by many US federal datasets. Distances computed in Module 2 depend on this step.

Mapping the raw variables
The following helper function draws a consistent choropleth with a state outline. It is redefined in each module so every notebook runs on its own.
Classification schemes affect how a map reads:

Quantiles put an equal number of counties in each class, which is good for showing relative position.
Natural breaks (Jenks) place class breaks at gaps in the data, which is good for skewed distributions.



Code
# Helper: draw a consistent county choropleth with a state outline overlay.
def choropleth(gdf, column, title, cmap="coolwarm", scheme="quantiles", k=5, **kw):
    # Plot the chosen attribute with a classified colour scheme and thin white edges.
    ax = gdf.plot(column, cmap=cmap, scheme=scheme, k=k, legend=True,
                  edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3,  # county boundaries
                  legend_kwds={"loc": "lower left", "fontsize": 8}, **kw)  # legend placement
    state.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#00000080", linewidth=0.8)  # semi-transparent state border
    ax.set_title(title)  # map title
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide axis ticks for a cleaner cartographic look
    return ax  # return axes for further annotation if needed

Observations

The oldest populations are in the Adirondacks and North Country (Hamilton, Essex) and in the Catskills and upper Hudson Valley (Delaware, Columbia, Greene).
Poverty is highest in the Bronx and Brooklyn, and in the western Southern Tier (Chautauqua, Cattaraugus, Allegany) and Broome County.
ICU capacity is concentrated in Manhattan and in the regional centers of Albany, Syracuse, Buffalo, and Long Island, with Warren County (Glens Falls) as a smaller hub.
The most rural counties (RUCC 6 and above) are scattered across the Southern Tier, the North Country, and the Catskills.

These patterns already suggest where the criteria will agree and where they will conflict.

title: Categorical (Boolean) Suitability Analysis
text:
Overview
Categorical (Boolean) Suitability Analysis is a transparent, rule-based, multi-criteria approach for evaluating potential locations (such as counties, regions, or pixels) based on fixed thresholds for each criterion. Each criterion, such as population need, distance to hospitals, presence of existing facilities, or rurality, is individually assessed using user-defined, domain-specific rules (for example, “need_index > 110” or “distance_to_hub < 100 km”).
For every location, each threshold is applied, and the location is assigned a value of 1 (suitable/True) if it passes the threshold or 0 (not suitable/False) if it does not. The specific choice of thresholds reflects planning priorities or constraints and should be adapted to the decision context.
Once all criteria are applied, their results are combined using logical rules, including: - Boolean AND (intersection): Only those locations that meet all individual criteria are deemed suitable. - Boolean OR (union): Locations that satisfy at least one criterion are considered suitable. - k-of-n logic (“at least k out of n”): Locations pass if they satisfy at least k out of n criteria, allowing for more flexible decision-making in situations where partial compliance is acceptable.
This method is prized for its simplicity and explainability: it provides an unambiguous, auditable record of how decisions are made. However, categorical suitability analysis is sensitive to the exact thresholds chosen, and in its basic form, treats each criterion as equally important unless weights are introduced using more advanced methods (not covered here).
In essence, categorical suitability analysis converts each evaluation into a series of yes/no (Boolean) questions and keeps only those locations answering “yes” to all (or enough, depending on the logic chosen). Mathematically, for Boolean AND, this is the intersection of all passing areas:
\[\text{Suitable}_i = C_{1,i} \land C_{2,i} \land \dots \land C_{n,i}\]
This approach is non-compensatory: a location that excels on several criteria but fails just one is excluded, no amount of strength on one factor can offset weakness on another. As such, categorical suitability is well-suited to cases with hard requirements (such as regulatory standards or minimum levels of access), and for initial screening of location candidates.
Apply crisp thresholds to each criterion, then combine them with Boolean AND / OR and k-of-n counting using geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis.

Overview
Defining Categorical Suitability for Health Access Analysis

2.1 Choosing Thresholds: Principles and Examples
2.2 Mapping individual criteria
2.3 Composite suitability (logical AND)
2.4 How much of the state passes the screen?
2.5 Logical OR: the opposite extreme
2.6 k-of-n analysis: how many criteria does each county meet?
2.7 Threshold sensitivity
2.8 Limitations of categorical suitability

Exercises
Key takeaways




Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup.
import warnings  # silence benign RuntimeWarnings
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for MCSM sample data

# Third-party numeric / plotting stack used throughout this notebook.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for Boolean maps
import numpy as np  # array ops kept available for threshold experiments
import pandas as pd  # tabular summaries of suitability flags

# ===================================================================
# Locate the repository root, import Boolean helpers, load criteria layers.
# ===================================================================
# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.
import geolattice

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if not (ROOT / "Data").is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

DATA_DIR = ROOT / "Data" / "03_spatial_analysis" / "MCSM_data"  # shared MCSM sample-data folder
DATA_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if missing

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)  # quiet numeric warnings
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)  # wider DataFrame previews
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = [9, 6]  # default figure size for maps

import geopandas as gpd  # vector GeoDataFrames for counties / hubs
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # two-class Boolean colormap

# GeoLattice Boolean overlay helpers: AND, OR, and per-feature criterion counts.
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis import (
    categorical_and,  # logical AND across Boolean criterion series
    categorical_or,  # logical OR across Boolean criterion series
    criteria_count,  # count how many criteria each feature meets
)

# Load the derived criteria GeoPackage written by the previous notebook.
counties = gpd.read_file(str(DATA_DIR / "ny_criteria.gpkg"), layer="counties")  # criteria counties
state = gpd.read_file(str(DATA_DIR / "ny_criteria.gpkg"), layer="state")  # state outline
hubs = gpd.read_file(str(DATA_DIR / "ny_criteria.gpkg"), layer="hubs")  # referral hubs

BOOL_CMAP = ListedColormap(["#d9d9d9", "#2c7fb8"])  # False = grey, True = blue


def boolean_map(gdf, column, title, show_hubs=False):
    """Plot a two-class Boolean choropleth and optionally overlay hubs."""
    # Map True/False to legend labels so categories plot in a fixed order.
    data = gdf.assign(_v=gdf[column].map({True: "Meets criterion", False: "Does not meet"}))  # legend labels
    ax = data.plot("_v", categorical=True, cmap=BOOL_CMAP, legend=True,
                   categories=["Does not meet", "Meets criterion"],  # fixed category order
                   edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3,  # county edges
                   legend_kwds={"loc": "lower left", "fontsize": 8})  # legend placement
    state.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#00000080", linewidth=0.8)  # state outline
    if show_hubs:
        hubs.plot(ax=ax, marker="*", color="black", markersize=120)  # optional hub markers
    ax.set_title(f"{title}  ({int(gdf[column].sum())} of {len(gdf)} counties)")  # title with pass count
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide axis ticks
    return ax  # return axes for further use

section: Defining Categorical Suitability for Health Access Analysis
text:
Defining Categorical Suitability for Health Access Analysis
In this section, we analyze which counties in New York State meet a set of operational criteria that indicate spatial need or vulnerability in the context of healthcare access. This approach is especially useful when criteria are best represented by clear, binary thresholds, translating complex, nuanced measures (like rurality, healthcare capacity, or proximity to specialist centers) into simple yes/no decisions.
Applications: - Identifying high-need areas for intervention, funding, or further study. - Supporting resource allocation by revealing gaps in capacity or access. - Highlighting places where multiple challenges overlap (e.g., rural counties with both high need and limited ICU availability far from major hubs). - Enabling transparent, replicable methods rooted in policy benchmarks or established research cutoffs.
The following analysis will show how these criteria can be combined to map counties according to whether, and how many, standards of vulnerability or access challenge they meet.

Choosing Thresholds: Principles and Examples
When establishing thresholds for spatial suitability analysis, it is essential to base cutoffs on policy, research evidence, or practical reference points rather than arbitrary values. This ensures the analysis remains meaningful and relevant to real-world needs.
Below are the criteria, operational definitions, and their justifications:








Criterion
Condition
Rationale




Need
need_index >= 100
At or above the New York State average need index


Capacity gap
icu_lq < 1
Fewer ICU beds per capita than the statewide benchmark


Rurality
rucc >= 4
Meets USDA non-metropolitan county definition


Referral access
hub_km <= 100
Within typical 1-1.5 hour drive (common referral radius)



These choices set criteria that can be interpreted consistently across the state and aligned with conventional standards in healthcare access and rural health research.


Code
# Define crisp thresholds for the four clinic-siting criteria.
THRESHOLDS = {"need_min": 100, "icu_lq_max": 1.0, "rucc_min": 4, "hub_km_max": 100}  # baseline cuts

# Build one Boolean flag per criterion (True = county meets that criterion).
counties["ok_need"] = counties["need_index"] >= THRESHOLDS["need_min"]  # need at/above state average
counties["ok_capacity"] = counties["icu_lq"] < THRESHOLDS["icu_lq_max"]  # below-average ICU capacity
counties["ok_rural"] = counties["rucc"] >= THRESHOLDS["rucc_min"]  # non-metropolitan RUCC
counties["ok_access"] = counties["hub_km"] <= THRESHOLDS["hub_km_max"]  # within 100 km of a hub

FLAGS = ["ok_need", "ok_capacity", "ok_rural", "ok_access"]  # ordered list of Boolean columns
counties[FLAGS].sum()  # how many counties pass each individual criterion

Composite suitability (logical AND)

The near-miss list shows which criterion is doing the excluding. Most near misses are metro counties that fail only on rurality. That is intended, since the program targets non-metro areas.
Others are more debatable. Chautauqua County has the fourth-highest need in the state but fails because its ICU-bed LQ is about 1.00, essentially equal to the state rate. Sullivan County fails because it is 106 km from a hub, just over the 100 km limit. These are the hard edges of categorical analysis.


Threshold sensitivity
Thresholds are judgments, so test them. The analysis below varies the distance and need thresholds and counts how many counties pass all four criteria.


Code
# Threshold sensitivity helper: count AND-suitable counties under alternate cuts.
def n_suitable(need_min=100, icu_lq_max=1.0, rucc_min=4, hub_km_max=100):
    """Return how many counties pass all four criteria at the given thresholds."""
    ok = ((counties["need_index"] >= need_min) & (counties["icu_lq"] < icu_lq_max) &
          (counties["rucc"] >= rucc_min) & (counties["hub_km"] <= hub_km_max))  # AND of four tests
    return int(ok.sum())  # suitable county count


distances = range(40, 241, 20)  # hub-distance thresholds to test (km)
needs = [90, 95, 100, 105, 110, 115]  # need-index thresholds to test

# Plot one-at-a-time sensitivity curves for distance and need thresholds.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))  # side-by-side sensitivity panels
axes[0].plot(list(distances), [n_suitable(hub_km_max=d) for d in distances], marker="o")  # distance curve
axes[0].set(xlabel="Maximum distance to hub (km)", ylabel="Suitable counties",
            title="Sensitivity to distance threshold")  # left panel labels
axes[1].plot(needs, [n_suitable(need_min=n) for n in needs], marker="o", color="tab:red")  # need curve
axes[1].set(xlabel="Minimum need index", ylabel="Suitable counties",
            title="Sensitivity to need threshold")  # right panel labels
for a in axes:
    a.grid(alpha=0.3)  # light grid on both panels
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure











The count levels off once the distance threshold passes about 120 km. Beyond that point, other criteria limit the result. Changing the need threshold between 95 and 105 matters little, but raising it above about 105 removes counties quickly. A robust candidate is one that stays suitable over a reasonable range of thresholds.

    index=pd.Index(needs, name="need_min"),  # rows = need thresholds
    columns=pd.Index([60, 80, 100, 120, 150], name="hub_km_max"))  # cols = distance thresholds

Limitations of categorical suitability

No ranking: the 12 suitable counties are treated as equally good.
Hard edges: a county with need index 99.9 fails while one at 100.0 passes, even though they are practically the same.
No trade-offs: a large strength cannot offset a small weakness.
Threshold dependence: results can change sharply with small threshold changes.

Weighted suitability analysis, covered in the next module, addresses the first three limitations by converting criteria to continuous scores and combining them with importance weights. In practice the two methods are often combined: hard constraints are applied categorically, and the remaining locations are ranked by weighted score.

import geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis as fz  # fuzzy helpers

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Why fuzzy?
Part I used crisp criteria. A county either had a need index of at least 100 or it did not. Chautauqua County, with an ICU-bed LQ of 1.00, failed the capacity criterion even though it was practically identical to counties that passed.
Real-world criteria rarely have sharp edges:

Is a 4% slope “gentle”? Mostly. Is 6%? Partly. Is 15%? Not really.
Is a site 105 km from a hospital “close”? Somewhat.

Fuzzy set theory (Zadeh, 1965) replaces the yes/no of crisp sets with a degree of membership μ between 0 and 1:



Set type
Membership of x in set A




Crisp
μ_A(x) ∈ {0, 1}


Fuzzy
μ_A(x) ∈ [0, 1]



A membership of 0.8 means “largely belongs to the set of suitable values”. It is a degree of truth, not a probability. Nothing is random: the slope is known exactly, and the uncertainty lies in what gentle means.


Code
# Compare a crisp slope threshold with a fuzzy "gentle slope" membership.
slope = np.linspace(0, 20, 401)  # slope (%) evaluation grid

crisp = (slope <= 5).astype(float)  # hard pass/fail at 5%
fuzzy = 1 / (1 + (slope / 5) ** 4)  # Small-style membership (midpoint at 5%)

plt.plot(slope, crisp, lw=2.5, label="Crisp: slope <= 5%")  # step function
plt.plot(slope, fuzzy, lw=2.5, label="Fuzzy: 'gentle slope'")  # smooth membership
for s in [4.9, 5.1]:
    plt.axvline(s, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)  # mark values just below/above the cut
plt.xlabel("Slope (%)")  # x-axis: slope percent
plt.ylabel("Membership mu")  # y-axis: membership in [0, 1]
plt.title("Crisp vs. fuzzy definition of a 'gentle slope'")  # panel title
plt.legend()  # show crisp vs fuzzy legend
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)  # light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure

# Print memberships at the two near-threshold slopes.
for s in [4.9, 5.1]:
    print(f"slope {s}% -> crisp {float(s <= 5):.0f} | fuzzy {1 / (1 + (s / 5) ** 4):.3f}")  # side-by-side











slope 4.9% -> crisp 1 | fuzzy 0.520
slope 5.1% -> crisp 0 | fuzzy 0.480


Under the crisp rule, 4.9% and 5.1% get completely different scores. Under the fuzzy rule, they are practically equal (about 0.52 and 0.48), which matches how a planner would actually think about them.

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
The fuzzy suitability workflow

Fuzzification: transform each criterion to a membership in the set suitable with a membership function.
Optional hedging: make a membership stricter or more lenient.
Fuzzy overlay: combine memberships with a fuzzy operator.
Interpretation: map, threshold, and rank the combined membership.

The next sections build each piece.

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Membership functions
The functions below follow the definitions in the ArcGIS Fuzzy Membership tool, so results can be checked against ArcGIS. In each formula, \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are the function’s two shape parameters.









Function
Formula
Shape
Use when




Gaussian
\(\mu = e^{-f_2 (x - f_1)^2}\)
Bell curve, peak at midpoint \(f_1\)
An ideal value exists (optimal temperature)


Near
\(\mu = \dfrac{1}{1 + f_1 (x - f_2)^2}\)
Narrow peak, heavier tails
Values near a target


Small
\(\mu = \dfrac{1}{1 + (x/f_2)^{f_1}}\)
Decreasing S-curve
Small values are favorable (slope, distance)


Large
\(\mu = \dfrac{1}{1 + (x/f_2)^{-f_1}}\)
Increasing S-curve
Large values are favorable (yield, need)


Linear
\(\mu = \dfrac{x - \min}{\max - \min}\), clipped to 0-1
Straight ramp
Simple monotonic relationship


MS Small
\(\mu = \dfrac{b s}{x - a m + b s}\) for \(x > a m\), else 1
Data-driven decrease
Skewed data, small values favorable


MS Large
\(\mu = 1 - \dfrac{b s}{x - a m + b s}\) for \(x > a m\), else 0
Data-driven increase
Skewed data, large values favorable



For Small and Large, \(f_2\) is the midpoint (where μ = 0.5) and \(f_1\) is the spread, which controls steepness. For Gaussian and Near, the midpoint is the peak. In MS Small and MS Large, m and s are the mean and standard deviation of the data, and a and b are user multipliers.
Small and Large require positive values. Gaussian, Near, and Linear accept any real values.

The GeoLattice fuzzy API
Membership functions and overlay operators live in geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis. Import the module as fz so later cells match the ArcGIS-oriented naming used in this series (fz.gaussian, fz.overlay, …). Every function:

accepts NumPy arrays, pandas Series, or scalars,
preserves NaN (NoData), and
returns values clipped to [0, 1].



Code
# List public lowercase helpers exposed by the fuzzy MCSM module.
print([f for f in dir(fz) if not f.startswith("_") and f[:1].islower()][:24])  # sample of API names




['annotations', 'block_mean', 'categorical_and', 'categorical_or', 'criteria_count', 'fuzzy_membership', 'fuzzy_overlay', 'gaussian', 'hybrid_suitability', 'interp_membership', 'jaccard_index', 'large', 'limiting_criterion', 'linear', 'locate_regions', 'mamdani', 'math', 'minmax_normalize', 'monte_carlo_weights', 'ms_large', 'ms_small', 'near', 'np', 'open_raster_data']




Code

print([f for f in dir(fz) if not f.startswith("_")][:25])  # first 25 public attributes

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Visualizing the membership functions


Code
# Plot the main ArcGIS-style membership functions on a common x-grid.
x = np.linspace(0.01, 100, 500)  # criterion-value grid (avoid exact 0 for some formulas)

curves = {
    "Gaussian (mid 50, spread 0.002)": fz.gaussian(x, 50, 0.002),  # peaked at 50
    "Near (mid 50, spread 0.01)": fz.near(x, 50, 0.01),  # ArcGIS Near shape
    "Small (mid 30, spread 5)": fz.small(x, 30, 5),  # smaller is better
    "Large (mid 70, spread 5)": fz.large(x, 70, 5),  # larger is better
    "Linear (20 -> 80)": fz.linear(x, 20, 80),  # ramp between 20 and 80
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))  # membership comparison figure
for name, mu in curves.items():
    ax.plot(x, mu, lw=2, label=name)  # one curve per membership type
ax.set(xlabel="Criterion value x", ylabel="Membership mu", title="Fuzzy membership functions")  # labels
ax.axhline(0.5, color="grey", lw=0.8, ls=":")  # crossover reference at mu = 0.5
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="center right")  # place legend away from curves
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure












How the spread parameter works
For Small and Large, the spread controls how quickly membership moves from 1 to 0 around the midpoint. Low spread produces a gentle transition and high spread approaches a crisp threshold. For Gaussian and Near, a larger spread produces a narrower peak, which can seem counterintuitive.


Code
# Show how the spread parameter changes Small and Gaussian membership shapes.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2))  # two side-by-side panels

# Left: Small membership at several spreads (midpoint fixed at 40).
for sp in [1, 2, 5, 10, 30]:
    axes[0].plot(x, fz.small(x, 40, sp), lw=2, label=f"spread = {sp}")  # steeper as spread grows
axes[0].set(title="Small (midpoint 40): effect of spread", xlabel="x", ylabel="mu")  # labels
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)  # spread legend

# Right: Gaussian membership at several spreads (midpoint fixed at 50).
for sp in [0.0005, 0.002, 0.01, 0.05]:
    axes[1].plot(x, fz.gaussian(x, 50, sp), lw=2, label=f"spread = {sp}")  # narrower as spread grows
axes[1].set(title="Gaussian (midpoint 50): effect of spread", xlabel="x")  # labels
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)  # spread legend

for a in axes:
    a.grid(alpha=0.3)  # light grid on both panels
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure













Choosing the parameters
The parameters translate expert knowledge into a curve. A practical recipe:

Pick the value where the criterion is “neither suitable nor unsuitable”. That value is the midpoint (μ = 0.5).
Pick a value that is “clearly suitable” (say μ = 0.9) and solve for the spread.

For the Small function, \(\mu(x_{0.9}) = 0.9\) gives \(f_1 = \ln(1/9) / \ln(x_{0.9}/f_2)\):


Code
# Solve for a Small-function spread so mu(3) ~= 0.9 when midpoint = 5 (gentle slope example).
sp = spread_for_small(midpoint=5, x_at_09=3)  # slope: 5% neutral, 3% clearly gentle
print(f"spread = {sp:.2f}")  # calibrated spread
print("check mu(3) =", round(float(fz.small(3, 5, sp)), 3), "| mu(5) =", float(fz.small(5, 5, sp)))  # verify




spread = 4.30
check mu(3) = 0.9 | mu(5) = 0.5




Data-driven membership: MS Small and MS Large
MS Small and MS Large set the transition point from the data’s mean and standard deviation, which helps when there is no expert threshold. They are applied here to a right-skewed (log-normal) sample.


Code
# MS Large / MS Small switch around the sample mean (data-driven memberships).
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)  # reproducible RNG
sample = rng.lognormal(mean=3, sigma=0.6, size=2000)  # skewed synthetic criterion sample

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))  # histogram + membership overlay
ax1.hist(sample, bins=60, color="lightgrey", edgecolor="white")  # data distribution
ax1.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="Count")  # left-axis labels
ax2 = ax1.twinx()  # right axis for membership curves
order = np.argsort(sample)  # sort for a smooth line plot
ax2.plot(sample[order], fz.ms_large(sample)[order], lw=2.5, label="MS Large (a=1, b=1)")  # larger better
ax2.plot(sample[order], fz.ms_small(sample)[order], lw=2.5, label="MS Small (a=1, b=1)")  # smaller better
ax2.axvline(sample.mean(), color="k", ls="--", lw=1)  # mean = MS switch point
ax2.set_ylabel("mu")  # membership axis
ax2.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=8)  # membership legend
ax1.set_title("MS functions switch at the mean (dashed line)")  # panel title
plt.show()  # render the figure













Cross-checking with scikit-fuzzy
scikit-fuzzy uses a different parameterization. Its gaussmf takes a standard deviation σ, which corresponds to an ArcGIS spread of \(1/(2\sigma^2)\). A quick numerical check confirms that the implementations agree:


Code
# Cross-check GeoLattice gaussian against scikit-fuzzy gaussmf under matched parameters.
import skfuzzy as skf  # scikit-fuzzy membership helpers

sigma = 10  # scikit-fuzzy Gaussian width
ours = fz.gaussian(x, 50, 1 / (2 * sigma ** 2))  # GeoLattice spread = 1/(2 sigma^2)
theirs = skf.gaussmf(x, 50, sigma)  # scikit-fuzzy Gaussian MF
print("max |difference| =", np.abs(ours - theirs).max())  # should be near machine epsilon




max |difference| = 1.1102230246251565e-16

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Hedges
Hedges modify a fuzzy set the way adverbs modify a word:

Very (concentration), \(\mu^2\), makes the set stricter: a value with μ = 0.7 drops to 0.49.
Somewhat (dilation), \(\mu^{0.5}\), makes it more lenient: 0.7 rises to 0.84.

Use them when stakeholders say a criterion should be applied “strictly” or “loosely” without changing its midpoint.


Code
# Demonstrate hedges: very (concentration) and somewhat (dilation) on a Small membership.
mu = fz.small(x, 40, 4)  # base membership "gentle"
plt.plot(x, mu, lw=2.5, label="gentle")  # original set
plt.plot(x, fz.very(mu), lw=2, ls="--", label="very gentle (mu^2)")  # concentration
plt.plot(x, fz.somewhat(mu), lw=2, ls="-.", label="somewhat gentle (sqrt(mu))")  # dilation
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("mu"); plt.title("Hedges")  # axis labels / title
plt.legend(); plt.grid(alpha=0.3)  # legend and light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Fuzzy overlay operators
After fuzzification, the criteria are combined. For memberships \(\mu_1 \dots \mu_n\) at a location:









Operator
Formula
Behavior
Analogy




AND
\(\min(\mu_i)\)
Result equals the weakest criterion
“All criteria must be met”, the fuzzy version of Boolean AND


OR
\(\max(\mu_i)\)
Result equals the strongest criterion
“Any criterion is enough”


Product
\(\prod \mu_i\)
Less than or equal to the smallest input; decreasive
Each weakness compounds


Sum
\(1 - \prod (1 - \mu_i)\)
Greater than or equal to the largest input; increasive
Each strength adds up


Gamma
\((\text{Sum})^{\gamma} \cdot (\text{Product})^{1 - \gamma}\)
Between Product (γ = 0) and Sum (γ = 1)
Tunable compromise



The fuzzy Sum is not an algebraic sum. Combining two memberships of 0.5 gives 0.75, not 1.0.
The order of the results always holds for any location: Product ≤ AND ≤ inputs ≤ OR ≤ Sum. Gamma can fall anywhere between Product and Sum.


Code
# Compare fuzzy overlay operators on four illustrative membership triplets.
mu_a = np.array([0.9, 0.9, 0.5, 0.2])  # criterion A across four cases
mu_b = np.array([0.8, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2])  # criterion B across four cases
mu_c = np.array([0.7, 0.9, 0.5, 0.9])  # criterion C across four cases

import pandas as pd  # (also imported at setup; kept here for self-contained cell)
table = pd.DataFrame({"mu_A": mu_a, "mu_B": mu_b, "mu_C": mu_c},
                     index=["All good", "One weak", "All average", "Mostly poor"])  # case labels
# Evaluate standard overlay operators column-wise.
for m in ["and", "or", "product", "sum"]:
    table[m.upper()] = fz.overlay([mu_a, mu_b, mu_c], m)  # AND/OR/PRODUCT/SUM
# Evaluate GAMMA at two gamma settings.
for g in [0.5, 0.9]:
    table[f"GAMMA {g}"] = fz.overlay([mu_a, mu_b, mu_c], "gamma", gamma=g)  # gamma blend
table.round(3)  # display rounded comparison table

Reading the table:

One weak (0.9, 0.3, 0.9): AND gives 0.3 because the weak criterion dominates. Product gives 0.24, which is even lower. Sum gives 0.99, so the weakness is almost ignored.
All average (0.5, 0.5, 0.5): Product falls to 0.125 while Sum rises to 0.875. The two operators diverge as more criteria are added.
Gamma 0.9 sits in between, but much closer to Sum, because γ near 1 weights the increasive component.


Response surfaces for two criteria
Plotting each operator over every pair of input values shows its logic at a glance.


Code
# Response surfaces: how each overlay operator combines two membership inputs.
g = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)  # membership grid on [0, 1]
A, B = np.meshgrid(g, g)  # all pairs (mu1, mu2)
ops = [("AND (min)", "and", None), ("OR (max)", "or", None), ("Product", "product", None),
       ("Sum", "sum", None), ("Gamma 0.5", "gamma", 0.5), ("Gamma 0.9", "gamma", 0.9)]  # panels

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 7.5))  # 2x3 grid of surfaces
for ax, (title, m, gm) in zip(axes.ravel(), ops):
    Z = fz.overlay([A, B], m, gamma=gm if gm is not None else 0.9)  # combined membership surface
    cs = ax.contourf(A, B, Z, levels=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), cmap="RdYlGn")  # filled contours
    ax.contour(A, B, Z, levels=[0.5], colors="k", linewidths=1)  # mu = 0.5 isoline
    ax.set_title(title)  # operator name
    ax.set_xlabel("mu1"); ax.set_ylabel("mu2")  # input membership axes
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # square panels
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Combined membership")  # shared colourbar
plt.suptitle("Fuzzy overlay response surfaces (black line: mu = 0.5)")  # figure title
plt.show()  # render the figure













How γ moves the result
As γ moves from 0 to 1, the result moves from Product to Sum. Values of γ between about 0.7 and 0.9 are common in practice because they balance the two. For the three-criterion “one weak” example:


Code
# Trace how gamma moves the combined membership for a fixed input triplet.
gammas = np.linspace(0, 1, 51)  # gamma from pure product-like to sum-like
case = [np.array([0.9]), np.array([0.3]), np.array([0.9])]  # one weak criterion among two strong
vals = [float(fz.overlay(case, "gamma", gamma=gm)[0]) for gm in gammas]  # gamma curve

plt.plot(gammas, vals, lw=2.5)  # combined mu vs gamma
plt.axhline(float(fz.overlay(case, "and")[0]), ls="--", color="grey", label="AND (min)")  # AND reference
plt.xlabel("gamma"); plt.ylabel("Combined mu")  # axis labels
plt.title("Gamma overlay for inputs (0.9, 0.3, 0.9)")  # panel title
plt.legend(); plt.grid(alpha=0.3)  # legend and light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Choosing an operator







Decision logic
Operator




All criteria are essential, and the weakest one limits suitability
AND


Any single criterion qualifies a site
OR


Weaknesses compound, so the result should be conservative
Product


Strengths reinforce each other
Sum


A balance between the two, tuned with γ
Gamma



Note that fuzzy overlay has no criterion weights. The operator controls how criteria interact, and importance can be expressed through membership parameters or hedges. Module 8 discusses weighting fuzzy criteria explicitly.

title: Fuzzy Logic Foundations for Suitability Modeling
text:
Key takeaways

A fuzzy membership is a degree of suitability between 0 and 1, not a probability.
Membership functions encode expert knowledge. The midpoint is the μ = 0.5 point and the spread controls steepness.
Hedges make sets stricter or more lenient.
Overlay operators range from strict (Product, AND) to lenient (OR, Sum), and Gamma moves smoothly between Product and Sum.

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
text:
Load and reproject the DEM
The DEM is stored in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326). Slope and distance calculations need equal-unit, metric cell sizes, so the DEM is reprojected to UTM zone 14N (EPSG:32614) at 90 m resolution. Bilinear resampling is used because elevation is continuous.


Code
# Download a small Texas DEM (geographic) if missing, then reproject to UTM 14N at 90 m.
DEM_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdbartos/pysheds/master/data/dem.tif"  # sample DEM URL
dem_geo = str(DATA_DIR / "dem_texas_geo.tif")  # local geographic GeoTIFF path
if not Path(dem_geo).is_file():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(DEM_URL, dem_geo)  # download once, then reuse

# Inspect the source DEM, then warp to a metric CRS for slope/distance work.
with rasterio.open(dem_geo) as src:
    print("CRS:", src.crs, "| size:", src.width, "x", src.height, "| res:", src.res)  # source metadata
    print("Bounds:", [round(b, 4) for b in src.bounds])  # geographic bounds

    DST_CRS, RES = "EPSG:32614", 90  # UTM zone 14N, 90 m cells
    transform, width, height = calculate_default_transform(
        src.crs, DST_CRS, src.width, src.height, *src.bounds, resolution=RES)  # target grid
    dem = np.full((height, width), np.nan, dtype="float32")  # destination elevation array
    reproject(rasterio.band(src, 1), dem,
              src_transform=src.transform, src_crs=src.crs, src_nodata=src.nodata,  # source georef
              dst_transform=transform, dst_crs=DST_CRS, dst_nodata=np.nan,  # destination georef
              resampling=Resampling.bilinear)  # bilinear for continuous elevations

# Shared GeoTIFF profile for saving derived rasters in the same grid.
PROFILE = dict(driver="GTiff", height=height, width=width, count=1, dtype="float32",
               crs=DST_CRS, transform=transform, nodata=np.nan, compress="lzw")  # write template


def save_tif(arr, path):
    """Write a float32 array to GeoTIFF using the shared PROFILE."""
    with rasterio.open(path, "w", **PROFILE) as dst:
        dst.write(arr.astype("float32"), 1)  # band 1


dem_utm = str(DATA_DIR / "dem_texas_utm.tif")  # projected DEM path
save_tif(dem, dem_utm)  # persist the UTM DEM for pysheds
valid = ~np.isnan(dem)  # True where elevation is defined
CELL_HA = RES * RES / 10_000  # cell area in hectares

print(f"Reprojected: {width} x {height} cells of {RES} m | valid cells: {valid.sum():,} "
      f"({valid.sum() * CELL_HA / 100:,.0f} km²)")  # grid summary
print(f"Elevation range: {np.nanmin(dem):.0f}-{np.nanmax(dem):.0f} m")  # elevation range



CRS: EPSG:4326 | size: 367 x 359 | res: (0.0008333333333333, 0.0008333333333333)
Bounds: [-97.485, 32.5225, -97.1792, 32.8217]
Reprojected: 325 x 374 cells of 90 m | valid cells: 117,478 (952 km²)
Elevation range: 147-298 m


The reprojected grid is slightly rotated relative to the original, so a few edge cells become NoData (NaN). Every later calculation must preserve those NaNs.

Hillshade for context
A hillshade simulates illumination from a light source and makes terrain easy to read. It is used as a backdrop for the maps in this module.


Code
# Build a hillshade and a helper that drapes arrays over it for quick maps.
def hillshade(z, res, azimuth=315, altitude=45):
    """Compute a simple Lambertian hillshade from an elevation array."""
    dy, dx = np.gradient(z, res)  # elevation gradients (row, col)
    slope = np.arctan(np.hypot(dx, dy))  # slope in radians
    aspect = np.arctan2(-dx, dy)  # aspect in radians
    az, alt = np.radians(azimuth), np.radians(altitude)  # light direction
    hs = np.sin(alt) * np.cos(slope) + np.cos(alt) * np.sin(slope) * np.cos(az - aspect)  # illumination
    return np.clip(hs, 0, 1)  # keep hillshade in [0, 1]


hs = hillshade(dem, RES)  # hillshade for basemap context
EXTENT = [transform.c, transform.c + width * RES, transform.f - height * RES, transform.f]  # imshow extent


def show(arr, title, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, label="mu", ax=None, alpha=0.75):
    """Drape an array over hillshade and add a colourbar."""
    ax = ax or plt.gca()  # use current axes if none provided
    ax.imshow(hs, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)  # hillshade basemap
    im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, extent=EXTENT, alpha=alpha)  # overlay array
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)  # panel title
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide ticks
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label=label)  # colourbar
    return ax  # return axes for further drawing


show(dem, "Elevation (m) over hillshade", cmap="terrain",
     vmin=np.nanmin(dem), vmax=np.nanmax(dem), label="m", alpha=0.6)  # elevation preview
plt.show()  # render the figure

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
text:
Deriving terrain criteria

Slope
The slope is computed from the elevation gradient using numpy.gradient with the 90 m cell size and expressed in percent rise, the usual engineering unit for site grading.


Code
# Derive percent slope from the DEM gradients (metres of rise per metres of run).
dz_dy, dz_dx = np.gradient(dem, RES)  # rows run north -> south; cols west -> east
slope_pct = 100 * np.hypot(dz_dx, dz_dy)  # slope as percent grade

print("Slope percentiles (%):", np.round(np.nanpercentile(slope_pct, [5, 25, 50, 75, 95, 99]), 2))  # slope stats



Slope percentiles (%): [0.25 1.05 1.82 2.9  5.29 8.39]




Aspect: a circular variable
Aspect is the compass direction a slope faces (0° = north, 90° = east, 180° = south). It is circular, so 359° and 1° are neighbors. Applying a membership function to raw degrees would be wrong.
The fix is to convert aspect to the angular deviation from due south (0-180°) and apply the membership to that. In NumPy array coordinates, rows increase southward, which sets the signs used below.


Code
# Aspect as compass bearing of the downslope direction (0 = N, clockwise).
aspect = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(-dz_dx, dz_dy)) + 360) % 360  # aspect in degrees [0, 360)
aspect[np.isnan(dem)] = np.nan  # keep NoData aligned with the DEM

# Angular deviation from south (0 = due south, 180 = due north).
dev_south = np.abs(((aspect - 180 + 180) % 360) - 180)  # circular distance to 180 degrees

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))  # aspect and south-deviation maps
show(aspect, "Aspect (deg from north)", cmap="twilight", vmin=0, vmax=360, label="deg", ax=axes[0])  # aspect
show(dev_south, "Deviation from due south (deg)", cmap="viridis_r", vmin=0, vmax=180, label="deg", ax=axes[1])  # deviation
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure












Topographic position index (TPI)
The TPI is a cell’s elevation minus the mean elevation of its neighborhood. Positive values mark ridges and upper slopes, negative values mark valleys and depressions. A 15 × 15 cell window (about 1.35 km) captures landform-scale position.
scipy.ndimage.uniform_filter does not handle NaN, so the neighborhood mean is computed as a ratio of two filtered arrays: the sum of valid values divided by the count of valid cells.


Code
# Topographic Position Index: elevation minus neighbourhood mean elevation.
def nanmean_filter(a, size):
    """Moving-window mean that ignores NaNs by normalising a filled sum by a weight sum."""
    vals = np.where(np.isnan(a), 0, a)  # replace NaN with 0 for summing
    wts = (~np.isnan(a)).astype(float)  # 1 where valid, 0 where NaN
    return ndi.uniform_filter(vals, size) / np.maximum(ndi.uniform_filter(wts, size), 1e-9)  # nan-aware mean


tpi = dem - nanmean_filter(dem, 15)  # 15-cell window TPI (m)
print("TPI percentiles (m):", np.round(np.nanpercentile(tpi, [5, 25, 50, 75, 95]), 2))  # TPI stats

show(tpi, "Topographic position index (m)", cmap="BrBG", vmin=-10, vmax=10, label="m")  # TPI map
plt.show()  # render the figure



TPI percentiles (m): [-6.12 -2.47 -0.23  2.26  6.95]











Distance to streams
Stream channels are derived from the DEM with a standard hydrological workflow in pysheds:

Condition the DEM by filling pits and depressions and resolving flats, so water can flow continuously.
Compute D8 flow direction, which sends each cell’s water to its steepest downslope neighbor.
Compute flow accumulation, the number of upstream cells draining through each cell.
Define streams as cells draining more than 500 cells (500 × 0.81 ha ≈ 4 km²).

The Euclidean distance from every cell to the nearest stream cell is then computed with distance_transform_edt.

Compatibility note: pysheds 0.4 calls np.in1d, which was removed in NumPy 2.0. The one-line shim below restores it. It has no effect on older NumPy versions.



Code
# Derive streams via pysheds hydrology, then compute Euclidean distance to stream cells.
if not hasattr(np, "in1d"):
    np.in1d = np.isin  # NumPy 2 shim for older pysheds

from pysheds.grid import Grid  # DEM-based flow routing

grid = Grid.from_raster(dem_utm)  # open the projected DEM
r = grid.read_raster(dem_utm)  # read elevation into a pysheds Raster
conditioned = grid.resolve_flats(grid.fill_depressions(grid.fill_pits(r)))  # hydrologically condition
fdir = grid.flowdir(conditioned)  # D8 flow directions
acc = np.asarray(grid.accumulation(fdir), dtype=float)  # upstream accumulation (cells)

STREAM_CELLS = 500  # accumulation threshold defining stream cells
streams = (acc > STREAM_CELLS) & valid  # stream mask on valid land
dist_stream = ndi.distance_transform_edt(~streams) * RES  # metres to nearest stream
dist_stream[~valid] = np.nan  # keep NoData outside the DEM

print(f"Stream cells: {streams.sum():,} ({100 * streams.sum() / valid.sum():.1f}% of area)")  # stream extent
print("Distance-to-stream percentiles (m):", np.round(np.nanpercentile(dist_stream, [5, 25, 50, 75, 95])))  # distance stats



Stream cells: 2,814 (2.4% of area)
Distance-to-stream percentiles (m): [  90.  450.  900. 1498. 2295.]




Code
# Map distance to streams and overlay the stream network in blue.
ax = show(dist_stream, "Distance to streams (m), streams in blue", cmap="magma_r",
          vmin=0, vmax=2500, label="m")  # distance surface
ax.imshow(np.where(streams, 1, np.nan), cmap="winter", extent=EXTENT, interpolation="nearest")  # stream overlay
plt.show()  # render the figure

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
text:
Hard constraints
Some conditions exclude a location no matter how good it is otherwise. These are applied as a crisp Boolean mask, separately from the fuzzy factors:







Constraint
Rule




NoData
Outside the DEM, or edge cells where slope cannot be computed


Steep terrain
Slope > 10% (impractical for fixed-tilt arrays)


Stream channel and setback
Within 90 m (one cell) of a stream


Probable open water
Contiguous areas ≥ 25 ha with slope < 0.1%



The last rule addresses a common pitfall. Reservoir surfaces are perfectly flat in a DEM, so a terrain-only model rates them as ideal solar land. Large, perfectly flat patches are flagged as probable water here. A real project would use a land-cover or hydrography layer such as NLCD or NHD instead.


Code
# Hard constraints: exclude water-like flats, steep slopes, stream buffers, and NoData.
flat = np.nan_to_num(slope_pct, nan=99) < 0.1  # near-zero slope candidates
flat_lab, n_flat = ndi.label(flat, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))  # connected flat patches
flat_ha = ndi.sum(flat, flat_lab, np.arange(1, n_flat + 1)) * CELL_HA  # patch areas (ha)
water = np.isin(flat_lab, np.where(flat_ha >= 25)[0] + 1)  # large flat patches (~open water)
print(f"Probable open water: {(flat_ha >= 25).sum()} areas, {water.sum() * CELL_HA / 100:.1f} km²")  # water summary

# Combine hard exclusions into a feasible-land mask.
excluded = (~valid) | np.isnan(slope_pct) | (slope_pct > 10) | (dist_stream <= 90) | water  # exclusion rules
feasible = ~excluded  # True where solar siting is allowed

print(f"Feasible area: {feasible.sum() * CELL_HA / 100:,.1f} km² "
      f"({100 * feasible.sum() / valid.sum():.1f}% of the study area)")  # feasible summary

show(np.where(valid, feasible.astype(float), np.nan), "Feasible land (green) after hard constraints",
     cmap="RdYlGn", label="feasible")  # feasible map
plt.show()  # render the figure



Probable open water: 6 areas, 23.6 km²
Feasible area: 850.2 km² (89.3% of the study area)

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
text:
Fuzzification









Factor
Function
Parameters
Meaning




Slope
Small
midpoint 4%, spread 4
2% ≈ 0.94, 4% = 0.5, 8% ≈ 0.06


Aspect
Gaussian on deviation from south
midpoint 0°, spread 1.49 × 10⁻⁴
Due south = 1, east or west (90°) = 0.3, north ≈ 0


Flatness override
Small on slope
midpoint 1%, spread 6
On flat land, aspect does not matter


TPI
Linear
-6 m → 0, +4 m → 1
Valley bottoms 0, ridges 1


Distance to streams
Large
midpoint 300 m, spread 3
90 m ≈ 0.03, 300 m = 0.5, 900 m ≈ 0.96




A conditional membership with fuzzy OR
On a 0.5% slope, aspect is irrelevant because the land is effectively flat and receives full sun. Applying the aspect membership everywhere would wrongly penalize flat, north-tilted fields. This condition is written as a fuzzy rule:

Exposure is good if the cell faces south OR the cell is flat.

That rule becomes \(\mu_{exposure} = \max(\mu_{south}, \mu_{flat})\). Fuzzy operators can be used inside a criterion as well as between criteria.


Code
# Fuzzify the four terrain criteria into membership rasters on [0, 1].
aspect_spread = -np.log(0.3) / 90 ** 2  # gives mu = 0.3 at 90 degrees from south
print(f"Aspect spread = {aspect_spread:.3e}")  # calibrated Gaussian spread

mu_slope = fz.small(slope_pct, 4, 4)  # gentler slopes preferred
mu_south = fz.gaussian(dev_south, 0, aspect_spread)  # prefer south-facing aspects
mu_flat = fz.small(slope_pct, 1, 6)  # very flat land also counts as exposed
mu_exposure = fz.overlay([mu_south, mu_flat], "or")  # south-facing OR nearly flat
mu_tpi = fz.linear(tpi, -6, 4)  # prefer mid-slope / lower positions
mu_stream = fz.large(dist_stream, 300, 3)  # prefer greater distance from streams

MEMBERSHIPS = {"Slope": mu_slope, "Exposure": mu_exposure, "Topographic position": mu_tpi,
               "Stream distance": mu_stream}  # named membership rasters

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
section: From suitability surface to candidate sites
text:
From suitability surface to candidate sites
A solar farm needs a contiguous block of good land, not scattered pixels. This step is the open-source equivalent of ArcGIS Locate Regions in its simplest form:

Threshold the suitability surface to define “highly suitable” land.
Label connected regions with 8-neighbor connectivity (scipy.ndimage.label).
Filter regions by a minimum area, here 40 ha, roughly a 5-8 MW array.
Rank regions by mean suitability and area.
Vectorize regions to polygons for mapping and reporting.


Choosing the threshold
The threshold should produce distinct, appropriately sized patches. If it is too low, highly suitable land merges into one huge, unhelpful region. If it is too high, too few patches remain. The table below compares several thresholds.


Code
# Threshold sensitivity: how patch count/size change as the suitability cut rises.
suit = results["Gamma 0.8"]  # working suitability surface

rows = []  # one summary row per threshold
for t in [0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9]:
    h = np.nan_to_num(suit) >= t  # high-suitability binary mask
    lab, k = ndi.label(h, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))  # connected patches
    sizes = ndi.sum(h, lab, np.arange(1, k + 1)) * CELL_HA  # patch sizes in hectares
    rows.append({"threshold": t, "area_km2": h.sum() * CELL_HA / 100,
                 "% of feasible": 100 * h.sum() / feasible.sum(),
                 "patches >= 40 ha": int((sizes >= 40).sum()), "largest patch (ha)": sizes.max()})  # stats
pd.DataFrame(rows).round({"area_km2": 1, "% of feasible": 1, "largest patch (ha)": 0})  # threshold table

At 0.6 and 0.7, highly suitable land merges into patches of more than 10,000 ha, which is too coarse to compare sites. A threshold of 0.85 keeps about a fifth of the feasible land and splits it into about 100 separate candidate patches, so it is used below.


Code
# Extract contiguous high-suitability patches and rank them by quality x log(area).
THRESH, MIN_HA = 0.85, 40  # membership threshold and minimum patch size (ha)

high = np.nan_to_num(suit) >= THRESH  # binary high-suitability mask
labels, n = ndi.label(high, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))  # label connected patches

ids = np.arange(1, n + 1)  # patch ids
cells = ndi.sum(high, labels, ids)  # cell counts per patch
mean_mu = ndi.mean(np.nan_to_num(suit), labels, ids)  # mean suitability per patch

regions = pd.DataFrame({"region": ids, "area_ha": cells * CELL_HA, "mean_mu": mean_mu})  # patch table
regions = regions[regions["area_ha"] >= MIN_HA].copy()  # drop undersized patches
regions["score"] = regions["mean_mu"] * np.log(regions["area_ha"])  # favour large AND good
regions = regions.sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)  # rank patches
regions["site"] = np.arange(1, len(regions) + 1)  # site numbers 1..N

print(f"Highly suitable cells: {high.sum():,} ({high.sum() * CELL_HA / 100:.1f} km²) in {n} patches")  # summary
print(f"Patches >= {MIN_HA} ha: {len(regions)}")  # retained patch count

title: Fuzzy Suitability for Rasters
text:
Key takeaways

Derive terrain criteria from a DEM in a projected, metric CRS, and keep NoData as NaN throughout.
Circular variables such as aspect need conversion (deviation from a target direction) before fuzzification.
Fuzzy operators can build conditional criteria inside a factor, such as south-facing OR flat.
Keep hard constraints crisp and soft factors fuzzy, and apply the mask after overlay.
Thresholding, connected-component labeling, area filtering, and vectorization turn a surface into actionable candidate sites.

Next: Module 8: Advanced Fuzzy Suitability: sensitivity, weighting, and rule-based fuzzy inference.
