title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Why sensitivity analysis matters
Every suitability model rests on judgments and imperfect data:







Source of uncertainty
Examples in this model




Preference (value judgments)
Criterion weights, whether slope matters more than flood risk


Model structure
Membership function shape and midpoint, aggregation rule (WLC or fuzzy)


Thresholds
Maximum slope of 10%, stream threshold of 4 km²


Data
DEM vertical error, cell size, zone boundaries (MAUP)



A map that presents one “best site” without testing these hides how fragile it may be. Decision-makers, regulators, and the public reasonably ask: would the answer change if someone else had chosen the weights?
Two related ideas are used in this module:

Sensitivity analysis (SA) asks which inputs the result responds to most. It tells you where to spend effort justifying inputs.
Uncertainty analysis (UA) asks how confident we can be in the result, given the plausible range of all inputs. It produces probability and confidence maps.

Sensitivity methods also differ in scope:








Scope
Method
What it reveals




Local
OAT (3)
Effect of small changes around the baseline, one input at a time


Global, preference
Monte Carlo weights (4)
Robustness to the full range of plausible weights


Global, variance-based
Sobol and Morris (5)
Share of output variance due to each input, including interactions


Data
Error propagation, resolution, MAUP (6)
Robustness to input data quality and spatial support

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
A reusable model pipeline
To test the model, it must be possible to re-run it from scratch with different inputs. The functions below rebuild the Module 7 workflow at any resolution: DEM → criteria → constraints → memberships → WLC score.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Reusable solar-suitability pipeline: terrain criteria, memberships, WLC.
# ===================================================================

def nanmean_filter(a, size):
    """Moving-window mean that ignores NaNs by normalising filled sums by weights."""
    vals = np.where(np.isnan(a), 0, a)  # replace NaN with 0 for summing
    wts = (~np.isnan(a)).astype(float)  # 1 where valid, 0 where NaN
    return ndi.uniform_filter(vals, size) / np.maximum(ndi.uniform_filter(wts, size), 1e-9)  # nan-aware mean


def flow_accumulation(dem, res, left=EXTENT[0], top=EXTENT[3]):
    """D8 flow accumulation (cells) with pysheds, via a temporary GeoTIFF."""
    prof = dict(driver="GTiff", height=dem.shape[0], width=dem.shape[1], count=1, dtype="float32",
                crs=CRS, transform=from_origin(left, top, res, res), nodata=np.nan)  # write profile
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".tif", delete=False) as tmp:
        path = tmp.name  # temporary DEM path for pysheds
    with rasterio.open(path, "w", **prof) as dst:
        dst.write(dem.astype("float32"), 1)  # write elevation band
    g = Grid.from_raster(path)  # open temporary DEM
    r = g.read_raster(path)  # read as pysheds Raster
    cond = g.resolve_flats(g.fill_depressions(g.fill_pits(r)))  # hydrologically condition
    acc = np.asarray(g.accumulation(g.flowdir(cond)), dtype=float)  # upstream accumulation
    os.remove(path)  # clean up temporary file
    return acc  # accumulation in cells


def terrain_criteria(dem, res, stream_km2=4.0):
    """Derive slope, south-deviation, TPI, stream distance, and a feasibility mask."""
    valid = ~np.isnan(dem)  # valid elevation cells
    dz_dy, dz_dx = np.gradient(dem, res)  # elevation gradients
    slope = 100 * np.hypot(dz_dx, dz_dy)  # slope as percent grade
    aspect = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(-dz_dx, dz_dy)) + 360) % 360  # aspect in degrees
    dev = np.abs(((aspect - 180 + 180) % 360) - 180)  # deviation from due south
    win = max(3, int(round(1350 / res)) | 1)  # odd window of about 1.35 km
    tpi = dem - nanmean_filter(dem, win)  # topographic position index (m)
    acc = flow_accumulation(dem, res)  # flow accumulation (cells)
    streams = (acc > stream_km2 * 1e6 / res ** 2) & valid  # stream mask from drainage area
    dist = ndi.distance_transform_edt(~streams) * res  # metres to nearest stream
    dist[~valid] = np.nan  # keep NoData outside DEM
    flat = np.nan_to_num(slope, nan=99) < 0.1  # near-zero slope candidates
    lab, n = ndi.label(flat, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))  # connected flat patches
    ha = ndi.sum(flat, lab, np.arange(1, n + 1)) * res * res / 1e4  # patch areas (ha)
    water = np.isin(lab, np.where(ha >= 25)[0] + 1)  # large flats treated as water
    feasible = valid & ~np.isnan(slope) & (slope <= 10) & (dist > 90) & ~water  # hard constraints
    return dict(slope=slope, dev=dev, tpi=tpi, dist=dist, streams=streams, feasible=feasible)  # criteria dict


PARAM0 = dict(slope_mid=4.0, south_mu90=0.3, tpi_lo=-6.0, stream_mid=300.0)  # baseline membership params


def memberships(c, slope_mid=4.0, south_mu90=0.3, tpi_lo=-6.0, stream_mid=300.0):
    """Stack the four membership rasters for a criteria dict c."""
    asp_sp = -np.log(south_mu90) / 90 ** 2  # Gaussian spread from mu(90 deg)
    mu_exp = np.maximum(fz.gaussian(c["dev"], 0, asp_sp), fz.small(c["slope"], 1, 6))  # exposure OR flat
    return np.stack([fz.small(c["slope"], slope_mid, 4), mu_exp,
                     fz.linear(c["tpi"], tpi_lo, 4), fz.large(c["dist"], stream_mid, 3)])  # (4, rows, cols)


CRITERIA = ["Slope", "Exposure", "Topographic position", "Stream distance"]  # criterion display names
W0 = np.array([0.35, 0.20, 0.15, 0.30])  # baseline weights (sum to 1)


def wlc(M, w):
    """Weighted linear combination of membership stack M with weights w."""
    return np.tensordot(np.asarray(w) / np.sum(w), M, axes=1)  # renormalised weighted sum




The rebuilt pipeline should reproduce Module 7. A few dozen cells may differ, because flow routing across flat areas is sensitive to tiny numerical differences in how the DEM is written and read. Differences below 0.1% of cells are negligible here.


Code
# Run the reusable pipeline on the Module 7 DEM and compare the feasibility mask.
t = time.time()  # start timer
crit = terrain_criteria(DEM, RES)  # derive terrain criteria + feasibility
print(f"Pipeline run time: {time.time() - t:.1f} s")  # elapsed seconds
diff = (crit["feasible"] != L["feasible"]).sum()  # cells disagreeing with Module 7
print(f"Feasible cells differing from Module 7: {diff} ({100 * diff / L['feasible'].sum():.2f}%)")  # QA

FEAS = crit["feasible"]  # feasibility mask used below
IDX = np.flatnonzero(FEAS)  # flat indices of feasible cells
M0 = memberships(crit)  # (4, rows, cols) membership stack
MF = M0.reshape(4, -1)[:, IDX]  # (4, n_feasible) matrix for fast WLC
BASE = wlc(MF, W0)  # baseline scores on feasible cells only
N_CELLS = len(IDX)  # number of feasible cells


def to_map(v, idx=IDX, shape=DEM.shape):
    """Scatter a feasible-cell vector v back onto a full raster map."""
    out = np.full(shape, np.nan)  # NaN background
    out.ravel()[idx] = v  # place feasible values
    return out  # map-shaped array


def show(arr, title, ax, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, label=None, alpha=0.85):
    """Drape an array over hillshade and optionally add a colourbar."""
    ax.imshow(HS, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)  # hillshade basemap
    im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, extent=EXTENT, alpha=alpha)  # overlay
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)  # panel title
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide ticks
    if label is not None:
        plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label=label)  # optional colourbar
    return im  # mappable for shared colourbars


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))  # baseline suitability map
show(to_map(BASE), "Baseline WLC suitability (weights 0.35 / 0.20 / 0.15 / 0.30)", ax, label="score")  # map
plt.show()  # render the figure
print(f"Feasible cells: {N_CELLS:,}")  # confirm sample size




Pipeline run time: 0.3 s
Feasible cells differing from Module 7: 68 (0.06%)









Feasible cells: 104,893



Comparison metrics
Every experiment is compared with the baseline using three metrics:

Jaccard index of the top 10%: the overlap |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| between the top-10% cells of two maps. It answers do we still pick the same best land?
Spearman’s ρ: agreement in the overall ordering, computed on a fixed random sample of 20,000 cells for speed.
Mean |Δ score|: the average absolute change in score.



Code
# Shared comparison metrics: Jaccard of top-10%, Spearman, and mean absolute change.
RNG = np.random.default_rng(42)  # reproducible RNG for subsampling
SAMP = RNG.choice(N_CELLS, 20_000, replace=False)  # subsample for fast Spearman
TOPQ = 0.90  # top 10% quantile threshold (keep cells above this)

BASE_TOP = top_quantile_mask(BASE)  # baseline top-10% Boolean mask


def metrics(v, ref=BASE, ref_top=BASE_TOP):
    """Return Jaccard / Spearman / mean |change| of alternate scores vs baseline."""
    return {"jaccard_top10": jaccard_index(top_quantile_mask(v), ref_top),  # top-set overlap
            "spearman": spearmanr(v[SAMP], ref[SAMP])[0],  # rank agreement on subsample
            "mean_abs_change": np.mean(np.abs(v - ref))}  # average absolute score change


print("Top-10% area (km²):", round(BASE_TOP.sum() * 0.0081, 1))  # 90 m cells -> 0.81 ha = 0.0081 km2




Top-10% area (km²): 169.9

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
One-at-a-time (OAT) weight perturbation
Each weight is changed by δ ∈ {±5, ±10, ±15, ±20%} while the others are rescaled proportionally, so the weights still sum to 1 and keep their relative proportions:
\[w_i' = w_i (1 + \delta), \qquad w_j' = w_j \cdot \frac{1 - w_i'}{1 - w_i} \quad (j \ne i)\]
For example, raising slope from 0.35 to 0.42 (+20%) scales the other three weights by (1 - 0.42)/(1 - 0.35) = 0.892.


Code
# One-at-a-time weight perturbation: move one weight, renormalise, recompute WLC.
print("Example, slope +20%:", perturb_weights(W0, 0, 0.20).round(4), "sum =", perturb_weights(W0, 0, 0.20).sum())  # demo

DELTAS = [-0.20, -0.15, -0.10, -0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20]  # relative weight changes to test
rows, max_change = [], np.zeros(N_CELLS)  # OAT table rows + per-cell max |delta score|
for i, name in enumerate(CRITERIA):
    for d in DELTAS:
        w = perturb_weights(W0, i, d)  # perturb criterion i by relative delta d
        v = wlc(MF, w)  # rescore feasible cells
        max_change = np.maximum(max_change, np.abs(v - BASE))  # track worst-case local change
        rows.append({"criterion": name, "delta": d, "weight": w[i], **metrics(v)})  # record metrics
oat = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # OAT results table
oat.pivot(index="delta", columns="criterion", values="jaccard_top10").round(3)  # Jaccard by delta

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Monte Carlo weight simulation (Dirichlet)

Why a Dirichlet distribution?
Weights must be positive and sum to 1. Drawing each weight independently and then normalizing gives poorly controlled distributions. The Dirichlet distribution samples directly on this space (the simplex). With concentration parameters \(\alpha_i = \kappa \, w_i^{(0)}\):

the mean weight vector equals the baseline \(w^{(0)}\), and
the concentration κ controls the spread. A small κ represents wide disagreement about the weights, and a large κ represents near-consensus.

For a weight with mean w, the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{w(1-w)/(\kappa+1)}\).


Code
# Visualise Dirichlet weight samples at three concentrations (kappa).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.8), sharey=True)  # three kappa panels
for ax, kappa in zip(axes, [10, 50, 200]):
    Ws = RNG.dirichlet(kappa * W0, 5000)  # sample weight vectors around W0
    ax.boxplot(Ws, tick_labels=[c.split()[0] for c in CRITERIA], showfliers=False)  # weight spreads
    ax.scatter(range(1, 5), W0, color="red", zorder=3, label="baseline")  # baseline markers
    sd = np.sqrt(W0 * (1 - W0) / (kappa + 1))  # analytic SD of Dirichlet margins
    ax.set_title(f"kappa = {kappa}  (SD of slope weight = {sd[0]:.3f})", fontsize=10)  # panel title
axes[0].set_ylabel("Sampled weight")  # shared y-label
axes[0].legend()  # baseline legend
plt.suptitle("Dirichlet weight samples: concentration kappa controls disagreement")  # figure title
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing
plt.show()  # render the figure













Running the simulation
The simulation uses N = 1,000 weight vectors with κ = 50, representing moderate disagreement (an SD of about 0.07 on the slope weight). Storing every simulated map would take about 800 MB, so statistics are accumulated in batches:

the running sum and sum of squares give the mean and SD of the score,
a count of top-10% membership gives the probability of being in the top 10%, and
the percentile rank of each cell in each run gives rank stability (mean and SD of rank).



Code
# Run Dirichlet Monte Carlo weight simulation (kappa=50, n=1000) on feasible cells.
t = time.time()  # start timer
mc = monte_carlo_weights(MF, W0, kappa=50, n=1000, batch=100, seed=1, top_q=TOPQ)  # MC results dict
print(f"1,000 simulations in {time.time() - t:.1f} s")  # elapsed time
print(f"Jaccard (top 10%) vs baseline: median {np.median(mc['jaccard']):.3f}, "
      f"5th-95th percentile {np.percentile(mc['jaccard'], 5):.3f}-{np.percentile(mc['jaccard'], 95):.3f}")  # summary




1,000 simulations in 6.7 s
Jaccard (top 10%) vs baseline: median 0.828, 5th-95th percentile 0.645-0.940




Uncertainty maps


Code
# Uncertainty maps from the Monte Carlo weight ensemble.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 12))  # four uncertainty panels
show(to_map(mc["mean"]), "Mean suitability (1,000 weight sets)", axes[0, 0], label="score")  # ensemble mean
show(to_map(mc["sd"]), "Standard deviation of suitability", axes[0, 1], cmap="magma_r",
     vmin=0, vmax=np.quantile(mc["sd"], 0.99), label="SD")  # score SD
show(to_map(mc["rank_sd"]), "Rank instability (SD of percentile rank)", axes[1, 0], cmap="magma_r",
     vmin=0, vmax=np.quantile(mc["rank_sd"], 0.99), label="percentile points")  # rank SD
show(to_map(mc["p_top"]), "Probability of being in the top 10%", axes[1, 1], cmap="viridis",
     vmin=0, vmax=1, label="P(top 10%)")  # selection probability
plt.tight_layout()  # tighten spacing

Robust, contested, and never-selected land
The probability map can be summarized in three classes that decision-makers can use directly:

Rule
Meaning

ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # legend and light grid
plt.show()  # render the figure

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Global sensitivity analysis with SALib
OAT and Monte Carlo show how much the result varies. Variance-based global sensitivity analysis shows which inputs cause the variation, including interactions, with all inputs varying together.

Inputs (factors) and their ranges








Factor
Range
Notes




imp_slope, imp_exposure, imp_tpi, imp_stream
baseline ± 50%
Importance factors, normalized to weights inside the model


slope_mid
3-5 %
Slope membership midpoint

0.15-0.50
Exposure membership value for east- or west-facing land


tpi_lo
-8 to -4 m
TPI value with membership 0


stream_mid
200-400 m
Stream-distance membership midpoint



Raw importance factors are sampled independently and then normalized. Sampling normalized weights directly would make them dependent, and the Sobol decomposition assumes independent inputs.


Model outputs

Y₁: Jaccard of the top 10% vs. the baseline, measuring how much the selection changes.
Y₂: mean score of the baseline top-10% cells, measuring how good the currently preferred land looks.

For speed, both outputs are computed on a fixed sample of 8,000 feasible cells.


Code
# Define an 8-factor SALib problem (4 weights + 4 membership parameters) on a feasible subsample.
from SALib.sample import sobol as sobol_sample, morris as morris_sample  # sampling designs
from SALib.analyze import sobol as sobol_analyze, morris as morris_analyze  # index estimators

FACTORS = ["imp_slope", "imp_exposure", "imp_tpi", "imp_stream",
           "slope_mid", "south_mu90", "tpi_lo", "stream_mid"]  # factor names
problem = {"num_vars": 8, "names": FACTORS,
           "bounds": [[0.5 * w, 1.5 * w] for w in W0] + [[3, 5], [0.15, 0.5], [-8, -4], [200, 400]]}  # factor bounds

SA_IDX = np.random.default_rng(3).choice(N_CELLS, 8000, replace=False)  # subsample for fast GSA
crit_s = {k: crit[k].ravel()[IDX][SA_IDX] for k in ("slope", "dev", "tpi", "dist")}  # criteria on subsample
base_s = BASE[SA_IDX]  # baseline scores on subsample
base_top_s = top_quantile_mask(base_s)  # baseline top-10% on subsample


def model(x):
    """Return (Jaccard of top-10%, mean score on baseline top-10%) for factor vector x."""
    w = np.asarray(x[:4]) / np.sum(x[:4])  # renormalise the four importance weights
    M = memberships(crit_s, *x[4:])  # rebuild memberships with perturbed params
    v = w @ M  # WLC scores on the subsample
    return jaccard_index(top_quantile_mask(v), base_top_s), v[base_top_s].mean()  # two outputs


print("Baseline check (should be 1.0 and the baseline mean):", model(list(W0) + list(PARAM0.values())))  # sanity




Baseline check (should be 1.0 and the baseline mean): (1.0, np.float64(0.9227860401470085))




Sobol indices

First-order index S1 is the share of output variance explained by a factor alone.
Total-order index ST is the share explained by a factor including all its interactions.
ST - S1 measures how much a factor acts through interactions.
ΣS1 < 1 means interactions matter.

With Saltelli sampling and calc_second_order=False, the model needs N × (D + 2) evaluations: 1,024 × 10 = 10,240 runs.


Code
# Estimate first-order and total Sobol indices for Jaccard and mean-score outputs.

Morris elementary effects (screening)
The Morris method is much cheaper, needing r × (D + 1) runs (here 100 × 9 = 900), and is often used to screen factors before a Sobol analysis:

μ* (mean absolute elementary effect) measures overall importance.
σ (standard deviation of the effects) measures non-linearity and interaction.

Factors near the origin can be fixed at their baseline values. Factors with high σ relative to μ* act non-linearly or through interactions.

Reading the global results.

Interactions dominate Y₁. For the Jaccard output, ΣS1 is only about 0.31, so most of the variance comes from interactions, and every ST is much larger than its S1. This is expected for a threshold-based output: whether a cell enters the top 10% depends on the combination of all inputs. For Y₂, the mean score of the preferred land, ΣS1 is about 0.94, so that output is almost additive.
The same leading factors from two methods. The TPI and exposure weights have the largest total effects, and Morris μ* ranks them first and second as well. Agreement between methods with different assumptions is strong evidence.
Influence is not the same as weight size. The TPI weight is the smallest baseline weight (0.15), yet it is the most influential factor. Its membership varies the most across the study area and is least correlated with the other criteria, so shifting its weight reorders cells the most. Criteria that are nearly uniform, such as slope on this gentle terrain, have little leverage however heavily they are weighted.
Transformation parameters matter too. The slope midpoint has a larger total effect than the slope or stream weights. Debates about suitability models tend to focus on weights, but where a membership function puts its midpoint can matter just as much.

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Data uncertainty

DEM error propagation
No DEM is exact. Vertical errors of a few meters are typical for 30-90 m national DEMs, and the error is usually spatially autocorrelated: neighboring cells tend to be wrong in the same direction. This matters because slope is computed from differences between neighbors:

Uncorrelated noise produces large spurious neighbor differences, which inflate slope and break up streams.
Correlated noise shifts neighbors together and has much less effect on slope.

The DEM is perturbed with Gaussian error fields (σ = 2 m), using both uncorrelated noise and noise with a correlation length of about 270 m (Gaussian-smoothed white noise rescaled to σ). The entire pipeline, including stream extraction, is re-run 20 times for each type, with the baseline weights.


Code
# DEM elevation-error Monte Carlo: uncorrelated vs spatially correlated noise (sigma = 2 m).
def error_field(shape, sigma_m, corr_cells, rng):
    """Gaussian elevation error field with optional spatial correlation (cells)."""
    e = rng.standard_normal(shape)  # white noise
    if corr_cells > 0:
        e = ndi.gaussian_filter(e, corr_cells)  # induce spatial correlation
    return e / e.std() * sigma_m  # scale to target RMSE (metres)


def run_full(dem, res=RES, w=W0):
    """Run the full terrain -> membership -> WLC pipeline on a DEM."""
    c = terrain_criteria(dem, res)  # derive criteria
    v = np.where(c["feasible"], wlc(memberships(c), w), np.nan)  # suitability map
    return v, c  # scores and criteria dict


def dem_error_mc(n=20, sigma=2.0, corr=0, seed=0):
    """Monte Carlo DEM error: return P(top 10%) map and summary stats."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # reproducible RNG
    ptop = np.zeros(DEM.shape); slope_med, feas, jac = [], [], []  # accumulators
    for _ in range(n):
        v, c = run_full(DEM + error_field(DEM.shape, sigma, corr, rng))  # perturb DEM and rescore
        thr = np.nanquantile(v, TOPQ)  # top-10% threshold for this realisation
        t_ = np.nan_to_num(v) >= thr  # top-10% mask
        ptop += t_  # accumulate selection counts
        jac.append(jaccard_index(t_, to_map(BASE_TOP.astype(float)) == 1))  # overlap with baseline top
        slope_med.append(np.nanmedian(c["slope"])); feas.append(c["feasible"].sum() * 0.0081)  # diagnostics
    return ptop / n, dict(median_slope=np.mean(slope_med), feasible_km2=np.mean(feas),
                          jaccard_mean=np.mean(jac), jaccard_min=np.min(jac))  # P(top) + stats


t = time.time()  # start timer
dem_res = {}  # store results by error model
for label, corr in [("Uncorrelated (sigma = 2 m)", 0), ("Correlated, ~270 m (sigma = 2 m)", 3)]:
    dem_res[label] = dem_error_mc(n=20, sigma=2.0, corr=corr, seed=corr)  # 20 realisations each
print(f"40 full-pipeline runs in {time.time() - t:.0f} s")  # elapsed time

tab = pd.DataFrame({k: v[1] for k, v in dem_res.items()}).T  # summary table
tab.loc["Baseline (no error)"] = [np.nanmedian(crit["slope"]), FEAS.sum() * 0.0081, 1.0, 1.0]  # reference row
tab.round(3)  # display

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6), layout="constrained")  # two error models
for ax, (k, (pt, _)) in zip(axes, dem_res.items()):
    im = show(np.where(FEAS, pt, np.nan), f"P(top 10%) under DEM error: {k}", ax, cmap="viridis")  # selection prob
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.6, label="P(top 10%)")  # shared colourbar
plt.show()  # render the figure











Uncorrelated noise of only 2 m raises the median slope by about 50% (1.8% to 2.7%) on this gentle terrain, because random neighbor differences of a few meters over 90 m create spurious slopes of several percent. The top-10% agreement with the error-free result drops to about 0.2, so most of the “best land” changes.
Correlated noise of the same magnitude is less damaging, with an agreement of about 0.44, but still substantial. The feasible area increases slightly under noise because the open-water rule fails: noise breaks up the perfectly flat reservoir surfaces, so they no longer qualify as water. An error model can reveal hidden weaknesses in other parts of the pipeline.
The practical implications are to know your DEM’s error structure, to smooth or filter noisy DEMs before deriving slope, and to report slope-based results with this uncertainty.


Raster resolution
The same analysis is repeated at 180, 270, and 450 m by block-averaging the DEM. Coarser cells smooth the terrain, which affects slope, TPI, and stream extraction. The stream threshold is kept constant in area (4 km²) and the TPI window in distance (about 1.35 km), so the only change is the cell size.


Code
# Aggregate the DEM to coarser resolutions and rescore suitability (scale effect).
from geolattice.spatial_analysis.multi_criteria_suitability_analysis import block_mean  # block averaging

res_maps, rows = {}, []  # suitability maps and summary rows by resolution
for f in [1, 2, 3, 5]:
    res = RES * f  # target cell size in metres
    d = DEM if f == 1 else block_mean(DEM, f)  # aggregate DEM by factor f
    v, c = run_full(d, res)  # full pipeline at this resolution
    up = np.kron(v, np.ones((f, f)))  # upsample scores back to the 90 m grid
    full = np.full(DEM.shape, np.nan)  # pad to original shape
    full[:up.shape[0], :up.shape[1]] = up  # place upsampled block
    res_maps[res] = full  # store map for plotting
    common = FEAS & ~np.isnan(full)  # cells comparable to baseline
    a = np.nan_to_num(full) >= np.nanquantile(full, TOPQ)  # top-10% at this resolution
    rows.append({"cell size (m)": res, "median slope (%)": np.nanmedian(c["slope"]),
                 "95th pct slope (%)": np.nanpercentile(c["slope"], 95),
                 "stream length (km)": c["streams"].sum() * res / 1000,
                 "feasible (km2)": c["feasible"].sum() * res * res / 1e6,
                 "Jaccard top10 vs 90 m": jaccard_index(a & common, to_map(BASE_TOP.astype(float)) == 1),
                 "Spearman vs 90 m": spearmanr(full.ravel()[IDX][SAMP], BASE[SAMP], nan_policy="omit")[0]})  # metrics
restab = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)  # resolution comparison table

# Map WLC suitability at each aggregated resolution (upsampled to 90 m for display).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 5.5), layout="constrained")  # one panel per resolution
for ax, (res, m) in zip(axes, res_maps.items()):

As cells get coarser, slopes flatten: the 95th-percentile slope falls from 5.3% at 90 m to 2.9% at 450 m. Total stream length stays similar, because the stream threshold is defined by area, but channel positions become coarser. The top-10% agreement with the 90 m result falls to about 0.4 at 180 m and 0.2 at 450 m, so a site that looks ideal at 450 m may contain steep gullies that a 90 m, or a 10 m, DEM would reveal. Cell size is therefore part of the model specification and should be chosen to match the size of the decision unit, here an array of tens to hundreds of hectares.


The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)
Results that are aggregated to zones depend on how the zones are drawn. This is the MAUP, which has two components:

the scale effect: changing zone size changes the result, and
the zoning effect: changing zone boundaries at the same size also changes the result.

To demonstrate both, the 90 m suitability is aggregated to square “planning blocks” (mean score per block, requiring at least 50% feasible land):

Scale: blocks of 1, 2.5, and 5 km.
Zoning: 2.5 km blocks with 16 different grid origins, shifted in 630 m steps in each direction.



Code
# Scale effect: mean suitability in 1 / 2.5 / 5 km blocks (modifiable areal unit).
SCORE = to_map(BASE)  # baseline suitability as a full raster


def zone_means(arr, size, dy=0, dx=0, min_frac=0.5):
    """Mean of arr in square zones of `size` cells, origin shifted by (dy, dx)."""
    rows_, cols_ = np.indices(arr.shape)  # row/col index grids
    zid = ((rows_ + dy) // size) * 10_000 + ((cols_ + dx) // size)  # zone ids
    ok = ~np.isnan(arr)  # valid cells
    df = pd.DataFrame({"z": zid.ravel(), "v": arr.ravel(), "ok": ok.ravel()})  # tidy table
    g = df.groupby("z").agg(mean=("v", "mean"), frac=("ok", "mean"))  # zone stats
    g.loc[g["frac"] < min_frac, "mean"] = np.nan  # drop mostly-empty zones
    return g["mean"].reindex(df["z"]).to_numpy().reshape(arr.shape)  # map-shaped zone means


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5.5), layout="constrained")  # three block sizes
scale_maps = {}  # store block-mean maps
for ax, km in zip(axes, [1, 2.5, 5]):
    size = int(round(km * 1000 / RES))  # block size in cells
    z = zone_means(SCORE, size)  # block-mean suitability
    scale_maps[km] = z  # store for later
    im = show(z, f"Scale effect: mean score in {km} km blocks", ax, alpha=0.9)  # map
    best = np.nanargmax(z)  # flattest index of the best block
    r_, c_ = np.unravel_index(best, z.shape)  # row/col of best block centre
    ax.plot(EXTENT[0] + (c_ + 0.5) * RES, EXTENT[3] - (r_ + 0.5) * RES, "*", color="magenta", ms=18,
            markeredgecolor="k")  # mark best block
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.6, label="block mean score")  # shared colourbar
plt.show()  # render the figure













Code
# Zoning effect: shift the 2.5 km block origin and track how the best block moves.
size = int(round(2500 / RES))  # 28 cells ~= 2.5 km
shifts = [(dy, dx) for dy in range(0, size, 7) for dx in range(0, size, 7)]  # 16 origin shifts
Z = np.stack([zone_means(SCORE, size, dy, dx) for dy, dx in shifts])  # (16, rows, cols)

zoning_range = np.nanmax(Z, 0) - np.nanmin(Z, 0)  # per-cell range of block means across zonings
best_pts = []  # best-block centres for each zoning
for z in Z:
    r_, c_ = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(z), z.shape)  # best block for this zoning
    best_pts.append((EXTENT[0] + (c_ + 0.5) * RES, EXTENT[3] - (r_ + 0.5) * RES))  # map coordinates

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6), layout="constrained")  # zoning comparison
show(Z[0], "2.5 km blocks: one of 16 zonings", axes[0], alpha=0.9, label="block mean score")  # example zoning
bx, by = zip(*best_pts)  # best-block coordinates
axes[1].imshow(HS, cmap="gray", extent=EXTENT)  # hillshade basemap
im = axes[1].imshow(np.where(FEAS, zoning_range, np.nan), cmap="magma_r", extent=EXTENT, alpha=0.85,
                    vmin=0, vmax=np.nanquantile(zoning_range, 0.99))  # zoning-range surface
axes[1].scatter(bx, by, marker="*", s=160, color="cyan", edgecolor="k", label="Best block in each zoning")  # stars
axes[1].set_title("Zoning effect: range of block mean across 16 zonings", fontsize=10)  # title
axes[1].set_axis_off(); axes[1].legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)  # legend
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.7, label="range of block mean")  # colourbar
plt.show()  # render the figure

print(f"Distinct locations of the 'best block' across 16 zonings: {len(set(best_pts))}")  # MAUP diagnostic
print(f"Median range of block mean at a cell: {np.nanmedian(zoning_range[FEAS]):.3f} "
      f"(baseline cell-level score SD: {BASE.std():.3f})")  # compare to cell SD











Distinct locations of the 'best block' across 16 zonings: 7
Median range of block mean at a cell: 0.105 (baseline cell-level score SD: 0.154)


The “best 2.5 km block” moves across the study area as the grid origin shifts, even though the underlying data never change. When suitability is reported for administrative units, parcels, or planning grids, the result is partly an artifact of the zone boundaries.
Ways to reduce the effect:

analyze at the native resolution and aggregate only for reporting,
use zones that are meaningful for the decision, such as actual parcels,
test several zonings, as done here, and
report zone results together with their within-zone variability.

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Deliverables

(a) Sensitivity ranking of the criteria
The evidence from every method is combined into one ranking. For each criterion, the following are collected:

OAT: the mean loss of top-10% agreement (1 - Jaccard) at ±20%,
Sobol ST on Y₁ for the criterion’s weight, and for weight and transformation parameter combined,
Morris μ* for the weight, and for weight and transformation parameter combined.

Each method’s scores are ranked, and the ranks are averaged.


Code
# Synthesise a cross-method sensitivity ranking of the four criteria.
crit_factor = {"Slope": ("imp_slope", "slope_mid"), "Exposure": ("imp_exposure", "south_mu90"),
               "Topographic position": ("imp_tpi", "tpi_lo"), "Stream distance": ("imp_stream", "stream_mid")}  # factor pairs
S1df = sobol["Y1 Jaccard top10"]  # Sobol table for Jaccard
mo = morris["mu_star"]  # Morris mu* series

rank_df = pd.DataFrame(index=CRITERIA)  # one row per criterion
rank_df["OAT: 1-Jaccard at +/-20%"] = [1 - oat[(oat["criterion"] == c) & (oat["delta"].abs() == 0.2)]["jaccard_top10"].mean()
                                    for c in CRITERIA]  # OAT sensitivity
rank_df["Sobol ST (weight)"] = [S1df.loc[crit_factor[c][0], "ST"] for c in CRITERIA]  # weight-only ST
rank_df["Sobol ST (weight + transform)"] = [S1df.loc[list(crit_factor[c]), "ST"].sum() for c in CRITERIA]  # combined ST
rank_df["Morris mu* (weight)"] = [mo[crit_factor[c][0]] for c in CRITERIA]  # weight-only mu*
rank_df["Morris mu* (weight + transform)"] = [mo[list(crit_factor[c])].sum() for c in CRITERIA]  # combined mu*

ranks = rank_df.rank(ascending=False)  # higher sensitivity -> better (lower) rank number? ascending=False means largest gets rank 1
rank_df["mean rank"] = ranks.mean(axis=1)  # average rank across methods
rank_df["SENSITIVITY RANK"] = rank_df["mean rank"].rank(method="min").astype(int)  # overall order
rank_df = rank_df.sort_values("SENSITIVITY RANK")  # most sensitive first
rank_df.to_csv(str(OUT_DIR / "criteria_sensitivity_ranking.csv"))  # export ranking
rank_df.round(3)  # display











OAT: 1-Jaccard at +/-20%
Sobol ST (weight)

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Reporting checklist
A credible suitability report should state:

The baseline inputs: weights, membership parameters, thresholds, and data sources with resolution and accuracy.
Local sensitivity (OAT): which weights change the selection, and by how much.
Weight uncertainty (Monte Carlo): the distribution used (here Dirichlet with κ = 50), the robust-core and contested maps, and site rank intervals.
Global sensitivity: Sobol and Morris rankings, including the transformation parameters.
Data uncertainty: the DEM error model and its effect, the resolution chosen and why, and MAUP checks for any zonal reporting.
A recommendation that reflects robustness. For this model, for example: “Site #10 ranks first in about 95% of plausible weightings, and Site #12 is in the top three in about 88%. Site #2 ranks anywhere from 1st to 10th depending on the weights, so its selection should be discussed with stakeholders. All site rankings assume an error-free DEM. Given its sensitivity to DEM noise, the top sites should be verified with higher-resolution elevation data.”

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Exercises

Repeat 9.3 with the fuzzy Gamma 0.8 model from Module 7 instead of WLC. Is the fuzzy model more or less weight-sensitive? (Use the weighted gamma operator from Module 8.)
Add slope_max (8-12%) and the stream threshold (2-8 km²) as Sobol factors. This requires re-running terrain_criteria, so use a smaller N, or compute the criteria once for a set of discrete levels.
Replace the Gaussian error model with σ = 1 m and σ = 4 m. Plot the median slope and top-10% Jaccard against σ.
Aggregate the 90 m suitability to real zones, such as Census block groups or parcels, and compare the ranking with 2.5 km blocks.
Run the κ analysis for a stakeholder group whose mean weights differ from the baseline (for example 0.2, 0.4, 0.1, 0.3). Map where the two groups’ robust cores overlap.

title: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of MCSM
text:
Key takeaways

Sensitivity analysis shows what drives the result, and uncertainty analysis shows how confident to be in it. Both are required for a credible decision.
OAT with proportional renormalization is a simple first check, but it is local and misses interactions.
Dirichlet Monte Carlo produces probability maps (P(top 10%)), rank stability measures, and robust versus contested land. Sites with tight rank intervals make defensible recommendations.
Sobol and Morris rank all inputs together. Membership parameters can matter as much as weights.
Data uncertainty is not secondary. DEM error, cell size, and zoning can change the answer as much as the weights do.

title: Geographic Embedding of Nodes and Edges
text:
Overview
A spatial network is a network whose nodes and edges are embedded in geographic space. Every node has coordinates, and edges usually have a physical form (road, pipe, river) or a cost that depends on distance (travel time, shipping cost, likelihood of a social tie).
This notebook uses geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis with the synthetic road network in Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/ to cover:

Node coordinates and CRS (lon/lat vs projected)
Edge lengths with haversine vs projected Euclidean distance
Graph ↔︎ GeoDataFrame conversion (OSMnx / NetworkX)
Spatial descriptors: circuity, Kansky α/β/γ, planarity
Spatially embedded random graphs (RGG, Waxman) and link-probability vs distance

text:
Part A: Nodes with coordinates
In NetworkX a node can carry any attribute. For a spatial network the essential ones are its coordinates and the CRS those coordinates are in. We start with a small network of New York cities in longitude/latitude (EPSG:4326).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Build a small New York city graph in lon/lat (EPSG:4326).
# Nodes store OSMnx-style x/y attributes; edges are unweighted until
# haversine lengths are attached in the next code cell.
# ===================================================================

# City names with longitude (x) and latitude (y) in WGS 84.
cities = pd.DataFrame({  # city names with lon/lat in WGS 84
    "city": ["Ithaca", "Syracuse", "Rochester", "Buffalo", "Albany", "Binghamton", "Elmira", "New York"],  # continue string literal
    "lon":  [-76.50, -76.15, -77.61, -78.88, -73.76, -75.92, -76.81, -74.01],  # degrees east
    "lat":  [ 42.44,  43.05,  43.16,  42.89,  42.65,  42.10,  42.09,  40.71],  # degrees north
})
# Undirected city-to-city links that define the toy transport graph.
links = [("Ithaca", "Syracuse"), ("Ithaca", "Binghamton"), ("Ithaca", "Elmira"),  # undirected city-to-city edges
         ("Ithaca", "Rochester"), ("Syracuse", "Rochester"), ("Rochester", "Buffalo"),  # continue multi-line call
         ("Syracuse", "Albany"), ("Binghamton", "Elmira"), ("Binghamton", "New York"),  # continue multi-line call
         ("Albany", "New York")]  # run this analysis or plotting step

# Empty undirected graph tagged with the geographic CRS of the coordinates.
G_ny = nx.Graph(crs="EPSG:4326")  # small New York city toy graph
# Add one node per city with OSMnx convention: x = lon, y = lat.
for r in cities.itertuples():  # iterate GeoDataFrame rows as named tuples
    G_ny.add_node(r.city, x=r.lon, y=r.lat)  # OSMnx convention: x = lon/easting, y = lat/northing
# Add the undirected edges listed above.
G_ny.add_edges_from(links)  # add graph elements
# Summarise the graph and inspect Ithaca's node attributes.
print(G_ny)  # status line for the notebook reader
G_ny.nodes["Ithaca"]  # notebook step



Graph with 8 nodes and 10 edges


{'x': -76.5, 'y': 42.44}



Edge lengths: never use Euclidean distance on degrees
One degree of longitude in New York is about 82 km, but one degree of latitude is about 111 km. Treating lon/lat as flat x/y therefore distorts distances. Two correct options:

Haversine (great-circle) distance directly on lon/lat.
Project to a metric CRS (e.g., UTM 18N) and use Euclidean distance.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Compare haversine, UTM Euclidean, and a naive degree*111 km shortcut.
# Haversine and UTM should agree; the naive shortcut overstates E-W spans.
# ===================================================================

# Edge lengths with geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis.haversine_km.
# Project city points to UTM 18N for a metric Euclidean comparison.
pts = gpd.GeoSeries(gpd.points_from_xy(cities.lon, cities.lat), crs="EPSG:4326").to_crs("EPSG:32618")  # projected city points for Euclidean km
proj = dict(zip(cities.city, pts))  # city name -> projected Point

rows = []  # accumulate one length comparison per edge
for u, v in G_ny.edges:  # iterate over the collection
    a, b = G_ny.nodes[u], G_ny.nodes[v]  # node attribute dicts with x/y
    hav = sna.haversine_km(a["x"], a["y"], b["x"], b["y"])  # great-circle km on lon/lat
    naive = np.hypot(a["x"] - b["x"], a["y"] - b["y"]) * 111.32  # degrees x 111 km shortcut
    utm = proj[u].distance(proj[v]) / 1000  # Euclidean km in UTM 18N
    G_ny.edges[u, v]["length_km"] = hav  # store haversine length on the edge
    rows.append({"edge": f"{u}-{v}", "haversine_km": hav, "utm_km": utm, "naive_deg_km": naive})  # append this record

# Round lengths for display and report the naive method's percent error.
dist = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1)  # haversine vs UTM vs naive length table
dist["naive_error_%"] = ((dist.naive_deg_km - dist.haversine_km) / dist.haversine_km * 100).round(1)  # run this analysis or plotting step

Drawing a graph in its true geographic position
nx.draw accepts a pos dictionary. Passing coordinates turns an abstract layout into a map.

# ===================================================================

# Left: force-directed spring layout (ignores geography).

    G_ny,  # notebook step
    nx.spring_layout(G_ny, seed=3),  # reproducible abstract layout
    ax=axes[0],  # draw into these axes
    with_labels=True,  # print city names on nodes

    G_ny,  # notebook step
    pos,  # geographic positions
    ax=axes[1],  # draw into these axes
    with_labels=True,  # print node labels on the graph

Same graph, two very different stories. The spring layout puts Ithaca in the middle because it has the highest degree; the geographic layout shows how stretched the Binghamton-New York connection really is.
Weighted shortest paths now respect real distances. An unweighted search cannot tell two equally short (in hops) routes apart:

# ===================================================================
# Elmira -> Albany: hop-count ties vs distance-weighted shortest path.
# Unweighted search cannot separate two equally short (in hops) routes.
# ===================================================================

# Print every unweighted shortest path and its total haversine length.
for p in nx.all_shortest_paths(G_ny, "Elmira", "Albany"):  # iterate over the collection
    hops = len(p) - 1  # number of edges on the path
    km = nx.path_weight(G_ny, p, "length_km")  # sum of haversine edge lengths
    print(f"{hops} hops: {' -> '.join(p):45s} {km:5.0f} km")  # status line for the notebook reader
# Distance-weighted shortest path (minimises length_km).
best = nx.shortest_path(G_ny, "Elmira", "Albany", weight="length_km")  # strategy with highest late-period adoption
print("Shortest by km:", " -> ".join(best))  # status line for the notebook reader

Part B: Edges with geometry: graphs ↔︎ GeoDataFrames
Real infrastructure edges are not straight lines. Each edge should carry a LineString whose length is the true travel distance. OSMnx standardises this representation:

section: Part C: Describing a spatial network
text:
Part C: Describing a spatial network

C1. Edge length and degree
Physical networks have bounded degree: you cannot fit 50 roads into one intersection. Compare this with the heavy-tailed degree distributions of social or web networks from Module 4.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Degree distribution and segment-length histogram for the road graph.
# Physical networks have bounded degree unlike many social graphs.
# ===================================================================

# Undirected view: one edge per road segment for descriptive stats.
Gu = ox.convert.to_undirected(G)  # undirected view for descriptive statistics
deg = pd.Series(dict(Gu.degree()))  # degree of every node
lengths = pd.Series([d["length"] for _, _, d in Gu.edges(data=True)])  # segment lengths (m)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))  # create a grid of subplot axes
# Left: how many nodes have each degree (bounded for street junctions).
deg.value_counts().sort_index().plot.bar(ax=axes[0], color="#6baed6")  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[0].set(title="Node degree (bounded)", xlabel="degree", ylabel="nodes")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
# Right: distribution of individual road-segment lengths in km.
axes[1].hist(lengths / 1000, bins=30, color="#fd8d3c")  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[1].set(title="Edge (segment) length", xlabel="km", ylabel="segments")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
# Print a one-line summary of degree and mean segment length.
print(f"mean degree {deg.mean():.2f}, max degree {deg.max()}, mean segment {lengths.mean()/1000:.2f} km")  # status line for the notebook reader










mean degree 3.23, max degree 6, mean segment 2.07 km




C2. Circuity (detour index)
Circuity = network distance ÷ straight-line distance. A value of 1.0 means a perfectly direct route; values of 1.2-1.4 are typical of real road networks. High circuity flags places where the network forces long detours (rivers without bridges, sparse rural grids).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Sample OD pairs and compare network distance with Euclidean distance.
# Circuity = network_km / euclid_km; median should sit around 1.2-1.4.
# ===================================================================

# Reproducible RNG for sampling origin-destination node pairs.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)  # reproducible random generator
node_ids = np.array(list(G.nodes))  # all junction ids as an array
pairs = rng.choice(node_ids, size=(400, 2))  # 400 random (o, d) draws
recs = []  # accumulate distance pairs for the scatter plots
for o, d in pairs:  # iterate over the collection
    if o == d:  # conditional branch
        continue  # skip degenerate same-node pairs
    # Shortest-path length along the road network (metres).
    network_len = nx.shortest_path_length(G, o, d, weight="length")  # network_len argument
    # Straight-line Euclidean distance in the projected CRS (metres).
    euc = np.hypot(G.nodes[o]["x"] - G.nodes[d]["x"], G.nodes[o]["y"] - G.nodes[d]["y"])  # euc argument
    recs.append({"euclid_km": euc / 1000, "network_km": network_len / 1000})  # append this record
circ = pd.DataFrame(recs)  # route circuity records
circ["circuity"] = circ.network_km / circ.euclid_km  # route detour index

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))  # create a grid of subplot axes
# Left: network km vs straight-line km (dashed line = circuity 1).
axes[0].scatter(circ.euclid_km, circ.network_km, s=8, alpha=0.5)  # scatter points on the axes
m = circ.euclid_km.max()  # axis limit for the 1:1 reference line
axes[0].plot([0, m], [0, m], "k--", lw=1, label="circuity = 1")  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
axes[0].set(xlabel="straight-line km", ylabel="network km", title="Network vs Euclidean distance")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
axes[0].legend()  # add a legend
# Right: circuity against trip length (short trips are more circuitous).
axes[1].scatter(circ.euclid_km, circ.circuity, s=8, alpha=0.5, color="#e6550d")  # scatter points on the axes
axes[1].set(xlabel="straight-line km", ylabel="circuity", title="Circuity falls with trip length")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
# Compare our route-level median with OSMnx edge-level circuity_avg.
print(  # status line for the notebook reader
    f"median circuity {circ.circuity.median():.3f}; OSMnx network-wide average: "  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"{ox.stats.circuity_avg(Gu):.3f}"  # run this analysis or plotting step
)










median circuity 1.266; OSMnx network-wide average: 1.016


Note the two numbers measure different things. Our route circuity compares origin-destination trips; OSMnx’s circuity_avg is edge circuity, the average bend of individual road segments (curved length ÷ chord length). Both are useful: edge circuity describes road geometry, route circuity describes how well the network connects places.
Short trips are the most circuitous because a single detour is large relative to the trip; long trips average out. This is a general property of grid-like networks and an important caveat when people use straight-line distance as a proxy for access (Section 03.06.4).


C3. Connectivity indices from transport geography
Three classic indices (Kansky, 1963) summarise how well-connected a planar network is, using \(v\) nodes, \(e\) edges and \(p\) connected components:

Beta \(\beta = e / v\): edges per node. Trees have \(\beta < 1\); meshed grids approach 2.
Alpha (meshedness) \(\alpha = (e - v + p) / (2v - 5)\): share of the maximum possible independent cycles in a planar graph (0 = tree, 1 = maximally meshed).
Gamma \(\gamma = e / [3(v - 2)]\): share of the maximum possible edges in a planar graph.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Kansky alpha / beta / gamma for the roads, a spanning tree, and a grid.
# The road network should sit between a tree and a perfect grid.
# ===================================================================

# Simple undirected graph required by the classic planar indices.
Gs = nx.Graph(Gu)  # simple undirected graph for planar indices
# Length-minimising spanning tree (no cycles; alpha near 0).
tree = nx.minimum_spanning_tree(Gs, weight="length")  # minimum spanning tree reference graph
# Dense planar reference: a 21x21 lattice.
full_grid = nx.grid_2d_graph(21, 21)  # dense planar grid for index comparison
# Side-by-side Kansky indices for the three graphs.
idx = pd.DataFrame({  # Kansky indices side-by-side
    "our road network": sna.kansky_indices(Gs),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    "its spanning tree": sna.kansky_indices(tree),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    "complete 21x21 grid": sna.kansky_indices(full_grid),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
}).T.round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

The road network sits between a tree (no redundancy at all) and a perfect grid. Removing about a fifth of local roads in the generator lowered meshedness, which means fewer alternative routes when a road is closed (Module 6 robustness ideas apply directly here).


C4. Planarity
A graph is planar if it can be drawn without edges crossing. Street networks are close to planar, but bridges and overpasses break planarity in real data, so planarity is a useful sanity check rather than a guarantee.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Planarity sanity checks on the road graph, city graph, and K5.
# Street networks are nearly planar; K5 is the classic non-planar case.
# ===================================================================

print("Road network planar?   ", nx.is_planar(Gs))  # synthetic roads should be planar
print("NY city network planar?", nx.is_planar(G_ny))  # small city graph is planar

title: Geographic Embedding of Nodes and Edges
section: Part D: Spatially embedded random graphs
text:
Part D: Spatially embedded random graphs
Generative models from Module 8 ignore space. Two classic models add it:

Random geometric graph (RGG): connect two nodes if they are within radius \(r\). Hard distance threshold.
Waxman graph: connect with probability \(p(d) = \beta\, e^{-d / (\alpha L)}\), where \(L\) is the maximum distance. Soft distance decay, allows occasional long links.

These are the null models for any relational network embedded in space, including the farmer advice network in 03.06.6.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Compare RGG, Waxman, and Erdos-Renyi embeddings with the same n.
# RGG uses a hard radius; Waxman soft distance decay; ER ignores space.
# ===================================================================

n = 300  # number of random nodes in the unit square
# Random positions shared by RGG and the ER comparison layout.
pos_rand = {i: tuple(p) for i, p in enumerate(np.random.default_rng(7).random((n, 2)))}  # random unit-square node positions
# Hard threshold: link nodes within radius 0.09.
rgg = nx.random_geometric_graph(n, radius=0.09, pos=pos_rand, seed=7)  # random geometric graph
# Soft decay: occasional long links allowed by the Waxman model.
wax = nx.waxman_graph(n, beta=0.6, alpha=0.06, domain=(0, 0, 1, 1), seed=7)  # Waxman distance-decay graph
wpos = nx.get_node_attributes(wax, "pos")  # Waxman stores its own positions
# Erdos-Renyi with the same edge count as the RGG (no spatial rule).
er = nx.gnm_random_graph(n, rgg.number_of_edges(), seed=7)  # Erdos-Renyi graph with matched edge count

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.3))  # create a grid of subplot axes
# Draw each generative model in geographic (or assigned) position.
for ax, g, p, title in [  # notebook step
    (axes[0], rgg, pos_rand, "Random geometric (r = 0.09)"),  # continue multi-line call
    (axes[1], wax, wpos, "Waxman (distance decay)"),  # continue multi-line call
    (axes[2], er, pos_rand, "Erdos-Renyi (no space)"),  # continue multi-line call
]:
    nx.draw(g, p, ax=ax, node_size=8, width=0.4, node_color="#3182bd", edge_color="#999")  # draw the NetworkX graph
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{g.number_of_edges()} edges")  # panel / map title
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook












Code
# ===================================================================
# Component summary for RGG, Waxman, and Erdos-Renyi (same edge budget).
# Expect higher clustering and longer paths under hard spatial thresholds.
# ===================================================================

pd.DataFrame({  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "RGG": sna.graph_component_summary(rgg),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    "Waxman": sna.graph_component_summary(wax),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    "Erdos-Renyi": sna.graph_component_summary(er),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
}).T.round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

Key lesson. A hard distance threshold (RGG) produces high clustering (your neighbours are close to each other, so they are also neighbours) and long path lengths (you can only hop a short distance at a time). The Erdős-Rényi graph with a similar number of edges has almost no clustering but short paths. The Waxman model’s few long links shorten paths, the same “small-world” effect we will exploit when seeding technology diffusion in 03.06.6.

Distance decay of link probability
Plotting the share of node pairs that are linked at each distance band reveals the distance-decay function, the signature of any spatial network.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Distance-decay curves: P(link) vs separation for each generative model.
# RGG drops at the radius; Waxman decays smoothly; ER is roughly flat.
# ===================================================================

bins = np.linspace(0, 0.6, 25)  # distance bands for the empirical P(link)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))  # create figure and primary axes
# Overlay link-probability curves for the three models.
for g, p, lab in [(rgg, pos_rand, "RGG"), (wax, wpos, "Waxman"), (er, pos_rand, "Erdos-Renyi")]:  # iterate over the collection
    sna.link_probability_by_distance(g, p, bins).plot(ax=ax, marker="o", ms=3, label=lab)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.set(  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    xlabel="distance between nodes",  # x-axis label
    ylabel="P(link)",  # y-axis label
    title="Distance-decay of link probability",  # plot or map title
    yscale="log",  # log scale highlights the decay shape
)
ax.legend()  # add a legend for mapped layers
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

title: Geographic Embedding of Nodes and Edges
text:
Summary
Helpers used here live in geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis (haversine_km, kansky_indices, graph_component_summary, link_probability_by_distance, load_road_graph). Tutorial data: Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/.

A spatial network = graph + coordinates + CRS + (often) edge geometries.
Compute lengths with haversine on lon/lat or project first; never use raw degrees.
OSMnx’s MultiDiGraph + graph_to_gdfs / graph_from_gdfs is the standard bridge between NetworkX and GeoPandas.
Spatial descriptors: bounded degree, circuity, alpha/beta/gamma, planarity, and the distance-decay curve.
Spatial embedding → high clustering, long paths; a few long-range links create small-world shortcuts.


Exercises

Add Plattsburgh (-73.45, 44.70) linked to Albany. How large is the naive-degree error on that north-south edge compared with east-west edges? Why?
Compute circuity separately for trips that start within 5 km of Centerville versus trips that start near the region’s edge. Which area is better served?
Delete all primary edges and recompute the alpha index and median circuity. What does the highway contribute?
Vary the Waxman alpha parameter (0.02 → 0.3) and plot average path length against average clustering.

Overview
Not every spatial network is downloaded ready-made. Often you start with a GeoDataFrame (census tracts, farms, monitoring stations, river lines) and must decide what counts as a connection. That choice defines neighbours in spatial regression, diffusion paths, and regions that clustering can form.

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
text:
Part A: Polygon contiguity networks

Rook: neighbours share an edge (a boundary segment of positive length).
Queen: neighbours share at least one point (edge or corner).

Queen therefore always has at least as many links as Rook. libpysal stores the result as a spatial weights object W; W.to_networkx() gives a graph whose nodes are row positions.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Queen and Rook contiguity weights on census tracts, then a NetworkX
# graph labelled by tract_id with centroids as geographic positions.
# ===================================================================

# Queen: share an edge or a corner; Rook: share a boundary segment only.
w_queen = weights.Queen.from_dataframe(tracts, use_index=False)  # Queen contiguity spatial weights
w_rook = weights.Rook.from_dataframe(tracts, use_index=False)  # Rook contiguity spatial weights
print(f"Queen: {w_queen.s0/2:.0f} links, mean neighbours {w_queen.mean_neighbors:.2f}, islands {w_queen.islands}")  # status line for the notebook reader
print(f"Rook : {w_rook.s0/2:.0f} links, mean neighbours {w_rook.mean_neighbors:.2f}, islands {w_rook.islands}")  # status line for the notebook reader

# Convert Queen weights to a NetworkX graph and label nodes by tract_id.
G_queen = w_queen.to_networkx()  # Queen contiguity NetworkX graph
nx.relabel_nodes(G_queen, dict(enumerate(tracts.tract_id)), copy=False)  # run this analysis or plotting step
# Geographic layout positions from tract centroids.
cent = tracts.geometry.centroid  # tract centroids (or related centre geometry)
pos = {tid: (p.x, p.y) for tid, p in zip(tracts.tract_id, cent)}  # node -> (x, y) layout dictionary



Queen: 271 links, mean neighbours 5.37, islands []
Rook : 271 links, mean neighbours 5.37, islands []




Code
# ===================================================================
# Map Queen contiguity edges over a population choropleth of tracts.
# ===================================================================

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))  # square figure for the contiguity map
tracts.plot(
    ax=ax,  # draw into the prepared axes
    column="population",  # choropleth attribute
    cmap="Blues",  # sequential colormap
    edgecolor="white",  # light tract boundaries
    lw=0.6,  # thin boundary lines
    legend=True,  # show colorbar
    legend_kwds={"label": "population", "shrink": 0.6},  # colorbar label and size
)
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G_queen, pos, ax=ax, edge_color="#d62728", width=0.8)  # contiguity links
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G_queen, pos, ax=ax, node_size=8, node_color="k")  # tract centroids
ax.set_title("Queen contiguity network over census tracts")  # map title
ax.set_axis_off()  # hide axes for a clean map
plt.show()  # render the figure









Why are Queen and Rook identical here? Our tracts are a Voronoi tessellation, where generically exactly three cells meet at every vertex, so any two cells that touch at a corner also share an edge. On regular grids (raster cells, many US county and township layouts) the two rules differ a lot:


Code
# ===================================================================
# On a regular square grid, Queen has more links than Rook (corners).
# Voronoi tracts above can make Queen and Rook identical.
# ===================================================================

from shapely.geometry import box  # axis-aligned unit squares

# Build a 6x6 lattice of unit squares.
grid = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[box(i, j, i + 1, j + 1) for i in range(6) for j in range(6)])  # regular square lattice for Queen vs Rook
print(  # status line for the notebook reader
    "6x6 square grid  -> Queen links:",  # continue string literal
    weights.Queen.from_dataframe(grid, use_index=False).s0 / 2,  # continue multi-line call
    "| Rook links:",  # continue string literal
    weights.Rook.from_dataframe(grid, use_index=False).s0 / 2,  # continue multi-line call
)



6x6 square grid  -> Queen links: 110.0 | Rook links: 60.0


Notice the uneven geometry: small, dense urban tracts near towns and large rural tracts at the edges. Contiguity networks inherit this, so a rural tract and an urban tract both have about six neighbours even though the rural neighbours are many kilometres away. Keep this in mind when interpreting path lengths on contiguity graphs (“number of boundaries crossed”, not distance).

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
text:
Part B: Point-based networks
For points (or polygon centroids) we need a rule based on distance or geometry.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Build several point/polygon neighbour rules and summarise each graph.
# Labels come from tract_id so graphs share a common node namespace.
# ===================================================================

xy = np.c_[cent.x, cent.y]  # centroid coordinates as an (n, 2) array
# Contiguity, k-NN, distance band, and classical proximity graphs.
nets = {  # dict of libpysal weights objects by neighbour rule
    "Queen contiguity": w_queen,  # continue string literal
    "Rook contiguity": w_rook,  # continue string literal
    "k-NN (k = 4)": weights.KNN.from_array(xy, k=4),  # continue multi-line call
    "Distance band (no islands)": weights.DistanceBand.from_array(  # continue multi-line call
        xy, threshold=weights.min_threshold_distance(xy), binary=True  # run this analysis or plotting step
    ),
    "Delaunay triangulation": weights.Delaunay(xy),  # continue multi-line call
    "Gabriel graph": weights.Gabriel(xy),  # continue multi-line call
    "Relative neighbourhood": weights.Relative_Neighborhood(xy),  # continue multi-line call
}

# Convert each libpysal W to a labelled NetworkX graph.
graphs = {k: sna.weights_to_graph(w, labels=list(tracts.tract_id)) for k, w in nets.items()}  # dict of labelled NetworkX graphs by neighbour rule

# Side-by-side spatial-graph descriptors (degree, components, etc.).

for ax, name in zip(  # continue multi-line call
    axes.flat,  # notebook step

plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










How to choose.

k-NN guarantees every unit has neighbours and adapts to density, but the relation is asymmetric before symmetrising and k is arbitrary.
Distance band has a physical meaning (“within 6.6 km”), but beware: min_threshold_distance only guarantees that every unit has at least one neighbour (no islands), not that the network is connected. Here it still leaves two components. And in uneven settlement patterns the threshold large enough to connect rural points links dense urban points to dozens of neighbours.
Delaunay → Gabriel → Relative neighbourhood form a nested hierarchy of increasingly sparse proximity graphs (RNG ⊆ Gabriel ⊆ Delaunay). They need no parameters and are planar, which makes them good stand-ins for “who can plausibly interact with whom” in the absence of real links.

Check the nesting directly:


Code
# ===================================================================
# Verify the nested proximity hierarchy: RNG ⊆ Gabriel ⊆ Delaunay.
# ===================================================================

# Undirected edge sets with sorted endpoint tuples for set comparison.
E = {  # edge-set dictionary for nesting checks
    k: {tuple(sorted(e)) for e in graphs[k].edges}  # run this analysis or plotting step
    for k in ["Delaunay triangulation", "Gabriel graph", "Relative neighbourhood"]  # notebook step
}
print("RNG ⊆ Gabriel  :", E["Relative neighbourhood"] <= E["Gabriel graph"])  # status line for the notebook reader
print("Gabriel ⊆ Delaunay:", E["Gabriel graph"] <= E["Delaunay triangulation"])  # status line for the notebook reader



RNG ⊆ Gabriel  : True
Gabriel ⊆ Delaunay: True

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
section: Part C: Choosing a distance threshold: the percolation curve
text:
Part C: Choosing a distance threshold: the percolation curve
For a distance-band network, plot the size of the largest connected component as the threshold grows. The curve shows a sharp percolation transition: below it the network is fragmented, above it almost everything joins one component. Here we use the 20 towns as nodes.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Percolation curve for town distance-band networks.
# Track largest-component share and mean degree as the threshold grows.
# ===================================================================

txy = np.c_[towns.geometry.x, towns.geometry.y]  # town coordinates (metres)
# Pairwise Euclidean distance matrix between towns.
D = np.hypot(txy[:, None, 0] - txy[None, :, 0], txy[:, None, 1] - txy[None, :, 1])  # pairwise distance matrix
thresholds = np.arange(2_000, 20_001, 500)  # metres
rows = []  # accumulate one record per edge / pair / scenario
for d in thresholds:  # iterate over the collection
    g = nx.from_numpy_array((D <= d) & (D > 0))  # undirected distance-band graph
    largest = len(max(nx.connected_components(g), key=len))  # nodes in giant component
    rows.append({  # append this record
        "km": d / 1000,  # continue string literal
        "largest component %": 100 * largest / len(towns),  # continue multi-line call
        "components": nx.number_connected_components(g),  # continue multi-line call
        "mean degree": 2 * g.number_of_edges() / len(towns),  # continue multi-line call
    })
perc = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # percolation curve table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))  # create figure and primary axes
ax.plot(perc.km, perc["largest component %"], marker="o", ms=3, label="largest component %")  # draw lines or edges on the axes
ax2 = ax.twinx()  # second y-axis for mean degree
ax2.plot(perc.km, perc["mean degree"], color="#e6550d", ls="--", label="mean degree")  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
first_full = perc.loc[perc["largest component %"] == 100, "km"].min()  # first fully connected km
ax.axvline(first_full, color="grey", ls=":")  # run this analysis or plotting step
ax.set(  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    xlabel="distance threshold (km)",  # x-axis label
    ylabel="% of towns in largest component",  # y-axis label
    title=f"Percolation curve: fully connected from {first_full:.1f} km",  # plot or map title
)
ax2.set_ylabel("mean degree", color="#e6550d")  # run this analysis or plotting step
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










A sensible threshold is often just above the transition: connected, but not so large that every town links to every other. Compare it with weights.min_threshold_distance, which is the smallest distance at which no town is isolated. For these towns the two nearly coincide; for the tract centroids in Part B they did not, which is why the percolation curve is the safer check.


Code
# ===================================================================
# min_threshold_distance: smallest radius with no isolated towns.
# Compare with the percolation transition from the previous cell.
# ===================================================================

print(f"min_threshold_distance for towns: {weights.min_threshold_distance(txy)/1000:.2f} km")  # status line for the notebook reader



min_threshold_distance for towns: 8.88 km

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
section: Part D: Using the network for spatial statistics
text:
Part D: Using the network for spatial statistics
A spatial weights matrix is a network, row-standardised so that each unit’s neighbour weights sum to 1. Two foundational quantities follow:

Spatial lag \(Wy\): the average value among a unit’s neighbours.
Moran’s I: correlation between \(y\) and its spatial lag, the standard measure of spatial autocorrelation.

\[I = \frac{n}{S_0}\frac{z^\top W z}{z^\top z}, \quad z = y - \bar y\]
We compute both directly with NumPy on the Queen network and test significance by randomly permuting values across tracts.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Moran's I for population, income, and pct_over65 on Queen weights.
# Significance from 999 random permutations of values across tracts.
# ===================================================================

# Adjacency matrix in tract_id order, then row-standardise to W.
W = nx.to_numpy_array(graphs["Queen contiguity"], nodelist=list(tracts.tract_id))  # adjacency matrix in tract_id order
Wr = sna.row_standardize(W)  # row-standardised spatial weights matrix

results = []  # collect index / scenario result rows
for var in ["population", "median_income", "pct_over65"]:  # iterate over the collection
    y = tracts[var].to_numpy(float)  # attribute vector aligned with W
    stats = sna.morans_i(y, Wr, permutations=999, seed=42)  # I, E[I], pseudo-p
    results.append({  # append this record
        "variable": var,  # continue string literal
        "Moran's I": stats["I"],  # continue string literal
        "E[I] under randomness": stats["E[I]"],  # continue string literal
        "pseudo p": stats["pseudo_p"],  # continue string literal
    })
pd.DataFrame(results).round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

# ===================================================================
# Moran scatterplot and map of the spatial lag of population.
# ===================================================================

# Spatial lag = average neighbour population under row-standardised W.
tracts["pop_lag"] = Wr @ tracts.population.to_numpy(float)  # run this analysis or plotting step
# Standardise y and Wy for the classic Moran scatterplot axes.
z = (tracts.population - tracts.population.mean()) / tracts.population.std()  # standardised attribute for Moran scatter
zl = (tracts.pop_lag - tracts.pop_lag.mean()) / tracts.pop_lag.std()  # standardised spatial lag

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4))  # create a grid of subplot axes
axes[0].scatter(z, zl, s=14)  # scatter points on the axes
b = np.polyfit(z, zl, 1)  # slope approximates Moran's I on z-scores
xs = np.linspace(z.min(), z.max(), 10)  # x grid for the fitted Moran line
axes[0].plot(xs, np.polyval(b, xs), "r-")  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
axes[0].axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.6)  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[0].axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.6)  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[0].set(xlabel="population (z)", ylabel="spatial lag of population (z)", title="Moran scatterplot")  # configure this subplot's labels or title

tracts.plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax=axes[1],  # draw into these axes
    column="pop_lag",  # attribute used for the choropleth
    cmap="Blues",  # colormap for continuous / categorical values
    legend=True,  # show a legend or colour bar
    edgecolor="white",  # polygon / marker edge colour
    lw=0.4,  # line width
    legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.7, "label": "mean neighbour population"},  # legend / colour-bar styling
)
axes[1].set_title("Spatial lag of population")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
axes[1].set_axis_off()  # configure this subplot's labels or title
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Population is strongly clustered (tracts near towns border other dense tracts). Income, simulated with only a weak link to population, shows little autocorrelation. Results depend on the network: try Exercise 2 to see how Moran’s I changes with k-NN or distance-band definitions.

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
section: Part E: Network measures on a contiguity graph
text:
Part E: Network measures on a contiguity graph

E1. Gateway tracts
Betweenness on a contiguity graph highlights tracts that sit between many others. They are natural candidates for monitoring in contagion problems, because anything spreading tract to tract is likely to pass through them.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Contiguity betweenness highlights gateway tracts on the Queen graph.
# ===================================================================

bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(graphs["Queen contiguity"])  # node betweenness
tracts["betweenness"] = tracts.tract_id.map(bc)  # run this analysis or plotting step

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))  # create figure and primary axes
tracts.plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax=ax,  # draw into these axes
    column="betweenness",  # attribute used for the choropleth
    cmap="magma_r",  # colormap for continuous / categorical values
    legend=True,  # show a legend or colour bar
    edgecolor="white",  # polygon / marker edge colour
    lw=0.4,  # line width
    legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6, "label": "betweenness"},  # legend / colour-bar styling
)
towns.plot(ax=ax, color="#1f77b4", markersize=10)  # towns for geographic context
ax.set_title("Gateway tracts (contiguity betweenness)")  # panel / map title
ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook












E2. Contiguous regions with community detection
Weight each contiguity link by similarity in the attributes of interest, then run Louvain. Because links exist only between neighbours, communities tend to be spatially contiguous regions (a lightweight alternative to dedicated regionalisation methods such as SKATER or max-p in spopt).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Similarity-weighted Queen edges + Louvain for contiguous regions.
# Edge weight decays with attribute distance (age share, income).
# ===================================================================

Gw = graphs["Queen contiguity"].copy()  # weighted contiguity graph for community detection
# Z-score the attributes used to measure neighbour similarity.
attrs = tracts.set_index("tract_id")[["pct_over65", "median_income"]]  # z-scored attributes for similarity weights
attrs = (attrs - attrs.mean()) / attrs.std()  # z-scored attributes for similarity weights
# Higher weight when neighbouring tracts have similar attributes.
for u, v in Gw.edges:  # iterate over the collection
    Gw.edges[u, v]["weight"] = np.exp(-np.linalg.norm(attrs.loc[u] - attrs.loc[v]))  # run this analysis or plotting step
# Louvain communities on the weighted contiguity graph.
comms = nx.community.louvain_communities(Gw, weight="weight", resolution=1.0, seed=7)  # Louvain communities / regions
tracts["region"] = tracts.tract_id.map({n: i for i, c in enumerate(comms) for n in c})  # run this analysis or plotting step
# Contiguity constraint check: each community should induce a connected subgraph.
contig = [nx.is_connected(Gw.subgraph(c)) for c in comms]  # whether each community is spatially connected
print(  # status line for the notebook reader
    f"{len(comms)} regions; all spatially contiguous: {all(contig)}; "  # run this analysis or plotting step
    f"modularity = {nx.community.modularity(Gw, comms, weight='weight'):.3f}"  # run this analysis or plotting step
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))  # create figure and primary axes
tracts.dissolve("region").reset_index().plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax=ax, column="region", cmap="tab20", edgecolor="k", lw=1.2, categorical=True  # draw into these axes
)
ax.set_title("Regions from similarity-weighted contiguity + Louvain")  # panel / map title
ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
# Region-level population sum and mean attribute profiles.
tracts.groupby("region")[["population", "pct_over65", "median_income"]].agg(  # continue multi-line call
    {"population": "sum", "pct_over65": "mean", "median_income": "mean"}  # notebook step
).round(1)  # run this analysis or plotting step

section: Part F: From a line layer to a routable graph
text:
Part F: From a line layer to a routable graph
Shapefiles of roads, rivers, pipelines or power lines are line GeoDataFrames without topology. A graph appears once we treat each line’s endpoints as nodes. Real data usually need snapping (rounding coordinates) so that lines that should meet actually share a node.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Treat road edges as a plain line GeoDataFrame and rebuild a graph
# by snapping shared endpoints (lines_to_graph).
# ===================================================================

# Pretend the road LineStrings came from a shapefile without topology.
lines = ox.graph_to_gdfs(sna.load_road_graph(DATA / "roads.graphml"), nodes=False).reset_index(drop=True)  # line GeoDataFrame treated as a shapefile
lines = lines[["highway", "geometry"]]  # pretend this came from a shapefile
print(type(lines), len(lines), "line features")  # status line for the notebook reader

# Snap endpoints within 1 m so lines that should meet share a node.
G_lines = sna.lines_to_graph(lines, snap=1.0)  # graph rebuilt from line endpoints
print(G_lines, "| components:", nx.number_connected_components(G_lines))  # status line for the notebook reader
# Sample shortest-path length between two arbitrary endpoints.
a, b = list(G_lines.nodes)[0], list(G_lines.nodes)[-1]  # run this analysis or plotting step
print(  # status line for the notebook reader
    f"shortest path between two endpoints: "  # continue string literal
    f"{nx.shortest_path_length(G_lines, a, b, weight='length')/1000:.1f} km"  # run this analysis or plotting step
)
