For production work, momepy.gdf_to_nx does the same with options for primal (intersections as nodes) and dual (streets as nodes) graphs, and momepy.nx_to_gdf returns to GeoDataFrames.

title: Building Networks from GeoPandas Data
text:
Summary

The connection rule is the model: contiguity, k-NN, distance band, and proximity graphs give very different networks from the same data.
libpysal W objects and NetworkX graphs convert freely (W.to_networkx(), weights.W.from_networkx).
Use a percolation curve or min_threshold_distance to pick distance thresholds defensibly.
Spatial lag and Moran’s I are network operations; betweenness and community detection on contiguity graphs give gateway areas and contiguous regions.
Line layers become graphs by joining shared endpoints, with snapping for messy data.


Exercises

Rebuild Part B with k = 2, 6, and 8. At what k does the k-NN graph become connected?
Recompute Moran’s I for pct_over65 with the k-NN (k = 4), distance-band and Gabriel networks. How sensitive is the conclusion?
Increase the Louvain resolution to 1.5 and 2.0. Do the regions remain contiguous?
Add random noise of ±3 m to line endpoints, then run lines_to_graph with snap=1 and snap=10. How many components does each produce?

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
text:
Overview
A flow network is a weighted, directed network where nodes are places and edge weights are volumes moving between them (commuters, migrants, freight, trade). Flow data are usually stored as an origin-destination (OD) matrix.
This notebook uses the synthetic commuting OD table in Data/00_shared/data_spatial_net/ with geolattice.spatial_analysis.network_analysis for symmetric flow graphs, gravity-model fit diagnostics, metapopulation SIR, and arrival times.
Topics:

OD table → directed weighted graph; in-/out-/net flows
Flow maps and distance decay
Gravity models (OLS vs PPML)
Dominant-flow hierarchy and Louvain functional regions
Metapopulation SIR on commuting flows

text:
Travel time between towns
Gravity models need a cost term. We compute fastest drive time on the road network (the same method as 03.06.2).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Attach network travel times and Euclidean km to every OD pair.
# Gravity models use minutes as the cost term.
# ===================================================================

G = sna.load_road_graph(DATA / "roads.graphml")  # road MultiDiGraph
G = sna.prepare_travel_times(  # impute speeds and edge travel times
    G,  # notebook step
    hwy_speeds={"residential": 50, "tertiary": 60, "secondary": 70, "primary": 90},  # fallback speeds by highway class
    minutes_attr=None,  # keep travel_time in seconds on edges
)
towns["node"] = sna.snap_points_to_nodes(towns, G)  # snap each town to a junction
# One Dijkstra per origin town -> seconds to every network node.
tt = {  # define tt
    o: nx.single_source_dijkstra_path_length(G, towns.loc[o, "node"], weight="travel_time")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    for o in towns.index  # notebook step
}
# OD travel time in minutes between snapped town nodes.
od["minutes"] = [tt[o][towns.loc[d, "node"]] / 60 for o, d in zip(od.origin, od.destination)]  # run this analysis or plotting step
# Straight-line km between town geometries (projected CRS).
od["km"] = [  # notebook step
    towns.loc[o, "geometry"].distance(towns.loc[d, "geometry"]) / 1000  # run this analysis or plotting step
    for o, d in zip(od.origin, od.destination)  # run this analysis or plotting step
]

    ylabel="origin",  # y-axis label
    title="Commuting OD matrix (log scale, sorted by population)",  # plot or map title
)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log(1 + commuters)", shrink=0.7)  # attach a colour bar
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
text:
Part B: Flow maps
Drawing all 380 flows produces a hairball. Two standard remedies: show only flows above a threshold (or the top n), and use curved arrows so A→B and B→A do not overlap.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Flow maps: top-n curved arrows, with and without Centerville.
# Filtering the hub reveals secondary commuting sub-systems.
# ===================================================================

def flow_map(ax, df, top=40, color="#08519c", title=""):
    """Draw the largest commuting flows as curved arrows on town locations."""
    sub = df.nlargest(top, "commuters")  # keep only the largest OD pairs
    wmax = sub.commuters.max()  # scale arrow size relative to the largest flow
    for r in sub.itertuples():  # iterate GeoDataFrame rows as named tuples
        p0, p1 = towns.loc[r.origin, "geometry"], towns.loc[r.destination, "geometry"]  # notebook step
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(  # add a shape / arrow patch to the axes
            (p0.x, p0.y), (p1.x, p1.y),  # continue multi-line call
            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.18",  # curve so A->B and B->A separate
            arrowstyle="-|>",  # arrow head style
            mutation_scale=8 + 10 * r.commuters / wmax,  # head size ~ volume
            lw=0.4 + 5 * r.commuters / wmax,  # stroke width ~ volume
            color=color,  # artist colour
            alpha=0.55,  # regularisation strength (0 = unpenalised PPML)
        ))
    # Town markers sized by population.
    ax.scatter(  # plot point markers
        towns.geometry.x, towns.geometry.y,  # notebook step
        s=towns.population / 250, color="#fd8d3c", edgecolor="k", zorder=3,  # marker size
    )
    for t, p in towns.geometry.items():  # iterate key/value pairs
        ax.annotate(t, (p.x, p.y), fontsize=6.5, xytext=(3, 3), textcoords="offset points")  # label a feature near its coordinates
    ax.set_title(title)  # panel / map title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # keep geographic proportions undistorted
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.8))  # create a grid of subplot axes
flow_map(axes[0], od, top=40, title="Top 40 commuting flows")  # run this analysis or plotting step
flow_map(  # continue multi-line call
    axes[1],  # notebook step
    od[(od.origin != "Centerville") & (od.destination != "Centerville")],  # continue multi-line call
    top=40,  # top argument
    color="#a50f15",  # artist colour
    title="Top 40 flows excluding Centerville (secondary structure)",  # plot or map title
)
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Removing the dominant node reveals secondary sub-systems: smaller towns exchange workers with nearby mid-sized centers. Filtering out a hub is a simple but powerful trick for any flow map.

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
section: Part C: Distance decay and gravity models
text:
Part C: Distance decay and gravity models
The gravity model of spatial interaction:
\[T_{ij} = k\, \frac{P_i^{\alpha} P_j^{\beta}}{f(c_{ij})}, \qquad f(c) = c^{\gamma}\ \text{(power)} \ \text{or}\ e^{\gamma c}\ \text{(exponential)}\]
Taking logs gives a linear model, but OLS on log flows has two well-known problems: it must drop zero flows, and it is biased under heteroskedasticity. Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) (Santos Silva & Tenreyro, 2006) keeps zeros and is the modern default for trade and migration flows.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Distance-decay scatters: raw flows vs mass-normalised flows.
# ===================================================================

od["Pi"] = od.origin.map(towns.population)  # origin population mass
od["Pj"] = od.destination.map(towns.population)  # destination population mass
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))  # create a grid of subplot axes
axes[0].scatter(od.minutes, od.commuters + 1, s=10, alpha=0.6)  # scatter points on the axes
axes[0].set(  # configure this subplot's labels or title
    xscale="log", yscale="log",  # xscale argument
    xlabel="travel time (min)", ylabel="commuters + 1", title="Raw distance decay",  # x-axis label
)
# Remove mass effects so the cost term's shape is easier to see.
od["norm"] = od.commuters / (od.Pi * od.Pj) * 1e6  # run this analysis or plotting step
axes[1].scatter(od.minutes, od.norm + 1e-3, s=10, alpha=0.6, color="#e6550d")  # scatter points on the axes
axes[1].set(  # configure this subplot's labels or title
    xscale="log", yscale="log",  # xscale argument
    xlabel="travel time (min)", ylabel="flow per (Pi*Pj) x 1e6",  # x-axis label
    title="Decay after removing mass effects",  # plot or map title
)
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook












Code
# ===================================================================
# Gravity coefficients: OLS on log flows (zeros dropped) vs PPML.
# PPML keeps zero flows and is the modern default for OD models.
# ===================================================================

X = np.c_[np.log(od.Pi), np.log(od.Pj), np.log(od.minutes)]  # design matrix
names = ["log P_origin (alpha)", "log P_dest (beta)", "log minutes (gamma)"]  # coefficient or town name labels

pos = od.commuters > 0  # OLS cannot take log of zero flows
ols = LinearRegression().fit(X[pos], np.log(od.commuters[pos]))  # OLS gravity fit on positive log flows
ppml = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000).fit(X, od.commuters)  # keep zeros

coef = pd.DataFrame(  # side-by-side gravity coefficients
    {  # notebook step
        "OLS (log flows, zeros dropped)": ols.coef_,  # continue multi-line call
        "PPML (Poisson, zeros kept)": ppml.coef_,  # continue multi-line call
    },
    index=names,  # index argument
)
print(f"OLS drops {(~pos).sum()} zero flows")  # status line for the notebook reader
coef.round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step



OLS drops 0 zero flows









OLS (log flows, zeros dropped)
PPML (Poisson, zeros kept)

0.946

Code
# ===================================================================
# Predicted vs observed flows for PPML and OLS gravity fits.
# ===================================================================

od["pred_ppml"] = ppml.predict(X)  # PPML predictions on the original scale
od["pred_ols"] = np.exp(ols.predict(X))  # exponentiate log-OLS predictions
print(  # status line for the notebook reader
    f"Fit (squared correlation, all pairs):  PPML {sna.pseudo_r2(od.commuters, od.pred_ppml):.3f}   "  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    f"OLS {sna.pseudo_r2(od.commuters, od.pred_ols):.3f}"  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 5))  # create figure and primary axes
ax.scatter(od.pred_ppml + 1, od.commuters + 1, s=10, alpha=0.6, label="PPML")  # plot point markers
ax.scatter(od.pred_ols + 1, od.commuters + 1, s=10, alpha=0.4, label="OLS", marker="x")  # plot point markers
lim = [1, od.commuters.max() * 1.5]  # axis limit or symmetric colour scale
ax.plot(lim, lim, "k--", lw=0.8)  # perfect-fit reference
ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel="predicted + 1", ylabel="observed + 1", title="Gravity model fit")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
ax.legend()  # add a legend for mapped layers
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook



Fit (squared correlation, all pairs):  PPML 0.998   OLS 0.994









The data were generated with exponents of roughly 0.75 (origin), 0.95 (destination) and -1.8 on (time + 5 minutes), so we can check how well each estimator recovers them. The fitted time exponent is flatter than -1.8 because we regress on log(time) rather than log(time + 5): a reminder that the functional form of the cost term matters. Residuals are informative too: pairs with far more commuters than the gravity model predicts point to connections the model does not capture (a shared employer, a fast highway, a cultural tie).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Largest positive residuals vs PPML: pairs with unexpectedly high flow.
# ===================================================================

od["resid_ratio"] = (od.commuters + 1) / (od.pred_ppml + 1)  # observed / predicted
od.sort_values("resid_ratio", ascending=False)[  # run this analysis or plotting step
    ["origin", "destination", "commuters", "pred_ppml", "minutes"]  # notebook step

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
section: Part D: Hierarchy and regions from flows
text:
Part D: Hierarchy and regions from flows

D1. Dominant-flow (Nystuen-Dacey) nodal regions
Each town sends its largest outflow to one destination. If that destination is larger than the town itself, the town is subordinate to it; otherwise the town is a central place. Following these links produces a tree (or forest) that reveals the urban hierarchy.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Nystuen-Dacey dominant-flow hierarchy among towns.
# Subordinate towns point to a larger destination that receives their
# largest outflow; sinks of that digraph are central places.
# ===================================================================

# Each origin's single largest outflow destination.
dom = od.loc[od.groupby("origin").commuters.idxmax(), ["origin", "destination", "commuters"]]  # each origin's single largest outflow
# Keep only links to a larger town (true dominant-flow subordination).
dom["dest_larger"] = dom.destination.map(towns.population) > dom.origin.map(towns.population)  # run this analysis or plotting step
T = nx.DiGraph()  # travel-time matrix or time budget
T.add_edges_from(dom.loc[dom.dest_larger, ["origin", "destination"]].itertuples(index=False))  # add graph elements
T.add_nodes_from(towns.index)  # add graph elements
centers = [n for n in T if T.out_degree(n) == 0]  # no dominant flow to a larger town
print("Central places (no dominant flow to a larger town):", centers)  # status line for the notebook reader

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))  # create figure and primary axes
posg = {t: (p.x, p.y) for t, p in towns.geometry.items()}  # geographic layout
nx.draw_networkx_edges(  # draw the NetworkX graph
    T, posg, ax=ax, arrowstyle="-|>", arrowsize=12, width=1.6, edge_color="#525252",  # notebook step
    connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.1",  # curve style so opposing arrows separate
)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(  # draw the NetworkX graph
    T, posg, ax=ax,  # notebook step
    node_size=towns.population.reindex(list(T)) / 150,  # hide or size junction markers
    node_color=["#e31a1c" if n in centers else "#fd8d3c" for n in T],  # NetworkX node colour
)
nx.draw_networkx_labels(T, posg, ax=ax, font_size=7)  # draw the NetworkX graph
ax.set_title("Nodal hierarchy from dominant commuting flows (red = central places)")  # panel / map title
ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook



Central places (no dominant flow to a larger town): ['Centerville']











D2. Functional regions with community detection
Community detection on the flow network finds groups of towns that exchange more workers among themselves than expected: functional regions (the logic behind US commuting zones and labor market areas). We symmetrise flows and compare two weightings:

Raw flows \(w_{ij} = T_{ij} + T_{ji}\).
Relative flows \(w_{ij} = (T_{ij} + T_{ji}) / \min(P_i, P_j)\), the normalisation used by Tolbert & Sizer (1996) to build US commuting zones. It asks how important the link is to the smaller place, which stops a dominant city from absorbing every region.



Code
# ===================================================================
# Louvain regions on symmetric flow graphs: raw vs relative flows.
# Relative normalisation down-weights links that are large only because
# both towns are large.
# ===================================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6.2))  # create a grid of subplot axes
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")  # categorical colormap for communities
for ax, norm in zip(axes, [False, True]):  # iterate paired sequences together
    U = sna.symmetric_flow_graph(od, normalise=norm)  # undirected flow weights
    comms = nx.community.louvain_communities(U, weight="weight", resolution=1.0, seed=3)  # comms argument
    lab = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(comms) for n in c}  # node -> community id
    Q = nx.community.modularity(U, comms, weight="weight")  # Q argument
    wmax = max(d["weight"] for _, _, d in U.edges(data=True))  # wmax argument
    # Draw only relatively strong links to reduce clutter.
    for u, v, d in U.edges(data=True):  # iterate over the collection
        if d["weight"] > 0.05 * wmax:  # conditional branch
            ax.plot(*zip(posg[u], posg[v]), color="#bdbdbd", lw=6 * d["weight"] / wmax, zorder=1)  # draw lines or edges on the axes
    ax.scatter(  # plot point markers
        [posg[n][0] for n in U], [posg[n][1] for n in U],  # notebook step
        s=towns.population.reindex(list(U)) / 150,  # marker size
        c=[cmap(lab[n]) for n in U], edgecolor="k", zorder=2,  # colour values or constant colour
    )
    for n in U:  # iterate over the collection
        ax.annotate(n, posg[n], fontsize=6.5, xytext=(3, 3), textcoords="offset points")  # label a feature near its coordinates
    ax.set_title(f"{'Relative' if norm else 'Raw'} flows: {len(comms)} regions, Q = {Q:.2f}")  # panel / map title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # keep geographic proportions undistorted
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks for a clean map
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Two lessons:

Low modularity is a finding, not a failure. This region is strongly monocentric, so almost every town is tied mainly to Centerville and no partition separates the flows cleanly. Report Q alongside any map of “functional regions”.
Normalisation changes the answer. Relative flows let smaller towns’ local ties count, producing geographically coherent western, central and eastern regions even though nothing in the algorithm knows the coordinates. Distance decay built into the flows makes regions compact; where a region is not compact, look for a corridor or a non-spatial tie.



D3. Flow-weighted centrality
Weighted PageRank on the commuting graph rewards towns that receive flows from towns that themselves receive flows: a measure of regional attraction that goes beyond raw inflow.


Code
# ===================================================================
# PageRank on the directed commuting graph vs raw inflow ranking.
# ===================================================================

pr = nx.pagerank(F, weight="commuters")  # importance via recursive inflow
cent = pd.DataFrame({  # tract centroids (or related centre geometry)
    "population": towns.population,  # continue string literal
    "inflow": flows.inflow,  # continue string literal
    "PageRank": pd.Series(pr),  # continue multi-line call
})
cent["inflow rank"] = cent.inflow.rank(ascending=False).astype(int)  # run this analysis or plotting step
cent["PageRank rank"] = cent.PageRank.rank(ascending=False).astype(int)  # run this analysis or plotting step
cent = cent.sort_values("PageRank", ascending=False)  # tract centroids (or related centre geometry)
cent.head(8).round(3)  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
section: Part E: Flows as pathways for contagion
text:
Part E: Flows as pathways for contagion
Commuting networks are among the strongest predictors of how infections spread between places. A metapopulation SIR model treats each town as a well-mixed population and couples towns through travel.
For town i, the force of infection combines local and imported contact:
\[\lambda_i = \beta \sum_j M_{ij} \frac{I_j}{N_j}, \qquad M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 - \sum_{k \ne i} m_{ik} & i = j \\ m_{ij} & i \ne j \end{cases}\]
where \(m_{ij}\) is the share of i’s residents’ contact time spent in j. We approximate it as 10% of the commuting share (commuters spend part of their day, and part of their contacts, at the destination). We seed one case in the peripheral town of Riverton and record the day each town’s prevalence first exceeds 1 in 10,000.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Metapopulation SIR on the commuting matrix, seeded in Riverton.
# Plot infection curves; highlight seed, Centerville, and Lakeview.
# ===================================================================

names_t = list(towns.index)  # stable town order for matrix axes
N = towns.population.reindex(names_t).values.astype(float)  # population vector
C = (  # square commuting matrix
    od.pivot(index="origin", columns="destination", values="commuters")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    .reindex(index=names_t, columns=names_t)  # run this analysis or plotting step
    .fillna(0)  # run this analysis or plotting step
    .values  # notebook step
)  # square commuting matrix aligned with names_t

seed = "Riverton"  # contagion / SIR seed place or farmer set
H = sna.metapopulation_sir(C, N, names_t.index(seed))  # prevalence over time by town
arr = sna.arrival_times(H, threshold=1e-4, index=names_t)  # first day above threshold

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))  # create figure and primary axes
for i, t in enumerate(names_t):  # iterate with a numeric index
    hl = t in (seed, "Centerville", "Lakeview")  # highlight a few towns
    ax.plot(H[:, i] * 100, lw=2.2 if hl else 0.6, color=None if hl else "#bdbdbd", label=t if hl else None)  # draw lines or edges on the axes
ax.set(xlabel="day", ylabel="% infected", title=f"Metapopulation SIR seeded in {seed}")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
ax.legend()  # add a legend for mapped layers
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook











Geography vs. network shortcuts
Because these commuting flows decay with distance, arrival time tracks geographic distance from the seed closely. Now add a long-range tie: 200 daily trips each way between Riverton and Lakeview, at opposite corners of the region (think of a large employer running a shuttle, or a regional school). Geographically nothing has changed.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Counterfactual: add a Riverton-Lakeview commuting shortcut and compare
# arrival times vs geographic distance (baseline vs shortcut).
# ===================================================================

C_short = C.copy()  # commuting matrix with the long-range shortcut
i, j = names_t.index("Riverton"), names_t.index("Lakeview")  # run this analysis or plotting step
C_short[i, j] += 200  # extra daily trips Riverton -> Lakeview
C_short[j, i] += 200  # and the return direction
arr_short = sna.arrival_times(  # arrival times with the shortcut added
    sna.metapopulation_sir(C_short, N, names_t.index(seed)),  # call a geolattice.network_analysis helper
    threshold=1e-4,  # distance-band threshold
    index=names_t,  # index argument
)

# Geographic km from the seed to every other town.
d_geo = pd.Series({  # geographic km from the seed town
    t: towns.loc[seed, "geometry"].distance(towns.loc[t, "geometry"]) / 1000 for t in names_t  # run this analysis or plotting step
})
res = pd.DataFrame({  # arrival-time comparison table
    "geo_km": d_geo,  # continue string literal
    "arrival (gravity flows)": arr,  # continue multi-line call
    "arrival (+ shortcut)": arr_short,  # continue multi-line call
}).drop(seed)  # seed has arrival day 0 by construction

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)  # create a grid of subplot axes
for ax, col in zip(axes, ["arrival (gravity flows)", "arrival (+ shortcut)"]):  # iterate paired sequences together
    r = np.corrcoef(res.geo_km, res[col])[0, 1]  # geo vs arrival correlation
    ax.scatter(  # plot point markers
        res.geo_km, res[col], s=25,  # notebook step
        c=np.where(res.index == "Lakeview", "#d62728", "#3182bd"),  # highlight Lakeview
    )
    ax.annotate(  # label a feature near its coordinates
        "Lakeview",  # continue string literal
        (res.loc["Lakeview", "geo_km"], res.loc["Lakeview", col]),  # continue multi-line call
        fontsize=8, color="#d62728",  # font size
        xytext=(-50, 5), textcoords="offset points",  # annotation text offset in points
    )
    ax.set(xlabel=f"geographic distance from {seed} (km)", title=f"{col}: r = {r:.2f}")  # set labels, title, or axis limits
axes[0].set_ylabel("arrival day (prevalence >= 1/10,000)")  # configure this subplot's labels or title
plt.tight_layout()  # reduce wasted whitespace between panels
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
res.sort_values("arrival (+ shortcut)").head(5)  # run this analysis or plotting step

One strong long-range tie moves Lakeview from the last town to be reached to the first, and the correlation between geography and arrival time collapses. The same mechanism explains why airline networks, not distance, govern international spread, and why Brockmann & Helbing (2013) proposed effective distance \(d_{ij} = 1 - \log P_{ij}\), built from the share \(P_{ij}\) of travel from i to j, as a better predictor of arrival time in global mobility networks (Exercise 3 tests it here).

title: Flow Networks: Commuting, Gravity, and Contagion
text:
Summary

OD tables become directed weighted graphs; in-, out-, and net flows separate employment centers from dormitory towns.
Flow maps need filtering (top n, removing dominant hubs) and curved arrows.
Gravity models quantify distance decay; prefer PPML over OLS on log flows.
Dominant flows reveal hierarchy; community detection reveals functional regions; PageRank measures attraction.
Flows are contagion pathways: with distance-decayed flows spread follows geography, but a few long-range ties break that link.


Exercises

Fit the gravity model with an exponential cost function (\(e^{\gamma t}\), i.e., use minutes instead of log minutes). Which fits better?
Add origin and destination fixed effects (dummy variables) to the PPML model, the “doubly constrained” gravity model. What happens to γ?
Compute Brockmann-Helbing effective distance from Riverton (shortest paths on \(1 - \log P_{ij}\)) with and without the shortcut. Does it predict arrival better than geography here? Why might it underperform when many parallel short-range paths carry the infection?
Download ACS county-to-county commuting flows for New York State and reproduce Parts A and D2.

title: Single-group segregation indices

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Overview
Single-group indices summarize how one group is distributed across spatial units relative to another group (or to everyone else) in a single number. They are the oldest and most cited segregation measures and still anchor most applied work in sociology, public health, and urban economics.
Buffalo is a good place to learn them. It has been one of the most segregated metropolitan areas in the United States for decades, with a Black population concentrated on the city’s East Side, east of Main Street, and a mostly white suburban ring. Its refugee resettlement since the 2000s has also brought fast growth of Asian and Hispanic populations.
Massey and Denton (1988) grouped segregation indices into five dimensions. This notebook covers the two that single-group indices measure most directly:








Dimension
Question
Indices here




Evenness
Are the two groups spread across tracts in the same proportions?
Dissimilarity \(D\), Gini \(G\)


Exposure
How much contact does a typical member of a group have with others?
Isolation \(xPx\), Exposure \(xPy\), Correlation ratio \(\eta^2\)



All functions come from geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation (seg). The notebook follows the PySAL segregation tutorial (Single-group indices), and Part G checks every value against PySAL itself.
Topics:

A worked toy example: computing \(D\) by hand
Evenness: dissimilarity, Gini, and the segregation curve
Exposure: isolation, exposure (interaction), and the correlation ratio
Pairwise contrasts vs. focal group against everyone else
Generalized spatial versions and the checkerboard problem
Validation against PySAL and the seg.compute() entry point

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo, imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation as seg, and loads the data.
Study area and data. The Buffalo-Cheektowaga metropolitan area: Erie and Niagara counties, New York (about 1.17 million people in 2020). Counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau decennial censuses of 2000, 2010, and 2020, by census tract, for five mutually exclusive groups:



Column
Census definition




white
Not Hispanic or Latino, White alone


black
Not Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American alone


hispanic
Hispanic or Latino (any race)


asian
Not Hispanic or Latino, Asian alone


other
Everyone else (other single races and two or more races)



Tract boundaries change between censuses. To compare years on the same units, the 2000 and 2010 counts have been moved onto the 323 tracts of 2020 with dasymetric interpolation weighted by 2020 housing units; notebook 03_07_07 shows how. Tracts with fewer than 100 residents (water, parks, the airport) are dropped. Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/make_buffalo_data.py rebuilds everything from the Census files in Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/.
Two map helpers keep every map in the same frame: add_context(ax) draws the county outlines, and metro_and_core(...) shows the whole metro area next to a 30 km window centred on the City of Buffalo, where most tracts are small.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

def metro_and_core(
    gdf, values, title="", cmap="RdBu_r", norm=None, vmin=None, vmax=None,
    label="", significant=None, axes=None,  # define label
):
    """Side-by-side metro-wide and city-window choropleths of the same values."""
    if axes is None:  # create defaults when the caller omitted them
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(  # run this analysis or plotting step
            1, 2, figsize=(13, 6.2),  # run this analysis or plotting step
            gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.25]},  # define gridspec_kw
            constrained_layout=True,  # define constrained_layout
        )
    else:
        fig = axes[0].figure  # figure handle
    g = gdf.assign(_v=np.asarray(values, dtype=float))  # attach plot column
    kw = dict(  # extra keyword arguments for compute()
        column="_v", cmap=cmap, norm=norm,  # define column
        vmin=None if norm else vmin, vmax=None if norm else vmax,  # define vmin
        edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2,  # define edgecolor
    )
    for ax, core in zip(axes, (False, True)):  # iterate paired sequences together
        g.plot(ax=ax, **kw)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
        if significant is not None:  # hatch tracts that fail significance
            # Hatch tracts that are not statistically significant.
            g[~np.asarray(significant)].plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
                ax=ax, facecolor="none", edgecolor="0.3", hatch="////", linewidth=0.2  # axes handle for drawing
            )

    axes[0].set_title(f"{title}\nBuffalo metro (Erie + Niagara)", fontsize=10)  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    axes[1].set_title("City of Buffalo and inner suburbs (star = City Hall)", fontsize=10)  # set labels, title, or axis limits

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Part A: The data
Each tract holds counts for five mutually exclusive groups. A single-group index uses two count columns: the focal group \(x_i\) and a comparison group \(y_i\) (or “everyone else”). The table gives the metro-wide shares, the baseline every index compares tracts against.

Two things stand out.

Where. Black residents are concentrated in a contiguous block of tracts on Buffalo’s East Side, north-east of City Hall and east of Main Street, with smaller concentrations in Niagara Falls and Lackawanna. A few isolated rural tracts with high shares most likely contain state correctional facilities, whose populations the census counts where they are held. Outside these places, most of the two counties’ tracts have very few Black residents.
Change. Between 2000 and 2020 the East Side core lightens at its edges and the Black population spreads north and east into neighbouring city tracts and inner suburbs such as Cheektowaga. Meanwhile the metro area’s composition shifts: the white share falls from 83% to 73%, the Hispanic share doubles, and the Asian share triples, largely through immigration and refugee resettlement. Unlike a fixed-composition example, both where people live and who lives in the region are changing, a distinction that matters again in notebook 03_07_07.

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Part B: A toy example
Before computing indices on the metro area, build intuition on a four-tract region where everything can be checked by hand. With \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) the counts of two groups in tract \(i\) and \(X\), \(Y\) their regional totals, the index of dissimilarity (Duncan and Duncan, 1955) is
\[D = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left| \frac{x_i}{X} - \frac{y_i}{Y} \right|.\]
It equals the share of either group that would have to move to another tract for every tract to have the regional composition.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part B: A toy example.
# Before computing indices on the metro area, build intuition on a four-tract region where everything
# ===================================================================

toy = pd.DataFrame({  # four-tract toy city for a by-hand D
    "tract": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    "x": [90, 80, 10, 20],
    "y": [10, 20, 90, 80],
})
X, Y = toy.x.sum(), toy.y.sum()  # run this analysis or plotting step
toy["x/X"] = toy.x / X  # group's share of its regional total
toy["y/Y"] = toy.y / Y  # group's share of its regional total
toy["|diff|"] = (toy["x/X"] - toy["y/Y"]).abs()  # group's share of its regional total
display(toy)  # show a rich table preview
D_hand = 0.5 * toy["|diff|"].sum()  # manual dissimilarity from the |diff| column
print(f"D by hand: {D_hand:.3f}   seg.dissimilarity: {seg.dissimilarity(toy, ['x', 'y']):.3f}")  # two-group dissimilarity index D

even = pd.DataFrame({"x": [50, 50, 50, 50], "y": [50, 50, 50, 50]})  # toy city with identical composition everywhere
apart = pd.DataFrame({"x": [100, 100, 0, 0], "y": [0, 0, 100, 100]})  # toy city with complete group separation
print(f"identical composition everywhere: D = {seg.dissimilarity(even, ['x', 'y']):.3f}")  # two-group dissimilarity index D
print(f"no tract shared by both groups:   D = {seg.dissimilarity(apart, ['x', 'y']):.3f}")  # two-group dissimilarity index D

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Part C: Evenness

C1. Dissimilarity and Gini
The segregation Gini (James and Taeuber, 1985) uses the same information as \(D\) but averages over every pair of tracts rather than taking a single maximum gap. With \(p_i = x_i / t_i\) the focal share in tract \(i\) (here \(t_i = x_i + y_i\)), and \(P\) the regional share,
\[G = \frac{\sum_i \sum_j t_i t_j \, |p_i - p_j|}{2 T^2 P (1-P)}.\]
seg.gini computes this through the Lorenz-curve trapezoid rule in \(O(n \log n)\) instead of the \(O(n^2)\) double sum. \(G \ge D\) always holds, because \(D\) is the largest vertical gap in the segregation curve while \(G\) is twice the area between that curve and the diagonal.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part C: Evenness.
# $D = 0.7$ means 70% of group *x* (or of *y*) would need to relocate. Note what $D$ ignores: it is
# ===================================================================

evenness = pd.DataFrame({  # D and Gini by year for the focal pair
    y: {"dissimilarity D": seg.dissimilarity(g, pair), "Gini G": seg.gini(g, pair)}  # two-group dissimilarity index D
    for y, g in tracts.items()  # loop over each year and its tract GeoDataFrame
}).T
evenness.round(3)  # round for readable display

C2. The segregation curve
Sort tracts by their focal share \(p_i\) and plot the cumulative share of the comparison group (horizontal) against the cumulative share of the focal group (vertical). Perfect evenness is the diagonal. \(D\) is the maximum vertical distance from the diagonal; \(G\) is twice the area between the curve and the diagonal.


Code
# ===================================================================
# C2. The segregation curve.
# Sort tracts by their focal share $p_i$ and plot the cumulative share of the comparison group
# ===================================================================

def segregation_curve(g, focal, other):
    p = g[focal] / (g[focal] + g[other])  # tract share of the focal group within the pair
    order = np.argsort(p.to_numpy())  # tracts sorted by focal-group share
    cx = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(g[other].to_numpy()[order]) / g[other].sum()]  # cum. share of the other group (segregation curve x)
    cy = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(g[focal].to_numpy()[order]) / g[focal].sum()]  # cum. share of the focal group (segregation curve y)
    return cx, cy  # return the computed result

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 5.4))  # create figure and axes
for y, col in zip(YEARS, ["#3f007d", "#807dba", "#bcbddc"]):  # loop over panel years  # iterate paired sequences together
    cx, cy = segregation_curve(tracts[y], "black", "white")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    ax.plot(cx, cy, color=col, lw=2, label=f"{y}  (D={evenness.loc[y, 'dissimilarity D']:.2f})")  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    k = np.argmax(np.abs(cx - cy))  # index of maximum vertical gap (links to D)
    ax.plot([cx[k], cx[k]], [cy[k], cx[k]], color=col, ls=":", lw=1.2)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="k", lw=0.8)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.set(xlabel="cumulative share of white residents", ylabel="cumulative share of Black residents",  # set labels, title, or axis limits
       title="Segregation curves, Buffalo metro (dotted = D)", aspect="equal")  # define title
ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Black-white dissimilarity is 0.77 in 2000 and 0.69 in 2020: in 2020 more than two thirds of Black (or white) residents would still have to move for every tract to match the metro composition. Values above 0.6 are conventionally called “high” (Massey and Denton, 1993), so Buffalo remains highly segregated despite a steady decline of about 0.04 to 0.05 per decade. The curves hug the horizontal axis on the left: a large share of white residents live in tracts with almost no Black residents.

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Part D: Exposure
Evenness asks whether proportions match. Exposure asks what a typical person’s neighbourhood looks like, so it depends on group sizes.

Isolation (Bell, 1954): the average focal-group share in the tract of a randomly chosen focal-group member, \(xPx = \sum_i \frac{x_i}{X}\frac{x_i}{t_i}\).
Exposure / interaction: the average share of group \(y\) in that tract, \(xPy = \sum_i \frac{x_i}{X}\frac{y_i}{t_i}\). It is asymmetric: \(xPy \ne yPx\) unless both groups are the same size.
Correlation ratio (Bell, 1954; White, 1986): isolation rescaled by the regional share \(P\), \(\eta^2 = \frac{xPx - P}{1 - P}\). Isolation can never drop below \(P\) (that is its value under perfect evenness), so \(\eta^2\) removes the group-size effect and runs from 0 to 1.

Here groups=ALL_GROUPS, so \(t_i\) is the full tract population.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: Exposure.
# Black-white dissimilarity is 0.77 in 2000 and 0.69 in 2020: in 2020 more than two thirds of Black
# ===================================================================

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for y, g in tracts.items():  # loop over each year and its tract GeoDataFrame
    for grp in ["black", "white", "hispanic", "asian"]:  # iterate over the collection
        rows.append({  # append this year/group record
            "year": y, "group": grp,  # field in the summary row
            "regional share P": composition.loc[y, f"{grp} share"],
            "isolation xPx": seg.isolation(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp),  # isolation (xPx) for the focal group
            "exposure to white": seg.exposure(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp, "white"),  # exposure of one group to another
            "exposure to Black": seg.exposure(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp, "black"),  # exposure of one group to another
            "correlation ratio": seg.correlation_ratio(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp),  # correlation ratio (eta-squared)
        })
exposure_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["group", "year"]).sort_index()  # isolation / exposure / eta2 by group and year

In 2020 the typical Black resident lives in a tract that is 45% Black, more than three times the metro share of 12.5%. Isolation has fallen from 0.59 in 2000, and the size-adjusted correlation ratio from 0.54 to 0.37.
White isolation (0.82) is high mainly because white residents are the large majority. Its decline tracks the falling white share; the correlation ratio shows the size-adjusted picture.
Asian residents move the other way. Their isolation more than triples (0.04 to 0.14) and their correlation ratio rises from 0.03 to 0.10: as the Asian population grows, newcomers settle in a limited set of neighbourhoods rather than spreading evenly.
Exposure is strongly asymmetric. The typical Black resident’s tract is 34% white, but the typical white resident’s tract is only 6% Black. The two numbers describe the same tracts from the two groups’ points of view, weighted by where each group lives.

title: Single-group segregation indices

Part E: Which comparison group?
“Segregation of group x” can mean x against one other group (a pairwise contrast) or x against everyone else. These answer different questions and can give very different numbers.

# ===================================================================

                     "G vs everyone else": seg.gini(g, [grp, "rest"])})  # segregation Gini index

The four groups follow different paths.

Black-white dissimilarity declines slowly and stays the highest pair.
Hispanic-Black falls fastest (0.64 to 0.46), and Hispanic segregation from everyone else drops from 0.49 to 0.35: Hispanic residents, historically concentrated on Buffalo’s West Side, are now spread more widely, including in East Side tracts.
Asian-white dissimilarity rises (0.50 to 0.59) while Asian-Black falls (0.70 to 0.50). Asian residents increasingly live in city neighbourhoods that also have Black residents, rather than in the mostly white suburbs.

A single “minority vs. rest” index would hide all of this. Notebook 03_07_02 handles the groups together.

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Part F: Spatial (generalized) single-group indices

F1. The checkerboard problem
Aspatial indices treat tracts as unrelated bins. White (1983) showed the consequence with a checkerboard: alternating all-Black and all-white squares and two solid halves give the same \(D = 1\), although a resident of the checkerboard lives one block from the other group.
The test below keeps every tract’s composition but shuffles which tract gets which composition (the “systematic” null used in notebook 03_07_05). Aspatial \(D\) does not change at all.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part F: Spatial (generalized) single-group indices.
# The four groups follow different paths.
# ===================================================================

g20 = tracts[2020]  # 2020 tracts GeoDataFrame
shuffled = g20.copy()  # same geography with reshuffled compositions
shuffled[ALL_GROUPS + ["total"]] = seg.systematic_null(g20[ALL_GROUPS + ["total"]].to_numpy(), n_sims=1,  # null: shuffle compositions across tracts
                                                       rng=np.random.default_rng(3))[0]  # reproducible random generator
print(f"D observed: {seg.dissimilarity(g20, pair):.4f}   D after shuffling tracts: {seg.dissimilarity(shuffled, pair):.4f}")  # two-group dissimilarity index D

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, gg, ttl in [(axes[0], g20, "observed 2020"), (axes[1], shuffled, "same tracts, compositions shuffled")]:  # iterate over the collection
    gg.assign(s=gg.black / gg.total).plot(column="s", cmap="Purples", vmin=0, vmax=0.9, ax=ax,  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
                                          edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2)  # define edgecolor
    add_context(ax, core=True); ax.set_title(ttl)  # county outlines and optional city zoom
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook



D observed: 0.6867   D after shuffling tracts: 0.6867











F2. Generalized spatial dissimilarity
The fix (Reardon and O’Sullivan, 2004) is to measure each tract’s composition over its local environment rather than its own boundary. A kernel neighbourhood pools counts from nearby tracts, weighted by distance, and the index is computed on those pooled counts:
\[\tilde{x}_i = x_i + \sum_j w_{ij}\, x_j, \qquad \tilde{D} = D(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}).\]
seg.kernel_weights builds the weights from tract centroids (bandwidth in metres) and Neighborhood.pooled_counts does the pooling. The small wrapper below gives a spatial version of any index in the package.


Code
# ===================================================================
# F2. Generalized spatial dissimilarity.
# The fix (Reardon and O'Sullivan, 2004) is to measure each tract's composition over its
# ===================================================================

def spatial_index(g, groups, index_fn, bandwidth, kernel="gaussian", **kw):  # aspatial index on kernel-pooled counts
    nb = seg.kernel_weights(g, bandwidth=bandwidth, kernel=kernel)  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights
    pooled = g.copy()  # tract table with kernel-pooled group counts
    pooled[groups] = nb.pooled_counts(g[groups].to_numpy(dtype=float))  # assign a derived column or cell
    return index_fn(pooled, groups, **kw)  # return the computed result

for gg, name in [(g20, "observed"), (shuffled, "shuffled")]:  # iterate over the collection
    print(f"{name:9s} aspatial D = {seg.dissimilarity(gg, pair):.3f}   "  # two-group dissimilarity index D
          f"spatial D (2 km Gaussian) = {spatial_index(gg, pair, seg.dissimilarity, 2000):.3f}")  # aspatial index on kernel-pooled counts



observed  aspatial D = 0.687   spatial D (2 km Gaussian) = 0.620
shuffled  aspatial D = 0.687   spatial D (2 km Gaussian) = 0.376


Shuffling tracts leaves aspatial \(D\) untouched, but spatial \(D\) drops from 0.62 to 0.38 once compositions are scattered. The observed spatial index is only a little below the aspatial one, because Buffalo’s Black neighbourhoods form one large contiguous area: pooling each tract with its neighbours mostly pools similar tracts. That is what “spatially segregated” means, and the aspatial index cannot see it.


F3. Sensitivity to bandwidth
The bandwidth is a modelling choice. Small bandwidths approach the aspatial index; very large ones pool much of the metro area and push every index toward zero. Plotting the index against bandwidth is a quick, informal scale profile (notebook 03_07_04 does this properly).


Code
# ===================================================================
# F3. Sensitivity to bandwidth.
# Shuffling tracts leaves aspatial $D$ untouched, but spatial $D$ drops from 0.62 to 0.38 once
# ===================================================================

bandwidths = [500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000, 12000]  # Gaussian bandwidths in metres
prof = pd.DataFrame({  # spatial D across kernel bandwidths
    y: [spatial_index(g, pair, seg.dissimilarity, b) for b in bandwidths] for y, g in tracts.items()  # aspatial index on kernel-pooled counts
}, index=bandwidths)
prof.loc[0] = [seg.dissimilarity(g, pair) for g in tracts.values()]  # two-group dissimilarity index D
prof = prof.sort_index()  # spatial D across kernel bandwidths

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))  # create figure and axes
for y, col in zip(YEARS, ["#3f007d", "#807dba", "#bcbddc"]):  # loop over panel years  # iterate paired sequences together
    ax.plot(prof.index / 1000, prof[y], marker="o", color=col, label=str(y))  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.set(xlabel="Gaussian kernel bandwidth (km); 0 = aspatial", ylabel="spatial dissimilarity",  # set labels, title, or axis limits
       title="Spatial D(Black, white) as the local environment widens")  # define title
ax.legend(); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

Part H: One entry point with confidence intervals
seg.compute() wraps every index behind one call and returns a SegregationResult. With ci=True it adds a spatial block bootstrap interval (tracts resampled in spatially contiguous blocks, so neighbouring tracts move together); notebook 03_07_06 explains why that matters.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part H: One entry point with confidence intervals.
# `seg.compute()` wraps every index behind one call and returns a `SegregationResult`. With
# ===================================================================

results = []  # list of CI records to stack into a table
for y, g in tracts.items():  # loop over each year and its tract GeoDataFrame
    for name, kw in [("dissimilarity", {}), ("gini", {}), ("isolation", {"group": "black"}),  # loop over index specifications
                     ("correlation_ratio", {"group": "black"})]:  # run this analysis or plotting step
        grp = pair if name in ("dissimilarity", "gini") else ALL_GROUPS  # focal demographic group
        r = seg.compute(g, index=name, groups=grp, ci=True, n_boot=299, n_blocks=30, seed=0, **kw)  # index with optional spatial-block bootstrap CI
        results.append({"year": y, "index": name, "value": r.value, "ci_lower": r.ci_lower, "ci_upper": r.ci_upper})  # append this year/group record
ci_tab = pd.DataFrame(results).set_index(["index", "year"]).sort_index()  # bootstrap CI table for key indices
print(seg.compute(tracts[2020], index="dissimilarity", groups=pair, ci=True, n_boot=299, n_blocks=30, seed=0).summary())  # index with optional spatial-block bootstrap CI

title: Single-group segregation indices
text:
Summary

Evenness (\(D\), \(G\)) compares the distribution of two groups across units. \(D\) is the share that would need to move; \(G\) averages over all pairs of units and is always at least \(D\).
Exposure (isolation, interaction, correlation ratio) describes the typical neighbourhood and depends on group size. Use \(\eta^2\) when comparing groups of different sizes.
The comparison group changes the answer. Report pairwise contrasts as well as “group vs. everyone else”.
Aspatial indices are blind to the arrangement of units (the checkerboard problem). Pooling counts over a kernel neighbourhood gives a generalized spatial index; check its sensitivity to bandwidth.
seg results match PySAL to floating-point precision, and seg.compute(..., ci=True) adds spatially aware uncertainty.

Next: 03_07_02 extends these ideas to all groups at once.
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Decennial Census 2000 (SF1 P004), 2010 (SF1 P5), 2020 (P.L. 94-171 P2); cartographic boundary files 2000, 2010, 2020.

title: Local measures of segregation
text:
Overview
Region-wide indices answer “how segregated is the Buffalo metro area?” with one number. Planners, health researchers, and housing agencies usually need the follow-up: where is it segregated, and are those places different from what chance alone would produce? Local measures give one value per tract, ready to map, much like LISA statistics do for spatial autocorrelation.
This notebook follows the PySAL segregation tutorial on local measures using geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation. Local measures use all five groups (ALL_GROUPS) so that each tract’s shares are computed from its full population.
Topics:

Location quotients and exposure deviations for each group
Local entropy and Simpson diversity
Each tract’s contribution to the dissimilarity index
Permutation significance with false-discovery-rate control
Spatially pooled (“generalized”) local measures
Local change between census years and export to causal models

title: Local measures of segregation
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo, imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation as seg, and loads the data.
Study area and data. The Buffalo-Cheektowaga metropolitan area: Erie and Niagara counties, New York (about 1.17 million people in 2020). Counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau decennial censuses of 2000, 2010, and 2020, by census tract, for five mutually exclusive groups:



Column
Census definition




white
Not Hispanic or Latino, White alone


black
Not Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American alone


hispanic
Hispanic or Latino (any race)


asian
Not Hispanic or Latino, Asian alone


other
Everyone else (other single races and two or more races)



Tract boundaries change between censuses. To compare years on the same units, the 2000 and 2010 counts have been moved onto the 323 tracts of 2020 with dasymetric interpolation weighted by 2020 housing units; notebook 03_07_07 shows how. Tracts with fewer than 100 residents (water, parks, the airport) are dropped. Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/make_buffalo_data.py rebuilds everything from the Census files in Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/.
Two map helpers keep every map in the same frame: add_context(ax) draws the county outlines, and metro_and_core(...) shows the whole metro area next to a 30 km window centred on the City of Buffalo, where most tracts are small.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup and warning control.
import warnings  # silence noisy third-party warnings during demos
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample data

# Third-party GIS / plotting / tabular stack used throughout the notebook.
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame I/O for tracts and counties
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for maps
import numpy as np  # array ops for shares, norms, and masks
import pandas as pd  # tabular display of composition and indices
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook

# Hide library warnings so the notebook output stays readable.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # run this analysis or plotting step

# ===================================================================
# Setup for Buffalo metro segregation demos.
# Import GeoLattice, point DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo,
# import segregation as seg, load the tract panel, and define map helpers.
# ===================================================================

# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.
import geolattice

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]
if not (ROOT / "Data").is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

# Buffalo metro sample data (Erie + Niagara tracts on a shared 2020 geography).
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "03_spatial_analysis" / "data_segregation" / "buffalo"  # define DATA

# Segregation indices, local measures, profiles, and inference helpers.
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import segregation as seg

# Compact figures with top/right spines removed for a cleaner look.
plt.rcParams.update(  # run this analysis or plotting step
    {"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}
)
GROUPS = ["white", "black", "hispanic", "asian"]  # main race/ethnicity count columns
ALL_GROUPS = GROUPS + ["other"]  # include residual other category in totals
YEARS = (2000, 2010, 2020)  # panel years available in the sample

# Panel on the 2020 tract geometry (2000 and 2010 interpolated onto it).
tracts = {  # define tracts
    2000: gpd.read_file(DATA / "tracts_2000_on2020.geojson"),  # 2000 counts on 2020 boundaries
    2010: gpd.read_file(DATA / "tracts_2010_on2020.geojson"),  # 2010 counts on 2020 boundaries
    2020: gpd.read_file(DATA / "tracts_2020.geojson"),  # native 2020 tracts
}
counties = gpd.read_file(DATA / "counties.geojson")  # Erie and Niagara outlines
CORE = (662_000, 4_738_000, 692_000, 4_768_000)  # 30 km window on the City of Buffalo (UTM 17N, m)
CITY_HALL = (673_249, 4_750_383)  # City Hall marker for the core window


def add_context(ax, core=False, labels=True):
    """Draw county boundaries and optionally zoom to the City of Buffalo window."""
    counties.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.25", lw=0.8)  # county outlines for context
    if core:  # apply the city-window zoom when requested
        ax.set_xlim(CORE[0], CORE[2])  # zoom to city window
        ax.set_ylim(CORE[1], CORE[3])  # run this analysis or plotting step
        ax.plot(*CITY_HALL, marker="*", color="k", ms=9, mec="white")  # City Hall star
    elif labels:
        for name, (x, y) in {  # iterate over the collection
            "Niagara Co.": (690_000, 4_790_000),  # run this analysis or plotting step
            "Erie Co.": (700_000, 4_715_000),  # run this analysis or plotting step
        }.items():  # run this analysis or plotting step
            ax.text(x, y, name, fontsize=8, color="0.25", ha="center")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    ax.set_axis_off()  # hide coordinate ticks on maps
    return ax  # return the computed result


def metro_and_core(
    gdf, values, title="", cmap="RdBu_r", norm=None, vmin=None, vmax=None,
    label="", significant=None, axes=None,  # define label
):
    """Side-by-side metro-wide and city-window choropleths of the same values."""
    if axes is None:  # create defaults when the caller omitted them
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(  # run this analysis or plotting step
            1, 2, figsize=(13, 6.2),  # run this analysis or plotting step
            gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.25]},  # define gridspec_kw
            constrained_layout=True,  # define constrained_layout
        )
    else:
        fig = axes[0].figure  # figure handle
    g = gdf.assign(_v=np.asarray(values, dtype=float))  # attach plot column
    kw = dict(  # extra keyword arguments for compute()
        column="_v", cmap=cmap, norm=norm,  # define column
        vmin=None if norm else vmin, vmax=None if norm else vmax,  # define vmin
        edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2,  # define edgecolor
    )
    for ax, core in zip(axes, (False, True)):  # iterate paired sequences together
        g.plot(ax=ax, **kw)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
        if significant is not None:  # hatch tracts that fail significance
            # Hatch tracts that are not statistically significant.
            g[~np.asarray(significant)].plot(  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
                ax=ax, facecolor="none", edgecolor="0.3", hatch="////", linewidth=0.2  # axes handle for drawing
            )
        add_context(ax, core=core)  # run this analysis or plotting step
    axes[0].set_title(f"{title}\nBuffalo metro (Erie + Niagara)", fontsize=10)  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    axes[1].set_title("City of Buffalo and inner suburbs (star = City Hall)", fontsize=10)  # set labels, title, or axis limits
    sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(  # mappable used to draw the colour bar
        cmap=cmap,  # define cmap
        norm=norm or plt.Normalize(  # matplotlib colour normalisation
            vmin if vmin is not None else np.nanmin(values),  # run this analysis or plotting step
            vmax if vmax is not None else np.nanmax(values),  # run this analysis or plotting step
        ),
    )
    fig.colorbar(sm, ax=list(axes), shrink=0.75, label=label)  # attach a colour bar to the figure
    return axes  # return the computed result


print("repo:", ROOT)  # run this analysis or plotting step
print("data:", DATA)  # run this analysis or plotting step
print("geopandas", gpd.__version__, "| CRS", tracts[2020].crs)  # run this analysis or plotting step
print({y: f"{len(g)} tracts, {g.total.sum():,.0f} people" for y, g in tracts.items()})  # run this analysis or plotting step

title: Local measures of segregation
text:
Part A: Location quotients
The location quotient compares a group’s share in a tract with its share in the region:
\[LQ_{ik} = \frac{p_{ik}}{P_k} = \frac{x_{ik}/t_i}{X_k/T}.\]
\(LQ > 1\): the group is over-represented in the tract; \(LQ < 1\): under-represented; \(LQ = 1\): the tract matches the metro area. Because it is a ratio, the LQ is unbounded above and becomes large for small groups, a point Part B returns to.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part A: Location quotients.
# The **location quotient** compares a group's share in a tract with its share in the region:
# ===================================================================

g = tracts[2020]  # working copy of one year's tracts
norm = plt.matplotlib.colors.TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=0, vcenter=1, vmax=6)  # define norm
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 5.4), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, grp in zip(axes, GROUPS):  # loop over demographic groups
    lq = seg.local_quotient(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp)  # define lq
    g.assign(lq=lq).plot(column="lq", cmap="RdBu_r", norm=norm, ax=ax, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    add_context(ax, core=True); ax.set_title(f"LQ {grp} (max {lq.max():.1f})")  # county outlines and optional city zoom
fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap="RdBu_r", norm=norm), ax=axes, shrink=0.75, label="location quotient (1 = metro average)")  # attach a colour bar to the figure
fig.suptitle("2020, City of Buffalo window: where each group is over- (red) and under-represented (blue)")  # run this analysis or plotting step
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook










Each group has its own geography in 2020:

White residents are over-represented almost everywhere outside the city core. Because they are 73% of the metro area, their LQ cannot exceed about 1.37, so the white map shows mainly where white residents are absent: the East Side.
Black residents are concentrated on the East Side, north-east of City Hall, with LQ up to 6.8, meaning tracts that are more than 80% Black.
Hispanic residents are concentrated on the West Side along the Niagara River north of downtown (LQ up to 10), with a second, weaker cluster in South Buffalo.
Asian residents form two separate clusters: north of the city around the University at Buffalo’s North Campus in Amherst, and in city neighbourhoods on the East and West Sides. The two clusters most likely reflect different migration streams, university and professional migration in the suburbs and refugee resettlement in the city.

title: Local measures of segregation
section: Part B: Exposure deviation and diversity
text:
Part B: Exposure deviation and diversity
The exposure deviation \(p_{ik} - P_k\) carries the same information as the LQ on an additive scale. It stays bounded in \([-1, 1]\), so it behaves better for small groups: a tract that is 17% Asian in a metro area that is 4% Asian has \(LQ \approx 4\), but a deviation of only 0.13.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part B: Exposure deviation and diversity.
# Each group has its own geography in 2020:
# ===================================================================

summary = []  # define summary
for grp in GROUPS:  # loop over demographic groups
    lq = seg.local_quotient(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp)  # define lq
    dev = seg.local_exposure_deviation(g, ALL_GROUPS, grp)  # define dev

section: Part C: Where does dissimilarity come from?
text:
Part C: Where does dissimilarity come from?
Because \(D = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i |x_i/X - y_i/Y|\) is a sum over tracts, each tract’s term is its contribution to the metro-wide index. seg.local_dissimilarity_contribution returns these terms (the focal group is groups[0]), and they add back to \(D\) exactly.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part C: Where does dissimilarity come from?.
# Because $D = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i |x_i/X - y_i/Y|$ is a sum over tracts, each tract's term is its
# ===================================================================

pair = ["black", "white"]  # focal two-group pairing for D / Gini
contrib = {y: seg.local_dissimilarity_contribution(gg, pair) for y, gg in tracts.items()}  # define contrib
for y, c in contrib.items():  # iterate key/value pairs
    s_ = np.sort(c)[::-1]  # define s_
    print(f"{y}: sum of contributions = {c.sum():.6f}   D = {seg.dissimilarity(tracts[y], pair):.6f}   "  # two-group dissimilarity index D
          f"{np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(s_) / s_.sum(), 0.5) + 1} tracts make half of D")  # run this analysis or plotting step

metro_and_core(g, contrib[2020], title="2020: each tract's share of D(Black, white)", cmap="Reds",  # side-by-side metro and city-window choropleths  # run this analysis or plotting step
               vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(contrib[2020], 99), label="contribution to D")  # define vmin
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))  # create figure and axes
for y, col in zip(YEARS, ["#3f007d", "#807dba", "#bcbddc"]):  # loop over panel years  # iterate paired sequences together
    s_ = np.sort(contrib[y])[::-1]  # define s_
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, len(s_) + 1), np.cumsum(s_) / s_.sum(), color=col, lw=2, label=str(y))  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=0.8)  # run this analysis or plotting step
ax.set(xlabel="number of tracts (largest contribution first)", ylabel="cumulative share of D",  # set labels, title, or axis limits
       title="How many tracts produce half of D?")  # define title
ax.legend(); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

2010: sum of contributions = 0.729950   D = 0.729950   66 tracts make half of D
2020: sum of contributions = 0.686749   D = 0.686749   68 tracts make half of D
















The largest single contributions come from the East Side core, where each tract’s Black share is far from the metro value; they produce the steep start of the curve. A long tail of suburban tracts each adds a little. The number of tracts needed for half of \(D\) rises from 59 to 68 between 2000 and 2020: the dissimilarity that remains is spread over more tracts as the Black population disperses beyond the East Side core.

title: Local measures of segregation
section: Part D: Is a local value more extreme than chance?
text:
Part D: Is a local value more extreme than chance?
Every tract has a finite population, so even in a perfectly integrated metro area some tracts would show \(LQ \neq 1\) by chance. seg.local_significance tests each tract against an evenness null:

Keep each tract’s total \(t_i\).
Redraw its group counts from a multinomial with the metro proportions \(P_k\) (999 times).
Compare the observed statistic with that tract’s simulated distribution (pseudo p-value).
Apply the Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all 323 tests.

Step 4 matters. At \(\alpha = 0.05\) about 5% of tracts would be “significant” by chance alone without a correction, the same multiple-testing problem that LISA cluster maps face.

D1. Choose a statistic centred on zero
With alternative="two-sided" the test counts a simulation as “at least as extreme” when \(|\text{null}| \ge |\text{observed}|\). That is correct for a statistic centred on 0, such as the exposure deviation \(p_{ik} - P_k\). The LQ is centred on 1 and always positive, so a two-sided test on the LQ can only ever flag over-representation. The cell shows the consequence.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: Is a local value more extreme than chance?.
# The largest single contributions come from the East Side core, where each tract's Black share is
# ===================================================================

lq_test = seg.local_significance(g, ALL_GROUPS, seg.local_quotient, group="black", permutations=999, seed=42)  # define lq_test
dev_test = seg.local_significance(g, ALL_GROUPS, seg.local_exposure_deviation, group="black", permutations=999, seed=42)  # define dev_test
pd.DataFrame({  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "LQ, two-sided": {"over-represented (sig.)": int((lq_test.significant_fdr & (lq_test.statistic > 1)).sum()),  # run this analysis or plotting step
                      "under-represented (sig.)": int((lq_test.significant_fdr & (lq_test.statistic < 1)).sum())},  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "deviation, two-sided": {"over-represented (sig.)": int((dev_test.significant_fdr & (dev_test.statistic > 0)).sum()),  # run this analysis or plotting step
                             "under-represented (sig.)": int((dev_test.significant_fdr & (dev_test.statistic < 0)).sum())},  # run this analysis or plotting step
})

Two safe options: test the deviation two-sided (used below), or test the LQ twice with alternative="greater" and alternative="less".


D2. Significance in each year

Almost every tract is significant in every year, and about two thirds of significant tracts are ones where Black residents are under-represented, mostly the suburban ring. With a median of about 3,400 residents per tract, a random draw almost never strays more than a few percentage points from the metro share, so even moderate real differences are detectable. Only a handful of tracts, mostly in the transition zone around the East Side, are indistinguishable from the metro average. Statistical significance says a tract is not a random draw of the metro population; the magnitude of the deviation says whether the difference matters. Report both.

What the evenness null does and does not test. It asks whether the tract differs from a random draw of residents. It does not ask whether the spatial pattern of tracts is unusual; for that, use the systematic or spatially constrained nulls in notebook 03_07_05.

title: Local measures of segregation
section: Part E: Spatially pooled local measures
text:
Part E: Spatially pooled local measures
A tract boundary is an administrative line. Residents experience the surrounding area too. Passing a Neighborhood to any local function pools counts from nearby tracts before computing the statistic:
\[\tilde{x}_{ik} = x_{ik} + \sum_j w_{ij}\,x_{jk}\quad\text{(weights row-standardized)}.\]
seg.kernel_weights uses a distance-decay kernel; seg.knn_weights uses the \(k\) nearest tracts.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part E: Spatially pooled local measures.
# Significance maps for the four groups side by side show the structure behind the indices.
# ===================================================================

neighbourhoods = {  # define neighbourhoods
    "own tract": None,
    "k = 6 nearest": seg.knn_weights(g, k=6),  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "Gaussian 1 km": seg.kernel_weights(g, bandwidth=1000),  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights
    "Gaussian 3 km": seg.kernel_weights(g, bandwidth=3000),  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 5.4), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
norm = plt.matplotlib.colors.TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=0, vcenter=1, vmax=7)  # define norm
rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for ax, (name, nb) in zip(axes, neighbourhoods.items()):  # pair each axis with a year or layer
    lq = seg.local_quotient(g, ALL_GROUPS, "black", neighborhood=nb)  # define lq

title: Local measures of segregation
text:
Summary

Location quotients and exposure deviations show where each group is over- or under-represented. The LQ is relative and large for small groups; the deviation is bounded.
Local entropy summarizes all groups; low values flag single-group tracts, in Buffalo both the suburban ring and the East Side core.
Dissimilarity contributions add up to \(D\) exactly, showing which tracts produce the metro-wide index.
Permutation tests with FDR correction separate real local concentration from small-number noise. Correct for running one test per tract, use a zero-centred statistic (or two one-sided tests) for two-sided questions, and report magnitudes next to significance.
Pooled local measures describe the residential environment rather than the tract, and the choice of neighbourhood changes the map.
Local measures on shared boundaries can be differenced across years and exported as a tract-by-year panel for modelling.

Next: 03_07_04 turns the neighbourhood size itself into the object of study with multiscale segregation profiles.

title: Null models and simulation for segregation

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
text:
Overview
A segregation index is only interpretable against a reference: what value would the index take if residents were not sorting by group? That reference is a null model, and simulating it answers three practical questions:

Bias. Even in a metro area where residents choose tracts at random, finite tract populations produce some unevenness. How large is that baseline?
Significance. Is the observed index larger than chance would produce?
Spatial pattern. Given the set of tract compositions, does their arrangement on the map matter?

Each question needs a different null. geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation.null provides three, all returning a stack of simulated count tables of shape (n_sims, n_units, n_groups). This notebook follows the PySAL tutorial on simulating population groups distributed randomly in space, applied to Buffalo’s census tracts.









Null
What is kept
What is randomized
Tests




evenness_null
each tract’s total population
group membership of every resident (multinomial with metro shares)
whether tracts differ from random draws (bias, aspatial significance)


systematic_null
the exact set of tract compositions
which tract gets which composition
whether the spatial arrangement matters


spatially_constrained_null
the set of compositions within each spatial block
which tract gets which composition, only within its block
whether fine-scale arrangement matters, given the large-scale pattern



Topics:

Small-unit bias of the dissimilarity index
Simulated “even” metro areas and bias-corrected indices
Shuffling tracts across space
Spatial blocks and constrained shuffles
Choosing the right null for the question

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
text:
Setup
The next cell finds the repository root, puts it on the import path, points DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo, imports geolattice.spatial_analysis.segregation as seg, and loads the data.
Study area and data. The Buffalo-Cheektowaga metropolitan area: Erie and Niagara counties, New York (about 1.17 million people in 2020). Counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau decennial censuses of 2000, 2010, and 2020, by census tract, for five mutually exclusive groups:



Column
Census definition




white
Not Hispanic or Latino, White alone


black
Not Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American alone


hispanic
Hispanic or Latino (any race)


asian
Not Hispanic or Latino, Asian alone


other
Everyone else (other single races and two or more races)



Tract boundaries change between censuses. To compare years on the same units, the 2000 and 2010 counts have been moved onto the 323 tracts of 2020 with dasymetric interpolation weighted by 2020 housing units; notebook 03_07_07 shows how. Tracts with fewer than 100 residents (water, parks, the airport) are dropped. Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/make_buffalo_data.py rebuilds everything from the Census files in Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/.
Two map helpers keep every map in the same frame: add_context(ax) draws the county outlines, and metro_and_core(...) shows the whole metro area next to a 30 km window centred on the City of Buffalo, where most tracts are small.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 2 (core plus spatial analysis): pip install "geolattice[analysis]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Display matplotlib figures inline in this Jupyter notebook.
%matplotlib inline

# Standard library imports for path setup and warning control.
import warnings  # silence noisy third-party warnings during demos
from pathlib import Path  # filesystem paths for locating sample data

# Third-party GIS / plotting / tabular stack used throughout the notebook.
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoDataFrame I/O for tracts and counties
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figure and axes creation for maps
import numpy as np  # array ops for shares, norms, and masks
import pandas as pd  # tabular display of composition and indices
from IPython.display import display  # rich table previews in the notebook

# Hide library warnings so the notebook output stays readable.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # run this analysis or plotting step

# ===================================================================
# Setup for Buffalo metro segregation demos.
# Import GeoLattice, point DATA at Data/03_spatial_analysis/data_segregation/buffalo,
# import segregation as seg, load the tract panel, and define map helpers.
# ===================================================================

# The installed package lives in src/; the repository root is its parent.

ROOT = Path(geolattice.__file__).resolve().parents[1]

    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find the GeoLattice repository root.")

# Buffalo metro sample data (Erie + Niagara tracts on a shared 2020 geography).
DATA = ROOT / "Data" / "03_spatial_analysis" / "data_segregation" / "buffalo"  # define DATA

# Segregation indices, local measures, profiles, and inference helpers.
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import segregation as seg

# Compact figures with top/right spines removed for a cleaner look.
plt.rcParams.update(  # run this analysis or plotting step
