title: Null models and simulation for segregation
section: Part A: Why an even metro area does not give D = 0
text:
Part A: Why an even metro area does not give D = 0
Under the evenness null every tract has the metro composition in expectation, but each tract is a finite random sample. Sampling noise makes some tracts a little more Black and others a little more white, so \(D > 0\). The smaller the units (or the smaller the groups), the larger this noise floor.
The cell rescales 2020 tract populations from their real size (median about 3,400) down to about 35 people per unit, roughly the size of a census block, and simulates 300 even metro areas at each size.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part A: Why an even metro area does not give D = 0.
# Under the evenness null every tract has the metro composition *in expectation*, but each tract is
# ===================================================================

g20 = tracts[2020]  # 2020 tracts GeoDataFrame
counts20 = g20[ALL_GROUPS].to_numpy(float)  # NumPy array view of the column
totals20 = counts20.sum(1)  # define totals20
P20 = seg.global_proportions(counts20)  # define P20
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)  # reproducible random generator

def D_of(counts, pair):
    return seg.dissimilarity(pd.DataFrame(counts, columns=ALL_GROUPS), pair)  # two-group dissimilarity index D

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for factor in [1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01]:  # iterate over the collection
    sims = seg.evenness_null(totals20 * factor, P20, n_sims=300, rng=rng)  # define sims
    for pair in (["black", "white"], ["asian", "hispanic"]):  # loop over group pairs
        vals = np.array([D_of(s, pair) for s in sims])  # define vals
        rows.append({"median unit population": np.median(totals20 * factor), "pair": "-".join(pair),  # append this year/group record
                     "mean D under evenness": vals.mean(), "95th pct": np.percentile(vals, 95)})  # run this analysis or plotting step
bias = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # build table bias

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))  # create figure and axes
for pair, m in [("black-white", "o"), ("asian-hispanic", "s")]:  # loop over group pairs
    b = bias[bias.pair == pair]  # kernel bandwidth in metres
    ax.plot(b["median unit population"], b["mean D under evenness"], marker=m, label=f"{pair} (mean)")  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax.fill_between(b["median unit population"], 0, b["95th pct"], alpha=0.12)  # run this analysis or plotting step
for pair, ls in [(["black", "white"], "--"), (["asian", "hispanic"], ":")]:  # loop over group pairs
    ax.axhline(seg.dissimilarity(g20, pair), color="0.4", ls=ls, lw=0.8, label=f"observed 2020 {'-'.join(pair)}")  # two-group dissimilarity index D
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="median unit population (log)", ylabel="D in a perfectly even metro",  # set labels, title, or axis limits
       title="Random variation alone produces dissimilarity")  # define title
ax.legend(fontsize=7); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

At real tract sizes the noise floor is small: about 0.02 for Black-white and 0.04 for the much smaller Asian-Hispanic pair, far below the observed values (0.69 and 0.43). With block-sized units of a few dozen people it rises to 0.2 for Black-white and 0.4 for Asian-Hispanic, values that would be mistaken for moderate or even high segregation. This is why studies using small units, or small groups, report bias-corrected indices (Allen et al., 2015) or compare with simulated nulls rather than with zero.

Part B: The evenness null

plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook












B2. Null distributions and bias-corrected indices
Running every index on all simulated metro areas gives its null distribution. A simple bias-corrected value subtracts the null mean from the observed value; the standardized value divides that difference by the null standard deviation.


Code
# ===================================================================
# B2. Null distributions and bias-corrected indices.
# Running every index on all simulated metro areas gives its null distribution. A simple
# ===================================================================

index_fns = {  # define index_fns
    "D Black-white": lambda c: D_of(c, ["black", "white"]),  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "D Asian-Hispanic": lambda c: D_of(c, ["asian", "hispanic"]),  # run this analysis or plotting step
    "Theil H": lambda c: seg.theil_h(pd.DataFrame(c, columns=ALL_GROUPS), GROUPS),  # run this analysis or plotting step
}
rows, null_store = [], {}
for y in YEARS:  # loop over panel years
    c = tracts[y][ALL_GROUPS].to_numpy(float)  # NumPy array view of the column
    sims = seg.evenness_null(c.sum(1), seg.global_proportions(c), n_sims=499, rng=np.random.default_rng(y))  # reproducible random generator
    for name, fn in index_fns.items():  # iterate key/value pairs
        obs = fn(c)  # define obs
        null = np.array([fn(s) for s in sims])  # define null
        null_store[(y, name)] = (obs, null)  # assign a derived column or cell
        rows.append({"year": y, "index": name, "observed": obs, "null mean": null.mean(),  # append this year/group record
                     "bias-corrected": obs - null.mean(), "z": (obs - null.mean()) / null.std(),  # run this analysis or plotting step
                     "p (greater)": seg.permutation_pvalue(obs, null, alternative="greater")})  # run this analysis or plotting step
corrected = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["index", "year"]).sort_index()  # build table corrected
corrected.round(4)  # run this analysis or plotting step

At tract scale the bias correction is small for Black-white (about 0.02), but it matters for trends in small groups. The Asian-Hispanic null mean falls from 0.069 to 0.042 between 2000 and 2020 simply because both groups grew. Of the observed 0.14 decline in Asian-Hispanic dissimilarity, about 0.03 is the shrinking noise floor; the bias-corrected decline is 0.12.

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
section: Part C: The systematic null (shuffling tracts)
text:
Part C: The systematic null (shuffling tracts)
The evenness null destroys all structure. A different question is whether the observed arrangement of tracts matters, given the tract compositions we have. The systematic null keeps the exact set of compositions and reassigns them to tracts at random.
An aspatial index cannot respond to this null; it is identical in every shuffle. A spatial index can. Below, the spatial statistic is Black-white dissimilarity computed on counts pooled over a 2 km Gaussian kernel (notebook 03_07_01, Part F).


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part C: The systematic null (shuffling tracts).
# Every observed value lies far outside its null distribution (note the log scale), so the p-values
# ===================================================================

nb20 = seg.kernel_weights(g20, bandwidth=2000)  # distance-decay neighbourhood weights

def pooled_D(counts, nb=nb20, pair=("black", "white")):
    return seg.dissimilarity(pd.DataFrame(nb.pooled_counts(counts), columns=ALL_GROUPS), list(pair))  # two-group dissimilarity index D

sims_sys = seg.systematic_null(counts20, n_sims=499, rng=np.random.default_rng(7))  # null: shuffle compositions across tracts
aspatial = np.array([D_of(s, ["black", "white"]) for s in sims_sys[:50]])  # define aspatial
print(f"aspatial D across 50 shuffles: min {aspatial.min():.4f}, max {aspatial.max():.4f} (observed {D_of(counts20, ['black', 'white']):.4f})")  # status line for the notebook reader

obs_sp = pooled_D(counts20)  # define obs_sp
null_sys = np.array([pooled_D(s) for s in sims_sys])  # define null_sys
print(f"spatial D observed {obs_sp:.3f}; systematic null mean {null_sys.mean():.3f} (sd {null_sys.std():.3f}); "  # status line for the notebook reader
      f"p = {seg.permutation_pvalue(obs_sp, null_sys, alternative='greater'):.4f}")  # run this analysis or plotting step

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, (name, c) in zip(axes, [("observed 2020", counts20), ("one systematic shuffle", sims_sys[0])]):  # pair each axis with a year or layer
    g20.assign(s=c[:, 1] / c.sum(1)).plot(column="s", cmap="Purples", vmin=0, vmax=0.9, ax=ax, edgecolor="white", lw=0.2)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    add_context(ax); ax.set_title(f"{name}: spatial D = {pooled_D(c):.3f}")  # county outlines and optional city zoom
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook



aspatial D across 50 shuffles: min 0.6867, max 0.6867 (observed 0.6867)
spatial D observed 0.620; systematic null mean 0.383 (sd 0.013); p = 0.0020









Aspatial \(D\) is exactly the same in every shuffle. Spatial \(D\) falls from 0.62 to about 0.38 when the same tract compositions are scattered at random: clustering of similar tracts accounts for a large part of the spatially pooled index. The single shuffled map makes the point visually: the same number of mostly Black tracts exists, but they no longer touch each other.

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
section: Part D: The spatially constrained null
text:
Part D: The spatially constrained null
The systematic null shuffles tracts across both counties, so it compares the real metro area with one in which the East Side has been scattered across Niagara and rural Erie County. Often the large-scale pattern is taken as given and the question is about finer-scale structure: within each part of the metro area, are similar tracts next to each other?
seg.spatial_blocks partitions tracts into contiguous-ish blocks (k-means on centroids, or a regular grid), and seg.spatially_constrained_null shuffles compositions only within each block.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: The spatially constrained null.
# Aspatial $D$ is exactly the same in every shuffle. Spatial $D$ falls from 0.62 to about 0.38
# ===================================================================

blocks = {name: seg.spatial_blocks(g20, n_blocks=k, method=m, seed=0)  # define blocks
          for name, k, m in [("k-means, 10 blocks", 10, "kmeans"), ("k-means, 30 blocks", 30, "kmeans"),  # iterate over the collection
                             ("grid, 4 x 4", 16, "grid")]}  # run this analysis or plotting step
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 6), constrained_layout=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, (name, lab) in zip(axes, blocks.items()):  # pair each axis with a year or layer
    g20.assign(b=lab).plot(column="b", categorical=True, cmap="tab20", ax=ax, edgecolor="white", lw=0.3)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    g20.dissolve(by=lab).boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.9)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    add_context(ax, labels=False); ax.set_title(name)  # county outlines and optional city zoom
plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
section: Part E: Calibrating intuition with partial integration
text:
Part E: Calibrating intuition with partial integration
A useful simulation is to mix the observed metro area with an even one: move a fraction \(a\) of every tract’s residents into a random draw from the metro composition. It shows how a given index responds to a known amount of integration, and helps translate “D fell from 0.77 to 0.69” into a more concrete statement.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part E: Calibrating intuition with partial integration.
# The more the null preserves, the closer it gets to the observed value:
# ===================================================================

def partially_integrate(counts, a, rng):
    t = counts.sum(1)  # define t
    even = seg.evenness_null(t, seg.global_proportions(counts), n_sims=1, rng=rng)[0]  # toy city with identical composition everywhere
    return (1 - a) * counts + a * even  # return the computed result

alphas = np.linspace(0, 1, 11)  # numeric grid for plotting or thresholds
curve = {name: [] for name in ["D Black-white", "Theil H", "spatial D (2 km)"]}  # define curve
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)  # reproducible random generator
for a in alphas:  # iterate over the collection
    vals = {k: [] for k in curve}  # define vals
    for _ in range(20):  # iterate over the collection
        c = partially_integrate(counts20, a, rng)  # define c
        vals["D Black-white"].append(D_of(c, ["black", "white"]))  # append this year/group record
        vals["Theil H"].append(seg.theil_h(pd.DataFrame(c, columns=ALL_GROUPS), GROUPS))  # append this year/group record
        vals["spatial D (2 km)"].append(pooled_D(c))  # append this year/group record
    for k in curve:  # iterate over the collection
        curve[k].append(np.mean(vals[k]))  # append this year/group record

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))  # create figure and axes
for k, v in curve.items():  # iterate key/value pairs
    ax.plot(alphas, v, marker="o", label=k)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
ax.axhline(seg.dissimilarity(tracts[2000], ["black", "white"]), color="gray", ls=":", lw=0.8)  # two-group dissimilarity index D
ax.text(0.98, seg.dissimilarity(tracts[2000], ["black", "white"]) + 0.015, "observed D 2000", ha="right", fontsize=7, color="gray")  # two-group dissimilarity index D
ax.set(xlabel="share of 2020 residents redistributed at random (a)", ylabel="index value",  # set labels, title, or axis limits
       title="How indices respond to a known amount of integration (from 2020)")  # define title
ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook
target = 0.5 * seg.dissimilarity(tracts[2020], ["black", "white"])  # two-group dissimilarity index D
print(f"Halving D(Black, white) from its 2020 value would require redistributing about "  # status line for the notebook reader
      f"{np.interp(target, curve['D Black-white'][::-1], alphas[::-1]):.0%} of residents at random.")  # run this analysis or plotting step










Halving D(Black, white) from its 2020 value would require redistributing about 50% of residents at random.


\(D\) falls almost linearly with \(a\): halving the 2020 Black-white index would take the equivalent of redistributing about half of all residents at random. Theil’s \(H\) falls faster than linearly (it is closer to quadratic in the departures), so the same change in sorting produces a larger proportional drop in \(H\). Keep this in mind when comparing percentage changes across indices: a 20% fall in \(H\) and a 10% fall in \(D\) can describe the same change.

title: Null models and simulation for segregation
text:
Summary

Finite units produce non-zero indices even in an even metro area; the bias grows as units or groups get smaller. Report bias-corrected or standardized values when units or groups are small.
The evenness null (multinomial draws with metro shares) tests whether tracts differ from random allocation of residents.
The systematic null (shuffling compositions across tracts) leaves aspatial indices unchanged and tests whether the spatial arrangement matters.
The spatially constrained null shuffles only within blocks, keeping the large-scale pattern and testing finer-scale structure. Block size sets the scale of the question.
Partial-integration simulations show how differently indices respond to the same change.

Next: 03_07_06 turns these simulations into formal tests: single values, comparisons between years, and confidence intervals that respect spatial dependence.

title: Segregation Over Time: Boundaries, Panels, and Decomposition
text:
Overview
Segregation research is mostly about change: did Buffalo integrate, and why? Two technical problems stand between census tables and an answer.

Boundaries move. The Census Bureau redraws tracts every decade: Erie and Niagara counties had about 300 tracts in 2000 and 2010 and 325 in 2020, with many split, merged, or reshaped. Indices computed on different geographies are not comparable (the modifiable areal unit problem, MAUP).
Change has more than one source. An index can fall because people moved (the spatial arrangement changed) or because the metro area’s group mix changed (composition). Policy implications differ, so the two need to be separated.

This notebook follows the PySAL tutorial on decomposition and extends it to a multi-period panel with seg.areal_interpolate, seg.dasymetric_interpolate, seg.harmonize_panel, seg.compute_panel, seg.trend, seg.decompose_change, and seg.chain_decomposition. It also shows how the harmonized panel used in notebooks 03_07_01 to 03_07_06 was built.
Topics:

Real tract boundary changes, 2000 to 2020, and the MAUP
Areal and dasymetric interpolation with a housing-unit raster from census blocks
Validating interpolation against block-level truth
A harmonized panel with trend test
Shapley decomposition of change into spatial and composition parts, chained across decades
Exporting a tract-by-year panel for causal models

Study area and data. The Buffalo-Cheektowaga metropolitan area: Erie and Niagara counties, New York (about 1.17 million people in 2020). Counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau decennial censuses of 2000, 2010, and 2020, by census tract, for five mutually exclusive groups:

title: Segregation Over Time: Boundaries, Panels, and Decomposition
section: Part B: Moving counts between geographies
text:
Part B: Moving counts between geographies

B1. Areal interpolation
seg.areal_interpolate(source, target, cols) intersects the two layers and splits each source polygon’s counts across the pieces in proportion to area:
\[\hat{x}_{jk} = \sum_s x_{sk}\,\frac{|s \cap j|}{|s|}.\]
It assumes people are spread uniformly within each source tract, which is badly wrong for a large suburban tract that is half farmland. Counts are conserved exactly.


B2. Dasymetric interpolation
seg.dasymetric_interpolate(..., raster_path=...) replaces area with the sum of an ancillary raster inside each piece:
\[\hat{x}_{jk} = \sum_s x_{sk}\,\frac{R(s \cap j)}{R(s)}.\]
Here the raster is housing_units_2020_50m.tif: the 2020 census count of housing units in each block, spread over 50 m cells. People are placed where homes are.

With areal weighting, each 2000 tract’s population is spread evenly over its land, including farmland and parks. Dasymetric weighting moves it toward the villages and subdivisions where the housing actually is, which is most visible in the large rural tracts of southern Erie and northern Niagara counties. Totals are identical under both methods.


B3. Does the raster help? A check against block-level truth
The interpolation can be tested where the truth is known. The 2020 census reports population for every block, so we can compute the true 2020 population of any polygon by summing the blocks whose internal point falls inside it. The test mimics the real task:

Sum 2020 block populations into the 2000 (or 2010) tract polygons. This is what a “2020 census on old boundaries” would report.
Interpolate those totals onto the 2020 tracts with each method.
Compare with the true block sums for the 2020 tracts.

The raster comes from 2020 housing units in the same blocks, so the test is favourable to the dasymetric method. It still answers the practical question: does placing people where homes are beat placing them evenly over land? The tracts that matter are those whose boundaries changed; for unchanged tracts both methods are exact.


Code
# ===================================================================
# B3. Does the raster help? A check against block-level truth.
# With areal weighting, each 2000 tract's population is spread evenly over its land, including
# ===================================================================

blocks = gpd.read_file(DATA / "blocks_2020_points.geojson")  # load vector features from disk

def block_sum(polys):
    j = gpd.sjoin(blocks, polys[["tract_id", "geometry"]], predicate="within", how="inner")  # define j
    return j.groupby("tract_id").pop20.sum().reindex(polys.tract_id).fillna(0).to_numpy()  # return the computed result

truth20 = block_sum(target)  # define truth20
rows, store = [], {}
for src_year in (2000, 2010):  # iterate over the collection
    src = native[src_year][["tract_id", "geometry"]].copy()  # mutable copy so originals stay unchanged
    src["total"] = block_sum(src)  # assign a derived column or cell
    changed = ~target.tract_id.isin(src.tract_id).to_numpy()  # NumPy array view of the column
    for name, est in [("areal", seg.areal_interpolate(src, target, ["total"]).total.to_numpy()),  # iterate over the collection
                      ("dasymetric", seg.dasymetric_interpolate(src, target, ["total"], raster_path=DATA / "housing_units_2020_50m.tif").total.to_numpy())]:  # run this analysis or plotting step
        err = np.abs(est - truth20); pct = err / np.maximum(truth20, 1)  # define err
        store[(src_year, name)] = est  # assign a derived column or cell
        rows.append({"from": f"{src_year} tracts", "method": name, "2020 tracts with new boundaries": int(changed.sum()),  # append this year/group record
                     "mean abs error, changed tracts": err[changed].mean(), "median % error, changed tracts": np.median(pct[changed]) * 100,  # run this analysis or plotting step
                     "tracts off by > 25%": int((pct > 0.25).sum())})  # run this analysis or plotting step
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["from", "method"]).round(1))  # show a rich table preview

changed = ~target.tract_id.isin(native[2000].tract_id).to_numpy()  # NumPy array view of the column
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4), sharey=True)  # create figure and axes
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["areal", "dasymetric"]):  # pair each axis with a year or layer
    est = store[(2000, name)]  # define est
    ax.scatter(truth20[~changed], est[~changed], s=8, color="0.7", label="tract unchanged since 2000")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    ax.scatter(truth20[changed], est[changed], s=14, color="#d95f02", label="tract boundary changed")  # run this analysis or plotting step
    lim_ = max(truth20.max(), est.max())  # define lim_
    ax.plot([0, lim_], [0, lim_], "k--", lw=0.8)  # draw geometries or a series on the axes
    ax.set(xlabel="true 2020 tract population (blocks)", ylabel="interpolated from 2000 tracts", title=name)  # set labels, title, or axis limits
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # render the figure in the notebook

title: Segregation Over Time: Boundaries, Panels, and Decomposition
section: Part D: Why did segregation change?
text:
Part D: Why did segregation change?

D1. The Shapley decomposition
Write the index as a function of two ingredients: the spatial pattern \(S\) (the relative distribution of the focal group across tracts) and the composition \(C\) (the focal group’s share of the two-group population). Between periods A and B, \(I(S_B, C_B) - I(S_A, C_A)\) can be attributed to each ingredient by switching it on while holding the other fixed, averaged over both orders (a two-player Shapley value):
\[\Delta_{S} = \tfrac12\big[(I(S_B, C_A) - I(S_A, C_A)) + (I(S_B, C_B) - I(S_A, C_B))\big],\] \[\Delta_{C} = \tfrac12\big[(I(S_A, C_B) - I(S_A, C_A)) + (I(S_B, C_B) - I(S_B, C_A))\big].\]
The counterfactuals \(I(S_A, C_B)\) rescale period A’s focal-group counts in every tract so the metro-wide share matches period B, keeping tract totals. By construction \(\Delta_S + \Delta_C = I_B - I_A\) exactly. The first group in groups is the focal group.


Code
# ===================================================================
# Part D: Why did segregation change?.
# Black-white and Hispanic-white dissimilarity fall by about 0.04 to 0.05 per decade, and Theil's
# ===================================================================

dc = seg.decompose_change(panel[2020], panel[2000], pair)  # define dc
print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in dc.items()})  # status line for the notebook reader
print("additive:", np.isclose(dc["spatial_component"] + dc["composition_component"], dc["total_change"]))  # status line for the notebook reader

rows = []  # accumulate one summary row per year / group
for p_ in (["black", "white"], ["hispanic", "white"], ["asian", "white"], ["hispanic", "black"], ["asian", "black"]):  # iterate over the collection
    for name, fn in [("dissimilarity", seg.dissimilarity), ("gini", seg.gini)]:  # iterate over the collection
        r = seg.decompose_change(panel[2020], panel[2000], p_, index_fn=fn)  # compute() result with value and CI
        share00 = panel[2000][p_[0]].sum() / panel[2000][p_].sum().sum()  # sum the selected values
        share20 = panel[2020][p_[0]].sum() / panel[2020][p_].sum().sum()  # sum the selected values
        rows.append({"pair": "-".join(p_), "index": name, "focal share 2000": share00, "focal share 2020": share20,  # append this year/group record
                     "2000": r["index_b"], "2020": r["index_a"], "change": r["total_change"],
                     "spatial": r["spatial_component"], "composition": r["composition_component"]})

title: Segregation Over Time: Boundaries, Panels, and Decomposition
text:
Summary

Census tracts change every decade. Indices computed on different geographies are not comparable (MAUP): put every year on common units before comparing.
Areal interpolation conserves counts and assumes uniform density; dasymetric interpolation with a housing-unit raster places people where homes are and, checked against block-level truth, is far more accurate for Buffalo’s large suburban and rural tracts.
harmonize_panel, compute_panel, and trend turn a multi-year collection into a panel of indices with a trend test in a few lines.
The Shapley decomposition splits change exactly into spatial re-sorting and composition shifts; chaining it across decades and across group pairs shows which part drives each trend.
export_for_causal produces tract-by-year tables for downstream causal models.

title: Spatial Confounding
section: Why an omitted smooth confounder biases regression
text:
Why an omitted smooth confounder biases regression
Suppose the outcome model is \(Y_i=\alpha+\tau T_i+X_i^\top\beta+\gamma U_i+\varepsilon_i\) and we regress \(Y\) on \((T,X)\) without \(U\). By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem the OLS coefficient is
\[\hat\tau_{\text{OLS}}=\frac{\sum_i \tilde T_i Y_i}{\sum_i \tilde T_i^2}
\;\xrightarrow{p}\;\tau+\gamma\,\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\tilde T,\tilde U)}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde T)},\]
where \(\tilde T\) and \(\tilde U\) are the residuals of \(T\) and \(U\) after regressing on \(X\). The bias is the product of the confounder’s effect on \(Y\) (\(\gamma\)) and its association with treatment that \(X\) does not explain. In our design \(\gamma=0.9\) and \(U\) enters the propensity, so the bias is large and positive.

Diagnostics
If the treatment residual \(\tilde T\) is spatially autocorrelated, a smooth omitted variable has room to bias the estimate. If the outcome residual is autocorrelated too, the risk is real, and i.i.d. standard errors will also be wrong. diagnose_spatial_confounding computes Moran’s I (via geolattice.spatial_statistics) for \(T\), \(Y\) and both residuals.

title: Spatial Confounding
section: Adding a spatial smooth, and why that is not enough
text:
Adding a spatial smooth, and why that is not enough
A natural fix is to add a spatial basis \(S\) (functions of location) to the regression,
\[Y_i=\alpha+\tau T_i+X_i^\top\beta+S_i^\top\theta+\varepsilon_i,\]
or a spatial random effect (notebook 06). Two bases are used here.

Moran eigenvector maps (Griffith; Dray et al.): eigenvectors of \(MCM\) with \(M=I-\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top/n\) and \(C=(W+W^\top)/2\). Ordered by eigenvalue, they run from the broadest positively autocorrelated patterns to finer ones.
Radial basis functions centred on \(k\) k-means knots \(c_m\): \(S_{im}=\exp\!\big(-\lVert s_i-c_m\rVert^2/2h^2\big)\).

By FWL, \(\hat\tau\) now uses only the part of \(T\) that is orthogonal to \(X\) and \(S\). If the basis is rich enough to span \(U\), the bias disappears; if not, the remaining confounding stays. Hodges & Reich (2010) and Paciorek (2010) add a subtler point. With a penalised smooth or random effect, the smooth and the treatment compete for the same large-scale variation, and the estimate can move in either direction. Adding “space” is not automatically a confounding adjustment.

spatial+
Dupont, Wood & Augustin (2022) remove the spatially smooth part of the treatment first:

Regress \(T\) on a rich basis \(S_t\): \(\;T_i=S_{t,i}^\top\gamma+\tilde T_i\).
Fit \(Y_i=\alpha+\tau\tilde T_i+X_i^\top\beta+f(s_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(f\) a penalised smooth.

The coefficient on \(\tilde T\) is identified from treatment variation that is spatially rough, which a smooth confounder cannot explain. In geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal step 1 uses \(k_t=\max(3k,\,n/10)\) unpenalised Moran eigenvectors and step 2 a ridge-penalised basis with the penalty chosen by generalised cross-validation.

title: Spatial Confounding
text:
Spatial double machine learning

The partially linear model
\[Y=\theta\,T+g(X,s)+\varepsilon,\qquad T=m(X,s)+v,\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X,s,T]=0,\ \mathbb E[v\mid X,s]=0.\]
Here \(g\) and \(m\) are unknown functions learned by machine learning. Including location \(s\) (coordinates, spatial lags, basis functions) lets \(g\) and \(m\) absorb a smooth confounder.


Neyman-orthogonal score and cross-fitting
Write \(\ell(X,s)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X,s]\). DML solves the sample analogue of \(\mathbb E[\psi]=0\) with the score
\[\psi(W;\theta,\ell,m)=\big(Y-\ell(X,s)-\theta\,(T-m(X,s))\big)\,\big(T-m(X,s)\big),\]
giving the residual-on-residual estimator
\[\hat\theta=\frac{\sum_i \hat v_i\,\hat u_i}{\sum_i \hat v_i^2},\qquad
\hat u_i=Y_i-\hat\ell(X_i,s_i),\quad \hat v_i=T_i-\hat m(X_i,s_i).\]
The score is Neyman orthogonal: its derivative with respect to the nuisance functions is zero at the truth, so first-order errors in \(\hat\ell,\hat m\) do not bias \(\hat\theta\). Cross-fitting predicts each \(\hat\ell(X_i),\hat m(X_i)\) from models trained on other folds, which removes overfitting bias. Under heterogeneous effects \(\tau(x,s)\) the PLM estimand is the overlap-weighted average
\[\theta_{\text{PLM}}=\frac{\mathbb E\big[\operatorname{Var}(T\mid X,s)\,\tau(X,s)\big]}{\mathbb E\big[\operatorname{Var}(T\mid X,s)\big]}
=\frac{\mathbb E[e(1-e)\,\tau]}{\mathbb E[e(1-e)]}\quad\text{(binary }T),\]
which is why notebook 00 computed that quantity as the target.


Spatial cross-fitting and its trade-off
With spatial dependence a neighbour in the training fold leaks information about a held-out county, so SpatialDML holds out spatial blocks (k-means clusters of locations). Block size involves a real trade-off that this dataset makes vivid:

blocks should be larger than the range of residual dependence (to stop leakage), but
smaller than the scale of any confounder the nuisance models must learn from location. A held-out block as large as the confounder’s range forces the models to extrapolate \(U\) into a region they never saw, and the confounding comes back.

The basis also has to be rich enough to represent a surface that varies every ~350 km across a 4,600 km domain. geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal therefore scales both defaults with \(n\): \(\max(25,\ n/15)\) blocks and \(\min(200,\ \max(30,\ n/20))\) radial basis functions. These defaults were revised in response to exactly this analysis.


Code

Without location features DML cannot see \(U\) and inherits the OLS bias.
Raw coordinates and spatial lags barely help a linear nuisance model: coordinates enter linearly, and a plane cannot represent a surface with several hills and valleys.

The random forest with coordinates and RBFs is less accurate than ridge here, because a smooth surface is easier for a linear model on a smooth basis than for trees.

title: Spatial Confounding
text:
Standard errors under spatial dependence
All estimators in the package are asymptotically linear, \(\hat\theta-\theta\approx\frac1n\sum_i\psi_i\), so a standard error only needs the influence contributions \(\psi_i\):

i.i.d.: \(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\psi_i^2\).
Conley (1999) spatial HAC: keep covariances between pairs closer than a cutoff \(d^*\), down-weighted by a kernel, \[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\text{C}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\sum_j K\!\Big(\frac{d_{ij}}{d^*}\Big)\psi_i\psi_j,\qquad K(u)=(1-u)_+\ \text{(Bartlett)}.\]
Block (cluster-robust): treat spatial blocks \(b\) as clusters, \(\frac{G}{G-1}\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_b\big(\sum_{i\in b}\psi_i\big)^2\).

The cutoff is a modelling choice. suggest_cutoff reads it off the residual correlogram, and a sensitivity curve shows how much it matters.


Code
best = fits["RBF basis (155), auto blocks"]
psi = best.score_
d_star = sc.suggest_cutoff(best.residuals_["y"], xy)
print(f"suggested Conley cutoff from the outcome-residual correlogram: {d_star:.0f} km")

cutoffs = [25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 600]
se_c = [sc.standard_error(psi, xy, "conley", cutoff=c) for c in cutoffs]
se_iid = sc.standard_error(psi, method="iid")
se_blk = sc.standard_error(psi, xy, "block")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(cutoffs, se_c, "o-", color=ts.BLUE, label="Conley (Bartlett)")
ax.axhline(se_iid, color=ts.MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2, label=f"i.i.d. = {se_iid:.3f}")
ax.axhline(se_blk, color=ts.ORANGE, ls=":", lw=1.6, label=f"spatial blocks = {se_blk:.3f}")
ax.axvline(d_star, color=ts.INK2, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Conley cutoff (km)"); ax.set_ylabel("standard error of θ̂")
ax.set_title("Spatially robust standard errors grow with the dependence range")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout()

title: Spatial Confounding
text:
Summary and Conclusions

A spatially smooth unmeasured confounder can flip the sign of a naive estimate and attenuate a covariate-adjusted one by ~70%.
“Adding space” works only if the spatial terms can actually represent the confounder. spatial+ achieves this by removing the smooth part of the treatment; DML achieves it with a rich basis.
Spatial cross-fitting needs blocks that are small relative to the confounder’s scale; large blocks bring the bias back through extrapolation.
Report spatially robust standard errors and show their sensitivity to the cutoff.

No method can adjust for a confounder that is not spatially smooth and not measured; spatial methods only help with the smooth part.

title: Spatially Varying Treatment Effects
text:
Overview
A single average effect hides where a program works. In Scenario A the true effect
\[\tau_i=-0.8-0.35\,z(\text{child poverty})_i-0.6\,\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{\lVert s_i-s_{\text{Jackson,MS}}\rVert^2}{2\cdot400^2}\Big)\]
is larger in poorer counties and in the Deep South. We try to recover this surface, still in the presence of the smooth confounder \(U(s)\). We use the outcome without spillovers (y_noint) because these estimators assume no interference.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
ts.use()

gA, w, truth = cc.scenario_program()
X = gA[cc.COVARIATES].to_numpy()
xy = cc.coords_km(gA)
tau = gA["tau"].to_numpy()
data = sc.SpatialCausalData(X, gA["T"], gA["y_noint"], xy, w=w, feature_names=cc.COVARIATES)
print(f"true ATE {truth['ate']:.3f};  tau ranges from {tau.min():.2f} to {tau.max():.2f}")

title: Spatially Varying Treatment Effects
text:
The conditional average treatment effect
The CATE is \(\tau(x,s)=\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x,\,s]\). Under unconfoundedness given \((X,s)\) it is identified, but it is a function, estimated with much more noise than an average.

The AIPW pseudo-outcome and the DR-learner
With cross-fitted nuisances \(\hat\mu_t(x,s)=\mathbb E[Y\mid T=t,X,s]\) and \(\hat e(x,s)\), define
\[\Gamma_i=\hat\mu_1(Z_i)-\hat\mu_0(Z_i)+\frac{T_i\,(Y_i-\hat\mu_1(Z_i))}{\hat e(Z_i)}-\frac{(1-T_i)\,(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(Z_i))}{1-\hat e(Z_i)} .\]
If either nuisance is correct, \(\mathbb E[\Gamma_i\mid X_i,s_i]=\tau(X_i,s_i)\). So \(\frac1n\sum_i\Gamma_i\) is the doubly robust ATE, and regressing \(\Gamma\) on effect modifiers gives the DR-learner (Kennedy, 2023), whose error depends only on the product of the two nuisance errors. The catch: \(\Gamma\) is very noisy. Its variance is about that of \(Y\) itself and more than ten times the variance of the signal \(\tau\), so the second stage needs strong smoothing. In SpatialDRLearner the nuisance models see covariates plus the spatial basis (to absorb \(U\)), and the final stage regresses \(\Gamma\) on covariates and coordinates. All CATEs reported below are out-of-fold: a county’s estimate never uses its own outcome.


Code
dr = sc.SpatialDRLearner(spatial_features=("rbf",), cate_features="X+coords", se="conley", cutoff=150).fit(data)
print(dr.summary())
print(f"variance of the pseudo-outcome: {dr.pseudo_outcome_.var():.2f}   of Y: {gA['y_noint'].var():.2f}   "
      f"of the true effect tau: {tau.var():.2f}")

title: Spatially Varying Treatment Effects
text:
Geographically weighted DML
GW-DML keeps the global, spatially cross-fitted residuals of notebook 01, \(\hat u_j=Y_j-\hat\ell(Z_j)\) and \(\hat v_j=T_j-\hat m(Z_j)\), and fits a local residual-on-residual regression around each county. With kernel weights \(K_{ij}=K(d_{ij}/h_i)\) the local estimating equation is
\[\sum_j K_{ij}\,(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)\big(\hat u_j-\bar u_i-\theta_i(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)\big)=0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\hat\theta_i=\frac{\sum_jK_{ij}(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)(\hat u_j-\bar u_i)}{\sum_jK_{ij}(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)^2},\]
with kernel-weighted means \(\bar u_i,\bar v_i\) (a local intercept). This is a geographically weighted regression of \(\hat u\) on \(\hat v\).

Kernel and bandwidth come from geolattice.spatial_statistics.gwmodel: bisquare \(K(r)=(1-r^2)^2\) for \(r<1\), and an adaptive bandwidth \(h_i\) equal to the distance to the \(k\)-th nearest county. \(k\) is chosen by golden-section search on the leave-one-out error \(\sum_j\big(\hat u_j-\bar u_{(-j)}-\hat\theta_{(-j)}(\hat v_j-\bar v_{(-j)})\big)^2\).
Local standard error (kernel sandwich, treating the residuals as independent): \(\widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\hat\theta_i)=\sqrt{\sum_jK_{ij}^2(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)^2\hat e_{ij}^2}\big/\sum_jK_{ij}(\hat v_j-\bar v_i)^2\), and the effective sample size is \(n_{\text{eff},i}=(\sum_jK_{ij})^2/\sum_jK_{ij}^2\).
What it estimates. As with the global PLM, \(\theta_i\) is a local overlap-weighted average of \(\tau\) in the kernel neighbourhood, and smoothing biases it toward neighbouring values.
Stationarity test. Is there spatial variation at all? The statistic is the SD of the \(\hat\theta_i\). Under \(H_0\) (constant effect) the residual pairs \((\hat u_j,\hat v_j)\) are exchangeable across locations, so permuting them gives the null distribution (cf. Brunsdon, Fotheringham & Charlton, 1998).

gw = sc.GWDML(model_y="ridge", model_t="logistic", spatial_features=("rbf",), kernel="bisquare", fixed=False).fit(data)

title: Spatially Varying Treatment Effects
text:
The geographically weighted causal forest
Local regression of \(\hat u\) on \(\hat v\) is linear and only uses location. The GW causal forest lets the effect also vary with covariates, nonlinearly:

Compute cross-fitted AIPW pseudo-outcomes \(\Gamma_i\) (as for the DR-learner).
Place \(K=50\) calibration knots (k-means of county centroids). At knot \(k\) fit a random forest of \(\Gamma\) on covariates with sample weights \(K(d_{jk}/h_k)\) (the same geolattice.spatial_statistics kernel).
Each county uses its nearest knot’s forest, blended with a global forest: \(\hat\tau_i=\lambda\,\hat\tau^{\text{local}}_i+(1-\lambda)\,\hat\tau^{\text{global}}_i\) (the geographical random forest idea of Georganos et al., 2021).
All predictions are out-of-bag, and \(\lambda\) and the leaf size are chosen by out-of-bag error (leaf size matters a great deal because \(\Gamma\) is so noisy).

The bandwidth is chosen as the scale at which a kernel-weighted mean of \(\Gamma\) best predicts held-out values. That smoothed mean is itself reported as a local ATE map with a kernel sandwich SE, \(\hat\tau^{\text{loc}}_i=\sum_jK_{ij}\Gamma_j/\sum_jK_{ij}\). This step uses the geolattice.spatial_statistics.gwmodel kernels; engine="spatialstats" would instead run geolattice.spatial_statistics.gwmodel.ensemble.GWRandomForest with one local forest per county.


Code
cf = sc.GWCausalForest(spatial_features=("rbf",), n_knots=50).fit(data)
print(cf.summary())

GW-DML captures the regional pattern, but the CV-selected bandwidth is small (about 20 effective counties per neighbourhood), so local estimates are noisy and a few with almost no local treatment variation are extreme (the minimum is below −10, with a standard error above 5). It also cannot express the within-region poverty gradient, because it uses location only. A larger bandwidth trades this variance for more smoothing bias.

Using CATEs: targeting a limited budget
Suppose the budget covers 20% of counties. Ranking counties by estimated effect and treating the top fifth targets those predicted to benefit most. We compare the true average effect in the targeted counties with random allocation and with oracle targeting by the true \(\tau\).

def gain(est):
    pick = np.argsort(est)[:k]                    # most negative = largest reduction in diabetes
    return tau[pick].mean()

                 "GW causal forest": gain(cf.cate_), "oracle (true tau)": gain(tau)},

title: Spatially Varying Treatment Effects
text:
Summary and Conclusions

CATE estimation is much harder than ATE estimation: pseudo-outcomes are noisy, so methods need heavy smoothing, and honest (out-of-fold / out-of-bag) predictions are the only fair basis for comparison.
GW-DML answers “where?”, with local SEs and a test of whether the effect varies at all. It cannot see covariate-driven heterogeneity, and pointwise intervals are not a joint band.
The GW causal forest combines location and covariates and recovers both drivers here.
Even imperfect CATEs can be useful for targeting. The relevant measure is the true benefit in the selected counties, not the accuracy of each county’s estimate.

Overview
With repeated observations over time, each county serves as its own control: fixed differences between counties cancel, and only changes are compared. Space complicates this in two ways: untreated neighbours may be affected (contaminated controls), and adoption often spreads across states over time.
Three semi-synthetic annual panels, 2014-2025, built on real county baselines (2024 diabetes prevalence) with simulated common trends, factor structure and noise:

title: Panel Designs: DiD with Spillovers, Staggered Adoption, Synthetic Control
text:
Difference-in-differences and contaminated controls
With treated group \(G_i\in\{0,1\}\) and post period \(P_t\), the two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) model
\[Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\tau\,D_{it}+\varepsilon_{it},\qquad D_{it}=G_iP_t,\]
identifies the ATT under parallel trends: \(\mathbb E[Y_{it}(0)-Y_{is}(0)\mid G=1]=\mathbb E[Y_{it}(0)-Y_{is}(0)\mid G=0]\).
Spillovers break the control group. If some untreated counties are affected, \(Y_{it}=Y_{it}(0)+S_{it}\) for them, with spillover \(S\). The DiD estimand becomes
\[\tau_{\text{naive}}=\tau-\mathbb E[S\mid G=0,\text{post}],\]
biased toward zero when spillovers share the sign of the effect (Butts, 2023).
Ring model. Let \(R_{r,i}=1\) if untreated county \(i\) lies at distance \((d_{r-1},d_r]\) from the nearest treated county. Then
\[Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\tau D_{it}+\sum_{r=1}^{R}\delta_r\,R_{r,i}P_t+\varepsilon_{it}.\]
Counties beyond \(d_R\) form a clean control group, \(\tau\) is the direct effect, and \(\delta_r\) the spillover in ring \(r\). The outer ring must extend beyond the true spillover range. Estimation uses the two-way within transformation (alternating projections, which also handle unbalanced panels) and standard errors clustered on spatial blocks of counties, which allows for correlation between neighbours.
Event study. Replacing \(P_t\) by period dummies (reference = last pre-period) gives group × period coefficients. Pre-period coefficients test parallel trends jointly; with \(G\) clusters and \(q\) restrictions the Hotelling-type statistic \(F=W\,(G-q)/\big((G-1)q\big)\sim F(q,G-q)\) avoids the over-rejection of a \(\chi^2\) test with few clusters.

title: Panel Designs: DiD with Spillovers, Staggered Adoption, Synthetic Control
section: Staggered adoption: group-time effects with clean controls
text:
Staggered adoption: group-time effects with clean controls
When states adopt at different times, static TWFE also compares late adopters with already-treated early adopters. With effects that grow over time those “forbidden comparisons” receive negative weights, and the estimate can even change sign (Goodman-Bacon, 2021). Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) instead estimate each group-time ATT separately. For cohort \(g\) (adoption year) and year \(t\),
\[\text{ATT}(g,t)=\mathbb E\big[Y_t-Y_{g-1}\mid G=g\big]-\mathbb E\big[Y_t-Y_{g-1}\mid \text{clean controls at }t\big],\]
using the year before adoption as the base. StaggeredSpatialDiD adds space:

every county has an exposure time \(E_i\), the first year some county within the exposure distance (60 km) has adopted;
clean controls at year \(t\) are counties neither treated nor exposed by \(\max(t,g-1)\), so exposed neighbours never act as controls;
never-treated counties first exposed in year \(e\) form spillover cohorts with their own \(\text{ATT}_s(e,t)\).

Cells are aggregated into an overall ATT and an event study \(\theta(k)=\sum_g w_g\,\text{ATT}(g,g+k)\) with cohort-size weights. Inference uses a cluster bootstrap over spatial blocks.


Code
p2, g2 = cc.scenario_panel_staggered()
print(p2)
for yr, sts in p2.truth["cohorts"].items():
    print(f"  cohort {yr}: {', '.join(sorted(map(str, sts)))}")
stag = sc.StaggeredSpatialDiD(exposure_distance=60, cluster="spatial", n_boot=199).fit(p2)
cells = stag.cells_
post = cells[(cells.kind == "direct") & (cells.rel_time >= 0)]
true_att = np.average(p2.truth["event_time"](post.rel_time), weights=post["size"])
r2 = stag.result_.to_frame()[["estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"]]
r2["truth"] = [true_att, -0.3, true_att]
print(f"pre-trend Wald p-value: {stag.pretrend_test_['p_value']:.3f}")
r2.round(3)

title: Panel Designs: DiD with Spillovers, Staggered Adoption, Synthetic Control
text:
Spatial synthetic control
When a single unit is treated, DiD has one treated observation per year. Synthetic control (Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller, 2010) builds a counterfactual as a weighted average of untreated donors that tracks the treated unit before treatment:
\[\hat{\mathbf w}=\arg\min_{\mathbf w}\ \sum_{t<T_0}\Big(Y_{1t}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}w_jY_{jt}\Big)^2
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad w_j\ge0,\ \sum_jw_j=1,\]
\[\hat\tau_t=Y_{1t}-\sum_j\hat w_jY_{jt}\ (t\ge T_0),\qquad \widehat{\text{ATT}}=\frac{1}{T-T_0}\sum_{t\ge T_0}\hat\tau_t .\]
The weights are solved as non-negative least squares with a heavily weighted sum-to-one row, which is exact to ~\(1/M\) and fast enough for hundreds of donors and placebos.
The spatial problem. Neighbours share regional trends, so they are the best-fitting donors, and also the ones a local policy spills onto. A contaminated donor carries part of the effect into the counterfactual and pulls the estimate toward zero. The spatial version drops donors within a buffer distance of the treated unit, estimates the spillover onto each excluded neighbour (each gets its own synthetic control from the far donors), and reports how the estimate changes with the buffer.
Inference: in-space placebos. Re-run the method pretending each donor was treated and compare post/pre fit ratios, \(\rho_j=\text{RMSPE}_{\text{post},j}/\text{RMSPE}_{\text{pre},j}\). The permutation p-value is the rank of the treated unit’s ratio among all placebos.


Code
p3, g3 = cc.scenario_synthetic_control(seed=32)
near = p3.truth["spillover_by_unit"] != 0
units = list(p3.units)
print(p3, f"\n{near.sum()} counties within 120 km of the treated county receive spillover")
rows, fits = {}, {}
for b in (0, 120):
    m = sc.SpatialSyntheticControl(buffer=b).fit(p3)
    fits[b] = m
    wn = m.weights_[[u for u in m.weights_.index if near[units.index(u)]]].sum()
    rows[f"buffer {b} km"] = {"ATT": m.att_, "permutation p": m.p_value_, "pre-period RMSPE": m.pre_rmspe_,
                              "weight on contaminated donors": wn, "donors": len(m.donors_)}
print("true ATT: -1.0")
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

correlation of estimated and true spillover: 0.34









Without a buffer the best-fitting donors are contaminated neighbours: about half the weight goes to counties that received spillover, and the estimate is pulled toward zero. A 120 km buffer removes them and recovers the effect. The cost shows in the buffer curve: far donors fit the pre-period less well.
Look at the permutation p-values: the biased no-buffer estimate looks significant (p ≈ 0.05), while the accurate buffered estimate does not (p ≈ 0.37). The ratio statistic divides by pre-period fit. With only 7 pre-treatment years and ~200 donors, a near-perfect pre-fit (RMSPE ≈ 0 without a buffer) makes the treated unit’s ratio enormous. So the p-value reflects fit quality as much as effect size, and here it rewards precisely the contaminated donors that bias the estimate. Synthetic control inference needs long pre-periods; with short ones, judge the estimate by its robustness to the buffer rather than by the p-value.

title: Panel Designs: DiD with Spillovers, Staggered Adoption, Synthetic Control
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Untreated neighbours make bad controls. Ring models turn their contamination into estimated spillovers and leave a clean control group.
With staggered adoption, estimate group-time effects with clean (unexposed, not-yet-treated) controls; static TWFE is biased.
Synthetic control favours neighbours, which are exactly the donors a local policy contaminates. Use a buffer, estimate spillovers on the excluded units, and show buffer sensitivity.

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Overview
The previous notebooks fought confounding and interference after the fact. A randomised experiment removes confounding by design, but with spillovers the design must also control exposure. Here we plan a hypothetical trial of the CHW program across counties of seven Deep-South states, using real county locations and real diabetes residuals to calibrate the outcome variability.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 3 (core, spatial analysis and spatial statistics): pip install "geolattice[statistics]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geolattice.spatial_analysis.spatialcausal as sc, countycausal as cc, tutorial_style as ts
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.weights import Queen

states = ["MS", "AL", "GA", "LA", "AR", "TN", "SC"]

reg = g[g.state_abbr.isin(states)].reset_index(drop=True)
xy = cc.coords_km(reg)
Xr = reg[cc.COVARIATES].to_numpy()
wr = Queen(reg)
exposure = sc.ExposureMapping(wr, kind="share", threshold=0.5)

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
section: Calibrating outcome variability from real data
text:
Calibrating outcome variability from real data
Power depends on how variable the outcome is after adjusting for what we know, and on how far that variability is spatially correlated. We regress real diabetes prevalence on the covariates and look at the residuals.


Code
from geolattice.spatial_statistics.esda import Moran
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(reg)), Xr])
res = reg.diabetes_pct.to_numpy() - A @ np.linalg.lstsq(A, reg.diabetes_pct.to_numpy(), rcond=None)[0]
mi = Moran(res, wr, permutations=199, seed=0)
print(f"residual SD = {res.std():.2f} points; Moran's I of residuals = {mi.I:.2f}")
SIGMA, SPATIAL_SD, LENGTH = 0.7 * res.std(), 0.7 * res.std(), 150.0     # iid + smooth (150 km) parts
print(f"simulation noise: iid SD {SIGMA:.2f} + spatial SD {SPATIAL_SD:.2f} (length scale {LENGTH:.0f} km)")


residual SD = 0.54 points; Moran's I of residuals = 0.31
simulation noise: iid SD 0.38 + spatial SD 0.38 (length scale 150 km)

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Cluster randomisation and buffer zones
Randomising clusters of neighbouring counties (here k-means clusters of centroids) means most counties share their neighbours’ assignment, so spillovers stay within arms. Counties on a cluster edge still border the other arm. A buffer of distance \(b\) excludes from analysis every county whose \(b\)-neighbourhood contains the other arm. If spillovers reach no further than \(b\), each analysed county’s exposure equals its own cluster’s assignment, and the comparison estimates the total effect (own + neighbourhood) cleanly (cf. graph cluster randomisation, Ugander et al., 2013).
Variance. With \(G\) clusters of size \(m\) and intra-cluster correlation \(\rho\), the variance of a difference in means is inflated by the design effect \(1+(m-1)\rho\) relative to unit randomisation. Inference must use the cluster as the unit: cluster-robust standard errors with a \(t_{G-1}\) reference distribution.


Code
crd = sc.ClusterRandomizedDesign(xy, n_clusters=40, buffer=40.0, random_state=1)
t_c = crd.sample(rng=3)
mask = crd.analysis_mask(t_c)
reg["arm"] = np.where(~mask, 2, t_c)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4.8))
reg["cluster"] = crd.clusters
reg.plot(ax=ax[0], color="#f0efec", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2)
reg.dissolve("cluster").boundary.plot(ax=ax[0], color=ts.INK2, linewidth=0.9)
ax[0].set_axis_off(); ax[0].set_title("40 randomisation clusters (k-means of county centroids)")
ts.county_map(reg, "arm", ax[1], categorical=True, colors=["#9ec5f4", ts.BLUE, "#e4e3df"],
              legend_labels=["control (analysed)", "treated (analysed)", "buffer: excluded from analysis"],
              title=f"Assignment and 40 km buffer: {mask.mean():.0%} of counties analysed")
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"average share analysed over 30 draws: {crd.interior_share(30, rng=0):.2f}")


average share analysed over 30 draws: 0.79

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Two-stage randomised saturation
To measure spillovers, vary how intensively each cluster is treated (Baird et al., 2018). Stage one randomises clusters to saturation levels \(\pi\in\{0,\ 0.33,\ 0.67\}\); stage two treats each county in a cluster with probability \(\pi\). Untreated counties in partially treated clusters versus counties in pure-control clusters identify the spillover on the untreated, and comparing saturations traces how spillovers grow with treatment intensity.


Code
sat = sc.SaturationDesign(xy, n_clusters=40, saturations=(0.0, 0.33, 0.67), random_state=1)
t_s, s_s = sat.unit_saturation(rng=5)
reg["sat"] = np.round(s_s, 2)
reg["t_s"] = t_s
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4.8))
ts.county_map(reg, "sat", ax[0], categorical=True, colors=["#e4e3df", "#9ec5f4", ts.BLUE],
              legend_labels=["saturation 0", "saturation 0.33", "saturation 0.67"], title="Stage 1: cluster saturation")
ts.county_map(reg, "t_s", ax[1], categorical=True, colors=["#e4e3df", ts.BLUE],
              legend_labels=["untreated", "treated"], title="Stage 2: county assignment")
plt.tight_layout()

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Balanced allocation and rerandomisation
GRTS (generalised random tessellation stratified sampling; Stevens & Olsen, 2004) orders units along a randomised hierarchical (quadtree) address and takes a systematic sample through cumulative inclusion probabilities. Every county keeps its intended probability \(\pi_i=n_T/n\), so design-based inference stays valid, but treated counties are spread evenly over space. We use geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.grts.
Rerandomisation (Morgan & Rubin, 2012) draws assignments until balance criteria hold, here every covariate’s standardised mean difference
\[\text{SMD}_k=\frac{|\bar x_{k,T}-\bar x_{k,C}|}{s_k}\le0.08\]
and Moran’s I of the assignment at most 0. The analysis must then use randomisation inference over the accepted assignments.
The diagnostics compare four designs on the same 30% treated share.


Code
n_t = int(0.3 * len(reg))
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
t_srs = np.zeros(len(reg), int); t_srs[rng.choice(len(reg), n_t, replace=False)] = 1
t_grts = sc.balanced_allocation(xy, n_t, seed=11)
t_rr, info = sc.rerandomize(xy, Xr, n_t, max_smd=0.08, max_moran=0.0, w=wr, n_draws=3000, seed=11)
t_cl = sc.ClusterRandomizedDesign(xy, n_clusters=40, p=0.3, random_state=1).sample(rng=4)
rows = {}
for name, t in [("simple random", t_srs), ("GRTS (spatially balanced)", t_grts),
                ("rerandomised", t_rr), ("cluster (40 clusters)", t_cl)]:
    d = sc.design_diagnostics(t, xy, Xr, wr, exposure=exposure, names=cc.COVARIATES)
    rows[name] = {"treated share": d["treated_share"], "max |SMD|": d["balance"].max(),
                  "Moran's I of T": d["moran"]["I"], **{f"n {k}": v for k, v in d["exposure_counts"].items()}}
print(f"rerandomisation acceptance rate: {info['acceptance_rate']:.2%} "
      f"({len(info['accepted'])} accepted assignments form the randomisation-inference reference set)")

GRTS and rerandomisation spread treatment out (negative Moran’s I), which minimises exposure contamination and gives few treated-high-exposure counties. Cluster assignment does the opposite: treatment is strongly clustered, nearly all treated counties are highly exposed, and nearly all controls are not. Which is better depends on the estimand: dispersed designs suit direct effects, clustered designs suit total (policy-scale) effects.

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Power by simulation
Analytic power formulas break down with spillovers and spatially correlated outcomes, so we simulate. Each replicate draws an assignment from the design and outcomes
\[Y_i=\tau_{\text{dir}}T_i+\delta\,H_i+\underbrace{\sigma\,\varepsilon_i+\sigma_s\,f(s_i)}_{\text{iid + smooth noise}},\]
with \(H_i\) the high-exposure indicator, then estimates the effect with cluster-robust SEs and tests at 5% using \(t_{G-1}\). Power is the rejection rate under the alternative. Size (the rejection rate with all effects set to 0) checks that the test itself is valid.


Code
common = dict(sigma=SIGMA, spatial_sd=SPATIAL_SD, length_scale=LENGTH, exposure=exposure, n_sims=200, seed=1)
pc = sc.power_curve(lambda G: sc.ClusterRandomizedDesign(xy, n_clusters=G, random_state=1), xy,
                    [10, 20, 40, 80, 160], direct=0.15, spillover=0.10, estimand="total", **common)

Each cluster contributes roughly one independent draw of the regional noise, so power rises with the number of clusters \(G\), not with the number of counties, which stays fixed at 588. The mean estimate also drifts down with many small clusters: no buffer is used here, so more counties sit on cluster edges where neighbourhood exposure does not match own assignment, diluting the total-effect contrast (true value 0.25 only for fully “interior” counties). The size_warning column flags designs whose null rejection rate is clearly above 5%; none is flagged here.
Spillover power: saturation versus unit randomisation.

rows = {}
for name, des in [("saturation, 40 clusters", sc.SaturationDesign(xy, n_clusters=40, random_state=1)),

For spillovers, independent county-level assignment has the most power because every county is a cluster of one. Saturation designs give up power in exchange for controlled variation in exposure intensity and a pure-control arm. But look at the size column: every design over-rejects (about 10-13% instead of 5%) and carries a size warning. The noise is correlated over ~150 km, so nearby counties (or nearby clusters) are not independent, and the spillover contrast compares groups that are spatially interleaved, which these standard errors ignore. The reported power is therefore optimistic. Larger clusters, buffers, or spatially robust (Conley) variance would be needed before trusting these designs for a spillover hypothesis.

title: Designing Spatial Experiments
text:
Summary and Conclusions

Match the design to the estimand. Dispersed (GRTS, rerandomised) assignments suit direct effects; clustered assignments suit total effects; saturation designs identify spillovers by intensity.
Buffers make exposure match assignment but discard counties; check what share remains.
Power with spatial outcomes is driven by the number of clusters, not the number of counties.
Always simulate the size of the test as well as its power. A design whose test over-rejects overstates its power.

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Overview
The haor basin of north-east Bangladesh is a bowl of wetlands, rice fields and villages between the Meghalaya hills of India to the north and the Meghna river system to the south. It floods every year. In the dry season (December to April) the haor beds are drained and planted with boro rice; from May onward, rain over the hills and over the basin fills them again. When intense pre-monsoon or monsoon rain comes early, the water arrives before the harvest, as a flash flood, and both crops and homesteads are lost.
A flood susceptibility map answers one question: where is water most likely to stand when a large flood occurs, given the terrain, soils and land? It does not say when or how deep, so it is a planning tool for embankments, shelters and crop calendars, not a forecast.
This capstone builds that map for a 1,962 km² window over the Sunamganj and Netrakona haors at 250 m resolution, using

a Sentinel-1 radar flood map from the 2025 monsoon as the flood inventory (training and test data);
national 250 m layers of elevation, land type, soil drainage, permeability and texture, 1 km NDVI and water-table depth for 2020, the LGED river network and a 2020 population grid;
dekadal rainfall by district (a CHIRPS-based subnational table) to put the 2025 event in context.

Three families of model are built and compared, following Module 03: a bivariate statistical model (frequency ratio), a knowledge-driven multi-criteria model (AHP-weighted fuzzy overlay) and machine learning (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting).

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
The flood inventory from Sentinel-1

Water from backscatter
Calm open water reflects radar away from the sensor, so it is dark in Sentinel-1 VH backscatter, typically below -22 dB, while fields, trees and villages return -18 to -10 dB. The folder holds a before and an after VH image (30 m, in dB) and the change-detection flood map made from them (sylhet_flood_extent.tif, 1 = backscatter fell sharply between the two dates). The file names do not record which two of the four scenes were used.
A susceptibility map needs where water stood at the peak, not only where backscatter dropped: haor beds already under water on the first date did not darken further, and the change map calls them dry. So the inventory is rebuilt here from the after image alone, with a threshold chosen by Otsu’s method (the value that best separates the two modes of the histogram), and compared with the change map.


Code
before, _, _ = dp.read_band(S1 / "output" / "sylhet_before_vh_db.tif")
after, _, _ = dp.read_band(S1 / "output" / "sylhet_after_vh_db.tif")
change, _, _ = dp.read_band(S1 / "output" / "sylhet_flood_extent.tif")
for arr in (before, after):
    arr[arr < -100] = np.nan  # -9999 fill outside the swath


def otsu(values, bins=256):
    """Otsu threshold: maximise the between-class variance of a 1-D sample."""
    v = values[np.isfinite(values)]
    hist, edges = np.histogram(v, bins=bins)
    centres = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2
    w0 = np.cumsum(hist)
    w1 = w0[-1] - w0
    m0 = np.cumsum(hist * centres) / np.maximum(w0, 1)
    m1 = (np.sum(hist * centres) - np.cumsum(hist * centres)) / np.maximum(w1, 1)
    return float(centres[np.argmax(w0 * w1 * (m0 - m1) ** 2)])


T_BEFORE, T_AFTER = otsu(before), otsu(after)
water_before = np.where(np.isfinite(before), before < T_BEFORE, np.nan)
water_after = np.where(np.isfinite(after), after < T_AFTER, np.nan)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 3.6), sharey=True)
for ax, arr, t, name in zip(axes, (before, after), (T_BEFORE, T_AFTER), ("Before", "After (peak)")):
    ax.hist(arr[np.isfinite(arr)], bins=120, range=(-40, -5), color="steelblue")
    ax.axvline(t, color="crimson", lw=2, label=f"Otsu threshold {t:.1f} dB")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: VH backscatter")
    ax.set_xlabel("dB")
    ax.legend()
axes[0].set_ylabel("30 m pixels")
plt.show()

ok = np.isfinite(water_before) & np.isfinite(water_after) & np.isfinite(change)
tab = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(np.where(water_after[ok] == 1, "water at peak", "land at peak"), name="this notebook"),
                  pd.Series(np.where(change[ok] == 1, "flagged", "not flagged"), name="change-detection map"),
                  normalize=True) * 100
print(f"Open water: {np.nanmean(water_before):.0%} of pixels before, {np.nanmean(water_after):.0%} after")

Reading the comparison. About two thirds of the pixels agree. The two groups that disagree are the reason for rebuilding the inventory: water at peak but not flagged are mostly haors already flooded on the first date, and flagged but land at peak are fields that became wetter or darker without standing water. Both maps are shown below.


From 30 m pixels to 250 m labels
Each 250 m cell gets its flooded fraction, the share of its 30 m pixels that are water at the peak (computed with block_fraction, which resamples to 50 m and averages 5 x 5 blocks). A cell is labelled

flooded if at least half of it is water,
dry if at most 10 % is water,
and left out of training if it is in between (mixed cells along flood edges).

There is no separate permanent-water mask. In the haor basin almost all water in May and June is seasonal: the same beds carry boro rice from January to April. The dry-season NDVI check below confirms it.


Code
like = S1 / "output" / "sylhet_after_vh_db.tif"
FLOOD_FRAC = dp.block_fraction(water_after, like, GRID)
PRE_FRAC = dp.block_fraction(water_before, like, GRID)
CHANGE_FRAC = dp.block_fraction(np.where(np.isfinite(change), change, np.nan), like, GRID)
FLOOD_FRAC[~STUDY] = np.nan
PRE_FRAC[~STUDY] = np.nan

FLOOD_MIN, DRY_MAX = 0.5, 0.1


def make_labels(frac, flood_min=FLOOD_MIN, dry_max=DRY_MAX):
    """1 = flooded, 0 = dry, NaN = mixed or outside the study area."""
    lab = np.full(frac.shape, np.nan)
    lab[frac >= flood_min] = 1
    lab[frac <= dry_max] = 0
    lab[~STUDY | ~np.isfinite(frac)] = np.nan
    return lab


LABEL = make_labels(FLOOD_FRAC)
n_f, n_d = int(np.nansum(LABEL == 1)), int(np.nansum(LABEL == 0))
print(f"Flooded cells: {n_f:,}  dry cells: {n_d:,}  mixed (not used): {int(STUDY.sum() - n_f - n_d):,}")
print(f"Share flooded among labelled cells: {n_f / (n_f + n_d):.0%}")

im = show(axes[1], FLOOD_FRAC, "This notebook: share of open water at peak", "Blues", 0, 1)

What the inventory says. About three fifths of the basin was under open water at the peak. Dry land is confined to the north-east and north-west corners at the foot of the hills, the levees along the main channels, and the higher ground in the south-west. This high prevalence is unusual for a flood study, where flooded cells are normally a small minority; Section 10 handles it with class weights instead of discarding data.

text:
Conditioning factors

Terrain and hydrology
All terrain factors come from the 250 m DEM, processed with the GeoLattice hydrology tools of Module 03.02:








Factor
Meaning for flooding
Tool




elev
Lower land floods first
DEM


hand
Height above the nearest drainage line: how far water must rise to reach the cell
fill_depressions, d8_pointer, d8_flow_accumulation, extract_streams, elevation_above_stream


depression
Depth of the closed depression the cell sits in (filled minus original DEM): haor beds
fill_depressions


slope
Gentle slopes hold water
slope


tpi
Position relative to the mean elevation within about 10 km; negative in basins
tpi with a 41-cell window


twi
Topographic wetness index \(\ln(a / \tan\beta)\) with D-infinity flow
surface_hydrology.twi



The stream network for HAND uses a threshold of 1,000 cells (62.5 km²), which keeps the main rivers and drains of the basin. With smaller thresholds every haor gets its own channel and HAND loses contrast. Flow that leaves the 40 km window before it meets a stream is measured against the grid edge where it leaves.


Code

dem = dem_raw.copy()
bad = ~np.isfinite(dem) | (dem < 0)
idx = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(bad, return_distances=False, return_indices=True)
dem = dem[tuple(idx)]  # nearest-valid fill for artefacts and the area outside Bangladesh
F = OUT / "factors"
F.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# treated as drainage too, so that every cell gets a height above its outlet.

The LGED river layer maps every river and khal (canal) of the country. Two factors come from it: distance to the nearest mapped channel and drainage density (km of channel per km² in a 2.75 km window).

Soil and land
The national soil-survey rasters are categorical. Their codes are documented in IDFILES/.

How well does each factor separate flooded from dry cells on its own?

Elevation, HAND and TPI are strongly correlated, as expected: all three measure how high a cell sits. Variance inflation factors stay below the usual alarm level of 10 (elevation comes closest, at about 9.8), so all are kept. Tree models are not hurt by correlated predictors; for the logistic model it means the individual coefficients should not be interpreted.


Frequency ratio by class
The frequency ratio (FR) of a class is the share of flooded cells that fall in the class divided by the share of all labelled cells that fall in it. FR > 1 means the class floods more often than average. Continuous factors are split into deciles of the study area.


Code
def classes_of(name):
    """Integer classes: deciles for continuous factors, codes for categorical ones."""
    if name in CAT:
        return np.where(np.isfinite(CAT[name]), CAT[name], -1).astype(int)
    v = FACT[name]
    edges = np.unique(np.nanpercentile(v[STUDY], np.arange(10, 100, 10)))
    return np.digitize(v, edges)


FR_FACTORS = ["elev", "hand", "depression", "slope", "tpi", "twi", "ndvi_dry", "wt_premonsoon", "LT", "DRC", "SPC",
              "TEX", "LU"]
CLASSES = {k: classes_of(k) for k in FR_FACTORS}


def fr_table(name, mask):
    """Frequency ratio of each class of one factor, from the labelled cells inside ``mask``."""
    c, lab = CLASSES[name][mask & LAB], LABEL[mask & LAB]
    df = pd.DataFrame({"c": c, "y": lab}).groupby("c").y.agg(["sum", "count"])
    share_f = (df["sum"] + 0.5) / (df["sum"].sum() + 0.5 * len(df))  # add-half smoothing for empty classes
    share_a = df["count"] / df["count"].sum()
    return np.log(share_f / share_a)  # log FR: 0 = average, > 0 = floods more often


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 3.6))
for ax, k in zip(axes, ["elev", "hand", "tpi", "LT"]):
    t = np.exp(fr_table(k, STUDY))
    labels = [LT_NAMES.get(i, i) for i in t.index] if k == "LT" else [f"D{i + 1}" for i in t.index]
    ax.bar(range(len(t)), t.values, color=np.where(t.values > 1, "tab:blue", "tab:brown"))
    ax.axhline(1, color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(t)), labels, rotation=60 if k == "LT" else 0, ha="right" if k == "LT" else "center",
                  fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"Frequency ratio: {k}")
axes[0].set_ylabel("FR")
plt.show()









The lowest elevation and HAND deciles reach a frequency ratio of about 1.4, close to the ceiling of 1.45 that a 69 % flooded share allows (1 / 0.69): nearly every cell there flooded. The top deciles almost never did. Land type behaves as the soil survey intends: highland is rarely flooded, very lowland nearly always.

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Model 1: frequency ratio
The flood susceptibility index (FSI) of a cell is the sum of the log frequency ratios of its classes over all factors. It is the simplest data-driven model: each factor is judged on its own and the evidence is added. Land type is left out, for the leakage reason given in Section 6.3.
The machine-learning models in Section 10 are tested on 5 km blocks they did not see. For a fair comparison the frequency ratios are recomputed from the training blocks of each fold in the same way, in Section 10.2; here they are fitted on all labelled cells to draw the map.


Code
FR_USE = [k for k in FR_FACTORS if k != "LT"]


def fsi(mask_fit):
    """Flood susceptibility index for every cell, with frequency ratios from ``mask_fit``."""
    out = np.zeros(GRID.shape)
    for k in FR_USE:
        t = fr_table(k, mask_fit)
        out += pd.Series(CLASSES[k].ravel()).map(t).fillna(0).values.reshape(GRID.shape)
    return out


SCORE = {"FrequencyRatio": fsi(STUDY)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
im = show(ax, SCORE["FrequencyRatio"], "Frequency-ratio susceptibility index", "inferno")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.035)
plt.show()

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Model 2: AHP multi-criteria model
The expert model does not look at the inventory. Each criterion is turned into a fuzzy membership between 0 (not flood-prone) and 1 (highly flood-prone), and the memberships are combined with weights from the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP).








Criterion
Membership
Reasoning




elev
small, midpoint 9 m
the basin floor lies at 2 to 8 m; levees and terraces above 10 m


hand
small, midpoint 2 m
a 2 m rise above the nearest drain is a common monsoon stage


depression
linear, 0 to 3 m
closed depressions hold water until it evaporates or is pumped


tpi
small, midpoint -1 m
below the 10 km mean elevation


twi
large, midpoint 10
wet, convergent cells


drainage
class scores
poorly and very poorly drained soils stay wet



The judgments put the two measures of relative height first, as the flood literature for deltas does.


Code
CRITERIA = ["hand", "elev", "depression", "tpi", "drainage", "twi"]
JUDGMENTS = {
    ("hand", "elev"): 1, ("hand", "depression"): 2, ("hand", "tpi"): 3, ("hand", "drainage"): 4, ("hand", "twi"): 5,
    ("elev", "depression"): 2, ("elev", "tpi"): 3, ("elev", "drainage"): 4, ("elev", "twi"): 5,
    ("depression", "tpi"): 2, ("depression", "drainage"): 3, ("depression", "twi"): 3,
    ("tpi", "drainage"): 2, ("tpi", "twi"): 2,
    ("drainage", "twi"): 1,
}
RANDOM_INDEX = {1: 0.0, 2: 0.0, 3: 0.58, 4: 0.90, 5: 1.12, 6: 1.24, 7: 1.32, 8: 1.41, 9: 1.45, 10: 1.49}


def ahp(criteria, judgments):
    """AHP weights (principal eigenvector) and consistency ratio for a reciprocal matrix."""
    n = len(criteria)
    A = np.ones((n, n))
    for (a, b), v in judgments.items():
        i, j = criteria.index(a), criteria.index(b)
        A[i, j], A[j, i] = v, 1.0 / v
    vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
    k = np.argmax(vals.real)
    w = np.abs(vecs[:, k].real)
    w = w / w.sum()
    ci = (vals[k].real - n) / (n - 1)
    return pd.Series(w, index=criteria), A, ci / RANDOM_INDEX[n]


W_AHP, A_MATRIX, CR = ahp(CRITERIA, JUDGMENTS)
