title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Model 3: machine learning

Predictors and design
The predictors are the ten numeric factors and the categorical layers drainage, permeability, texture and land use, one-hot encoded. Two feature sets are fitted:

base: without land type;
+LT: with land type, to measure how much it adds and how much of that is leakage.

All labelled cells are used (about 27,000). Because 69 % are flooded, the logistic model and random forest weight the classes inversely to their frequency, and gradient boosting uses the same weights.


Code
def one_hot(name, codes):
    v = CAT[name][LAB_ALL]
    return pd.DataFrame({f"{name}_{int(c)}": (v == c).astype(np.int8) for c in codes})


LAB_ALL = STUDY  # build the design matrix for every study cell, then select rows
CAT_ML = ["DRC", "SPC", "TEX", "LU"]
CODES = {k: [c for c in np.unique(CAT[k][STUDY & np.isfinite(CAT[k])])
             if np.sum(CAT[k][STUDY] == c) >= 50] for k in CAT_ML + ["LT"]}
X_num = pd.DataFrame({k: FACT[k][STUDY] for k in NUM})
X_cat = pd.concat([one_hot(k, CODES[k]) for k in CAT_ML], axis=1)
X_lt = one_hot("LT", CODES["LT"])
X_SETS = {"base": pd.concat([X_num, X_cat], axis=1), "+LT": pd.concat([X_num, X_cat, X_lt], axis=1)}
for k, X in X_SETS.items():
    print(f"{k}: {X.shape[1]} predictors")

y_study = LABEL[STUDY]
use = np.isfinite(y_study)  # labelled rows of the study-cell table
y = y_study[use].astype(int)
rows_, cols_ = np.nonzero(STUDY)
BLOCK_KM = 5
blocks = (rows_ // int(BLOCK_KM * 1000 / GRID.res)) * 1000 + cols_ // int(BLOCK_KM * 1000 / GRID.res)
groups = blocks[use]
weights = np.where(y == 1, 0.5 / y.mean(), 0.5 / (1 - y.mean()))
print(f"Labelled cells: {use.sum():,} in {len(np.unique(groups))} blocks of {BLOCK_KM} km")


base: 39 predictors
+LT: 46 predictors
Labelled cells: 26,994 in 90 blocks of 5 km




Spatial cross-validation
Neighbouring cells are almost copies of each other, so a random split would test the model on cells it has effectively seen. Instead the 5 km blocks are split into five folds (GroupKFold): each model is always scored on blocks it never saw. Out-of-fold predictions are kept for the validation in Section 12. The frequency-ratio model is refitted on the training blocks of every fold; the AHP model is not fitted at all and is scored on the same test cells.


Code
def make_models():
    return {
        "Logistic": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=3000)),
        "RandomForest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, max_features="sqrt",
                                               n_jobs=-1, random_state=1),
        "GradientBoosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.06, max_iter=300,
                                                           l2_regularization=1.0, random_state=1),
    }


def tss_max(y_true, p):
    """Maximum true skill statistic (sensitivity + specificity - 1) over all thresholds."""
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, p)
    return float(np.max(tpr - fpr))


N_FOLDS = 5
FOLDS = list(GroupKFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS).split(np.zeros(len(y)), y, groups))
lab_idx = np.flatnonzero(use)  # positions of labelled rows in the study table
OOF = {}
rows = []
t0 = time.time()
for fs, X in X_SETS.items():
    XA = X.values.astype(np.float32)[use]
    for name in make_models():
        OOF[(name, fs)] = np.full(len(y), np.nan)
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(FOLDS):
        for name, model in make_models().items():
            fit_kw = {f"{model.steps[-1][0]}__sample_weight" if name == "Logistic" else "sample_weight": weights[tr]}
            p = model.fit(XA[tr], y[tr], **fit_kw).predict_proba(XA[te])[:, 1]
            OOF[(name, fs)][te] = p
            rows.append((fs, k, name, roc_auc_score(y[te], p), tss_max(y[te], p)))

# Frequency ratio refitted per fold, and the unfitted AHP model, on the same test cells.
OOF[("FrequencyRatio", "base")] = np.full(len(y), np.nan)
for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(FOLDS):
    fit_mask = np.zeros(GRID.shape, bool)
    fit_mask[rows_[lab_idx[tr]], cols_[lab_idx[tr]]] = True
    p = fsi(fit_mask)[rows_[lab_idx[te]], cols_[lab_idx[te]]]
    OOF[("FrequencyRatio", "base")][te] = p
    rows.append(("base", k, "FrequencyRatio", roc_auc_score(y[te], p), tss_max(y[te], p)))
    p = SCORE["AHP-MCDA"][rows_[lab_idx[te]], cols_[lab_idx[te]]]
    rows.append(("base", k, "AHP-MCDA", roc_auc_score(y[te], p), tss_max(y[te], p)))
OOF[("AHP-MCDA", "base")] = SCORE["AHP-MCDA"][rows_[lab_idx], cols_[lab_idx]]

cv = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["features", "fold", "model", "AUC", "TSS"])
print(f"Cross-validation: {len(cv)} scores in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
perf = cv.groupby(["model", "features"])[["AUC", "TSS"]].agg(["mean", "std"])
perf = perf.sort_values(("AUC", "mean"), ascending=False)

Reading the cross-validation. All models rank held-out flooded cells well above held-out dry ones. Final models and susceptibility maps
Each model is refitted on all labelled cells and applied to every study cell.


Code
t0 = time.time()
XA_all = X_SETS["base"].values.astype(np.float32)
FITTED = {}
for name, model in make_models().items():
    fit_kw = {f"{model.steps[-1][0]}__sample_weight" if name == "Logistic" else "sample_weight": weights}
    model.fit(XA_all[use], y, **fit_kw)
    FITTED[name] = model
    out = np.full(GRID.shape, np.nan)
    out[STUDY] = model.predict_proba(XA_all)[:, 1]
    SCORE[name] = out
print(f"Final fits and predictions in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")


def pct_rank(arr):
    """Percentile rank (0 to 1) of every study cell, so that all models share one scale."""
    out = np.full(GRID.shape, np.nan)
    out[STUDY] = pd.Series(arr[STUDY]).rank(pct=True).values
    return out


PCT = {k: pct_rank(v) for k, v in SCORE.items()}
PCT["Ensemble"] = pct_rank((PCT["RandomForest"] + PCT["GradientBoosting"]) / 2)

Comparing the maps. All six agree on the structure: the basin floor is highly susceptible, the piedmont, levees and southern terraces are not. They differ in texture. The frequency-ratio and AHP maps follow the DEM, and the AHP map is noisier because drainage class and TWI change from cell to cell. title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
What drives susceptibility?
Permutation importance measures how much the held-out AUC of the random forest falls when one predictor is shuffled; one-hot columns of a layer are shuffled together. Partial dependence shows the average modelled response to one predictor.


Code
tr, te = FOLDS[0]
XA = XA_all[use]
rf_imp = make_models()["RandomForest"].fit(XA[tr], y[tr], sample_weight=weights[tr])
FEATS = X_SETS["base"].columns.tolist()
layer_of = {c: (c.split("_")[0] if c.split("_")[0] in CAT_ML else c) for c in FEATS}
base_auc = roc_auc_score(y[te], rf_imp.predict_proba(XA[te])[:, 1])
imp = {}
for layer in dict.fromkeys(layer_of.values()):
    cols = [FEATS.index(c) for c, l in layer_of.items() if l == layer]
    drops = []
    for rep in range(3):
        Xp = XA[te].copy()
        Xp[:, cols] = Xp[RNG.permutation(len(Xp))][:, cols]
        drops.append(base_auc - roc_auc_score(y[te], rf_imp.predict_proba(Xp)[:, 1]))
    imp[layer] = np.mean(drops)
imp = pd.Series(imp).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"Held-out AUC of this fit: {base_auc:.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.7]})
axes[0].barh(imp.index[::-1], imp.values[::-1], color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Drop in held-out AUC when shuffled")
axes[0].set_title("Random forest: permutation importance")

rf = FITTED["RandomForest"]
sample = XA_all[RNG.choice(len(XA_all), 3000, replace=False)]
for name, col in zip([c for c in imp.index if c in NUM][:4], ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green", "tab:red"]):
    j = FEATS.index(name)
    q = np.nanpercentile(XA_all[:, j], [2, 98])
    xs = np.linspace(*q, 30)
    resp = []
    for v in xs:
        Xs_ = sample.copy()
        Xs_[:, j] = v
        resp.append(rf.predict_proba(Xs_)[:, 1].mean())
    axes[1].plot((xs - q[0]) / (q[1] - q[0]), resp, color=col, lw=2, label=f"{name}: {q[0]:.1f} to {q[1]:.1f}")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Position within the 2nd to 98th percentile range of the factor")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Mean predicted probability of flooding")
axes[1].set_title("Partial dependence (random forest)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Held-out AUC of this fit: 0.967









Elevation dominates by a wide margin, and its response is a threshold: the predicted probability is high below about 8 m and falls steeply over the next 2 to 3 m. HAND comes next, adding the local picture (a cell 2 m above the nearest drain floods less than one at the same absolute height beside it), followed by soil drainage class and land use. TWI, slope and the river-network factors add almost nothing once elevation is known.

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Validation of all models

ROC curves and prediction-rate curves
Two complementary views of the out-of-fold predictions:

ROC curve and AUC: how well each model separates flooded from dry cells over all thresholds.
Success and prediction rate curves, standard in susceptibility mapping: rank all labelled cells from most to least susceptible and plot the cumulative share of flooded cells against the cumulative share of cells. The success rate uses the final model on the cells it was fitted to; the prediction rate uses out-of-fold predictions. A steeper curve is better, and a large gap between the two signals overfitting.



Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.5))
for m in MODELS[:-1]:
    p = OOF[(m, "base")]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p)
    axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{m} (AUC {roc_auc_score(y, p):.3f})")
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("False positive rate")
axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
axes[0].set_title("ROC, out-of-fold (held-out blocks)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)


def rate_curve(score, yy):
    order = np.argsort(-score)
    return np.linspace(0, 1, len(yy)), np.cumsum(yy[order]) / yy.sum()


rows = []
for m, col in zip(["FrequencyRatio", "AHP-MCDA", "RandomForest", "GradientBoosting"],
                  ["tab:orange", "tab:green", "tab:blue", "tab:red"]):
    x, s = rate_curve(SCORE[m][STUDY][use], y)
    x, pr = rate_curve(OOF[(m, "base")], y)
    axes[1].plot(x, s, color=col, ls=":", lw=1.5)
    axes[1].plot(x, pr, color=col, lw=2, label=m)
    rows.append((m, np.trapezoid(s, x), np.trapezoid(pr, x)))
axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Cumulative share of labelled cells, most susceptible first")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Cumulative share of flooded cells")
axes[1].set_title("Prediction rate (solid) and success rate (dotted)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

Because 69 % of the labelled cells are flooded, even a perfect model reaches all flooded cells only after 69 % of the cells, so the area under these curves cannot exceed about 0.65 (1 minus 0.69 / 2). Susceptibility classes and model agreement
Each map is cut into five equal-area classes (quintiles of the study area): very low, low, moderate, high and very high. Equal-area classes make the models directly comparable, and the share of each class that actually flooded should rise steadily from very low to very high.

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Uncertainty
Three sources of uncertainty are examined:

AHP weights. monte_carlo_weights draws 500 weight vectors from a Dirichlet distribution around the AHP weights and reports how often each cell stays in the top 40 % (the high and very-high classes).
Label thresholds. The flooded label needs at least 50 % open water. The random forest is cross-validated again with 30 % and 70 %, and the very-high classes are compared with jaccard_index.
Method. The Jaccard overlap of the very-high classes of each pair of models.



Code
M = np.stack([MEMBERS[k][STUDY] for k in CRITERIA])
t0 = time.time()
mc = monte_carlo_weights(M, W_AHP.values, kappa=50.0, n=500, batch=50, top_q=0.6, seed=11)
p_top = np.full(GRID.shape, np.nan)
p_top[STUDY] = mc["p_top"]
print(f"Monte Carlo weights in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s; median Jaccard of top-40 % sets vs AHP baseline "
      f"{np.median(mc['jaccard']):.2f}")

rows = []
top_ref = CLS["RandomForest"][STUDY] == 4
for fmin in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7):
    lab_t = make_labels(FLOOD_FRAC, flood_min=fmin)[STUDY]
    u = np.isfinite(lab_t)
    yt = lab_t[u].astype(int)
    wt_ = np.where(yt == 1, 0.5 / yt.mean(), 0.5 / (1 - yt.mean()))
    gt = blocks[u]
    aucs = []
    for tr, te in GroupKFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS).split(np.zeros(len(yt)), yt, gt):
        mdl = make_models()["RandomForest"].set_params(n_estimators=150)
        p = mdl.fit(XA_all[u][tr], yt[tr], sample_weight=wt_[tr]).predict_proba(XA_all[u][te])[:, 1]
        aucs.append(roc_auc_score(yt[te], p))
    mdl = make_models()["RandomForest"].set_params(n_estimators=150).fit(XA_all[u], yt, sample_weight=wt_)
    pr = mdl.predict_proba(XA_all)[:, 1]
    top = pr >= np.quantile(pr, 0.8)
    rows.append((f">= {fmin:.0%} water", u.sum(), yt.mean(), np.mean(aucs), jaccard_index(top, top_ref)))
display(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["flooded label", "labelled cells", "share flooded", "spatial-CV AUC",
                                    "Jaccard of very-high class vs 50 % run"]).set_index("flooded label").round(3))

jac = pd.DataFrame(index=MODELS[:-1], columns=MODELS[:-1], dtype=float)
for a in MODELS[:-1]:
    for b in MODELS[:-1]:
        jac.loc[a, b] = jaccard_index(CLS[a][STUDY] == 4, CLS[b][STUDY] == 4)
display(jac.round(2).rename_axis(columns="Jaccard of very-high classes"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 7))
im = show(ax, p_top, "AHP: probability of staying in the top 40 % under weight uncertainty", "YlGn", 0, 1)

Two findings stand out. title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Limitations

A 250 m DEM in a flat basin. Relief across the AOI is about 15 m. Village platforms, embankments and channels are narrower than one cell, so the maps describe neighbourhoods, not individual plots. Because elevation dominates, errors in the national DEM pass straight into every model.
One season of labels. The inventory is one flood peak in one year. A large but different event, such as an April flash flood before the boro harvest, can flood land in a different order. Several years of radar would turn the single map into a flood frequency.
What radar misses. Water under dense vegetation and in built-up areas can look like land in VH backscatter, and wind-roughened water can look like land too. The Otsu threshold is a single global value.
Mixed seasons of the factors. NDVI and water table are from 2020, land use from 2020, soils from the national survey; they describe typical conditions, not 2025.
Forcing outside the AOI. The cause of the floods, rain on the Meghalaya plateau and the flow of the Surma and Kushiyara from India, lies outside the window. A susceptibility map cannot represent it; a hydrodynamic model can.
Legends. The land-use and texture rasters have no legend in the folder, so they are used as unnamed categories; the meaning of the SDC depth classes should be confirmed before it is used.

title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping in the Sylhet Haor Basin, Bangladesh
text:
Where to go next

Rebuild the inventory from all four Sentinel-1 dates (24 May, 5 June, 11 July, 16 August) and model the number of dates under water, not a single map. The raw scenes are in Sylhet_sentinel1/.
Replace the 250 m DEM with Copernicus GLO-30 or FABDEM at 30 m and compare the maps, as the landslide capstone does for its covariate grid.
Add embankments and roads from OpenStreetMap: in the haors they decide which beds fill first.
Compare the susceptibility classes with a HEC-RAS or LISFLOOD-FP inundation model driven by the 2025 rainfall.
Use the upazila exposure table with the network analysis of Module 03.05 to locate flood shelters within reach of the most exposed villages.

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Problem statement
The crop calendar. Wheat in Bangladesh is sown from about 15 November to 5 December and harvested from mid-March to early April, a season of roughly 110 to 120 days. Sowing waits until the land has drained after the monsoon; sowing late pushes grain filling into the hot second half of March.
What limits it.

Heat during grain filling (mid-February to March) is the main climatic limit. The north-west (Panchagarh, Thakurgaon, Dinajpur) has the coolest and longest winter of the country.
Land type and drainage: lowland that is still wet in November cannot be sown in time.
Soil: wheat prefers near-neutral soils; strongly acid terrace and hill soils reduce yield.
Water: two or three irrigations are needed. Shallow tubewells serve land with a shallow water table; the Barind Tract relies on deep tubewells.

Where it is grown. According to the Bangladesh Wheat and Maize Research Institute, 14 districts produce about 90 % of the country’s wheat: Thakurgaon, Chapainawabganj, Natore, Rajshahi, Pabna, Faridpur, Naogaon, Panchagarh, Meherpur, Kushtia, Rajbari, Bhola, Kurigram and Dinajpur (The Daily Star, 16 August 2025). This list is the reference for the validation in Section 13. It reflects where farmers choose wheat, which also depends on prices and on competing crops such as boro rice, maize and potato; a suitability map should agree with it broadly, not perfectly.
Question. Where in Bangladesh is land physically suitable for irrigated rabi wheat, what limits it elsewhere, and how robust is that picture?

text:
Checking the temperature grids

Mean, minimum and maximum
The folder has three temperature variables. Their names follow ERA5: t2m (mean 2 m temperature), mn2t and mx2t (minimum and maximum). In ERA5, mn2t and mx2t are the extremes within each hour, not within each day. Averaged over 16 days they stay within about a degree of the mean, so they cannot be used for daily-maximum rules such as “days above 30 °C”. The model uses t2m.


Code

A daily temperature range in Bangladesh in January is 10 to 12 °C; here mx2t - mn2t is under 3 °C, confirming that these are hourly extremes.


Which way is north?
A simple test of any climate grid is its gradient with latitude. In January, Bangladesh is coolest in the far north-west (Panchagarh and Thakurgaon, typically 15 to 17 °C) and warmest on the south-east coast (Cox’s Bazar and Teknaf, 20 to 22 °C). The grids as stored show the opposite.


Code

LAND1 = dem1 > -1000

              axis=0)

for ax, arr, title in zip(axes, (jan, np.flipud(jan)), ("As stored", "Rows reversed (north and south swapped)")):
    im = ax.imshow(arr, extent=ext1, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=13, vmax=23)
    dist.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.3", linewidth=0.25)

What this shows. As stored, the far north is the warmest part of the country in January and the coast the coldest, which is impossible. With the rows reversed, the values follow the known pattern, but the land mask no longer fits: the values were turned upside down before the files were clipped to Bangladesh. This is a common error when a NetCDF file whose latitudes run south to north is written to GeoTIFF without flipping the array. The water-table grid in the same folder does not have this problem: it is deepest under the Barind Tract (Rajshahi, Naogaon, Chapainawabganj), as expected.


Correction
The values for each land cell are recovered by reversing the rows. About a third of the land then has no value, because its mirror cell lay outside Bangladesh and was masked. Temperature at this scale is very smooth (the source reanalysis has cells of about 10 km), so the gaps are filled in two steps:

a trend: a cubic polynomial in position plus mean elevation, fitted to the recovered cells;
the residuals of the recovered cells, spread into the gaps as a Gaussian-weighted mean of nearby residuals (normalised convolution, σ = 15 km).

A hold-out test removes a 60 km wide north-south band of recovered cells, fills it the same way and compares.


Code
R1, C1 = np.indices(T_SHAPE)
Y1, X1, Z1 = R1 / T_SHAPE[0], C1 / T_SHAPE[1], np.where(LAND1, dem1, 0) / 1000


def design(m):
    return np.c_[np.ones(m.sum()), Y1[m], X1[m], Y1[m] ** 2, X1[m] ** 2, X1[m] * Y1[m], Y1[m] ** 3, Z1[m]]


def correct(stored):
    """Reverse the rows of a stored 1 km grid and fill the cells lost to masking."""
    f = np.flipud(stored)
    ok = np.isfinite(f) & LAND1
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design(ok), f[ok], rcond=None)
    trend = (design(np.ones(T_SHAPE, bool)) @ coef).reshape(T_SHAPE)
    resid = np.where(ok, f - trend, 0.0)
    # Normalised convolution: a Gaussian-weighted mean of the residuals of nearby recovered cells.
    num = ndimage.gaussian_filter(resid, 15)
    den = ndimage.gaussian_filter(ok.astype(float), 15)
    resid_fill = np.where(den > 1e-3, num / np.maximum(den, 1e-3), 0.0)
    out = np.where(ok, f, trend + resid_fill)
    out[~LAND1] = np.nan
    r2 = 1 - np.var(resid[ok]) / np.var(f[ok])
    return out, r2, ok


fixed, r2, recovered = correct(jan)
test = recovered & (C1 > 200) & (C1 < 260)
held = np.flipud(jan).copy()
held[test] = np.nan
refill, _, _ = correct(np.flipud(held))
err = refill[test] - np.flipud(jan)[test]
print(f"Trend R²: {r2:.3f}; land cells filled: {1 - recovered[LAND1].mean():.0%}")
print(f"Hold-out band: mean absolute error {np.abs(err).mean():.2f} °C, largest {np.abs(err).max():.2f} °C")


Trend R²: 0.853; land cells filled: 32%
Hold-out band: mean absolute error 0.10 °C, largest 0.77 °C


The trend explains most of the variation (R² about 0.86 for early January) and the residual fill does the rest: in the hold-out band the mean error is under 0.1 °C and the largest under 0.8 °C, far below the 3 to 4 °C differences between regions that matter for wheat. The correction is a workaround, not a fix: re-exporting the temperature series with the latitude axis handled correctly is the proper solution. The function correct checks nothing by itself, so if corrected files replace the current ones, the call to it in the next section must be removed.

Climate criteria
Two climate criteria are computed from 18 seasons (2000/01 to 2017/18) of 16-day composites. Each composite starts on the day of year in its file name.

A few December composites are missing for some years; each mean uses the composites available. The 1 km means are corrected (Section 4.3) and interpolated to the 250 m grid.


Code
SEASONS = range(2001, 2019)  # harvest years


def composite_files(doys, years=SEASONS):
    files = []
    for y in years:
        for d in doys:
            f = TEMP / "t2m" / f"t2m_{y - 1 if d >= 300 else y}_{d:03d}.tif"
            if f.exists():
                files.append(f)
    return files


def to_mem(arr1km):
    """Wrap a 1 km array as an in-memory GDAL dataset on the temperature grid."""
    mem = gdal.GetDriverByName("MEM").Create("", T_SHAPE[1], T_SHAPE[0], 1, gdal.GDT_Float32)
    mem.SetGeoTransform(T_GT)
    mem.SetProjection(T_WKT)
    band = mem.GetRasterBand(1)
    band.WriteArray(np.where(np.isfinite(arr1km), arr1km, dp.NODATA))
    band.SetNoDataValue(dp.NODATA)
    return mem


def climate_mean(doys, years=SEASONS):
    files = composite_files(doys, years)
    stored = np.mean([gdal.Open(str(f)).ReadAsArray().astype(float) for f in files], axis=0)
    fixed1, _, _ = correct(stored)
    return dp.warp_to_grid(to_mem(fixed1), GRID, resample="bilinear"), len(files)

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Land, soil and water criteria

Land type and drainage
The soil-survey land type classifies land by its normal depth of seasonal flooding. Highland and medium highland are above normal flood level or drain by October; lowland and very lowland stay wet into the dry season, too late for wheat. Drainage class describes how fast the soil dries after rain or irrigation; poorly drained soils waterlog at sowing.


Soil pH and organic carbon
Both are continuous national maps. Wheat does best at pH 6.0 to 7.5; the acid terrace soils of the Madhupur and Barind tracts and the hill soils fall below 5.5. Organic carbon is a proxy for soil fertility and structure.


Water: groundwater and drought
Irrigation in the dry season comes mostly from groundwater. The depth to the water table from February to April 2020 (the irrigation period) is the criterion. Shallow tubewells stop working below about 7 to 8 m, but wheat needs far less water than boro rice and the Barind Tract irrigates it from deep tubewells, so the membership only falls off past about 12 m. The drought class describes how prone the land is to moisture stress; it is weighted low because irrigated wheat is drought tolerant compared with transplanted rice.

AHP weights
The pairwise judgments put grain-filling heat and land type first: they decide whether wheat can be sown in time and whether it can fill its grain. Drainage and irrigation follow; soil chemistry, season temperature and drought are secondary.

    ("grainfill_T", "season_T"): 3, ("grainfill_T", "land_type"): 1, ("grainfill_T", "drainage"): 2,
    ("grainfill_T", "irrigation"): 2, ("grainfill_T", "pH"): 3, ("grainfill_T", "OC"): 5, ("grainfill_T", "drought"): 4,
    ("season_T", "land_type"): 1 / 3, ("season_T", "drainage"): 1 / 2, ("season_T", "irrigation"): 1 / 2,
    ("season_T", "pH"): 1, ("season_T", "OC"): 2, ("season_T", "drought"): 2,
    ("land_type", "drainage"): 2, ("land_type", "irrigation"): 2, ("land_type", "pH"): 3, ("land_type", "OC"): 5,
    ("land_type", "drought"): 4,
    ("drainage", "irrigation"): 1, ("drainage", "pH"): 2, ("drainage", "OC"): 3, ("drainage", "drought"): 3,
    ("irrigation", "pH"): 2, ("irrigation", "OC"): 3, ("irrigation", "drought"): 2,
    ("pH", "OC"): 2, ("pH", "drought"): 1,
    ("OC", "drought"): 1 / 2,
}
RANDOM_INDEX = {1: 0.0, 2: 0.0, 3: 0.58, 4: 0.90, 5: 1.12, 6: 1.24, 7: 1.32, 8: 1.41, 9: 1.45, 10: 1.49}


def ahp(criteria, judgments):
    """AHP weights (principal eigenvector) and consistency ratio for a reciprocal matrix."""
    n = len(criteria)
    A = np.ones((n, n))
    for (a, b), v in judgments.items():
        i, j = criteria.index(a), criteria.index(b)
        A[i, j], A[j, i] = v, 1.0 / v
    vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
    k = np.argmax(vals.real)
    w = np.abs(vecs[:, k].real)
    w = w / w.sum()
    ci = (vals[k].real - n) / (n - 1)
    return pd.Series(w, index=criteria), A, ci / RANDOM_INDEX[n]

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Combining the criteria
Three rules, from fully compensatory to not compensatory at all:

Weighted linear combination (WLC): a weighted mean. A poor score on one criterion can be offset by good scores on others.
Weighted fuzzy gamma (γ = 0.8): between the fuzzy product (all criteria must be good) and the fuzzy sum. Low scores pull the result down more than in WLC.
Limiting factor (minimum): the cell is only as suitable as its worst criterion, following Liebig’s law of the minimum and the FAO practice of classing land by its most severe limitation.



Code
def combine(members, weights):
    stack = [members[k] for k in CRITERIA]
    out = {
        "WLC": weighted_linear_combination(members, weights.to_dict()),
        "Gamma": weighted_fuzzy_overlay(stack, weights.values, gamma=0.8),
        "Minimum": np.min(np.stack(stack), axis=0),
    }
    return {k: np.where(OK, v, np.nan) for k, v in out.items()}

The break points are a choice: they are set so that S1 picks out land with no serious limitation, and their effect is tested in Section 14.

def fao_classes(score_, breaks=BREAKS):
    c = np.full(GRID.shape, np.nan)

    s = np.where(OK, score_, np.nan)
    c[OK] = 1 + np.digitize(s[OK], breaks)  # 1 = N1, 2 = S3, 3 = S2, 4 = S1
    return c

Reading the limiting factors. In N1 land the weakest criterion is mostly land type (lowland that is still wet at sowing), followed by drainage. In S3 land it is mostly drainage: the national soil map classes much of the floodplain as poorly drained. In S2 and S1 land the weak points are organic carbon and pH, criteria that liming, manure and residue management can improve. Grain-filling heat is rarely the single weakest criterion, because its membership falls gradually; its effect shows in the weighted score and in the hot-season test of Section 14.

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Validation against the wheat districts
The 14 districts named in Section 2 grow about 90 % of the country’s wheat. If the map is right, they should rank high. Two measures per district:

the mean WLC score of land passing the constraints (only for districts where at least a quarter of the land passes them; otherwise a few valley cells in the hill districts would stand for the whole district);
the share of land that is S1 or S2.

The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen wheat district scores higher than a randomly chosen other district (0.5 = no better than chance). Because farmers’ choices also depend on markets and on competing crops, a perfect score is not expected.
The model is also run with the strict water criteria an analyst might start from: irrigation falling off past 7 m (shallow-tubewell depth) and drought scored 0.2 for very severe to 1.0 for none.


Code
MAJOR = ["Thakurgaon", "Nawabganj", "Natore", "Rajshahi", "Pabna", "Faridpur", "Naogaon", "Panchagarh", "Meherpur",
         "Kushtia", "Rajbari", "Bhola", "Kurigram", "Dinajpur"]  # Nawabganj = Chapainawabganj in the boundary file


MIN_FARMLAND = 0.25  # districts with less land passing the constraints are not ranked on the mean score


def district_table(score_, cls):
    rows = []
    for i, name in enumerate(dist.ADM2_EN, start=1):
        m = (DIST_ID == i) & LAND
        ok = m & OK
        share_ok = ok.sum() / max(m.sum(), 1)
        rows.append((name, np.nanmean(score_[ok]) if share_ok >= MIN_FARMLAND else np.nan,
                     np.mean(cls[m] >= 3) * 100, share_ok * 100, name in MAJOR))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["district", "mean_score", "S1_S2_pct", "farmland_pct", "major_wheat"]) \
        .set_index("district")


strict = memberships(irrigation_midpoint=7.0, drought_table={1: 0.2, 2: 0.4, 3: 0.7, 4: 0.9, 5: 1.0})
strict_wlc = combine(strict, W_AHP)["WLC"]
RUNS = {"WLC (headline)": (SCORES["WLC"], CLS), "Gamma": (SCORES["Gamma"], fao_classes(SCORES["Gamma"], (0.4, 0.5, 0.6))),
        "Minimum": (SCORES["Minimum"], fao_classes(SCORES["Minimum"], (0.3, 0.4, 0.5))),
        "WLC, strict water criteria": (strict_wlc, fao_classes(strict_wlc))}
rows = []
for name, (s, c) in RUNS.items():
    t = district_table(s, c)
    tr_ = t.dropna(subset=["mean_score"])
    top14 = tr_.mean_score.nlargest(14).index
    rows.append((name, roc_auc_score(tr_.major_wheat, tr_.mean_score), roc_auc_score(t.major_wheat, t.S1_S2_pct),
                 int(np.sum(t.loc[top14, "major_wheat"]))))
display(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["model", "AUC (mean score)", "AUC (S1+S2 share)", "wheat districts among top 14"])
        .set_index("model").round(3))

DT = district_table(SCORES["WLC"], CLS).dropna(subset=["mean_score"]).sort_values("mean_score", ascending=False)
print(f"Districts ranked: {len(DT)} of {len(dist)}; not ranked (less than {MIN_FARMLAND:.0%} farmland): "
      f"{', '.join(sorted(set(dist.ADM2_EN) - set(DT.index)))}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(18, 4.5))
ax.bar(DT.index, DT.mean_score, color=np.where(DT.major_wheat, "#1a9641", "#bdbdbd"))
ax.set_ylim(0.5, DT.mean_score.max() + 0.03)
ax.set_ylabel("Mean WLC score")
ax.set_title("Districts ranked by suitability; green = one of the 14 main wheat districts")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90, labelsize=8)
plt.show()

Reading the validation. Agreement is moderate (AUC about 0.67 on the mean score and 0.70 on the S1 + S2 share). The four hill districts (Bandarban, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari, Rangamati) are not ranked: less than a quarter of their land passes the constraints. The north-western wheat districts (Thakurgaon, Panchagarh, Dinajpur, Kurigram) are among the highest-ranked districts in the country. The Ganges-floodplain wheat districts (Rajshahi, Natore, Naogaon, Pabna, Kushtia, Meherpur, Faridpur, Rajbari) sit in the middle: warmer during grain filling, with deep water tables in the Barind and much poorly drained land. Several high-ranking districts that are not on the list lie in the same cool north (Nilphamari, Lalmonirhat, Rangpur, Gaibandha, Bogura) or in the north-centre (Sherpur, Jamalpur, Mymensingh), where potato, maize and boro rice compete for the same land in the same season. Bhola, a coastal island district, is on the list although its grain-filling temperatures are high: the model would need sowing dates and local soil detail to explain it.
The strict water criteria rank the Barind districts much lower and agree clearly less with where wheat is grown (AUC about 0.5, no better than chance), which is why the headline model uses the deep-tubewell setting. The minimum rule ranks the wheat districts worst of all on the mean score: one poor criterion anywhere in a district drags it down.

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Uncertainty

Weights
monte_carlo_weights draws 300 weight vectors from a Dirichlet distribution centred on the AHP weights and records, for every cell, how often it stays in the top 30 % of WLC scores (roughly the S1 and S2 classes).


Code
idx_ok = np.flatnonzero(OK.ravel())
M = np.stack([MEMBERS[k].ravel()[idx_ok] for k in CRITERIA])
t0 = time.time()
mc = monte_carlo_weights(M, W_AHP.values, kappa=50.0, n=300, batch=10, top_q=0.7, seed=3)
P_TOP = np.full(int(np.prod(GRID.shape)), np.nan)
P_TOP[idx_ok] = mc["p_top"]
P_TOP = P_TOP.reshape(GRID.shape)
print(f"Monte Carlo weights in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; median Jaccard of the top-30 % set vs the AHP baseline: "
      f"{np.median(mc['jaccard']):.2f}")


Monte Carlo weights in 40 s; median Jaccard of the top-30 % set vs the AHP baseline: 0.80




A hot season
The climate criteria use the 18-season mean. To see how a single season changes the picture, the share of seasons in which the grain-filling mean exceeded 24 °C is mapped (about 3 °C above the coolest districts). The WLC is also recomputed with the grain-filling temperature of the hottest season in the record.


Code
HOT = 24.0
hot_share1 = np.mean(GF_YEARS > HOT, axis=0)
HOT_SHARE = dp.warp_to_grid(to_mem(np.where(LAND1, hot_share1, np.nan)), GRID, resample="bilinear")
hottest = int(np.argmax(nat))
hot_gf = dp.warp_to_grid(to_mem(GF_YEARS[hottest]), GRID, resample="bilinear")
hot_members = dict(MEMBERS)
hot_members["grainfill_T"] = np.where(OK, np.clip(linear(hot_gf, 27.0, 21.0), 0, 1), np.nan)
hot_cls = fao_classes(combine(hot_members, W_AHP)["WLC"])
print(f"Hottest grain-filling period: {list(SEASONS)[hottest] - 1}/{list(SEASONS)[hottest]} "
      f"(national mean {nat[hottest]:.1f} °C vs {nat.mean():.1f} °C on average)")
comp = pd.DataFrame({"average season": [np.sum(CLS == i) * 0.0625 for i in range(5)],
                     "hottest season": [np.sum(hot_cls == i) * 0.0625 for i in range(5)]}, index=CLASS_NAMES)

for a, b in [("WLC (headline)", "Gamma"), ("WLC (headline)", "Minimum"), ("WLC (headline)", "WLC, strict water criteria")]:

Reading the uncertainty. The weights matter moderately: a typical random weight vector keeps about 80 % of the baseline top-30 % set, and the core of the north-west stays in it under almost every vector. Moving the class break points by 0.02 keeps 85 to 88 % of the S1 + S2 land. The combination rule matters much more: the minimum rule shares only about a fifth of its S1 + S2 land with WLC, because it ignores everything except the weakest criterion. Heat is the largest source of year-to-year risk. In the hottest season of the record (2005/06), S1 + S2 land shrinks from about 49,600 to 28,400 km², and the share of seasons above 24 °C rises steadily from the north-west, where it is near zero, to the coast, where it is nearly every season. That is the practical case for early sowing and heat-tolerant varieties outside the north-west. (The straight-edged contours in the heat map are already in the source grids: the reanalysis was interpolated to 1 km by triangulation before export.)

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Limitations

Temperature grids. The stored files are upside down. The correction recovers two thirds of the land cells exactly and fills the rest from a smooth trend; it is accurate to a few hundredths of a degree in a hold-out test, but the files should be re-exported. Only mean temperature is usable; the mn2t and mx2t grids are hourly extremes, so daily-maximum heat rules cannot be applied.
Salinity is missing. Large parts of the south-western and south-central coast are saline in the dry season, which rules out wheat. No salinity map is in the folder, so the coastal classes are too optimistic where salinity, not temperature, is the binding limit.
Soil maps are generalised. Land type, drainage, pH and organic carbon come from the national soil survey at reconnaissance scale. A 250 m cell carries the dominant class of a mapping unit, not the field.
Water. The water table is from one year (2020) and does not include surface-water irrigation or the cost of pumping.
Validation is coarse. The reference is a list of districts, not wheat fields, and it mixes suitability with economics. District statistics of wheat area (BBS) or a wheat map from Sentinel-2 would allow a much sharper test.
Unused layers. Texture has no legend; permeability, depth class and thermal zone are undocumented or redundant.

title: Land Suitability for Wheat in Bangladesh
text:
Where to go next

Re-export the 2000 to 2018 temperature composites with the latitude axis handled correctly and rerun without correct.
Add a soil salinity layer (SRDI) as a constraint or criterion for the coastal districts.
Validate against upazila wheat area from the BBS Yearbook of Agricultural Statistics, or against a wheat map classified from Sentinel-2 time series in February.
Model sowing date: flood recession from Sentinel-1 in October and November decides when each field can be sown, and therefore how much March heat the crop meets.
Add wheat blast risk zones for the south-western districts affected since 2016.
Repeat the analysis for maize, which competes with wheat for the same land in the same season, and map where each crop has the advantage.

Problem statement, study area and data
Study area. The Huanglong Mountains, south-east of Yan’an, Shaanxi Province (about 109.6°E to 110.6°E, 35.3°N to 36.4°N; 7,293 km²). The climate is temperate continental monsoon, annual precipitation is 400 to 600 mm and forest covers at least 65 percent of the land. Three nature reserves lie inside the area; two were designated for the brown eared pheasant, one for musk deer.
Question. Where is habitat for the forest musk deer, which patches are large enough to support home ranges, and where is movement between patches most constrained?
Data (Dryad, doi:10.5061/dryad.qbzkh1902, CC0):

text:
Data preparation
The ASCII grids carry no projection file. Their header (cell size 0.000303°) shows geographic coordinates, so they are read as WGS 84, then projected to UTM zone 49N (the projection used in the paper) on a 90 m grid. A 90 m cell keeps the fine-scale detail the multi-criteria model needs while keeping the notebook fast.

Continuous layers use bilinear resampling.
Landcover uses the majority (mode) of the 30 m cells.
A road mask is built on the original grid (Dis_road == 0) and kept wherever any 30 m road cell falls in the 90 m cell, so thin roads are not lost.



Code
CRS_UTM = "EPSG:32649"  # WGS 84 / UTM zone 49N
CELL = 90.0  # analysis cell size (m)

t0 = time.time()
GRID = {}  # name -> path of the 90 m UTM raster

    dst = OUT / f"{name.lower()}_90m.tif"
    if not dst.exists():
        reproject_raster(
            SRC / "current" / f"{name}.asc", dst, CRS_UTM, src_crs="EPSG:4326",
            resample="mode" if name == "Landcover" else "bilinear", resolution=CELL, overwrite=True,

    GRID[name] = dst

# Road mask on the source grid, then "max" so any road cell marks the 90 m cell.

section: The scale problem: what coarsened records can support
text:
The scale problem: what coarsened records can support
A presence-background model compares conditions at occurrence points with conditions across the study area. That only works if the occurrence point and the predictor describe the same place. Here each record is known only to lie somewhere in a 0.1° block, while a predictor cell is 90 m wide.
Two quantities make the problem concrete for slope, the dominant driver:

the value at the grid centre, which is what a naive model would use;
the block mean over the 0.1° block around the centre, which is what the record can honestly represent.



Code
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", CRS_UTM, always_xy=True)
sites["x"], sites["y"] = to_utm.transform(sites.longitude.values, sites.latitude.values)
rc = [dp.xy_to_rowcol(x, y, GT) for x, y in zip(sites.x, sites.y)]
sites["row"] = [r for r, _ in rc]
sites["col"] = [c for _, c in rc]
inside = (sites.row.between(0, valid.shape[0] - 1)) & (sites.col.between(0, valid.shape[1] - 1))
print("Dropped (outside the predictor extent):", sites.loc[~inside, ["longitude", "latitude"]].values.tolist())
sites = sites[inside].reset_index(drop=True)

# A centre that falls on a masked cell (outside the study-area outline) moves to the nearest valid cell.
near_r, near_c = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(~valid, return_distances=False, return_indices=True)
moved = ~valid[sites.row, sites.col]
sites["row"], sites["col"] = near_r[sites.row, sites.col], near_c[sites.row, sites.col]
print(f"Centres moved onto the study area: {int(moved.sum())}")

# Block size in cells: 0.1 degree of longitude and of latitude at the study-area centre.
LAT0 = 35.85
BLOCK_X = int(round(0.1 * 111_320 * np.cos(np.radians(LAT0)) / CELL))  # ~ 9.0 km
BLOCK_Y = int(round(0.1 * 110_950 / CELL))  # ~ 11.1 km
print(f"0.1-degree block = {BLOCK_X} x {BLOCK_Y} cells ({BLOCK_X * CELL / 1000:.1f} km x {BLOCK_Y * CELL / 1000:.1f} km)")


def block_mean(arr, mask, size=(BLOCK_Y, BLOCK_X)):
    """Moving-window mean over valid cells only (NaN outside ``mask``)."""
    a = np.where(mask, arr, 0.0)
    num = ndimage.uniform_filter(a, size=size, mode="constant")
    den = ndimage.uniform_filter(mask.astype(float), size=size, mode="constant")
    return np.where(mask & (den > 0), num / np.maximum(den, 1e-12), np.nan)


slope = layers["Slope"]
slope_block = block_mean(slope, valid)
steep_block = block_mean((slope > 22).astype(float), valid)
sites["slope_at_centre"] = [slope[r, c] for r, c in zip(sites.row, sites.col)]
sites["block_mean_slope"] = [slope_block[r, c] for r, c in zip(sites.row, sites.col)]
sites["block_share_gt22"] = [steep_block[r, c] for r, c in zip(sites.row, sites.col)]

summary = pd.DataFrame(

        "whole study area": [np.nanmean(slope[valid]), np.nanmean(slope[valid]), np.mean(slope[valid] > 22)],
    }
)

What this shows.

Around the occurrence blocks, mean slope is about 3° above the landscape average and the share of land steeper than 22° is more than twice as high. The habitat signal survives at block scale.
The centre cell itself is an arbitrary point. It has no ecological link to where a sample was collected, so treating centres as exact locations would train a model on noise at 90 m.

Design consequence. The notebook uses each kind of information at the scale it supports:









Model
Information
Scale
Role




A, multi-criteria
The species’ habitat requirements as published
90 m cells
Where local conditions are suitable


B, machine learning
The 22 occurrence blocks against the background
0.1° block summaries, mapped on a 270 m grid
Where the surrounding landscape resembles occupied blocks



The final map requires both. A cell that meets the habitat requirements but lies in a landscape unlike any occupied block, or the reverse, is not treated as primary habitat.

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Model A: knowledge-driven habitat suitability
Each predictor is converted to a membership between 0 and 1 that follows the response the paper reports (Section 3.2 and Figure 2 of Zheng et al. 2026):









Criterion
Membership
Parameters
Reason




Slope
large (sigmoid)
midpoint 20°, spread 12
Steep terrain preferred, above 22° in the paper


Annual precipitation
gaussian
optimum 462 mm
Peak of the response curve


Max. warm-month temperature
small (sigmoid)
midpoint 27 °C, spread 30
Suitability rises below 27 °C


Land cover
class scores
needle-leaved 1.0, broadleaf 0.8, grassland 0.3, croplands 0.1, built-up 0
Ranking of classes in the response curve


Distance to settlement
linear
0 at 0 m, 1 at 5,000 m
Preference for > 5 km


Distance to river
linear (decreasing)
1 at 500 m, 0 at 4,000 m
Preference for proximity


Distance to road
linear
0 at 0 m, 1 at 1,000 m
Minor avoidance



Aspect is left out: its transformation is not documented in the data release, so its direction cannot be interpreted.
Weights follow the paper’s relative contributions where they are reported: slope 56.2, precipitation 19.1, temperature 12.8. The paper gives only an upper bound (< 5 % each) for the rest; the remaining 11.9 points are split here as land cover 4.5, settlements 3.4, rivers 2.5 and roads 1.5. That split is a modelling choice, and Section 9 tests how much it matters.


Code
# Membership functions (GeoLattice) applied to every 90 m cell.
lc_scores = {1: 0.1, 2: 0.1, 3: 0.1, 4: 0.8, 5: 1.0, 6: 0.3, 7: 0.1, 8: 0.05, 9: 0.0, 10: 0.0, 11: 0.0}
lc_member = np.full(lc.shape, np.nan)
for k, v in lc_scores.items():
    lc_member[lc == k] = v

members = {
    "slope": large(np.maximum(slope, 1e-6), midpoint=20.0, spread=12.0),
    "precipitation": gaussian(layers["Bio12"], midpoint=462.0, spread=0.004),
    "warm_temperature": small(layers["Bio5"], midpoint=27.0, spread=30.0),
    "land_cover": lc_member,
    "settlement_distance": linear(layers["Dis_resident"], 0.0, 5000.0),
    "river_distance": linear(layers["Dis_river"], 4000.0, 500.0),
    "road_distance": linear(layers["Dis_road"], 0.0, 1000.0),
}
members = {k: np.where(valid, np.clip(np.asarray(v, float), 0, 1), np.nan) for k, v in members.items()}

WEIGHTS_A = {"slope": 56.2, "precipitation": 19.1, "warm_temperature": 12.8, "land_cover": 4.5,
             "settlement_distance": 3.4, "river_distance": 2.5, "road_distance": 1.5}

# Plot the membership curves over the observed range of each variable.
curve_vars = [("slope", slope, "Slope (deg)"), ("precipitation", layers["Bio12"], "Annual precipitation (mm)"),
              ("warm_temperature", layers["Bio5"], "Max temp. warmest month (°C)"),
              ("settlement_distance", layers["Dis_resident"], "Distance to settlement (m)"),
              ("river_distance", layers["Dis_river"], "Distance to river (m)"),
              ("road_distance", layers["Dis_road"], "Distance to road (m)")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(22, 3.4))
for ax, (key, raw, label) in zip(axes, curve_vars):
    x, y = raw[valid], members[key][valid]
    idx = RNG.choice(x.size, 4000, replace=False)
    order = np.argsort(x[idx])
    ax.plot(x[idx][order], y[idx][order], color="darkgreen")
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax2.hist(x, bins=40, color="grey", alpha=0.25)
    ax2.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
    ax.set_xlabel(label)
    ax.set_title(f"{key} (w={WEIGHTS_A[key]})", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Membership")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Code
# Weighted linear combination (weights are normalised to sum to 1).
stack_A = {k: np.nan_to_num(v) for k, v in members.items()}
hsi_A = np.where(valid, weighted_linear_combination(stack_A, WEIGHTS_A), np.nan)

# Which criterion contributes most in each cell?
contrib = score_contributions(stack_A, WEIGHTS_A)
names_A = list(contrib)
w_norm = np.array([WEIGHTS_A[k] for k in names_A]) / sum(WEIGHTS_A.values())
# Shortfall = weight x (1 - membership): the criterion that costs each cell most.
shortfall = np.stack([w * (1 - stack_A[k]) for w, k in zip(w_norm, names_A)])

Block-scale predictors
Every predictor is summarised over a 0.1° moving block, the precision of the records. Land cover becomes two shares (needle-leaved forest; all forest), and slope gets a second summary, the share of land steeper than 22°. The block summaries are computed on the 90 m grid and sampled on a 270 m grid, which is ample for surfaces this smooth.


Code
AGG = 3  # 90 m -> 270 m
CELL_B = CELL * AGG


def coarsen(arr, how="mean"):
    """Aggregate a 90 m array to 270 m blocks of AGG x AGG cells."""
    r, c = (arr.shape[0] // AGG) * AGG, (arr.shape[1] // AGG) * AGG
    blocks = arr[:r, :c].reshape(r // AGG, AGG, c // AGG, AGG)
    return np.nanmean(blocks, axis=(1, 3)) if how == "mean" else np.nanmax(blocks, axis=(1, 3))


feature_src = {
    "slope_mean": slope,
    "slope_share_gt22": (slope > 22).astype(float),
    "precipitation": layers["Bio12"],
    "warm_temperature": layers["Bio5"],
    "needleleaf_share": (lc == 5).astype(float),
    "forest_share": np.isin(lc, [4, 5]).astype(float),
    "dist_settlement": layers["Dis_resident"],
    "dist_river": layers["Dis_river"],
    "dist_road": layers["Dis_road"],
}
t0 = time.time()

valid270 = coarsen(valid.astype(float)) >= 0.5

      f"{valid270.sum():,} cells")

# Collinearity screen: correlations and variance inflation factors on the study area.
F = pd.DataFrame({k: v[valid270] for k, v in feat270.items()}).dropna()


def vif(df):
    out = {}
    for col in df.columns:
        X = df.drop(columns=col).values
        X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
        beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, df[col].values, rcond=None)
        resid = df[col].values - X @ beta
        r2 = 1 - resid.var() / df[col].values.var()
        out[col] = 1 / max(1 - r2, 1e-9)
    return pd.Series(out, name="VIF")

Presences and background

Presences: the 22 block centres inside the area, one per block. Repeated records at a centre do not add information about habitat, only about survey effort, so they are not used as weights.
Background: eight sets of random cells (two each of 300, 500, 800 and 1,000), as in the paper, drawn across the study area excluding presence cells.

tile_rows = int(np.ceil(3 * BLOCK_Y / AGG))
tile_cols = int(np.ceil(3 * BLOCK_X / AGG))


def tile_id(cells):
    r, c = np.divmod(cells, valid270.shape[1])
    return (r // tile_rows) * 1000 + (c // tile_cols)

Algorithms and evaluation
Five algorithms cover the families the paper ensembled (it retained RF, GBM, MARS, MaxEnt, GLM and CTA):

Each is scored two ways, with AUC and the True Skill Statistic (TSS, at the threshold that maximises it):

Spatial cross-validation: folds are 0.3° tiles, so a model is always tested on blocks far from the ones it learned from.

With only 22 presences, the difference between the two is part of the lesson.


Code
def make_models():
    return {
        "GLM": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False),
                             LogisticRegression(C=1.0, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=5000)),
        "MAXENT": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SplineTransformer(n_knots=5, degree=1),
                                LogisticRegression(penalty="l1", solver="liblinear", C=0.5,
                                                   class_weight="balanced", max_iter=5000)),
        "CTA": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=5, class_weight="balanced", random_state=1),
        "RF": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, class_weight="balanced_subsample",
                                     n_jobs=-1, random_state=1),
        "GBM": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=200,
                                              class_weight="balanced", random_state=1),
    }


def tss_max(y, p):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p)
    return float(np.max(tpr - fpr))


def assemble(bg):
    X = np.vstack([X_pres, Xgrid[bg]])
    y = np.r_[np.ones(len(X_pres)), np.zeros(len(bg))]
    groups = tile_id(np.r_[pres_cells, bg])
    return X, y, groups


t0 = time.time()
rows = []
oof_presence = {}  # (background set, model) -> out-of-fold predictions at the 22 presences
for s, bg in enumerate(pa_sets):
    X, y, groups = assemble(bg)
    # Random 80/20 splits (paper design).
    for rep, (tr, te) in enumerate(StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=10, test_size=0.2, random_state=s).split(X, y)):
        for name, model in make_models().items():
            p = model.fit(X[tr], y[tr]).predict_proba(X[te])[:, 1]
            rows.append(("random 80/20", s, name, roc_auc_score(y[te], p), tss_max(y[te], p)))
    # Spatial cross-validation on 0.3-degree tiles; predictions pooled across folds.
    n_groups = len(np.unique(groups[y == 1]))
    oof = {name: np.full(len(y), np.nan) for name in make_models()}
    for tr, te in GroupKFold(n_splits=min(5, n_groups)).split(X, y, groups):
        if y[tr].sum() < 3 or y[te].sum() == 0:
            continue
        for name, model in make_models().items():
            oof[name][te] = model.fit(X[tr], y[tr]).predict_proba(X[te])[:, 1]
    for name, p in oof.items():
        oof_presence[(s, name)] = p[: len(X_pres)]
        ok = np.isfinite(p)
        rows.append(("spatial (0.3° tiles)", s, name, roc_auc_score(y[ok], p[ok]), tss_max(y[ok], p[ok])))
evals = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["scheme", "pa_set", "model", "AUC", "TSS"])
print(f"Evaluation runs: {len(evals)} in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

Reading the evaluation. Two things stand out.

Random splits are mostly noise here. A 20 percent test set holds only about four presences, so a single split can give an AUC anywhere from 0.4 to 0.9. Mean AUC under random splits is about the same as, or lower than, under spatial tiles; only TSS comes out higher, because with four test presences one lucky threshold separates them easily. Spatial cross-validation pools out-of-fold predictions for all 22 presences, which gives a far more stable estimate.
The honest skill is moderate. Spatial AUCs of 0.72 to 0.78 for GLM, MaxEnt-style, RF and GBM, and 0.64 for the single tree, describe a model that ranks occupied blocks above the background clearly but far from perfectly.

The paper’s very high scores (mean ROC up to 0.999 for RF) come from random splits on 177 precise points. They measure something different and are not comparable with the scores here.
The ensemble below uses the spatial scores: an algorithm enters only if its mean spatial AUC is at least 0.70, and members are weighted by that AUC (the paper’s EMwmean rule, with a lower bar suited to an honest test on 22 blocks).


Code
spatial_auc = evals[evals.scheme.str.startswith("spatial")].groupby("model")["AUC"].mean()
members_B = spatial_auc[spatial_auc >= 0.70]
if members_B.empty:  # never leave the ensemble empty
    members_B = spatial_auc.nlargest(2)
print("Ensemble members and AUC weights:")
display(members_B.to_frame("weight (spatial AUC)"))

# Fit every member on all presences with each background set, predict every 270 m cell, average.
t0 = time.time()
pred = {}
fitted = {name: [] for name in members_B.index}
for name in members_B.index:
    maps = []
    for bg in pa_sets:
        X, y, _ = assemble(bg)
        model = make_models()[name].fit(X, y)
        fitted[name].append(model)
        p = np.full(Xgrid.shape[0], np.nan)
        p[valid_idx] = model.predict_proba(Xgrid[valid_idx])[:, 1]
        maps.append(p)
    pred[name] = np.nanmean(maps, axis=0)
w = members_B / members_B.sum()
hsi_B270 = sum(w[name] * pred[name] for name in members_B.index).reshape(valid270.shape)
hsi_B270 = np.where(valid270, hsi_B270, np.nan)
print(f"Ensemble prediction in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")


def ensemble_predict(X):
    """AUC-weighted mean over members, averaged over the eight background sets."""
    return sum(w[n] * np.mean([m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] for m in fitted[n]], axis=0) for n in members_B.index)

Reading the importance and response curves. The response shapes agree in direction with the paper: suitability rises with mean slope and with the share of steep land, falls as warm-month temperature rises, rises with distance from settlements and falls with distance from rivers. Precipitation has an almost flat response.
The ranking differs. Distance to settlements carries about 45 percent of the importance and distance to roads about 18 percent, while slope and climate together carry less than a third. The paper found the reverse (slope 56 %, precipitation 19 %, temperature 13 %, every disturbance variable < 5 %). Three reasons are likely, and they are worth stating because each is a general lesson:

Survey design. The transects were laid out in and around the three reserves, which sit in the remote, road-poor centre of the area. At 10 km resolution “far from villages and roads” is what most distinguishes the surveyed blocks from the rest of the landscape, whether or not the deer select for it.
Unit of analysis. Inside a 10 km block, almost every block contains some steep land, so block-mean slope varies less than cell slope. The paper’s strong slope effect is partly a fine-scale effect that block summaries cannot see.
Correlated predictors share credit. Remote blocks are also the steep, forested, cooler ones; permutation importance assigns the shared signal to whichever variable the models used first.

This is why Model B is used only as landscape context and is combined with Model A, whose weights come from the paper’s fine-scale analysis.

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Combining the two models
The two maps answer different questions. Model A asks whether a 90 m cell offers what the species needs. Model B asks whether the surrounding 10 km of landscape looks like the landscapes where the species was found. The combined suitability is their geometric mean,
\[
h = \sqrt{A \cdot B},
\]
which stays low when either model is low: one model cannot compensate for the other.


Code
B90 = np.repeat(np.repeat(hsi_B270, AGG, axis=0), AGG, axis=1)  # back to 90 m
B90 = np.pad(B90, ((0, valid.shape[0] - B90.shape[0]), (0, valid.shape[1] - B90.shape[1])), constant_values=np.nan)
B90 = np.where(valid, B90, np.nan)
hsi = np.sqrt(np.clip(hsi_A, 0, 1) * np.clip(B90, 0, 1))

for ax, arr, title in zip(axes, [hsi_A, B90, hsi], ["Model A (local habitat)", "Model B (landscape context)",

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Primary habitat patches
The paper defines primary habitat in two steps: a presence-based threshold on the suitability map, then a minimum patch size. The threshold step needs care here.
Why a presence threshold cannot be set at 90 m. The paper’s threshold (the lowest presence threshold at 90 percent, LPT90) is the suitability value exceeded at 90 percent of the occurrence points. With precise points that is well defined. Here each record is a 10 km block, so the 90 m value “at” a record does not exist.
What is done instead.

Landscape mask from Model B. LPT90 is applied to Model B, which works at block scale. The values used are out-of-fold predictions from the spatial cross-validation: what the ensemble predicts for each occurrence block when that block was left out. In-sample predictions would set the bar far too high, because the tree ensembles reproduce their 22 training blocks almost perfectly.
Equal-area selection on the combined map. Within that mask, the cells with the highest combined suitability \(h\) are kept until they cover 11.8 percent of the study area, the share the paper classed as primary habitat (863 of 7,293 km²). This is an explicit decision, not an estimate: it makes the configuration of habitat directly comparable with the published map, and the sensitivity table below shows what other shares would give.

def primary_patches(top_share=TOP_SHARE, b_thr=lpt90, min_ha=MIN_PATCH_HA):
    """Top `top_share` of h inside the Model B mask, then patches of at least `min_ha`."""
    mask = valid & (B90 >= b_thr)
    h_thr = np.nanquantile(hsi[valid], 1 - top_share)  # equal-area cut on the whole study area
    suitable = mask & (hsi >= h_thr)
    lab, n = ndimage.label(suitable, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))
    sizes = np.bincount(lab.ravel())[1:] * CELL_HA
    keep_ids = np.flatnonzero(sizes >= min_ha) + 1
    order = keep_ids[np.argsort(-sizes[keep_ids - 1])]
    relabel = np.zeros(lab.max() + 1, dtype=int)
    relabel[order] = np.arange(1, len(order) + 1)
    lab = relabel[lab]
    tab = pd.DataFrame({"patch": np.arange(1, len(order) + 1), "area_km2": np.sort(sizes[keep_ids - 1])[::-1] / 100})
    return lab, tab, h_thr

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Resistance surface
Connectivity starts from a resistance surface: the cost for an animal to cross a cell. The paper converts suitability \(h\) into resistance with a negative exponential (Keeley et al. 2016):
\[
R = 100 - 99 \cdot \frac{1 - e^{-c h}}{1 - e^{-c}}
\]
\(R\) runs from 1 (best habitat) to 100 (worst). The parameter \(c\) sets the curvature. A habitat specialist may tolerate mediocre habitat while dispersing, so resistance should stay low over intermediate suitability and rise sharply only in poor habitat; the paper uses \(c = 8\) as baseline and tests 4 to 16.
Connectivity is computed on the 270 m grid.


Code
def resistance(h, c):
    return 100.0 - 99.0 * (1.0 - np.exp(-c * h)) / (1.0 - np.exp(-c))


hh = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)

for c in [4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16]:
    ax.plot(hh, resistance(hh, c), label=f"c = {c}", lw=2.5 if c == 8 else 1)
ax.set_xlabel("Habitat suitability h")
ax.set_ylabel("Resistance R")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title("Suitability-to-resistance transformation")

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Least-cost corridors
The cost-weighted distance (CWD) from a patch to any cell is the minimum sum of resistance times distance along a path. Following Linkage Mapper (McRae and Kavanagh 2011), patches are linked when their cost-distance zones touch, that is, when no third patch lies between them in cost space. For each link the notebook reports:

the least-cost path (LCP) and its length;
the CWD between the patches and the Euclidean distance between their edges;
the ratio CWD : EucD. A ratio near 1 would mean an easy, straight route through good habitat; larger values mean detours or costly ground.

Cost distance is computed with Dijkstra’s algorithm (scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra) on the 8-neighbour cell graph. The cost of moving between neighbouring cells is the mean of their resistances times the step length.


Code
NR, NC = valid270.shape
node_of = -np.ones(NR * NC, dtype=np.int64)
node_of[valid_idx] = np.arange(valid_idx.size)
STEPS = [(0, 1, 1.0), (1, 0, 1.0), (1, 1, np.sqrt(2)), (1, -1, np.sqrt(2))]  # each undirected edge once


def edges_for(R):
    """Undirected 8-neighbour edges (i, j, step_length_m, mean_resistance)."""
    I, J, L, RM = [], [], [], []
    rr, cc = np.divmod(valid_idx, NC)
    for dr, dc, s in STEPS:
        r2, c2 = rr + dr, cc + dc
        ok = (r2 >= 0) & (r2 < NR) & (c2 >= 0) & (c2 < NC)
        nb = np.full(rr.shape, -1)
        nb[ok] = node_of[r2[ok] * NC + c2[ok]]
        ok &= nb >= 0
        a, b = np.arange(valid_idx.size)[ok], nb[ok]
        I.append(a); J.append(b); L.append(np.full(a.size, s * CELL_B))
        Rf = R.ravel()[valid_idx]
        RM.append(0.5 * (Rf[a] + Rf[b]))
    return np.concatenate(I), np.concatenate(J), np.concatenate(L), np.concatenate(RM)


def cost_graph(R):
    I, J, L, RM = edges_for(R)
    n = valid_idx.size
    return sparse.coo_matrix((L * RM, (I, J)), shape=(n, n)).tocsr()


patch_nodes = {p: node_of[np.flatnonzero(patch270.ravel() == p)] for p in np.unique(patch270) if p > 0}
patch_nodes = {p: v[v >= 0] for p, v in patch_nodes.items() if (v >= 0).any()}
print(f"Patches on the 270 m grid: {len(patch_nodes)}")


def corridors(R):
    """Cost distances from each patch, adjacent links, least-cost paths and their statistics."""
    G = cost_graph(R)
    cd, pred = {}, {}
    for p, nodes in patch_nodes.items():
        d, pr, _ = csgraph.dijkstra(G, directed=False, indices=nodes, min_only=True, return_predecessors=True)
        cd[p], pred[p] = d, pr
    # Allocation: nearest patch in cost space for every node; links where allocation zones touch.
    ids = np.array(list(cd))
    D = np.vstack([cd[p] for p in ids])
    alloc = ids[np.argmin(D, axis=0)]
    I, J, _, _ = edges_for(R)
    pairs = {tuple(sorted(x)) for x in zip(alloc[I], alloc[J]) if x[0] != x[1]}
    xy = np.column_stack(dp.rowcol_to_xy(*np.divmod(valid_idx, NC), (ext270[0], CELL_B, 0, ext270[3], 0, -CELL_B)))
    links = []
    for a, b in sorted(pairs):
        tot = cd[a] + cd[b]
        k = int(np.argmin(tot))
        cwd = float(tot[k])
        # Trace the least-cost path from the best meeting node back into each patch.
        def trace(p):  # nodes from the meeting node k back to patch p
            n, seg = k, []
            while n >= 0:
                seg.append(n)
                n = pred[p][n]
            return seg

        path = np.array(trace(a)[::-1] + trace(b)[1:])  # patch a -> k -> patch b
        # Drop links whose least-cost path runs through a third patch (Linkage Mapper rule).
        others = patch270.ravel()[valid_idx[path]]
        if np.any((others > 0) & (others != a) & (others != b)):
            continue
        steps = np.hypot(*np.diff(xy[path], axis=0).T).sum() if len(path) > 1 else 0.0
        # Edge-to-edge Euclidean distance between the two patches.
        from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

        tree = cKDTree(xy[patch_nodes[b]])
        euc = float(tree.query(xy[patch_nodes[a]])[0].min())
        links.append({"from": a, "to": b, "cwd": cwd, "lcp_length_m": steps, "euclid_m": max(euc, CELL_B),
                      "path": path})
    links = pd.DataFrame(links)
    links["cwd_to_euclid"] = links.cwd / links.euclid_m
    return links, cd

title: Habitat Suitability and Landscape Connectivity for the Forest Musk Deer
text:
Pinch points with circuit theory
A least-cost path is one line. Circuit theory (McRae et al. 2008) treats the landscape as an electrical network in which each cell conducts in proportion to \(1/R\). Current injected in one patch and drained in another spreads over all routes in proportion to their ease, so it shows how many alternatives a corridor has. Where current is forced through a narrow strip, current density peaks: a pinch point, the place where losing a little habitat breaks the link.
For each link the notebook

restricts the network to the corridor, the cells where \(CWD_a + CWD_b \le CWD_{ab} + 10{,}000\) (the paper’s cutoff);
sets the voltage to 1 in one patch and 0 in the other, and solves Kirchhoff’s equations \(L\,v = 0\) for the remaining cells with a sparse solver;
scales the solution to 1 A and records the current through every cell.

Summing over links gives cumulative current density.


Code
CWD_CUTOFF = 10_000.0


def current_density(R, links, cd):
    """Pairwise circuit current, summed over links, on the 270 m node set."""
    I, J, L, RM = edges_for(R)
    g = (CELL_B / L) / RM  # conductance: 1 / (mean resistance x relative step length)
    n = valid_idx.size
    total = np.zeros(n)
    for _, lk in links.iterrows():
        a, b = int(lk["from"]), int(lk["to"])
        inc = (cd[a] + cd[b]) <= lk.cwd + CWD_CUTOFF
        inc[patch_nodes[a]] = inc[patch_nodes[b]] = True
        sub = np.flatnonzero(inc)
        loc = -np.ones(n, dtype=np.int64)
        loc[sub] = np.arange(sub.size)
        e = inc[I] & inc[J]
        ii, jj, gg = loc[I[e]], loc[J[e]], g[e]
        m = sub.size
        Lap = sparse.coo_matrix((np.r_[-gg, -gg], (np.r_[ii, jj], np.r_[jj, ii])), shape=(m, m)).tocsr()
        Lap = Lap + sparse.diags(-np.asarray(Lap.sum(axis=1)).ravel())
        fixed = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
        v = np.zeros(m)
        src, snk = loc[patch_nodes[a]], loc[patch_nodes[b]]
        fixed[src] = fixed[snk] = True
        v[src] = 1.0
        free = ~fixed
        if free.sum() == 0:
            continue
        A = Lap[free][:, free].tocsc()
        rhs = -Lap[free][:, fixed] @ v[fixed]
        v[free] = spsolve(A, rhs)
        flow = gg * np.abs(v[ii] - v[jj])  # current on each edge
        node_cur = np.zeros(m)
        np.add.at(node_cur, ii, flow)
        np.add.at(node_cur, jj, flow)
        injected = (Lap[src] @ v).sum()  # total current leaving the source patch
        if injected > 0:
            total[sub] += 0.5 * node_cur / injected
    return total

The network topology hardly changes with \(c\): the same links appear (one extra at \(c = 16\)). Costs fall as \(c\) rises, because a larger \(c\) makes resistance drop faster with suitability, so intermediate habitat becomes cheap to cross; the CWD : EucD ratios between the largest patches fall accordingly. The pinch-point cells overlap only partly with the baseline (Jaccard about 0.3 to 0.4), so the exact bottleneck cells depend on \(c\) more than the paper reports, although they stay within the same corridors. When locating crossing structures, treat a pinch point as a stretch of corridor rather than an exact cell.

Comparison with the published study, and limitations








Aspect
Zheng et al. (2026)
This notebook




Occurrence data
177 precise points
Same records, coarsened to 23 block centres (22 inside the area)


Model
Ensemble of 6 algorithms on 30 m cells
Model A (published requirements, 90 m) x Model B (5-algorithm ensemble on 0.1° block summaries)


Validation
Random 80/20 splits
Random and spatial cross-validation


Dominant drivers in the published model
Slope 56 %, precipitation 19 %, temperature 13 %
Used as Model A weights


Dominant drivers in the data-driven model
Slope, precipitation, temperature
Distance to settlements and roads (Model B, block scale); see Section 6.4


Primary habitat
19 patches, 863 km²; largest 421, 362, 21 km²
Area set to the paper’s share (857 km²); 6 patches, one of about 830 km²


Corridors
25, Linkage Mapper
7 cost-allocation links with least-cost paths


Pinch points
Circuitscape, CWD cutoff 10,000
Pairwise circuit solves, same cutoff



Limitations.

Coordinate generalisation. The public coordinates are deliberately imprecise. Model B can only learn what distinguishes 10 km landscapes, and its maps are smooth for that reason. Precise points would allow a cell-level model and would almost certainly sharpen and shift the patches.
Model A is only as good as its translation of the paper. Membership shapes were read from published response curves, and four of the seven weights were assigned here.
Presence-background design. Background points are not absences; the outputs are relative suitability, not probability of occurrence. Survey effort was concentrated in and around the reserves, which can bias both the occurrence blocks and the inferred preferences.
Sampling bias. Model B’s emphasis on distance from settlements most likely reflects where surveys were done. Target-group background sampling (background drawn from surveyed areas only) would reduce it, but the survey tracks are not part of the data release.
Static connectivity. Resistance from suitability assumes that animals disperse through the habitat they would live in, which telemetry or landscape genetics would need to confirm.
No reserve boundaries. The protected-area gap analysis needs an external boundary file.
